And now that Harada is leaving, there's absolutely ZERO hope for this to ever be fixed. He was arguably not in much control anyway, so I guess it's just going to get worse now that he's not there at all.  First of all... What's good about the game? This is the most stylish Tekken has ever been... Fancy graphics, cool outfits and customization, the music is really good too and the updated animations are just chef's kiss... Also, hitting your opponent has never felt more satisfying than this. The sound direction (excluding voice acting) is amazing. And if you're a combo artist, you're gonna love the overcomplicated combo system and the crazy stuff you can do with it, especially with the new Heat system. The practice mode is also one of the most elaborated and helpful systems I've seen on any fighting game (with one caveat in the bad section). But that's about it... If it were S1, there'd be more, but sadly that's not the case...  Onto the bad: The game is riddled with so many issues, I have to section them off. I'll try to be short and to the point with each:  Sidestepping: Doesn't work. You WILL get clipped 90% of the time and this seems to be by design, because they amped up the tracking in S2 after "buffing" sidestepping. That should tell you what mindset these devs are on...  Hitboxes: Inconsistent as hell... You will get hit from a back turned opponent, whiffing attacks will randomly connect and sometimes you can literally catch your character's fist go through the heart of your opponent sticking out the other side and still not connect. On top of that, nearly every character has been given a ton of evasive moves, that randomly duck under highs and jump over lows, sometimes even mids are skipped... This is one of the main factors leading into the next issue:  Fundamentals: Tekken 8 prides itself in giving every character so many options to skip the fundamentals of Tekken, that it stops being Tekken... The evasive moves allow anyone to steal their turn back with little thought. Specialty moves like Yoshi's flash, Xiaoyu's AOP stance and lots and lots of power crush moves allow most characters to steal their turn back and skip neutral. So many moves are overtuned, that you hardly even need to use the moveset. And for most of these, the counter is often a hard read or just playing like a turtle...  Inputs: Generally the inputs feel ok. But every now and then, this game decides not to register some moves or completely misfire, often killing you in turn. Like for example ducking inputs randomly not registering. I've seen other people complain about this and I know it's not controller related, because I've gone through 4 of them and a keyboard and all exhibit the same issues.  Overall Character Design: By this I mean gameplay design. Most characters had their weaknesses removed in S2 and are now easy Jack of all Trades characters. Character identity is a thing of the past... Lots of interesting interactions and mixups were removed, lots of characters became harder focussed on stance rushdown type gameplay and overall, it just doesn't feel like the characters stand out from each other as they did pre S2.   50/50 Casino Gameplay: Most characters have had legacy moves altered or new moves introduced, that make this game more of a guessing game than a fighting game. Almost every character has stances that force a 50/50 you can't react to based on character knowledge... It's just awful, because there's no depth to it like there was before.  Combo System: Tekken 8's combo system is an absolute abomination... It's the result if adding more and more layers to extend the combos, without considering what happens on the receiving end. To simplify: You launch an opponent, perform a couple moves to juggle, sprinkle in some tailspins, usually follow up with a combo extension (in this case the Tornado, it's easy to pick up too), then perform a couple more hits, before engaging heat to resplat them on the ground, carry them to the wall and end with a wall combo, which may or may not engage a stage gimmick and resplat the opponent for a couple more hits (be it on the ground, wall or through an explosion). All that, while the receiving end gets nothing to do but watch their healthbar get deleted, usually 50% or more... Not every combo is like this obviously, but once you get to higher ranks you usually spend half the round just waiting to be able to do anything again... It's a very frustrating system, that could be easily fixed by giving the receiving player something to do to break / reduce combo damage or just by reducing the amount of combo extensions there are... There's a reason so many people get easily tilted in this game...  Community: I'm gonna get hate for this, but the community straight up sucks for the most part... Everyone works on a "Every character sucks except my character, everyone else is carried" mindset. 80% of people are either abusing broken ♥♥♥♥ constantly, taunting / teabagging you after winning a round, not rematching if they lose once or just one and doneing you, plugging on you or straight up cheating... Which brings me top the next issue:  Cheating: Be it lag switching, auto ducking, auto punishing, whatever, cheating is rampant in this game and the devs do nothing against it. There's people blatantly cheating on social media, bragging about it and they still aren't banned... The report button may as well not exist in this game.  DLC: This is where the greedy execs come in. Legacy outfits are being locked behind DLC. Stages are locked behind DLC and one of them was even rugpulled form the first Season Pass. DLC characters are all becoming annoying, gimmicky, do it all casino simulators, just like the rest of the cast. But they come with that extra caveat I mentioned in the practice system... You can't lab them unless you pay up... Oh, Anna is currently the most broken character, can do everything and is basically impossible to defend against? Well you can't even learn how to counter her the same way you did the others. Better pay up even tho you may not even want to use her...   Overall, I do have to say, the game CAN be fun when it works... The problem is it doesn't work 90% of the time. The most fun you will have here, is if you're a casual or just playing with friends. If either of those apply to you, go ahaed, it's a great game for you and a lot of the issues I was talking about don't apply for you. Story mode is decent too, but it definitely misses sometimes as well.   But if you have any intention to play this online or competitively or especially if you are a Tekken veteran expecting a Tekken experience and are not a troll or don't thrive on masochism, stay as far away from this trash as you can... Maybe consider it after Season 3 drops, but with Harada gone, I highly doubt this game will ever be saved...

TEKKEN 8 - A good game ruined by a lack of balancing and pay-to-win, and so much more.  Tekken 8 is a game with great visual effects, composed of new and returning characters, some of them more iconic than others. It is a game where you can enjoy the story mode, the goofy moments (fighting an army of armed soldiers with King—need I say more?), and playing with friends regardless if your friends own the game or not.  It serves as a good local multiplayer or online if you use remote play or tools like Parsec, whatever fits your taste.  You'll be golden if you play this game casually, but if you are one of those people who want to take the experience a step further and hop onto ranked matches, the nightmare begins.  I say this because Tekken 8 requires you to dedicate a good portion of your leisure time to get to an average level of expertise. Things like side-stepping, side-walking, neutral game, blocking, combos, opening up your opponent's defense, power crush usage, punishments, grab-breaks, turn awareness, and so on. Whenever you hit the current average ranks, which currently in season 2 are blue ranks, you'll have a huge necessity of labbing characters if you haven't done so already. Essentially what this means is you'll need to hop on the practice mode and start learning when to sidestep strings, moves that track to one side or the other, and when to duck and punish your opponent properly with every character in the game.   WHERE THE PROBLEMS START... Pay-to-win philosophy is quite present in this game, because if you want to have a chance against DLC characters, you have two solutions: either pay up and lab/learn the character, which means -8€ on your wallet for a character you don't even want in the first place, or you randomly find them in quick matches and take loss after loss until you eventually get the hang of them, and even then those who properly learn it in practice mode will still be better off than you. This bothers me and many others because in ranked, each loss will cost you time and effort to build back up again, and if you are unfortunate enough to so much as find a DLC character on the other side, you will lose ranked points, so your only out is to either pay and lab or get taxed in ranked points by a DLC character user.  FLAWED BALANCING I'm not the first and certainly not the last to say it, but this game is not in favor of those who want to enjoy a few ranked matches in their free time. This game features heavily and effectively broken characters like Anna Williams, Nina Williams, Hwoarang, Yoshimitsu, Bryan Fury, Jack-8, and so on. In theory, each character in this game has something that makes them flawed when it comes to balancing, be it string jailing, unpunishable lows with heavy mix-up options that make you gamble your HP bar each time those come out (Hworang mains will know what I am talking about), strings that track even when side walked (heavy position re-adjusting on Bryan's strings is an example), heat smashes with wall splats (Jin Kazama), heavy tracking, priority stealing (Yoshi's flash "parry" is as much of a threat as a rage art, basically working as a turn steal at a button's notice, so you must play around that whenever it is your turn), and the list goes on so be prepared to not have fair odds against every match up you face. HEAT BAR... In my opinion, it should not be a thing. A mechanic which changes how your character works, sometimes more or sometimes less than others depending on who you main, and that poses a threat for your opponent whenever it is activated since you can heat smash at any time and respond to most moves the other makes.  That being said, if it is meant to stay, make it so it goes down in the middle of a combo instead of it stopping or, in some cases, even regenerating it for some unknown design choice for certain characters.  CONCLUSION and TLDR If you like the game, play it. If you get enjoyment from it, keep at it. But if your red flags include modern Tekken, poor balancing or long waits for fixes, praying for your character NOT to be buffed, pay-to-win / save time, rage-inducing (for some), and a long and arduous journey to become actually good at the game essentially requiring you to only pay attention to this game to learn it from top to bottom, do not go for this game. Play something else, enjoy it, and make sure your free time is used for things worth your time and that are FUN, especially FUN and ENJOYABLE, not a competitive game with this many issues.

Namco has truly excelled with Tekken 8, featuring 32 characters at launch, including both legacy favorites and newcomers like Reina, Victor, and the coffee-loving Azucena. The game boasts a memorable soundtrack that includes the entire series library, allowing players to customize their own stage tracks. With a steady online experience, fighter customization options, and a story mode, there’s a lot to enjoy. Most fighting games should take notes on how to deliver a solid $70 package.  In terms of gameplay, Tekken 8 is the most aggressive of its predecessors. It introduces a new mechanic called "heat," which enhances fighters’ offensive capabilities with an expanded moveset, quicker recovery, and chip damage on block—perfect for making comebacks when health is low. At first, I was unsure about this concept, but once I learned how to utilize it, I grew to appreciate the heat mechanic and the direction Tekken is taking.  I particularly love the addition of Arcade Quest, a personal story mode that not only teaches new players the mechanics but also provides a glimpse of what to expect when competing online. It’s a great introduction for those who aren't ready to play online yet.  The story mode is decent; while not groundbreaking, it serves well enough to pass the time and showcases the developments in each character’s legacy.  Tekken has also introduced a fight pass, which is a timely addition. Players can enjoy grinding for artwork, cosmetics, and more if they choose to, all at an affordable price of $10, with rewards given upon completion.  One disappointment I have regarding Tekken 8 is the DLC roster. It’s frustrating that legacy characters need to be repurchased, and some guest characters leave much to be desired. For instance, where's Tifa Lockhart? A character like her, being a boxer, would fit perfectly within Tekken's roster of martial artists. Instead, we get Clive, who seems more suitable for Soul Calibur—this is quite confusing, Namco.  Tekken 8 might not be the definitive title for every veteran player, especially with its new comeback system, but it’s still a lot of fun to play with family and friends from time to time. I would rate this fighting gem a 9/10.  But seriously, Namco, where's Tifa Lockhart?

Tekken 8 had all the hype in the world, but the final product feels like a step backward wrapped in pretty graphics. Yes, the visuals are impressive, but once you’re actually playing, the problems start piling up fast.  The new Heat system feels more like a gimmick than an evolution of the gameplay. Instead of adding depth, it pushes the game toward aggressive, brain-off rushdown that removes a lot of the strategic spacing and mind games the series is known for. Matches feel chaotic—not in a fun way, but in a sloppy, unbalanced way.  The story mode is a mess. It’s filled with cheesy dialogue, uneven pacing, and fights that feel more like interruptions than actual gameplay. Character episodes are short and forgettable, and several fan-favorite fighters feel like they were included at the last minute with almost no meaningful development.  Online play is another disappointment. Despite promises of rock-solid rollback, matchmaking is slow, unstable, and inconsistent. You either wait forever for a match or get thrown into a laggy one that ruins any sense of competition.  And don’t even get me started on the customization system. It’s shallow, limited, and somehow manages to look worse than past games that were nearly a decade old.  Overall, Tekken 8 looks good from a distance, but the moment you pick up the controller, the cracks show. Flashy graphics can’t save a fighting game that forgets what made the series great in the first place. Not worth full price.

There’s no chance to learn, no room to breathe, and definitely no “fun” when every match turns into a stun-lock highlight reel for someone who’s been grinding the optimal routes for months. It’s not even about skill—it's about how the community leans obsessively into whatever the most broken, efficient combo of the week is. Instead of matches feeling like fights, they feel like cutscenes you’re forced to watch while your health bar evaporates. For a game that markets itself on excitement and accessibility, Tekken 8 ends up feeling like a gated club where newer players exist only to get farmed. Honestly, the whole experience gets old fast.

Tekken 8 is a lot different than the earlier games, it is nostalgic seeing old characters* but they have changed visually, it is still great to see them again though in new and revived forms; and this game is visually impressive and runs well enough.   The gameplay is different in that it's not all about memorising moves and spacing, since now they have an easy mode that you can press that spams out moves and combos for you, again we all agreed not to use this, new players will bear the brunt of and with this feaure though.  There is also now heat and heat smashes, basically a limited resource per round that lets you do extra moves, more damage, or press a button that uses up all heat but performs an instant combo deleting a portion of the opponents health if it lands, again, not something we were proud of using but you get to smirk at them when it lands.  The least proud button that we didn't want to put people through (Or at least the animations are quite novel and cool to watch the first time around) is something called Rage, basically if you are low health you can press "the funny button", if this single strike hit lands the opponent has to watch as you perform a 20 second long cutscene that will remove over half of their health. Usually these don't land but if they do, boy they are going to *love* you so much.  *Ah yes, the asterix, under characters...Yes charging players money for characters that are classically base game characters, they themselves being replaced mostly by characters that bore me or I haven't heard of, a lot of the roster was hit or miss for me but this is personal preference, there are definitely some new favourites of mine in tekken 8. TL;DR- Good outweighs the bad. Lots of great features and fun to be had if you put aside the small amount of issues. Heat system is a load of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and ruins a lot of matches.  I decided to update my review, as I have learned a lot since I originally posted it. Right off the bat, I just want to say it is painfully clear that the reason for most of the negative reviews is, "It's not Tekken 7." Ok, so go play Tekken 7, it's right there.  With that out of the way, I want to address the actual issues I have with the game, the biggest of which isn't a problem with the game itself- it's the monetization. There is no reason why a game that costs $60 should have paid DLC characters, with the exception of crossovers; and crossover characters should absolutely NOT be stronger than originals (*cough*Clyde*cough*). I got the game at an 85% discount, but this is a valid excuse for a negative review. The second issue I have is with how weak defense feels in relation to damage output. It feels like characters do way too much damage across the board. It's not a case of "if everyone is OP, nobody is." It's genuinely boring, because the matches feel rushed. I don't feel accomplished pressing one button to initiate a heat chain, just to follow it up with a combo that ends the round. It's not even annoying when it happens to me- it's just a really stupid mechanic. The craziest part is, I started playing AFTER they increased the max HP to 200. They need to either nerf damage across the board, or get rid of Heat chains.  Despite that major gripe I have, the good outweighs the bad. For starters, the graphics are absolutely stunning, especially for this genre. The amount of detail in the character models and environment are genuinely beautiful, and it adds a special level of immersion. Next thing I really like is the Rage Art mechanic. It can completely change the outcome of a match, and it adds a level of strategy to both offense and defense that is genuinely exciting. The Ghost Battle features are incredible. Wanna practice against that guy that just destroyed you in a set? Download his ghost data and go to town. Wanna fight YOURSELF? Pick one of your own ghosts and smash your monitor after you lose to yourself. The AI learning is really f*cking cool, and it will help you improve. The replay system is another strong-suit. Can't figure out why you lost that match? Watch the replay and the game will pause it and tell you what you could have done differently at any given moment. I could keep going on and on about features like this, from learning combos, to a full blown story mode, the offline content is plentiful AND worthwhile. Online is obviously why most people are going to buy it. The rollback netcode is great, the ranked grind is fun, and the Fight Lounge is actually really cool, and a great place to socialize in a PlayStation Home kinda way. Also, boobs. Can't forget about boobs.

Tekken 8 is a competitive 3D fighting game that advances the long-running series with refined mechanics, aggressive pacing, and a strong focus on character individuality. Built on Unreal Engine 5, it delivers high visual fidelity and fluid animations that enhance both readability and impact during matches. The game maintains Tekken’s core movement system while introducing new features designed to make offense more rewarding and dynamic.  The narrative continues the Mishima family conflict, centering on Jin Kazama’s confrontation with Kazuya. The story mode blends cinematic sequences with playable segments, emphasizing dramatic stakes and character motivations. While the plot follows familiar themes of power, legacy, and revenge, its presentation benefits from improved visuals and more cohesive mission structure.  Combat remains deeply technical but leans further toward forward pressure. The Heat system is the centerpiece, granting characters temporary offensive boosts that expand combo routes, extend pressure, and enable new strategic layers. Rage Arts return as cinematic finishers, giving matches dramatic closing moments. Movement precision, punishment knowledge, and matchup awareness remain essential to high-level play.  The roster showcases a mix of returning favorites and newcomers, each with unique mechanics, stances, or signature techniques. Characters feel distinct without losing cohesiveness within the core system. The soundtrack blends electronic, rock, and thematic stage tracks to match the intensity of matches and narrative tone. Visual clarity during high-speed sequences helps maintain focus despite the increased aggression of the new mechanics.  Tekken 8 succeeds by modernizing the series with an offense-oriented system, robust online features, and high production values. It preserves the strategic complexity that defines Tekken while offering tools and mechanics that encourage more active play. For veterans and newcomers seeking a refined, high-intensity 3D fighter, it stands as one of the most polished entries in the franchise.

A very good TEKKEN game with some major flaws that let it down.  One of the major flaws being that the game is way too offensive now. Playing it smart and safe is dis-encouraged, and sometimes you are forced into unwinnable or near-impossible 50/50s purely due to pressure and the fact that you usually have to do some sort of maneuver to get out of the situation, leaving you vulnerable.  Even worse is the disgustingly advantageous Special Styles. While I understand that, in higher ranks, this is quite counterable and not much of an issue (if it gets used at all), it can really unbalance the lower ranks and lower the skill gaps meaning a beginner with Special Style and a decent idea of the game's mechanics has an advantage over someone who prefers not to use it. This would be all right as an optional feature - but it is allowed in RANKED, with no option to filter it out!  The heat system is MEH, I wouldn't care if it was removed altogether but I haven't ever found it game-breaking or grossly unbalanced. I especially like the risk/reward factor that the Rage Arts bring to the game. And they are great to look at, although they can drag on sometimes.  I feel this is why this game has become controversial amongst TEKKEN fans, mostly the competitive high-rank players. But I don't think this is so much the case for more casual or semi-serious players. The game offers plenty of Online and Offline content and doesn't feel unfinished.  What the game partially lacks in substance it makes up for in style. TEKKEN 8 is by far the best looking TEKKEN game I have ever played. The character models look outstanding, the stages are gorgeous, and the amount of detail in ever corner of the game graphically is impressive. The visual effects during fights are maybe a little overdone, but it definitely looks flashy, and it feels responsive.  I would recommend this game GENERALLY but there are some very major flaws that need to be ironed out. I can definitely understand people's point of view with the glaring issues in the game. If you are buying purely for story content and offline modes, there is a lot to be enjoyed. If you are a ranked player who is fairly competitive and high rank, and you are coming from a previous TEKKEN, do not set your expectations too high.

They made back dash easier for new people, which was a good change, whereas back dash cancel is still better, due to it being faster and easier to create space. BUT, none of that matters, because you can't get away from anything, as I said moves reach so far and your back dashes are tiny, slow and feel sluggish compared to older games.    But, this is a 3D game so you should side step! Right!? Nope because they've also made side steps useless. Actually, wait they IMPROVED side step in S2! Except, they also improves everyone's tracking on moves and added new homing moves. So, basically it's even worse now. A 3D game that plays like a 2D game. The more I played this game, the more I realized Tekken 8 wasn't made for me. I came back after a long break and yet I only find anger and resentment towards this game. Whenever I took a break from Tekken 7, I felt refreshed and re-engergize to improve my skill set, but Tekken 8 doesn't give me any sort of accomplishment and satisfaction. Everything felt artificial, almost all my  wins are due to the game's oppressive style over a strong defense that many players have honed for years.   In Tekken 7, being aggressive may result in opponent outmaneuvering you, and tiny little things like Korean Back Dash, sidestep and various Tekken fundamentals are what determines what kind of player you are. Tekken 8 removed many of those fundamentals and normalize all the characters. Everyone has a running + moves, everyone has a stance mixups, everyone have the same gameplan, everything just felt the same.  Despite Tekken 7's final 3 seasons catering to an offensive gameplan, it never felt as overwhelmed as Tekken 8, and special effects are one of the biggest gripe I have with this game, I just can't cant see ♥♥♥♥. It's my first time playing a Tekken, and I have to admit that I find it fun that each character has their own fighting style and combos. Some combat dynamics are great, but there is something that bothers me a lot, and that is that Bandai Namco doesn't make an effort to retain new players. First of all, several characters (if not many) are ridiculously unbalanced. By just spamming a couple of buttons with those characters, you can even achieve a perfect. Some moves and hitboxes are absurdly weird (I'm talking about you, Alisa and Yoshimitsu), and there are characters that are too complicated to even counter or parry, like King. Many times, you can't even put into practice what you learned in tutorials because the opponent doesn't even let you stand up after spamming the same two attacks. If only they balanced the characters and made some technical adjustments, I feel the game would be more enjoyable for new players.  Another thing that I found annoying was the enormous number of smurfs in quick match and ranked games. They pair you a lot with accounts that have no ratings and the default 100 points, but when you fight them, those players seem like they came straight from EVO. I understand that sometimes you lose or have a losing streak, but it's not even close to normal to see people with default accounts having 7 or even 9 consecutive wins without it being reflected in their accounts. I think I could understand it if it were about playing ranked matches because we've all been ambitious and want to win, but it's too boring to fight people who clearly already have experience with the game that just want hunting rookies in categories that are technically for beginners and new players.  I don’t understand how Namco expects to attract new audiences and players to Tekken if they technically do nothing to prevent veteran players from scaring off rookies for feeling superior with their techniques and combos. They should improve their matching system. Anyway, I recommend the game for playing with friends; the online can sometimes be stressful or tedious if you want play alone.

Tekken players all agree certain aspects of the games design are fundamentally flawed, and overlook them hoping the game will change for the better. Tekken devs double down on their mistakes and make the game fundamentally worse, alienating players more. Despite the failure of Soul Calibur 6, Bandai Namco and it's tragically misled team have decided to carry it's worst problems into tekken. Instead of focusing on the rich complexities of the game, we are being drowned in system mechanics that are designed to make it easier for people who simply do not care about it.  The roster is full of duds who wouldn't see play if it wasn't for them being overtuned to have "competitive" value. Most of the cast has been flanderized into "emotionless stick of wood" or "guffawing joke idiot". The story is nonsense, and mostly still boring. The music is a significant downgrade from prior games, the graphics are better, but the visual clutter of turning a game that used to be about martial arts into wizard fighting doesn't even do that slight improvement much justice.  The actual archetypes of characters have been eroded to ensure most players can swap without adapting their play style much, because ultimately there is only one playstyle; aggressive. This is the keyword of tekken 8's design philosophy as expressed by it's devs many times. The focus on creating an aggressive game has led them to make a game where defense is heavily punished. Chip damage on guard, chip damage on throw breaks, insane plus frame attacks on guard, all designed to stop players from feeling rewarded for maintaining a solid defense, and instead encourage them to take needless risks and gamble arbitrarily.  Multiplayer content aside, the games weird AI training "ghost" battle BS is absurd, and the single player content is mostly boring.   When you take the colossal failures of tekken 8 in all at once, it paints a picture of a company desperately trying to appeal to the lowest common denominator, in any way possible. All that's left to do is remind yourself slop is for pigs and move on.

EDIT:  Everything has, dare I say it, been going smoothly for the last few patches. The game is going in a better direction and it's the best it's been since release imo. If they keep it up I'll keep it positive. I'm leaving my old complaints however to remind people what we had to deal with and if we're not careful, what we'll have to deal with again.  I am definitely in the camp of enjoying this game a lot and even love it sometimes, but it has a lot of decisions that make me question the competence and sanity of the designers. I'm really into the game competitively and dive into it quite a bit deeper than the average player so I tend to get familiar with the game's inner workings; so when I see so many exceptions to rules to an absurd degree it makes my head hurt.  Again I totally agree that the game needs to be criticized harshly especially with the horrifying U-Turn they took in S2 directly towards a more toxic, volatile game, and the absolute radio silence for 6 plus months is ridiculous. Unfortunately I'm stuck still enjoying the game even with all of it's stupid flaws and stupid decisions, because there just is NOT a game like this anywhere. VF is too old and outdated for me and I will 100% play the new one when it comes out but for 3D fighters there's just no competition to be found.  Many people mention "ugh constant 50/50 at all times" but I think it goes much deeper than that. 50/50 is an important fundamental part of all fighting games; there HAS to be a mixup at some point to open up the opponent, otherwise holding back at all times is just an option select to any offence. Now I think people need to specify and focus their dislike of 50/50's, namely the easy access to them with relatively low risk.  If I'm going to put you into a situation where you have to guess the mixup or eat a bunch of damage, I should have to work for it. I should need to condition you to block first so even a slow move will make you hesitate, or make you whiff, or punish you first with something other than a 10f. I should not be able to just mindlessly run across the screen with a big, homing while running mid and make you guess for your life because you didn't react to the 20 frame move (a third of a second, quick reminder how fast that is) with a jab or sidestep. I also should not be able to put you into a guess or die situation off a 10f punish, that idea is stupid as hell because that means you cannot take ANY risks against me or you're not only going to eat the guaranteed punish, but you're going to be mixed up for daring to use the least unsafe option possible while not being outright safe. Personally, I believe 12f punishes should be the minimum for a hard mixup situation, especially from stance.  To top it all off because I can keep going on about this for so long I'll write a thesis; I know they wanted to up the aggression and make it less backdash and whiff focused like T7 which is understandable, but gutting backdash to this extent is too much. I shouldn't be able to backdash out of any mixup situation granted, but if I block a move that's, say, -4 on block, and the opponent mashes something afterwards, I should be able to quickly backdash out of the way to avoid immediate retaliation. The opponent then has to use half a brain cell to use a longer range linear move or dash forward before continuing their pressure, creating mind games and counterplay. As it stands, backdashing is rarely an option even on block, and only on some characters do you have strong backdashes, others barely move. A small buff to backdash along with a slight reduction to constant forward movement when attacking, I believe, would help lessen volatility.  Their buffs to sidesteps have been steps in the right direction for sure, but it's counteracted by their addition of ridiculous new moves in S2 that cover character weaknesses for no reason, and the infamous wonky hitboxes and re-aligning strings that even when you whiff let you just press an attack and turn back around to continue hitting your opponent. I'm thinking of a couple of specific characters when I say this but I don't want to make this a character balance issue, more of a systemic issue.  TL;DR I love the game but it has a lot of highly questionable decisions that make it far too volatile and difficult to deal with. I understand their desire to make comebacks and even lesser skilled players able to compete, but as of right now it's taken to an absurd degree that severely frustrates players that do not have the "I MUST MASH CONSTANTLY" mindset. Defensive play, while plausible and can be done, is VERY difficult to execute in order to compete with even an intermediate player, as it takes ten times the knowledge, reflexes and execution to be defensive than offensive. I also have not touched on the lackluster story mode, single player arcade content, or lackluster customization. Hell, even their PAID stuff is often mid or just not worth the money and just screams laziness and greed.  As it stands right now, I cannot recommend this game because so far the developers have not shown that they are in touch with the general sentiment of the playerbase and want to cater to the super casuals, which with respect, are not the bread and butter that keeps the franchise alive. If they take steps to make the game less volatile and casino-like I will change my review to a positive one, until then, I cannot in good faith reward their bad behavior.

this one sits oddly and has a weird barrier for entry skill requirement than the previous games. in some aspects, the game is easier and more lenient on execution heavy inputs which allows for people with not a lot of time and dedication on their hands to play the game at a decent level, but at the same time eliminating the flaws characters had in previous installments.. this makes Tekken 8 a game where knowledge checks and +frame mixup pressure easily win you games if you aren't a pro or have fundamental skills from other Tekken games.   on the surface, this isn't a bad thing, but in the first season and even well into season 2, defense is still taking a backseat compared to everyone's offense. at higher levels of skill, however, you cannot get away with a lot of cheese and you need to revert back to fundamentals from previous games to SOME level.. it's just not as necessary as it was in Tekken 7 and before. i've been playing Tekken since 2009 irc with Tekken 6 on the Xbox, i dont consider myself a pro, but i do have legacy knowledge. with the addition of more complex characters and movesets comes more homework for you and your opponent, needing to remember every string or frame trap to be able to reliably deal with early rank cheese. you're not compelled to play carefully against people most of the time, as they will do their usual flowcharts and expect you to mash. since the damage is so high, you wont be able to adapt mid-match as much as you could from previous games.   if you are planning to play Tekken 8, please dont be discouraged from playing after seeing the move lists. allow your brain and body to build muscle-memory, practice using your tools and punishes correctly.. and most importantly, do not sweat misinputing. most people cannot even do King's chain throws, let alone electrics.   tl;dr: lower barrier to entry but overall higher skill ceiling; average experience is flowcharting and doing 50/50 mixups to win. take your time and adjust accordingly if you want to try it out.

Review for Tekken 8 (Ultimate Edition) – Buyer Beware  I’m a long-time fan of the Tekken series and was excited to support the latest installment by purchasing the Tekken 8 Ultimate Edition. However, I’m extremely disappointed with what “Ultimate” actually means here.  When you label something as an Ultimate Edition, it implies that you're getting the complete experience — all future DLC, characters, stages, costumes, etc. That’s standard across the industry, and many of us bought this edition in good faith, expecting full content coverage.  Instead, Bandai Namco has now released a Season 2 which is not included in the Ultimate Edition. So what exactly did we pay a premium for? Turns out it only covers Season 1 — a fact that wasn't clearly communicated during the game's launch or in the edition's description at the time.  This is misleading marketing. If you're only getting Season 1 content, it should have been labeled something like “Complete Season 1 Edition” — not “Ultimate.” Naming it otherwise feels intentionally deceptive and designed to squeeze more money out of loyal fans down the line.  I don’t blame Steam for this. The blame lies squarely with Bandai Namco for pushing a false sense of value. As it stands, the Ultimate Edition is not worth the price if future seasons are going to be sold separately.  Very disappointed.

So, I bought this game because I am a fan of tekken franchise. I played Tekken 2, Tekken 3, Tekken 5, Tekken Tag Tournament 2, Tekken 7, and now this Tekken 8.  I was already disappointed with Tekken 7. But I have to say that Tekken 8 is complete garbage, an absolute waste of money. The game is heavily unbalanced, cheats and exploits are common, and what made tekken different from other fighting games has been completely removed in this one. Tekken 8 is a fighting game as many others, and arguably the worst tekken game in the franchise and the worst fighting game out there,  Tekken 8 uses a heat system and rage art system. The rage art system is completely unbalanced and terrible. I understand the idea behind it, but it is horrible. This is also why Tekken 7 honestly sucked. But the heat system is the worst: it advantages characters that are inherently aggressive, such as Brian. However, characters that are slow or with slow animations, or that are inherently defensive or that use primarily counters are incredibly disadvantaged.   The game is absolute trash for this price. I regret buying it. The only positive thing is that it is flashy and what not. Besides this, it is a terrible game.  A tip for Jun players: Jun, in this game, is definitely better compared to how she was in Tekken Tag Tournament 2. However, Jun results to be bad nonetheless. Why? Simple. The design of the character seemed to be that she had the capability of regenerating her health bar with certain moves, and that could benefit of the heat system by recharging her health, besides of course using amazing counters. There's a problem: every character restores health, with or without heat system, at the same rate Jun does, in practice. One could argue "but Jun can restore health beyond the white bar", yeah, but the amount that she restores is negligible. Second problem, Jun's damage is low compared to the damage that certain characters, such as Devil Jin or Heihachi, can deal on a single hit. Third problem, like in Tekken 7, there is "armor", i.e. moves that momentarily make the character shine and that cannot be stopped, unless one uses a low hit or a throw. I think the armour system is often abused by a lot of players, making the game practically unplayable with certain characters. Fourth problem, Jun gets staggered by almost every hit from aggressive characters, unlike other characters. So, it is significantly more difficult to punish with Jun compared to punishing with, in practice, any other character. Finally, fifth problem... Jun is slow as hell in this game. She is the slowest character of the game as far as I am concerned. Her move animations are quite long, and they can be interrupted by faster characters with shorter hit animations (namely, any other character, since most characters can produce a strike in 0.1 ms, compared to Jun that often takes between 0.3 and 0.8 ms from button input).    Note on Yoshimitsu: Yoshimitsu's counter can counter everything and stagger, namely it can counter low hits, high hits, and throws. I think it is a bit busted and unbalanced.   Note on Heihachi and similar characters that, to be used, need to be bought separately: I wouldn't say they are "pay to win" characters, because that's not the case. However, they definitely come with some incredible moves that, in my opinion, can be heavily abused by players, and increased damage. For instance, Fakhumram, the new released character, can punish from great distances of the ring... I find it a bit odd and somewhat heavily unbalanced.   Final thought: I truly hope the makers of this game have a huge loss in terms of sales, because this game is just terrible, a waste of money, and not so entertaining at all, but more frustrating than anything else.

I have played every single Tekken since the very first one, each one thousands of hours, and by far the worst one of them all is Tekken 8. Sure, it looks good, has very good production value etc, but outside of all that - the actual game itself, it is just bad and I am tired of pretending that it is not. Bandai Namco likes to gaslight the player base - it wasn't bad netcode, it was YOUR bad internet. It is not bad game, it is YOUR skill issue etc, while in fact - it is the game. Everything is for the offense. Skill ceiling is destroyed, there is nothing to lab anymore, since everything follows, moves, tracks, is plus and launchers. Everything is a 25 second combo, everything takes you to the wall and all walls sticks like a fly paper. Everything auto corrects, so at this point this game might as well just be fully AI, no need for any player, because essentially you are just watching cut scenes and not really playing. So many long animations that interrupt the flow. Even basic knockdowns have built in followups into guaranteed oki, that cannot be avoided. Risk-reward is like 9 to 1 in favor of the attacker. All defensive tools are removed or nerfed, so you just have to guess. Tekken 8 is a casino, where you just have to be lucky. Never has there been a Tekken game where max rank is filled with player with 0 knowledge about the  game, movement, later movement, ducking etc, because you can just keep mashing since plus, plus, plus, mid, mid, launcher, launcher, no execution. This game is hell on training wheel and a perfect example when 12-year olds design a game thinking "lets give everyone everything with no drawbacks", so it will be fun fun fun. If this game frustrated you - don't worry, the problem is not you, but the game. It punishes skill, time and patience, rewards recklessness and fast brain dead rewards. Utterly disgusting and sad remnant of a franchise that used to be the best fighting game in history.

Original review: Having come back to this game for the third time as of writing this, I really want to like this game but I don't. The focus on aggressiveness is not fun to me. Heat as a get out of jail card without any risk, rage art as a semi get out of jail card, power crush as a get out of jail card, auto parries as a get out of jail card, stances with auto parries as a get out of jail card, the overuse of stance and install based character overhauls, lack of poking, lack of movement, chip damage from mashing your face on the controller, guard breaking moves, unblockable moves, teleporting moves on characters, guns/weapon moves on characters, projectiles on characters, exploding stage hazards, emphasis on forced 50/50 mixups, the simplification of the cast neglecting the hours spent by players to master aspects of a character (e.g. Law's DDS or Drag's WR2), cast being stripped of their flaws by getting moves that are a mix of mids/lows that are plus on block, homing, heat activating, counter hit launching, power crushing and active from range 3 (or full screen almost). All because the dev team designed a character that had a specific set of flaws but in this game decided that said flaws "made it difficult for *insert your character here* at the particular situation". Overtuned characters and a general homogenization of it.  High level Tekken is less interesting to watch since they are forced to constantly press buttons to not get overwhelmed by the opponent.  The aesthetic is too much. The particle effects makes the game look worse and at times it is hard to see what is going on. No option given to turn it off locally. Yes, Tekken has had influences from fantasy/anime before but Tekken 8 doubles down on this for some reason. Every character shoots laser and lightning out of their ass and spouts annoying nonsense to a larger degree than in Tekken 7, it is baffling. The rage arts are ridiculous flashy short movies. Stages follows this trend and many look oversaturated, making it difficult to see the characters. Getting juggled allows one to take a five minute stretch. New combos are added that makes the game look even dumber and take even longer time (e.g. Jim and pigeon Jim in S2).  There is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ monetization practices and annoying collaborations forced upon the game post launch. The DLC decisions to lock knowledge check monsters needing to be labbed (e.g. Eddy, Lidia) behind DLC or adding mismatched characters (Clive) to the game and acting all surprised when the character focused on martial arts from the same franchise, that have been requested since Tekken 7, was neglected.   I wanted a game with the clean look of previous Tekkens with a focus on the martial arts, movement, reading your opponent and slowly growing as a player from putting in the hours. Tekken 8 does not provide that. I had problems with the game in S1 and S2 just doubled down on the aspects I do not like. No, Tekken 7 was not a perfect game by any means but the parts that I did not like about it, often found in the different DLC characters, seems to have been the base that Tekken 8 was built from. It is not a bad game, only a disappointing "Tekken" that has gone in the direction I did not want to. Bandai won't have to bother with adjusting anything no matter how much I and others complain if they are satisfied and we keep coming back to play this game and keeping the player count up. As someone who’s played Tekken for years, I came into Tekken 8 with excitement—but after spending time with it, I can’t help but feel let down. The main culprit? The Heat System.  it’s supposed to add intensity and give players more offensive options, but in reality it feels like Tekken trying too hard to copy Street Fighter’s mechanics without understanding what makes Tekken… Tekken. Instead of rewarding skillful play, Heat often feels like a “win button” that tilts the balance in favor of already strong characters. Characters who were solid before now become absurdly overpowered in Heat, with safe-on-block moves that deal insane chip damage and extend pressure far beyond what feels fair.  Tekken has always been about high-risk, high-reward gameplay, where mastering movement and punishes defined the experience. With Tekken 8’s Heat system, that balance feels broken. Right now, the game feels less like Tekken and more like a flashy experiment trying to imitate Street Fighter—without capturing what made Tekken special in the first place.

Review Tekken 8 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   Tekken 8 is without a doubt one of the most exciting and polished entries in the legendary fighting game franchise. Bandai Namco has truly delivered a game that feels modern, fast, and visually stunning, while still staying true to the roots that long-time fans love. From the moment you boot it up, it’s clear this is a celebration of the series’ history and a bold step forward for competitive fighters.  Pros  Spectacular Visuals: The graphics are some of the best in any fighting game to date. Character models, stages, and effects look incredibly detailed, bringing every punch, kick, and special move to life.  Fluid Combat: The fighting feels smoother and more dynamic than ever. The new Heat System adds an exciting layer of strategy that rewards aggression and creativity.  Character Variety: The roster is well-balanced and diverse, offering both fan favorites and fresh faces. Each character feels unique with their own style and personality.  Story Mode: The cinematic presentation makes the story engaging and impactful, adding emotional weight to the long-standing Mishima saga.  Online Play with Cross-Play: A huge win! Tekken 8 finally brings cross-play, making it easier than ever to fight friends and rivals no matter what platform they’re on.  Accessibility: With simplified control options, newcomers can jump in without feeling overwhelmed, while veterans still have all the depth and complexity they crave.  Cons (Room for Improvement)  Balancing Tweaks Needed: Some characters and moves may feel slightly overpowered in the early days, but this can be fine-tuned with patches.  More Single-Player Content: While the story is strong, additional modes, challenges, or arcade-style extras would give solo players more reasons to keep coming back.  Customization Variety: Character customization is good but could use even more depth and creativity to truly stand out.  Learning Curve: Although accessible, mastering Tekken 8 still requires dedication. A more robust tutorial system could help beginners ease into advanced techniques.  And yes… I miss Lucky Chloe: Tekken 7’s dancing queen was goofy, flashy, and fun — I’m crossing my fingers she moonwalks back into Tekken 8 someday!  Final Thoughts  Tekken 8 is a powerhouse of a fighting game that pushes the series into a new era. It’s beautiful, fast, and fun — perfect for both casual players and competitive fans. While there’s always room to grow with future updates and DLC, what’s here at launch is already fantastic. This game feels like a love letter to fighting game fans and a clear sign that Tekken remains one of the kings of the genre.  Reviewed by Zulandin from Zul TV on YouTube and TikTok

Tekken 8 Review: The King Is Back, and He's a Beast  Listen up, fighting game fans. Tekken 8 isn't just a new game; it's a statement. Tekken 7 brought the series back to life, but Tekken 8 is here to push the genre into a whole new era. With jaw-dropping visuals, a super aggressive new combat system, and a story that feels like a full-on movie, this game blew my expectations out of the water.  Looks and Vibe Right from the jump, the first thing you notice is how damn good Tekken 8 looks. Built on Unreal Engine 5, every character model, stage, and special effect is packed with insane detail. You can see the sweat on Jin's face, the fiery glow from Kazuya's moves, and even individual snowflakes falling in the Siberia stage. The stages are dynamic and destructible, which just amps up the drama and makes every fight feel like a cinematic showdown. The music is also fire—a mix of rock, electronic, and orchestral tracks that get your blood pumping the second the match starts.  The New Combat System Tekken has always been about deep 3D combat, and Tekken 8 takes that to the next level with the Heat system. This is the core of the game and what makes it feel so fresh. By activating a Heat Burst or Heat Engager, your character enters a 'Heat' state for a few seconds. In this state, you can use a Heat Dash to extend combos or a Heat Smash for a powerful finisher.  The Heat system pushes you to be more aggressive. It's not just about waiting for an opening; it's about going on the offensive and creating your own chances. Combos that used to be a nightmare are now easier to pull off, which makes the game more welcoming for newcomers. For the veterans, it adds a whole new layer of strategy. Managing your Heat becomes a huge part of dominating a fight.  They also brought in the Tornado mechanic, which replaces the old Bound system from Tekken 7. Tornado lets you launch opponents high into the air, setting them up for some sick combos. This, along with the return of Rage Arts, makes the pace of the game feel fast and frantic. Every hit feels impactful, and every combo is super satisfying.  Story Mode: A Blockbuster Experience One of the most impressive things about Tekken 8 is its story mode, "The Dark Awakens." After years of fighting, the clash between Jin Kazama and Kazuya Mishima finally comes to a head. The story is full of drama, plot twists, and epic cinematic fights that feel like something straight out of a Hollywood movie. The cutscenes are gorgeous, and the voice acting is on point, pulling you deep into the emotional narrative.  The story mode is a great way to get a feel for the game's mechanics in a real-world setting. While the story might be a bit cheesy for some, the execution is so good that it stands as one of the best story modes in any fighting game.  Besides the main story, there are also Character Episodes that give you a deeper look into each fighter's backstory. It's a great way to get to know your favorite characters and see how they fit into the bigger Tekken world.  Content and Replay Value Tekken 8 is stacked with content. Besides the story mode, you've got Arcade Quest, which helps new players learn the ropes, and the Tekken Fight Lounge, a 3D social hub where you can hang out with other players, have casual matches, or just watch fights.  The training and tutorial modes are top-tier. The Tekken 8 Practice Mode is one of the best I've ever seen, with easy-to-read frame data, combat simulations, and customizable training scenarios. It's an invaluable tool for anyone looking to get better.  And for all you fashionistas out there, the character customization is insane. You can find all kinds of cosmetic items—from costumes to accessories—to make your favorite fighter totally unique.  Final Thoughts Tekken 8 is the peak of 3D fighting games. It nails the perfect balance between keeping the old school feel and adding awesome new stuff. The mind-blowing visuals, aggressive combat, and cinematic story make this a must-buy.  Whether you've been playing Tekken since the PlayStation 1 days or you're new to the genre, Tekken 8 has something for everyone. This is a game you'll love playing, learning, and mastering. Every fight is a blast, and you'll feel the energy and adrenaline that makes Tekken 8 so special.  If you're looking for a game that's deep, engaging, and visually stunning, Tekken 8 is it. It's a masterpiece that not only respects its past but also confidently steps into the future.  Overall Score: Highly Recommended

Opinion of a 35 year old Azucena main (Tekken King on Xbox and PC.) Also this is my first Tekken game since Tekken 3, and honestly I was a child at that time lol. I've played a lot of fighting games over the years, and  gotten pretty good on a casual level, but this is the first game I've truly tried to learn and be good at. So, some may say i'm a scrub, and some may say i'm still a noob. Anyways, this is not only my favorite Tekken, but it's also my favorite fighting game. I've spent thousands of hours on Xbox learning, and grinding. I've met countless friends, and spent hours scrubbing it out and conversing as we learn the match-ups and deep mechanics of this game. It's a very hard game to learn, and there will be growing pains. You will get perfects done to you. You will struggle with character match-ups. You have to learn and study to find your way in dealing with large move lists, and a variety of different play styles. It's all been worth it. If you stick with it you will eventually stop fighting against characters, and you will finally start fighting the pilot. Then the flow of Tekken will start becoming what I consider a work of art. It's a fighting game with so many mechanics and moves, and in the hands of good players it's just some of the most satisfying gameplay a fighting game can offer. If you are the pilot it gives you such a satisfying rush to break down someones fighting style, and then dismantle their defense into a 100+ damage combo. The FGC is divided it seems on this game for various reasons. Personally, I think the devs have made an amazing game. It will never be perfect for everyone, but I trust that the devs are doing their best to make Tekken 8 the best it can be. Things will be broken sometimes, some things may be unbalanced sometimes, and characters can be over tuned. Underneath it all is a fighting game that I consider the best in it's class, and I will be here to ride the wave until the end. I've made some great memories through this game. If you're reading this, I hope you chose to do the same also. Win or lose, trash talk or respect. I look forward to seeing everyone in the que.

Why Tekken 8 Fails the Legacy of Fighting Games (Review from a Bushin Jin)  Main Character: Jin Kazama Highest Rank Achieved: Bushin (Top ~5% of global players) Time Played: 100+ Hours  I am a 51-year-old gamer who grew up on the arcade and early console era of fighting games, where fundamentals actually meant something. I am not writing this review out of rage or after a bad loss streak; I am writing it after successfully grinding to the elite blue ranks, analyzing the system, and deciding to permanently uninstall the game for my own mental health.  If you are a working adult with a family and limited free time, or if you love traditional fighting games that reward spatial awareness, patient defense, and human-to-human reads, stay far away from Tekken 8.  Here is a breakdown of why this game is fundamentally flawed:  1. The System-Enforced "Unga Bunga" Meta The developers explicitly stated they designed Tekken 8 for "forced aggression." They succeeded, but they completely destroyed tactical depth in the process. Because of the Heat system, massive chip damage on block, and tracking moves that skip the spacing game entirely, pure defense is dead. High-level Tekken 8 is not chess; it is a series of chaotic, forced 50/50 coin flips. Guessing wrong twice shouldn't cost you a round, but in this game's hyper-optimized landscape, it does.  2. A Fraudulent Visual Loop The visual presentation frequently lies to the player. You can physically connect a punch or kick directly into an opponent's face, but because the internal system loop has granted them "priority" mid-combo, your hit becomes invisible, their animation overrides yours, and you are punished for making a correct physical read. A fighting game should accurately reflect its mechanics visually. Tekken 8 forces you to play a frame-data spreadsheet rather than reacting to what your eyes actually see.  3. The Game as a Second Job Older games (and entries like Dead or Alive) allowed you to win on intuition, timing, and fundamentals. Tekken 8 reduces organic fighting to an academic memory test. You are required to lab and memorize frame advantages, combo paths, and tedious matchup strings for a massive roster. If you cannot treat this game like a part-time job, the mechanics actively lock you out of having fun, completely disregarding your actual combat IQ.  Verdict: I reached the top single-digit percentage of the player base, looked at the "forced-aggression" meta, and realized it wasn't a rewarding challenge, it was just an artificial, exhausting cortisol spike. The community's toxic response to honest critique is just the cherry on top of a deeply hostile environment.  I chose my sanity and my family over a digital badge. If you value your peace of mind, do not waste your time or money here. Currently things are looking a lot better. The last few patches have been great and new characters have been quite well balanced as well. Devs are fixing a lot of the major issues the community has had with the game since launch, many of which I mentioned in the previous review (still below). Things are looking bright for the future of the game. I'm actually enjoying the game a lot now.  ---  Old review (Before Season 3):  TL;DR  Sadly Tekken 8 is not fun anymore for a player like me. Trying to improve is a nightmare due to massive system and game design changes that appear to be catering to absolute beginners at the cost of pro play and especially so for the average player looking to get good.  If you want to just play the story and dabble a bit with combos and online, the game is great and everything around that has never been better. If that's what Tekken means to you, you'll love Tekken 8. But I'm writing this from the point of view of me. I'm an average skilled ranked player who tries to improve and learn. I was around purple ranks in Tekken 7 and it was hard getting there. My playstyle is more defensive and movement focused. I spent a lot of time practicing movement and other "fundamentals".  Game looks and sounds great. There's new additions to game modes and practice functionality that is top notch, but there's very little replay value anywhere outside online. Online is fun with friends and casual play, but a nightmare for taking seriously, due to how oppressive offense is now. Backdashing has been all but removed. Without match-up knowledge it's just about who can attack first and better. Defense is now only effective for the absolute top tier players who want to spend absurd hours practicing match-ups, and even then there's a lot of pure guessing where there used to be option selecting and using movement to defend.   ---  This is really sad to write as I love the franchise.  Tekken 8 is brutal and not in a good way like it used to be. Unless you know each match-up pretty well, you're just gonna get killed by offensive stances, which pretty much every character now has, or by plus on block moves into more, or by otherwise blatantly overtuned moves, or by free combos through the new heat system, character specific power-ups, or guard breaks who pretty much everyone seems to have now etc. Pretty much all characters have been dumbed down and execution requirements removed to the point where a toddler can run pretty decent offense on most of the cast. The downside is that countering that offense requires more of you than ever before, making offense incredibly potent. Most matches from absolute beginner to the upper ranks are decided by who can just do better button mashing, which to me is a complete antithesis to what Tekken is all about. If you enjoy party games where you can just press buttons and lots of effects happen on the screen, Tekken is pretty close to that now.  There's no backdashing anymore. Pretty much all moves and strings advance so much that backdashing only makes it possible to get hit by their mids with little to no upside. A lot of strings have mix-ups built in. So good luck learning any counter-play as the opponent can just choose another version of the same string that shuts down any possibility for counter-play. One upside to movement is that sidestepping has been improved in Season 2, which feels great. The problem is that they also added so many good homing moves - of which a lot are launchers - that sidestepping is often a death sentence.  And god forbid if you get launched. Combos last 20 seconds now and every character gets wall-to-wall carry into wall combo and disgusting oki. So most rounds are decided by a launch into guessing for your life. None of that option selecting stuff, just pure guess.  So all in all, the game has devolved into mashing and 50/50's on an unprecedented scale. This sadly is reflected even at the highest level of play where neutral is not seen for the most of the time. It's just 20 seconds of pressure from one side into a guess from the defender and if they guess right, it's 20 seconds of pressure and guessing games for the other.  If all you do is play with a good group of people you know, private lobbies are still fun. But if your main goal is playing ranked and trying to improve, I can't recommend the game with a good conscience. Ranked is just not fun anymore.  And the eSports scene is pretty boring too. Heck, the biggest tournament of the year just finished where the top 8 was two of the same disgustingly overpowered character against another where both are just pressing god moves that require no execution to pull off. It was a snooze fest.  The development team are dragging their feet which to me only indicates that this is the direction they want the game to go. There's a lot of echoes of other competitive games where they started making it easier to get wins, in order to lure in the casual players. In the end they always end up making the game absolutely unplayable for anyone wanting to take the game seriously, which sadly puts off many casuals from engaging with the game long term. I really hope this is not the direction they are intending, but that's exactly what it looks like at the moment, and that's extremely disheartening.  The game looks gorgeous. I like that they're adding in new costumes and stuff to buy (Tekken Store) and earn (through a Battle Pass system). The practice functionality is better than it's ever been and they keep building on it which is a huge plus. The story was pretty dope, perhaps the best in the series. There's a new "Arcade Quest" story as well, which kinda teaches you the basics of Tekken which I really enjoyed even as a seasoned player. There's a new "Ghost Battle" system where you can play AI powered CPU opponents that learn from actual players, which is really interesting. You can even play your own Ghosts that learn new stuff from you on the fly. But outside of the stories, Tekken Ball, classic Arcade mode and the AI Ghost battles, but sadly there's very few ways to play the game with replay value. There's no treasure battle, no survival, tekken force etc. Outside of online, the game kinda runs out of offline content after you finish everything once.

I have very mixed feelings about this game.  I started with Tekken 7 (despite its issues: Marduk), and I really enjoyed the defensive play, movement, and spacing. Tekken 8 moves heavily toward aggressive mechanics (Heat system, chip damage) too hard, making it feel less like... what I expect and loved from Tekken. It takes much longer in T8 to experience the strategic, defensive play that I think defines the series compared to T7.  And okay.. let’s talk about the learning curve. I keep hearing people say Tekken 8 is “easier” than Tekken 7. First of all: WHAT? Because I see nothing. If anything, I get knowledge checked way more here, and for the dumbest reasons. Sometimes I feel like I'm being punished for trying to play like a level-headed person instead of a full-blown unga gorilla. Granted, I like games like Guilty Gear Strive (Game Pass Free Trial) and I enjoy some monkey gameplay from time to time. But I don’t come to Tekken for that. This game constantly throws transitions into stances into more stances into more stances. After the 20th stance I’ve seen in a match, I feel like I’ve had enough.  Ooookay, to be fair, the tutorials in Tekken 8 are better cuz mostly because they actually exist, unlike Tekken 7. It’s a step forward, and worth mentioning, especially since proper detailed tutorials are a new invention for fighting games in general. So, cool, here's the medal. It helps, but it doesn’t fix how unnecessarily overwhelming the rest of the game is.  The game itself looks great, has solid netcode, and a decent roster. Still, visually, there's an odd imbalance: male characters have excellent animation quality and detail (though weirdly dry-skinned), while female characters look pretty but overly doll-like and lack expressiveness. SF6 handled this balance way better, making all characters feel expressive and dynamic.  DLC-wise, Season Pass 1 felt forgettable, and Season Pass 2 was even more disappointing... mostly predictable picks that didn't excite me. After seeing what is up on offer... my expectations of Season Pass 3 are VERY low. And if this game ever adds Marduk as DLC? Yeah, that’ll seal the deal for me.  Also, just a personal nitpick: Tekken's male characters aren’t very attractive, and its female characters aren't particularly cool. Other games, like Guilty Gear or Granblue Fantasy Rising, nail character attractiveness way better, even considering they're anime games (though Tekken is pretty anime at this point anyway).  Overall, Tekken 8 feels like polished mechanics stacked awkwardly on legacy systems. It's not a bad game, but for me personally, it just didn't click like how it did with T7 for me.

Tekken 8 – 600 Hours In: A First-Time Player’s Perspective  As someone who came into Tekken 8 fresh — no prior Tekken experience, just raw curiosity and the willingness to grind — I’ve dropped over 600 hours into this game. I wanted to love it. And for a while, I did.  Season 1 felt rough, no doubt. The mechanics were flashy, Heat System felt like a gamble, and damage was through the roof. But at least there was some learning curve, some level of commitment required to climb the ladder. Even when the balancing was questionable, wins still felt like they were earned.  Season 2, though? Somehow worse. The balancing is completely off the rails. The game is now so “beginner-friendly” that it actively rewards button mashing. I get that fighting games need to attract new players, but we’ve gone from helping newcomers to handing them the keys to the kingdom. You can mash your way up the ranks now. It happens. I’ve seen it. I’ve played against it. And worst of all? It works.  Characters like Hwoarang and Anna are absolutely cracked, able to overwhelm with relentless pressure and flowcharts that are way too safe. There’s no risk vs reward when you're rewarded for just pressing buttons faster than your opponent can think. Bryan’s damage output is ridiculous, and it’s getting to the point where one clean read turns into a 70% health swing. That’s not rewarding skill — that’s just bloated numbers on top of unbalanced mechanics.  I’m not complaining because I’m bad. I’ve stuck with this game longer than any other fighter. I’ve practiced, labbed, watched high-level play, and fought through the grind. I’ve earned my frustration. And it’s frustrating to see the game I dedicated myself to turn into something where neutral, spacing, and decision-making are losing value in favor of autopilot offense and spam-heavy strategies.  Accessibility shouldn't mean brainless. You should still need to learn how to play neutral, how to whiff punish, how to condition, how to block under pressure. But in its current state, Tekken 8 feels like it’s punishing players for thinking, and rewarding those who just go full throttle and pray.  There’s still potential. The core of Tekken is amazing — legacy mechanics, mind games, matchup knowledge. But the current direction? It’s not sustainable for serious players. If this is what Tekken 9 will look like too, I might be out.  (I'd still recommend this game to people attempting to get into fighting games, but be ready for that unimaginable Tekken rage to come out)

The netcode is a joke, the connection strength filter does absolutely nothing, online the game forces you to just sit there and watch as you eat mix up after mix up after mix up.  Poor balancing has plagued the game in season two, and the devs have consistently shown no interest in making meaningful changes with only minor changes being made at sporadic intervals. (Most of the season two patches have been poor at best, game breaking at worst.)   The poor balance is exacerbated by the netcode and connectivity issues, making certain characters unbearable to fight online that are otherwise manageable offline.  Unreal Engine 5 bloat and bad optimization also rears its head, which is a shame because the game often works well on lower spec PCs but UE5 gets in the way of that for seemingly no reason.  The game is better offline, but if you wanted to play offline, I think you would be better off with either of the console versions.

Tekken 8 is the latest instalment in BANDAI NAMCO's long-running Tekken series of arcade-style, 1-on-1 fighting games. This game offers a broad range of unique characters, both newcomers and veterans alike, each with their own fighting style.  This game's newest in-game mechanic is the Heat Meter which, when activated in each round, grants players a temporary boost of power, namely chip damage, and the ability to perform a powerful Heat Burst move. This mechanic can be easily compared to the MAX MODE mechanic in SNK's King of Fighters series.  Tekken 8 also offers a broad range of varied game modes, including the fan-favourite Tekken Ball mode and two new virtual lobby modes: the offline Arcade Quest, and the online Battle Lounge.  Alas, although Tekken 8 has so much content for players old and new alike, the PC version of this game is shockingly bugged and thus almost unplayable, even for players with computers made for gaming.  In particular, Tekken 8 has the longest loading times between matches in Tekken history thus far. In my experience, offline matches often take at least 2 or 3 minutes to load. In all the previous Tekken games, in-game matches only took up 15 seconds to load.  Worse yet, online matchmaking, in my experience, is almost impossible without cross-play. When I first tried out the online Battle Lounge mode, I was only able to play 1 out of 15 online matches, because the other 14 online matches ended up disconnecting for some unknown reason, even when my opponents and I agree to face off with each other.  As a result, it becomes painstakingly clear why many fellow Tekken players feel disappointed with Tekken 8. To add insult to injury, the previous instalment, Tekken 7, ran much more smoothly with faster loading times and accessible online matchmaking.  All in all, Tekken 8 has plenty of content for fighting game fans old and new, but I would not recommend the PC version, not unless you cannot play this game on console and thus you can only play on PC.

I've been following, studying and competing in Tekken for over 10 years at this point. I've always pushed through the difficulties of learning such a complex series and I can appreciate Tekken from both a casual and a competitive perspective. I'm all for having a different change of pace and being able to do different things. However, this is not how you do it properly.  There are good things about this game. I've always liked the visuals, designs and animations and this game is no different. Practice mode has just about anything you need. Matchmaking works well overall. The jukebox feature to change stage music is welcome and I hope it returns for future games.  With that said, everything else is a colossal disappointment. The main issue with the gameplay itself is not one big erroneous mechanic or feature. It's the amalgamation of everything that adds up to a cocktail of absolute chaos and uncertainty, where the game is stressful and uncontrollable for both player and opponent.  If you want to make a game where you have to overwhelm your opponent with offense, that's the developers' vision and I respect that, but if you spoonfeed solutions by adding unreasonably strong moves and systems instead of having the player think to get around a situation or work around a character's weakness, you lose character type variety, play style variety and player intelligence.  The story had potential but it was nonsensical, adding the micro-transaction shop after the game reviews were out was filthy, the balance team is clueless and doesn't know who to listen to or what to do, the combos are way too long now having about 3 different extension mechanics, every character has lost their gameplay identity, their collaboration works are boring and wasted opportunities to do something actually meaningful or substantial and there are no signs or intentions of making major improvements, given that the last few "fix" patches were, in the grand scheme of things, meaningless and useless.  I've tried every character, gone to offline tournaments, played with friends, and given Tekken 8 a fair chance since release. I'm posting my first review on Steam as a testament to my disappointment with a 30 year old series that has been consistently enjoyable despite some flaws and has taught me so much, yet has fallen so low.  Mr.Harada, please be in charge of Tekken 9, make it a classic, end the Mishima story once and for all and get some rest in Lee's resort in the Bahamas.
