Edit after end of season 2:  Having played almost the whole roster and still coming back to casual lobbies daily/weekly it would be hypocritical not to recommend the game. For the "original tekken" experience we still have the old games but for what tekken 8 is it can be a ton of fun with other people in discord. This iteration is the most unforgiving as you have to literally know every interaction if you wan't to know what is going on. Playing basic movement tekken is not a viable strategy anymore and sidestepping/backdashing is mostly for hard reads for very specific situations. Offence is king in this game and "holding block" will just get you killed.  Every patch has been going to the right direction and making it the best it can be with the overly offensive design in mind. I would not recommend this version to casual players who just want to press buttons as it can be very frustrating experience with all the heat stuff and simplified and opressive offensive options that anyone can perform. For fighting game fans, this is still the best 3D fighting game experience (as there is not much competition) that we currently have in the market.   If you want "traditional tekken" with movement options and varied neutral game this is not the game for you, however especially for newcomers this games provides easy access to start playing a fighting game as all characters are loaded with easy to execute moves and strategies. It is a good party game to play in lobby with other people but if you want to play the game competitively you will be faced with a ton of unfair situations where only control you have as a player is to guess from 2 options.   Positive things:  -A lot of characters to choose from -Playing with other people is made a lot easier -Loading times are manageable -Free frame-data in practice with relatively easy options compared to older titles  -Removal of hard legacy inputs for moves that did not need them (universal throw inputs, easier while running input etc.) -Sidestep from ducking was reintroduced (provided, everything tracks so there are rare occasions you actually want to press it)  Negative things:  -This game is 3D in paper but every move tracks making the most viable strategy to spam ob+ tracking moves into pure unearned 50/50 coinflip gameplay -Neutral skip buttons -Magic 4 was removed  -Ki charge counterhit was removed -DLC characters cannot be tested in practice mode -Combos take a ton of time to execute -Mechanics that take you out of playing the game with very long animations (rage arts, heat activations etc.) -Higher health makes poking a lot less viable -Ranked system is still a mixed bag so quality of games is a coinflip  The dev team seems to listen to social media outrage instead of constructed criticism. Players are also promised things that eventually are not what was said like infamous "season 2 defensive patch" where all characters were given more oppressive attacks with low risk high reward type of playstyle. Latest few patches after season 2 farce have been steps to right direction but the road is about 100 steps long so I am not holding my breath on this game actually ever becoming the nuanced competitive game that the earlier installations have been.

This review is written after the v2.03.01 update with the early access release of Fahkumram.  This patch shows the developers have now tripled down on the game's direction, aggression. The skill floor for beginner players has been lowered with heat burst, heat smash, chip damage, unblockables, improved lows, armor moves, homing throws, low risk high reward strings, realigning strings, infinite range weapons, safer/fewer getup options, and rage art. Mechanically difficult options have been made easier or replaced with simpler moves, lowering the skill ceiling for intermediate to advanced players. Professional level players have been affected too but they sit above the ceiling at mastery of the game. They can still be the best, but the removal of depth only removes enjoyment from the game. Everybody can now do the highest damage combo with ease. Combo variety is gone, the best damage and wall carry is accessible to all. Single hit pokes and fast counter hit moves have been being selectively nerfed to encourage the use of big moves. Defensive movement is a non-option with far advancing moves, bigger hit boxes, forced 50/50 sequences, and weaker movement. Too many situations come down to a raw guess. Option selects are almost nonexistent, because characters have been given new coverage moves to their move list from Tekken 7 or added in the season 2 patch. The devs refuse to delete these moves or at least make them terrible. Weakness and character identity has been patched out. Online cheating has gone unanswered, and the best solution was a spreadsheet of Twitter reports. These problem have existed since the launch of Tekken 8 and have not been addressed to a satisfactory extent. The developers have had plenty of time to listen to the community which they pretend to be close to and improve the game, but they would rather appease to the greatest common factor in the hopes of greater player retention.  Bandai Namco has gotten what they wanted. A game for the spectators and casuals. Fast-paced rushdown fights with little neutral or spacing, where your best option is to be the first one swinging. Infinite stages have been removed and tournament rules changed on stage selection to discourage defense and make sure all stages are shown. Matches are now flashy particle effects, lengthy combos with cinematics for flare, and the combo and damage counters to let the audience know that was a big combo. There is a lower time investment to pick up the game and feel like you're good at it by flying up the meaningless online ranks, just enough to get the cash cows into the Tekken Shop to buy the uninspired battle pass and costumes while selling Unreal Engine default shapes and assets from previous games. Bandai Namco has taken the momentum from the success of Tekken 7 and turned it into a game that demands less, provides less, and respects less of the community that made it great.  I know casuals don't want a hard game, but there were better alternatives than to turn Tekken into a party game. Investments should have been made on secondary game modes for casual players. Expand on Arcade Quest, why can I finish a visual novel and a couple bot battles in an afternoon? Why not have modifiers, character leveling, a continued story? Bring in extra features to Tekken ball. Train your ghost. Where is tournament mode? Why is Tekken Force one level in the story? Give character episodes that mean something and advance their story. Add in all the cool cinematics and super moves there. Leave online matches for those that want to make the investment and don't ruin it for those that have already invested.  This game had the legacy and potential to be the best fighting game ever, but now it's a disappointment.  Positives: [list] [*]Roster is good. [*]Graphics are good. [*]Story mode is good. [*]More story expansions like Unforgotten Echoes should be done. [*]Fight lounge and Arcade Quest are great for new players to become familiar with the game. [*]Tekken Ball is fun. [*]Music is good. [*]Jukebox is great. [*]Practice and match queue mode settings and UI display tools are great. [*]My Replay is great, replay takeover is an amazing tool. [*]Customization is good. [/list]

this game has less depth than other modern fighters on the market, because every character has so many moves that they have access to all the same tools, resulting in a very stagnant neutral that functions almost the same regardless of who you're playing. it also means the best characters in the game just have the best versions of those tools without any drawbacks. archetypes don't really exist, everyone is a stance mix-up character, and i don't even mind that the game is more aggressive (i am not an old tekken player), but i do mind the linearity of it. because the game makes itself seem deep by having so many moves, but really it just means you have to dedicate hundreds of hours to knowledge check moves that you'll only see once a month. you have to memorize endless gimmicks and know when to low parry certain strings that leave the opponent safe if you don't, and memorize chains that are only used by players hoping you haven't cuz otherwise they're useless. it's busywork disguised as depth, complexity purely for complexity's sake. if every character had the 30ish moves that characters in other fighting games do, it wouldn't make the game less deep or interesting, it would just mean you get to do the fun stuff faster. functionally high/mid/low isn't really different than the overhead/high/low system of 2D fighters, you just hold back instead of down-back by default, and sidestepping isn't functionally different than 2D sways or parries except it's way less consistent because they're really really bad about making the results of sidestepping even the same move consistent. rage arts are a braindead mechanic that has all the drawbacks of comeback supers with none of the benefits (restraining meter use, rewarding patient play). they only slow down the match once they're online since they can't be jab checked and there's no such thing as a safejump. plus the animations are insanely long and boring to watch more than once, yet alone in half your matches. "then don't get hit by rage arts", ok should i also never use my own rage art and never get combo'd? be for serious. also the music sucks, probably the worst fighting game music ever.  and lastly, having new stages not be free when they affect competitive play and not having the DLC characters available in training mode is a scummy business practice. bring back soulcalibur

The game is in a very rough state. Here's the good and the bad.  The good:  More fluent gameplay, more responsive controls, new mechanics make the game feel fresh and new, yet still feeling very similar and helping players that have legacy skill with Tekken. Roster is good, characters feel nice, look nice, play nice. Great visuals, great stages, nice new moves, and they add more moves every season. Game was sort of tuned in terms of notations and input to make complex and difficult moves become easier for all, for example some Just Frame moves are not that strict as it used to, and most command grabs got rid of the old "know the button" character specific inputs, and instead all characters now have the uf1+2 input for command grabs. Heat mode is good, and helps in comebacks and cool combos. Makes it look impressive. A bit of a dumbed down version of Tekken compared to older titles.  The bad:  The game *IS* a dumbed down version of Tekken. Lots of moves and new mechanics make the game very imbalanced, and some characters just have better moves that others, and are now easier to perform. Why play my old favourite character (Lee Chaolan) who has very difficult gameplay and difficult inputs and demanding playstyle while I can simply pick another character that does the same, with less effort? It feels unfair and silly. The Tekken Store is a joke, it makes you pay for cosmetics by paying extra money, while you already paid money for it. The Tekken gold coins you get from the game are essentially useless, even more so that it was in Tekken 7. Online play is trash, ranked games have no satisfying rewards when winning, and losing hurts a lot more that winning feels good. Lots of intentional disconnects make the experience worse, cheaters even more. Frequent game disconnects for no reason while it wasnt your fault at all, and yet STILL you get punished by the game, letting you know that if you leave frequent matches, you'll get a penalty. Game is too dumbed down, thus making learning the game mean nothing, since new players and moderate players can spam powerful moves at you (and with the help of Special Mode, which is TOURNAMENT OK), and make winning a match a tedious and tiring process. New season's changes and modifications made the game very awful, and the price tag for the new season pass is basically half the game's FULL PRICE (40€).  Utterly absurd, you can try joining the party and try not taking the game seriously, because I cannot. But you won't have a nice time. Wait for a discount on the game and the season passes, and check again. It's a fun game at some times, but most of the times, I want to break my desk in half. That's all.

Now that in season 2 even BRYAN has a true 50/50 in heat, that just loses his identity and loops him in with the rest of the cast. I miss in Tekken 7 that when characters had their own identity. For example: Bryan was a defensive counter hit character that had good wall carry and wall damage. But to get the good damage, you had to do harder combos that were harder to execute and had A LOT less leniency. Now, all his combos are easier to some degree to execute. He was considered a skill character along with Kazuya, Lee, and Steve. Now he is washed with the same tools and offensive capabilities that the rest of the cast have that he didn't have before. It is mind numbingly boring and repetitive. I would like to see a change to Heat where you get 1 bar of heat per match and 1 rage art per match. BUT, if you use heat, you lose access to Rage Arts and vice versa. Which would make for maybe one crazy round per player, then it would make for some actual decision making. Then to top it off, let people get 2 strong heat moves per bar, OR 1 heat smash, if you use one of the moves, no heat smash. Which would make players internalize more scenarios for more interesting interactions. Then the change to the frame data on moves for heat, and heat burst. I have unfortunately decided to take a permanent hiatus from the game until actions are taken to fix the game and overhaul it for a more consistent and not forced interaction game play. Only a recommendation for a fair price.  I wish this could be a review of the mechanics and the art style and the normal things you'd talk about reviewing a videogame, but unfortunately games are such slimy scans nowadays that the entirety of this review will be answering the question of, "will you be getting ripped off buying this for the price they are asking?"  TL;DR is: Base game is fair, with a decent roster and probabky the most robust single player experience if any tekken to date. However, there are moderate cosmetic microtransactions and overpriced DLC.  To preface, I'm a casual. I have no idea what a 50/50 is or plus on block, so the season two balance changes that have upset everyone are completely beyond my perception. Instead this review will be fore the casual button masher who cannot even comprehend competitive play.   The gane has a respectable base roster and there is a lot of single player content to keep you busy. There is a full story mode with animated cutscenes- definitely the best implementation of a story mode in any tekken. I wish every Tekken had a story mode of this format and quality. And they seem to add more stories for free with each season. And beyond that there is the Arcade Quest. A separate, meta-story mode about ranking up through the arcade circuit. There are ghost battles, character story modes, and a traditional arcade mode.  However the monetization is where things become frustrating and off-putting. Character customization is depressingly limited, with only the same palette of ill-fitting streetwear for every character. Compare that to the multitudes of unique and interesting customization options for each character in tekken 6. And of course most of the customization is behind the mtx paywall, but even what's for sale is generic and uninteresting. There are really cool throwback outfits also behind the paywall, too, which nothing says, "they don't care they just want to extract as much money from you as they can" like making fan service hidden behind a paywall. What a reward for my brand loyalty or whatever.  And beyond that, for customizables for your boring xbla avatar for the arcade quest that im sure nobody cares about, character portraits, title cards, etc, all hidden behind microtransactions.   And to top off the egregious monetization FORTY DOLLAR season passes that only include four characters and a few maps. Amd judging by the fact that Tekken 7 is trying to charge over $100 for the complete edition, it's unlikely that it will ever be sold at a reasonable price.  But in conclusion, the now $60 is more than enough content to play through by myself, for my own entertainment with no aspirations of becoming a professional, and there is always multi-player with friends. Microtransactions are upsetting to see, but they're not super egregious and are not difficult to ignore. DLC is overpriced, however.  If you can, I recommend getting whatever complete edition you can for sale if it ever goes up for a reasonable price. Otherwise, although the base isn't unreasonably prices at the current moment, considering how new it still (kinda) is; with time it'll start to feel like less of a value, and if the price doesn't go down with it's age, the recommendation will turn into a "don't pay near full price for an almost ten year old game" situation like tekken 7 is.

There are so many explosions and effects even when you throw a jab. It is hard to see where the jab would land.   3. Tekken translates to iron fist. Tekken is supposed to  be a tournament of the iron fist. A martial arts game, and here we are with ana bazooka, victor's bs, alisa chainsaw, and nina's guns. These moves are so fast, keep you stunned, and have crazy effects. This is not what a tournament of the iron fist should be about. Keep that stuff in mortal kombat.   4. 60fps in the big 2024 or 2025. Outrageous.   5. System mechanics-  heat gauge/heat smash. Basically you get two overpowered supers every round that are hard and boring to deal with. You just have to block the whole 10-15 seconds someone activates their heat mechanic.   6. Rage- tekken 7 had this as well. But this game shows how the developers do not understand what tekken 5 Dr was all about. (their best game). In the final moments of tekken 7, the reason the final matches were so  slow was because rage, rage drive, and rage arts were too powerful. Rage is a passive given to a fighter when their health is low, their damage increases by 10%. Rage drive is basically a super from street fighter. Rage arts are stronger normal moves that do more damage and stun the opponent.  Back to the point- The two fighters realized that rage was so beneficial that they would purposefully not hit each other. The devs tried to attack this problem in Tekken 8. However, their fix was to help the aggressive player engage by using a heat smash which is not fun for either player, (the defender has to block, the attacker looks at a cutscene). If rage was not on the table the matches would be faster. If rage was not on the table, the comebacks would be way cooler because knowing the person in rage gets a flat 10% increase in damage is not as cool as being equal to your opponent and beating him with less health.   Pros When the effects are off, its pretty cool to see bryan, dragunov, and kazuya fight.

I feel compelled to write my first game review ever on Steam because there are so many negative reviews, but I think this game is pretty awesome. Maybe I like it because I'm not "normal"?  [h2] My background - Old School Gamer [/h2] I'm an old school gamer, most of my fighting game experience was in the arcades playing Tekken 2, Tekken 3, and TTT, like a million years ago. I've never played Tekken 5, 6, 7 or TTT2. I played a tiny bit of T4 on PS2.  I was fairly competitive in the arcades. Me and my buddy would usually clear out whichever arcade we went to. I know, that's local and I'm sure there places I'd get schooled but hey I was pretty good in my home town. My point is I didn't super suck and I'm not a button masher.  I was pleasantly surprised to find all of my old school Tekken skill pretty much directly worked as soon as I started Tekken 8, even without understanding "heat" or "rage". Did I get my butt handed to me several times? Yes I did. I still enjoyed it. I'm learning the new stuff and getting better.  [h2] Yeah a lot of offense and harder to punish, that's fine [/h2] As everyone complains about, yes this game rewards offense. I think that's fine. Also, I like the how the devs beefed up the down parry and added the high parry (back+1+2) to every character. This seems to pretty directly stop predictable offense. I'm still learning though... Leroy destroys me every game, which is fine.  When I first saw the "special" input mode I laughed in disbelief and thought the game was broken. This mode lets players mash one button and perform fairly long combos. But after playing online I found that most people playing with mode were pretty bad and I would be able to beat them. So, meh, whatever. I'm glad people can smash buttons and do something cool. It does not bother me.  I suppose all fighting games were "broken" back in the day. I remember people complaining about Eddy Gordo in T2 (or was it T3?). A true button mashing character. People would smash the kicks and win. Although once you learn his patterns you could super punish him. Today's button mashers are a bit more complex but seems like the same ideas still work. Learn their mashing and punish them.  I'll admit there are a lot of high/low mix-ups combos for like every character. Once they start laying into you, even if blocking, it is harder to punish than back in the day. Still, I find if I can control the game in neutral.  [h2] Dude, it's good, seriously [/h2] Maybe I'll change my review later to say I hate it, but for now I'm enjoying playing Tekken again. If you just want to play Tekken, this will probably have the biggest player base. I was going to pick Tekken 7 because of all the negativity, but I gave T8 a chance and don't regret it in the slightest.

As a casual player, I do like how some of the mechanics of Tekken were made easier to understand and use with this release. From what I've seen with T7, the game does play drastically different so I can see how some more experienced players might be dissatisfied from the state of the game as-is.   Outside of gameplay, I've always had an interest in this franchise's story. As wacky and nonsensical as it can get, I've always believed that this game has some of the most interesting concepts for fighters on both a visual and narrative level. But lately, it's felt like this game's story no longer has any discernable direction beyond the conflict between the Mishimas. I realize that this isn't new as far as Tekken is concerned but I really thought that things would be different this time, especially with how this and Tekken 7 were marketed on that front.  I have no problem with some characters being more important and/or stronger than others, but I do think it's still possible to have this in a way that respects all characters' stories and developments without making them seem insignificant.  This is why Unforgotten Echoes was the last straw for me. At first, I was excited that we were going to explore the perspectives of characters who hadn't had their chance to become the focus yet, and while I think that that was the case for at least the first half of the expansion, the second half completely obliterates any and all development they go through in the service of a poorly-explained plot twist without allowing them to achieve anything of substance.  I'm happy that Heihachi mains can play their character again, but I think he could have been re-included without making the story suffer. Tekken 7, which did a lot to add depth to his story and motivations, is made completely irrelevant as a result.  The base game's story was good though, it had its flaws but it hit the mark in terms of shifting the status quo and delivered on a conflict that has been brewing for years both in and out of the game.  TLDR: Filthy casual here. I like the gameplay and effort to appeal to players of my skill level as someone who's never been skilled at Tekken but I can empathize with the more skilled players who see this title as unrecognizable from the rest of the series. This game's characters and story has always been the thing getting me to come back, but the latest story DLC has left me dissatisfied with the narrative thus far. I feel as though it didn't do justice to all of the characters it was supposed to highlight, including Heihachi, who despite coming out on top, deserved a more interesting explanation for his return. If you are a newcomer to the series and are interested in gameplay alone, give this title a try. If you are looking for a meaningful development to the game's story, this title is not it.  Might change this review in the future when more story content is released but the thought of having to wait years for a continuation of the story at the point where Unforgotten Echoes leaves it leaves a bad taste in my mouth and has killed my enjoyment of the game for the time being.

The fun I had playing with friends, laughing at each other’s over-the-top moves, made it more than worth it.  That said, hackers are a real issue right now. They're not even subtle — pixel-perfect ducks, low blocks, parries, you name it. It sucks the fun out of online play, and I seriously hope it gets addressed soon.  Overall, Tekken 8 is beginner-friendly and still a blast for newcomers. But if you’re going in with a competitive mindset, be mentally prepared for a fair bit of frustration.

Oh, man.  I could write a full, genuine review, on exactly why I can't recommend this game, but honestly: you're not going to read that whole thing.  You wanna know quickly why you should or shouldn't buy this, right?  Well, I'll tell you, but easily-digested short answers will only lead to more questions (or assumptions) on your part.  Still, it's better than nothing, so I'll ***try*** to be as concise as possible from here:  DO NOT BUY  Why?  1. The biggest and most important reason is this: they have completely betrayed everything Tekken built in the games 1-5, betraying the long-term hardcore fans at the same time. 2. If you're brand new to the game, there are other games in the genre which are less technical, faster paced, and whose devs actually listen to their communities 3. If you fall in love with this game, they will inevitably completely change what you love about it in upcoming titles 4. It has become a completely shameless cash-grab.  In all Tekken titles prior to 7, you either had all characters unlocked right away (and as part of the base game's price) OR you could actually play the game to unlock "secret" characters (which was the most fun, especially when some of those characters were genuinely secret/hidden/difficult to unlock).  Now you pay a full game price just to unlock one or two characters and maybe an extra level. 5. The levels in which you fight are so irrelevant that previous versions of the game literally had stages that were just infinite darkness, or an infinite plane of shallow water, featureless "grass", etc.  The stages literally don't matter at all for how the game is played, but they sell you new ones as if they're important.  Disgusting.  I could honestly go on, but that's enough.  I could go *very deep* into the betrayals, but if you're new, you won't care, and if  you're an old fan, you already know.  Suffice it to say, Tekken was one of the greatest games of all time, and starting with Tekken 6, they decided to head in the direction of laziness, exploitation, and dishonour.   All that said, they still have one of the best stories and character development of any fighting game.  It's just not enough.

I recommend giving TEKKEN 8 a shot, but it's not a game for everyone (and I think this unfortunately includes myself as I've come to realize). I was struggling in TEKKEN 7 against players who either mash or knowledge check you into oblivion and TEKKEN 8 ups the ante by doubling down on character gimmicks and player aggression. The addition of the Heat system is a big contributor to this and Season 2 introduced even more safe, homing moves that are plus on block and/or transition into 50/50 mix-ups for a lot of the cast, causing very one-sided gameplay if you don't know what to do in retaliation.  Learning how to pilot a single TEKKEN character is already a big ask for casual players like myself, but learning to defend kind of equals that same effort but for the entire cast so to speak. So if you're not willing to spend a lot of time learning what each character does, let alone the frame data, you're again incentivized to rely on gimmicks and aggressive play to carry you to victory. I say 'again' because the focus on safe but powerful moves and 50/50 mix-ups greatly reduces mind games and often boils down to you just having to guess correctly, making it less rewarding to learn defense at all. Kind of antithetical to the big thing a "3D" fighting game enables—stronger defense because you're now able to sidestep moves.  This ties in to my biggest gripe with the game and online play specifically. The inherent complexity of a TEKKEN game combined with the current vision for TEKKEN 8 made ranked matchmaking a nightmare for a guy like me. I don't like playing aggressively, it's the reason I gravitate towards characters like Bryan, Lee, or even Paul (though the unique identity of Lee and Bryan specifically have been kind of lost at this point). I also don't like to rely on overpowered moves too much because it's boring and it makes me feel like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ playing the game. This puts me at a huge disadvantage, and I'll be forever stuck in purple ranks as a result. I'm also just not very good at the game period.  Most people will do whatever they think they gotta do to get the W, and this often results in a frustrating and overwhelming experience for me personally. Put more simply, there's just so much stuff you have to deal with when you're trying to play defensively and look for openings. Don't get counter-hit, don't get launched, watch out for grabs, don't press into plus moves, pull back when your opponent enters Heat, don't get baited into a rage art, be mindful of power-crushing and evasive moves, and yeah correctly guess a 50/50 every 5 seconds.  I want to play defensively and land CH launchers all day but I don't want to spend hours labbing the cast in order to do so more effectively. This puts me at an impasse, so I've put the game to rest for now feeling like the franchise isn't for me after all, especially after Season 2 of TEKKEN 8.   I realize this review sounds very negative but a lot of that has to do with me and not the game per se so I'm still going to recommend it. It's got a lot of potential to be the best TEKKEN game ever made in 20 years. I really want this game to be great actually, because it can be highly addictive and immensely rewarding when the matches are fun. The series has given me some of the most intense moments I've ever experienced playing a video game. Also, BANDAI NAMCO are coming out with new updates more frequently, and it looks like they're slowly making progress in the right direction. Who knows, maybe I'll pick it up again after a few balance patches.

Longtime casual player here since Tekken 2.  I took a break from from Tekken during Tekken 6 and jumped in a couple years after Tekken 7 launched and found it to be too technical to really get stuck into after so much time away. Tekken 8 gets announced with great new features and an attack forward focus, which sounded great! However after playing it for a year and a bit, I don't really get the direction the game is going in. It showed a lot of promise in the beginning by being a bit faster paced and requiring more intuitive thinking but the longer I play, the less the game delivers on intuitive, quick and adaptive thinking and rather favours a flow chart approach based on calculated chance.  I was pretty content with the game up until the Season 2 adjustments started and since then it's just thrown the whole game off balance. I get that there are future fixes scheduled in an attempt to rectify this but I can't help but feel the devs have dropped the ball massively here. Playing Tekken online used to be a very frustrating but super rewarding experience when you manage unlock a tricky opponent. With more opponents banking on such formulaic approaches to playing, it removes the rewarding aspect entirely and just becomes frustrating playing against people who lean into this style of play and uninspiring because the characters lose all their uniqueness and flair when you see the same 5 moves and 85-100+ damage combo.  Sure, the devs are working on patches but it's such a shame with how it's started - that's a whole year of Tekken 8 off to an awful start.  - Defence isn't valued or rewarded and sidestepping is buffed unnecessarily to compensate which doesn't make sense because you rarely have an option besides hard reading your opponent's next move - Some iconic and longstanding moves have been removed - Max combo chains and thus max combo damage has increased (and we know that because it's displayed on screen now - why exactly?) - Anna can inflict a temporary chip damage increase on her opponent (??!) - Even down to the ungodly AI ghost arena they've clumsily placed in the Fight Lounge where there used to be a fountain (I get that the fountain was purely aesthetic and served no function but from a design perspective, what the hell is an arena doing there?!) - The AI ghost mode itself, I understand that machine learning takes time but I'm not really seeing the benefit here. The ghosts still don't play like actual people so fighting them serves what purpose exactly? Literally none of these features are things that the core fanbase have asked for en masse, nor are they responding well to them, so why continue as though the opinions of the people paying money to play this game don't matter at all?!  I'm all for moving the series forward but the way Tekken 8 devs promised so much, delivered only some of it due to subpar execution and then slowly started taking what they did deliver away from players is just wild to me. I'm going to begrudgingly continue playing this game for now in the hope that future patches do some good, but devs, please, just make this game balanced in the way it plays and how it caters to new and existing players and don't make such drastic changes to core features of the game between seasons unless it's to actually fix something. You must have so much game data collected from every single match played in game to do your due diligence and understand why people are enjoying this game less and less and work towards avoiding it in future decisions.

If you are a casual player, Tekken 8 is a fantastic game and you definitely get your money's worth. It has arguably the best story mode in a Tekken game, CGI cutscene endings for every character, Arcade Quest to help learn the game, a Tekken Lounge to meet other players, Tekken Ball and a solid customization system. The cast is large and diverse with a variety of different fighting styles to play around with and it's easy to find a character you like.  The problem arises once you step into ranked and run into the abomination that is other ranked players. With the season 2 update, the game's balance was thrown completely off as almost every character received buffs and new moves, some of which were broken and spammable and others which covered up characters' unique weaknesses. Forced mix-ups and 50/50s became commonplace, with no counter-play except to take a guess. The devs have recognized the issue and are slowly taking steps to fix it, but they are taking their sweet time.   Some of the glaring issues have been fixed, but problems still remain. The core issue is the direction that the game directors and balancing team are pushing this game in. They are replacing the calculated & nuanced gameplay and interesting mind-games that Tekken is known for in favor of mindless aggression and forced 50/50 situations. Unfortunately, I don't think that this part of the game will change substantially.  However, this is mostly an issue for higher level players, others may not notice a difference.  Therefore, there is a large disconnect between the opinion of a casual vs. a dedicated player on this game. If I could give a mixed review I would, but I think that, since the game is worth the time and money for the average player, it is enough to justify a positive review.

Tekken 8 is a Tekken game not meant for Tekken players.  Where past Tekken titles rewarded players for mastering complex combo and chain throw combinations,Tekken 8 continues to simplify move inputs for casuals and newcomers alike by reducing their execution down to just one button - or stringed together instantly on autopilot while using Tekken 8's combo assist feature.  Keeping a safe distance or being mindful of a player's surroundings during matches are no longer needed as Tekken 8's new new 'Heat Engine' creates inescapable cutscenes that send players dashing across the screen; allowing players to string together combos with little thought required.    Just about every character features a glut of overpowered, unbalanced or just downright broken moves at their disposal; allowing matches to be ended in a matter of seconds.  Fans of paying for DLC skins in Fortnite will feel right at home with Tekken 8's new predatory Tekken Shop feature; a built-in store that charges real money to purchase customizable items, events and avatars all locked behind a paywall. The price for these edit packs ranges from an average of $6 a piece with more customization items on the way.    PRO's: -------------------- - Beautiful graphics; the best the series has looked to date.  - Interactive, multi-tiered stages.   - Expansive roster of newcomers and series favourites.  - Plenty of offline and online modes to keep players busy.   - The classic Tekken Ball mode is back.   - Photo Mode allows players to freeze frames, rotate angles and apply a wealth    of customization during matches.  - Fully supported by the modding community, with an ever-growing number of   free-to-download skins, level redesigns and gameplay add-ons.   - The ability to download Ghosts which use A.I. to simulate the behaviour of real-life players. - Players can also simulate CPU vs CPU matches using their own Ghost's play data.     CON's: ---------------------------- - Horribly unbalanced fight engine with many overpowered attacks and combos   that plague the entire roster.  - Heat Engine - a new gameplay addition that dumbs down matches with inescapable   cutscenes and move tracking. With Heat moves, players don't have to worry about   distance getting in the way of stringing together combos.  - A built-in store called the Tekken Shop; which uses predatory micro-transaction   that charge players real money for a large number of items all locked behind   a paywall.    - Classic modes such as Team Battle, Survival and Time Attack modes are nowhere to   be found.   - While the Ghosts in Tekken 8 replicate the playstyle of human players, the difficulty   of the regular CPU is too easy, even on the harder difficulty settings.

I have played this game over 200+ hours not including steam.   I had fun for the first 10-20 hours of the game because it did feel like "beginner friendly". However that's where the positives end. T  This game has gotten so bad that it's not worth it's price tag or your time.  Some general qualms that I have:  - Poor Balancing - Poor Connections - Ranked System is not functional (Season 1 and 2) - Cheaters are streaming while they are cheating (no, they won't get banned) - Customizing options are very bare bones - Punches and hits sometimes connect, but most times they won't because of random bugs - Reporting system doesn't work - JIN  I have only one giant issue with the game and that IT IS WASTING YOUR TIME MORE THAN IT SHOULD. Just to give you some perspective of how bad the game has gotten.   I've recorded my gameplay for 10 hours straight (wanted to see how I can improve) and aprox. 4-5 hours out of those were cutscenes and combos by the opponent.  I understand combos need to exist, but sitting for 30 seconds waiting and asking "when do I get to continue playing" EVERY. SINGLE. ROUND. is not fun nor should it cost 80$.  If you want a smaller example, any fight may have 3-5 rounds all of them 60sec each.  If you miss a punch and the opponent manages to punish your mistake, YOU WILL SIT THERE AND LOOK AT THE CUTSCENE/COMBO FOR 20-30 SECONDS WHILE THE OPPONENT DOES A 15 HIT COMBO. Doesn't matter what character you are playing vs, IF YOU MESS UP ONE TIME you will sit and look at the pretty lights for 30 sec. The more annoying part of this, is that skill is proportional to how long the combo is.  If someone has mastered a character that means the longer the combos are going to be, which means you get to sit and watch the pretty lights longer.  Let me say, I don't mind jugling and combos (every fighting game has them), I have a problem with not playing 50% of the time for the game I paid 80$ for.  If you enjoy watching a fighting movie, but you also get to interact with it once in a while, THIS IS THE GAME FOR YOU.   Otherwise, do not buy this,   EDIT: It's been over 2 Months and the game is in the same state as it was before. This should give you an idea of how broken this game is. This game genuinely started off fun and much less overwhelming than other Tekken titles, excellent UI, great slew of features, beautiful graphics compared to Tekken 8, core of the game remains the same, albeit with the addition of the heat system. I never played other Tekkens competitively before, so I just took what I got at face value and had great fun, though I did feel as I played more that the heat system breaks up the flow of the fight too much, that so many moves are very spammable and incredibly difficult to counter without hard reads, movement that is less emphasized as all the systems push you towards offense more and more.  As I played more I agreed that the game needs to move away from the excess offense and reward good defense more - tone down many moves, such as heat engaging power crushes. Tone down chip damage, tone down the advantages characters get in heat, buff sidesteps and reward good fundamentals with opportunities for whiff punishes and block punishes.  But that is not what the game devs did - in season 2 they have added even more BS that takes away any joy, fun or complexity from the game. Defense is not possible to play well because no human can react to so many threats with very specific answers - and if you guess wrong, you will eat a huge punish.  I main Reina, and she also got more ways to enter her stances, her already amazing offense got amped up for no reason.   This game is confused in its vision and doesn't know what it wants to do. The gamedevs respond to criticism with blocking, and telling the players they are stupid and should how to play.   I have NEVER seen such a negative response to a patch or a game, this feels like post-release Street Fighter 5... except SF5 got better over time.  Tekken 8 got worse with time. Tekken 8 has given me a wonderful community within locals, a thriving competitive scene, and has introduced me to a lot of people I consider close friends. My commitment to this game since the start made me grind and compete more than any other game I have before. However, the increased instability in games due to the metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of + on block into mix up situations and the loss of identity among the cast has dramatically ruined the integrity of this game.  The top players will continue to be the best as they've ingrained fundamentals over years, but all of this makes the intermediate to low upper tier player particularly miserable. At the end of the day, the most skilled player will USUALLY win, but the increased instability has made that division fuzzier. While season 2 follows the same game design through line as season 1, season 1's ability for skill expression from unique characters and their pilots was clearly higher than it is now.  Outside of standard critique of season 2, there are a lot of good QoL features added. Online practice has allowed me to introduce concepts to completely new players in a less stressful environment. Practice settings have been incredible for drills and practice. The current ranked system leaves a lot to be desired however, and feels like rewarding than the admittedly still flawed system in season 1.

When Tekken 8 first released I've had a lot of fun. No other fighting game makes a constant exchange of blows while dancing around the opponent as fun for me as this game does. Compared to Tekken 7 things such as graphics/netcode/load times have been improved. We've got interesting gameplay changes and new characters/features. But in time the game started showing its problems, culminating in Season 2 update. Still, let's start from the beginning.  Netcode finally has been made good enough so that I don't feel like I'm messing up due to the input delay. Though it's still far away from games like Skullgirls or Guilty Gears Strive which have the best netcodes I've had a chance to play with.  Gameplay wise the biggest new thing has been the Heat System making you temporarily more powerful. Which is a lot of fun - at least on paper, more on that later.  Unfortunately, Rage Arts are still in the game and they're neither satisfying to land or fun to watch more than once.  The new feature that I've loved and feel like should be a new standard for fighting games is the interactive replay system. You're now able to simply take control of your character during replays and try out things to see how to play better next time. This is great as in the past you'd have to rewatch the replays, then figure out which move the opponent used, then manually setup the same situation in the training mode.   Good stuff! But this is where our honeymoon period ends.  At some point micro-transactions and battle pass have been added to the game - they have not been mentioned before the game's release. You can't unlock all of the fun costumes by just playing the game anymore.  At some point DLC characters have been released just to render the interactive replay system useless for them as you can't even control YOUR OWN character during the replays.  At some point you realise that the game wants you to be aggressive all the time which is exacerbated by the Heat System. It's best to rush down and make your opponent guess your next move with 50/50 mixups till they die. Good defence is not rewarded.  And finally. Patch 2.0 - aka Season 2 happened. Which flipped the game on its head, tuned the aggression up to the extreme and changed some the characters completely.  This is the first time I'm seeing such a terrible patch. It feels like it has been made by somebody who has no idea what they're doing and what the players of their game want. The developers have noticed the players' backlash since then as we got an emergency patch 2.00.02 a while ago. But this is only one step forward after the previous 100 steps back. So realistically, we're looking at months that it will take to fix a mess this game has become.  Thus, sadly, as the game stands now I can NOT recommend it at all. Just play anything else, seriously.

I really like this game.  This review is focused mostly on the community aspects of tekken as a fighting game since I think that has become more relevant as of recent, but I also touch on what constitutes tekken 8's identity as of now.  People have recently started showing how much they'd rather not play whatever mess that became of the game after the season 2 changes, these changes not only included a couple of game breaking bugs for certain characters that certainly, evidently did not motivate people to keep playing (these have been fixed) but also large amounts of changes that served to dumb down and/or homogenize many of the cast effectively turning tekken 8's characters into more of what previous titles strayed far from, and for good reason: a HIGHLY aggressive cast with "stance" oriented 50/50 mixups strewn all throughout their movelists. I hear this is not too unlike how games such as Mortal Kombat operate- the difference being how tekken players never expected nor asked for these radical changes to the game.   This however met much controversy and the developers seem to now be attempting a "repair" of what the community saw as frankly stated "broken" while I presume still pertaining to much of tekken 8's aggressive but rewarding identity. As to whether this trend in changes will continue, and whether the developers will lean too heavily into the "aggression" yet again I am as uncertain as could be since the developers have shown little understanding with the higher concepts of what historically has been attractive about the game (namely defensive strategy). - but I am hopeful for what is to come because I truthfully don't believe the game could ever be beyond repair.  If you have ever played a previous title of the game I want you to recognize that the game might be a bit on the "spammy" side of things- it might get better, it might not.  To those that haven't and don't necessarily feel the need to be best, I think there is plenty of fun and learning to be had experiencing this iteration of tekken and I would say the same about the game even during it's rough stages. Those willing to get good, might want to pertain to a flexible, problem-solving mindset above all else, many characters have multiple complex mix ups that they might derive high rewards from and your "labbing" sessions per character might be a tad more frequent than in most fighting games.  It is a game where information and knowledge often is key.  The many characters range from anywhere between difficult and easy, specialized and multifaceted. There is definitely at least ONE character among the 32 in the base roster that might interest you, presuming the general aesthetic and playstyle of the game overall already appeals to you.  Above all else and obvious to some: It is a game and any sane man or woman would tell you to find enjoyment and entertainment in what you choose to play rather than how some choose to play particularly fighting games where they neurotically force themselves and find strife with how the game is, and find little to no enjoyment and much more negativity. I urge you not to be like that- We are all responsible for our own happiness.  This frankly mentally-ill, try-hard mindset is rampant in the fighting game community as a whole and it is important to be aware of, at times I am no exception. I would ask of you to not let this intimidate you and thus prevent you from playing what I consider, and probably always will, a fantastic game with much depth and a, I hope, mostly-parted, well-minded, welcoming community.  Good luck, tekken-player or not.  Sidenote- The many haters of the season 2 changes, and specifically those that directly targeted the developers and creators with threats and other belligerent comments should be ashamed and I as well as many others would rather you not be a part of this community, or that you at least stay silent in the future. I fashion myself as a fan of Tekken. I've owned and played every game in the franchise since Tekken Tag on the PS2. I put 350 hours (give or take) into Tekken 7 on the PS4, and I figured I'd be locked in on T8 when it released. I bought T8 on release day on PS5 and immediately didn't like it. It felt too simplified. Heat, chip damage, grey health... all of these things didn't feel very "Tekken" to me. Tekken is about movement, spacing, poking, and baiting a whiff before punishing with big damage. T8, meanwhile, seems to be more focused on aggression and constant pressing.  I recently migrated my Tekken 8 gameplay to PC with the launch of Season 2, and while i'm not giving a bad review because of Season 2 specifically (as basically everybody has said their piece on why it's bad), I do want it to be known that this game, Tekken 8, is not for anybody. Is it for casuals? No. Casuals only want cool characters, cool stages, and tons of offline modes. They don't really understand the functional difference between, say, Law in T7 and Law in T8. He's just Law to them. Is it for competitors? No. Competitors (the ones not being cut checks by Bandai Namco), since day one, have spoken endlessly about Tekken 8's move towards aggression and spectacle over more classic methods of play.  Tekken 8 is, for all intents and purposes, a spectator sport. It's as loud, flashy, and insane as it is to try and generate hype in an attention economy. Namco isn't competing with Capcom, SNK, or SEGA. They're competing with TikTok, with Fortnite, with your cell phone, with anything else you could be doing and spending microtransaction money on. I don't want the visual equivalent of a nuclear bomb going off while I perform a high damage wall-splat combo. I just want Tekken. Good, old-fashioned, defense-based Tekken. And this? This isn't that.

The recent 3.02.00 update made the game feel a little more bearable to play compared to the previous Season 2 iteration of the game. There are still glaring issues with certain characters being super over-tuned like Lidia and the amount of stance transitions into stance transitions lie Victor but I'll list down the more positive changes.  - Heat launching moves being almost removed from the faster buttons (Law's 1,1,1) but kept within the slower heavy hitting buttons that are above 15f. - Lateral Movement being more viable than before with the indirect nerfs and buffs towards both movement and character hit-boxes and hurt-boxes. - Heat specific moves costing a significant amount of heat gauge so you're less in a position of having to eat those powerful heat mix and have more breathing room while the enemy is in heat.  I think the game is going a step towards the right direction for the looks of things, not to mention the Yuujiro Hanma guest character, but I am also not too hopeful until they address some of the glaring over-tuned characters. The game is more rewarding towards the offenders and being able to push out more buttons which is Tekken 8's core idea of how they want to approach the game but I also hope that they should be able to tone it down a bit while also not making it feel very stuffy to play as a defender.

Gave the game a bad review in season 2, but I decided to try this game again after the 2nd emergency patch, and I am sad to say this game is now EVEN WORSE! I put 20 more hours into the game just to give as fair an assessment as possible, and I completely agree with all the other players who are trashing this game in the reviews.  I have been a gamer for almost 30 years, and I never felt like a game robbed me of my time the way Season 2 did. I literally wanted to make something of myself after playing this game, I swear to god! I went outside, touched all of the f****ing grass after playing Season 2.  This is easily the worst major fighting game release in decades. I'm not just some old head who hates change, either. Season 1 of Tekken 8 had it's problems, but it was still a fantastic game. This is not.   You can play ranked right now, and all you go up against is players spamming heavy, plus-framed mids with tracking, and all you can do is sit there and block until you get pressed to a wall. EVERYTHING IS PLUS ON BLOCK, with no cool down, and even if your opponent messes up and gives you frame advantage, you have to guess if they are going for a low, or mid, with a 50/50 chance you might guess it wrong before you continue to get pressed. In other words, you're guessing your way through every round, and your're fishing for counter-hit like you're playing a slot machine!  As soon as you hit purple ranks, all you are going to see online is LAUNCH, LAUNCH, LAUNCH, and LAUNCH! Even if you get a trade, you still get launched, and your opponent still gets frame advantage. You can't even punish a launch attempt, because they are mostly always plus on block. You can't side-step most of them, because the Season 2 moves gave them tracking, meaning they can hit side-walking players. The only viable strategy is to 1, 1+2  over and over again in the hope that you might interrupt the opponent's pressure, since the Season 2 update turned blocking into a frame-trap. The defensive style is completely dead now, and the only thing you can do to be competitive in this game is spam!  Every online set will go to whoever is mashing the controller the hardest. If you're not hate-f****ing your controller into the ground at the start of every round, you're never going to get out of Ganryu.  Gone are the days of skillful, tactical gameplay, and in are the brain-dead, pressure-into-launch, launch-into mix up gameplay that always goes to Dragunov and Jun players every time. All the high-skill gameplay with zoning, side-stepping, and solid defense that put Tekken 7 on the map is gone, and replaced with a gameplay style akin to Marvel Versus Capcom arcade from 1998.  There are so many 50/50s, the game feels like I'm playing a slot machine, rather than actually fighting someone. You're going to guess wrong half the time, get launched, and end up watching a mix-up montage, that lasts as long as my *** damn lunch break at my job! I could file my taxes and knit a sweater in the time it takes for these wall-carry mix-ups to finish! I'm sure my opponent is feeling the same way, when I'm playing Hwaorang, and it takes like 72 years for me to finish my floor-break mixup with heat smash! That MF probably went grocery shopping in the time it took me to get that over with, only for all that to only eat 30% my opponent's health bar!  Season 2 is a disaster, even after the Emergency patch. I almost can't believe Namco Bandai screwed up this badly.

TEKKEN 8  A love letter.  I ended up going to the party anyway, even though I worked a 10 hour shift. I don’t even play these kinds of games, but I really should go. A couple introduces themselves. I stumble past, nearly ignoring them by accident. Zombified by life, I am exhausted, and burnt out.  I try socializing, in a different room, but nothing sticks. I plant myself next to them with a drink in hand. I’ve been a lifelong gamer. I’ve tried to play Fighters before- Honestly, I don’t really think I even like them. One of them is playing a game by herself in a practice mode- with numbers, information, and crazy looking data sprawling across the screen. She’s destroying some poor ultra-hard CPU. I don’t know what I’m looking at, but it’s… incredible to witness. She must know what she’s doing.  I finally decide to make some small talk. “If you could explain Fighting games to someone who has never played them before… what would you tell them?”  She sheepishly points to the different buttons and explains their functions. One one two. Shows simple strings and combos most characters have. Explains basics to me in a simple way, but enough to get me started.   I didn’t touch alcohol for the rest of the night. What started as a “I’ll maybe show up for a little while” turned into a night-long session. The girl and her partner, who both seemed quiet and shy at first, smiling ear to ear, laughing with everyone towards the end of the night. We’ve become fast friends and I would take a bullet for them.   I return home and boot Super Smash Bros. “That 'Kazuya' guy was in there… wasn’t he?” My mind is COMPLETELY blown. He’s a TEKKEN character- not a Smash character!! Little did I know how much this night would blow my entire gaming experience wide open.  I found myself so suddenly, and blissfully addicted.   A whole community of new friends suddenly emerged. By the next day, I was playing Tekken 8 every single night, with groups I met at that party- Labbing with them, sharing in this new excitement of the wonderful mechanics of Tekken.   Watching people in the lounge- Friends, groups, clans gathering of all different skill levels to watch each other’s battles, talk strategies, mentor, cheer each other on,  learning more about this game they love.  I’ve made so many friendly acquaintances by playing with others that just want to play, too. The amount of clips I have with sounds of lighthearted cackling while just generally having fun messing around brings such a warm healing touch to my soul. I’ve also been so lucky as for strangers to help out in the online practice modes, too. People want you to learn, because they want you to play. Voluntarily, they will work with you to get better, simply so they can get better, with complete strangers, no less, that simply share a passion for these chess-like mind games, an exploration of mechanics and how far they can be pushed. I started keeping notes in a leather bound notebook I keep by my desk of things people have taught me in passing.   This community LOVES Tekken.  And so do I.   - - -   At the same time, I have never, EVER met a community that hates its game as much as Tekken. I don't think any game is flawless, but the community online is all crickets when they're having fun, because they're too roped up in playing.   There are mechanics that are frustrating that, to fight it, simply may need to learn how to deal with. The game's lab tools are SO good, but half of the complainers in these reviews don't even try to use them. Game is fun, but the company you choose to engage with matters as well. This is true for any competitive game.   Anyways final thoughts, Kazuya is literally so hot he is my husband, fighting games are funny, and y'all if you hate the game so much then stop playing it, lmfao.   - - -  [⇒★⇓⇘+2]

I can see players that would love that, though. I recently started playing King and his changes make it so that I can basically force anyone into a casino situation with no real options of escape.  The design philosophy behind Heihachi from season 1 was most excellent. The flaws of the character made you have to excel in other areas and that used to be true for most characters. I'm doing my part and writing a negative review.  I am pretty new to Tekken, as this is the first Tekken game I have ever owned. The devs promised that they'd add more defensive options to counter the over-aggressive fighting system where the only counter to a damaging blow is to throw your own damaging blow and hope yours wins the coin toss. The devs decided that the best defense is more offense, and these negative reviews for season two's release are the predictable fallout.   I main Lee, so I have already been having a hard time surviving online match-ups against the rest of the roster because they are a lot more accessible to new players. One of the only accessible things I had going for me as a beginner was Hitman style (it scares off beginner opponents because it has a lot of defensive capabilities), but the devs nerfed it by making the 1, 1, 1 a heat activator and taking it away from the uf3+4. Now I have to wait for an opponent to get within range of my jab to hit them with a heat combo instead of being able to reach them with the uf3+4 kick from a further distance. I now run a much bigger risk of my opponent landing a hit than being able to land that jab on them. Lee's lows also seem nerfed, but I can't really explain what they did to them that feels slower. All I know is that doing the silver tail move from a crouched position is a lot harder to successfully input now.  During season one, I put about 50 hours into training mode as Lee. I know about 75% of his moves now and when to use them. Despite this, I am still stuck at warrior rank because of the insane amount of reach and damage that the S-tier characters have. My best strategic move usage is no match for the average Eddy Gordo, Clive, Azucena, Hwoarang, or Victor masher.  The devs try to balance the game so that everyone can pick their favorite character and still have a fighting chance, but it seems that the rift between the low tiers and the high tiers just grew twice as big. I really like Lee Chaolan as a character and I don't want to play any other character because of the time (and customization outfits) I have invested in him so far, so I probably won't be playing Tekken 8 for a while until they give him back some of his identity.

Unfortunately, the game is not in a playable state for anyone right now.  The development and balance team clearly thought they were doing the right thing for the "silent majority" and think that they will enjoy whatever slop they throw at them.  Tekken players continue playing Tekken because there is so much to learn. I started playing in 2022 and I was still learning new stuff everyday. But it seems the intent of Bandai Namco is to simplify the game by removing lasting and appreciated mechanics, such as the get-up system or the spike setups. They added homing, mid, plus on block moves to almost all characters so whatever buffs they added to sidestepping becomes virtually useless.  It still is possible to learn the matchups and perform well when you possess the knowledge of what strings to duck, how minus is the move you just blocked. But with all of the changes and new options every character has, they can play in such a way that they never have to take a risk anymore. Homing mid covers all defense and starts offense, then you need to guess an option from unreactable and unreadable stances. Rinse and repeat. These move are often running moves or projectiles, making spacing compeletely useless or impossible to whiff punish since they will be so far away.  This reviewbombing is not about veterans wanting the game to stay the exact same. It wouldn't have reached such numbers. Casuals are not having fun with the game. Intermediate are not having fun with the games. Pro players are reconsidering their career. This is how bad this patch impacted the game.  Tekken is such a special game in my heart and was the only fighting game I truly connected with and wanted to keep getting better and play as long as my hands would allow me to. I love a lot of characters, I love the story, and overall I love the feel of a 3D fighting game. But this is simply Soul Calibur 7 with a Tekken skin. Everything that made me fall in love with the game is almost gone.   The identity of my main, Lee Chaolan, has been reduced to ashes. He used to be defined by his wall carry. Now every character can do wall-to-wall combos. His evasiveness, including evading mids, is gone. D2 is completely useless now. His excellent counter hit game has been nerfed in damage. Lee was defined by being horrible at offense but was backed by having a near-perfect defensive kit. Now everything is jumbled. He still has great defense tools but they absolutely do not complement the new heat moves. What do i do when i'm +8 in Hitman after my D1+2 ? I have no 50/50 options worth going for since LEE IS NOT AN OFFENSIVE CHARACTER TO BEGIN WITH. And since they couldn't stop there, they nerfed the damage and wall carry potential of WS2,3. What did we get in return ? a plus on block heat mid, and a homing neutral on block mid (which is a recycled animation from T7). Great. Just Excerrent as the man would say. Tekken 8 is a flawed fighting game that leans into the modern formula with all of its weight. There is an abundance of offensive tools. Lots of plus frames, high damage combos, 50/50 mix-up situations and the core system mechanics heavily favour this play-style. Unfortunately not every player can fit into that play-style and it has become, in its most recent update, a slot machine but the result always yields 777 on the damage counter. With a few honest tweaks this game can achieve the greatness it strives to reach.  What Tekken 8 Does Well: +Comprehensive and interactive tutorial in the form of Arcade Quest. You will create an avatar (which you will also use in the games online modes) to engage in a short story mode (approx. 3 hours in length) where you simulate going to local tournaments and as the story progresses you will learn the different layers to Tekken 8.  +Fully in-depth Training Mode. Complete with everything you'd expect from a fighting game with some modern era tweaks, such as Punishment Training. Frame data, combo trials, replay takeover, reset states, wake-ups, stage interactions. It's all there. You'd be hard pressed to find something this games training mode genuinely lacks. Tekken 8 gives you the tools and labbing has never been more fun for me personally.  +Ghost Mode. Another modern addition that enhances player experience. I personally used this in tandem with training mode almost exclusively for 9 months before regularly fighting my friends or playing opponents online. It takes the stress of learning out of the equation while not holding your hand (too tightly mind you) as a CPU would.  +Customisation is back and while its a step down from other games before it namely Tekken 7 and Soulcalibur 6, it does have pretty fun options. You can make almost anything and most customs encountered online are also in good taste. I have literally seen thousands of customs in this game. It definitely allows creative minds to flourish. But there is 100% room for improvement.  +Roster and DLC are quite good. I don't have too much to say about this one. I fortunately have all of my mains already available, though my main Lidia should have been on the launch roster. Coming from Soulcalibur I never cared about Bamco showing all of the DLC at once, because they have never done it like that. Modern sensibilities and economics dictate that more players want to know who exactly they are getting in each season so I understand players now wanting a shift from how Bamco does reveals. I think their current model of at least telling us if the character is returning, new, or guest is a fair middle ground. Bamco also said they would revisit this strategy pending more and more people asking for open reveals. Very fair.  +Music, the game launched with a very catchy OST of its own but also with a complete jukebox of music from the previous games. I especially like that if they use music from an older game like they did with the reveal of Anna Williams, I can just go and find that. I do mostly play with music off though, to help my concentration. Can't say too much here, but I think music is the least of anyones worries.  +Lots of player expression with titles, artwork, frames, banners, etc. +Lots of single player content.  Things Tekken 8 can work on: -Netcode can be shaky especially if one player is wired and one is playing on wifi. In fact, about 4 months after the games launch it has rejected all LAN cables I have tried to use. I'm not an elitist tho and will play with pretty much anyone. Netcode is usually part of the games skeleton and any changes to this framework is difficult to improve without disrupting the user experience. I get it. It's serviceable and way better than pre-covid titles. But it does leave more to be desired when you look at the rollback of other modern fighting games.  -The games core mechanic "HEAT" can feel overbearing in the sense that there is not much counterplay to it. You take increased damage off of Heat specific attacks, if you block an attack during Heat you will take chip damage, Heat dashes will leave you at disadvantage and will put you in a guess for game situation in many scenarios, Heat Smashes are "Level 1 type Supers" that will deal respectable damage if they connect, if they are blocked they will deal a decent amount of chip and will leave the defender at disadvantage and in yet another guess for game scenario. There just aren't enough defensive options. Game can feel like Street Fighter: Oops All Cammy's Edition sometimes. Heat in general I do not mind but it can use tweaks.  -Way too many moves give you plus frames. This makes it so that the game just plays like "Whoever Hits First WINS". There is not much room for neutral based gameplay because you will likely win neutral after your first interaction and won't relinquish it until you yourself make a mistake in your own gameplan. It can be very boring. And while I don't think combos are "too long" per se, I can understand the sentiment where the round ended quickly based off of two interactions "in neutral".  Overall I would rate Tekken 8 an 9/10. I thoroughly enjoy the game and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys fighting games. But I do want to make known that the game has its issues. Those issues aren't insurmountable and I do think the dev team will ultimately make the changes the game needs. I say this as a person who plays nearly everyday, with anyone, at any level and even in my local scene. Not as an emotional bot who is vocalising what a doomtuber or twitterhead told them to think. At the end of the day I do believe EVERYONE wants Tekken to succeed. I write this review mostly to catalog my own thoughts and encourage others to try the game and make their own judgements.

I’ve never felt the need to post a review before, but this time I just can’t stay silent. What’s happened with this game is honestly mind-blowing. It’s hard to believe how far off the mark the developers are when it comes to understanding their player base.  With the release of the new season, the direction the game has taken feels completely misguided. Every character now seems to revolve around overly simplified, aggressive playstyles, making it easier than ever to spam mix-ups and overwhelm opponents with little thought. The most shocking part? There’s been no attempt to balance this out with better defensive tools. From the start, fans have been raising concerns about how defense has been gutted compared to earlier titles in the series, and instead of addressing that, this update doubles down on the exact problems the community has been vocal about for months.  What’s even more confusing is that these changes appear to come out of nowhere. There was no real demand—veterans and newcomers alike weren’t asking for more offense or less strategy. The current gameplay encourages reckless aggression and button mashing, which strips away the thoughtful decision-making that Tekken used to be known for.  Tekken used to stand out in the fighting game scene, especially during the height of Tekken 7’s competitive era. It was respected for rewarding strong fundamentals—things like smart movement, neutral game awareness, and defensive precision. Now, those qualities are being pushed aside in favor of flashy, shallow mechanics that make every character feel the same. Even viewer interest in tournaments seems to be dropping, which speaks volumes about how these design choices are affecting the game’s appeal.  What’s most disappointing is that there was still a chance to course-correct. Players were vocal, passionate, and willing to stick with the game through growing pains. But rather than listening, it feels like the developers chose to ignore all the feedback and went all-in on a vision that almost no one supports—all supposedly for the sake of “new player accessibility.” But that logic doesn’t hold up when you consider that Tekken 7 managed to bring in new players and maintain depth, making it one of the most successful entries in the franchise.  At this point, it’s hard not to feel let down. There was so much potential, but it’s being buried under design decisions that go against everything the community loved about the series

After adjustments, the game is in a better place than the initial launch of S2, but I can't help but feel that Tekken 8 isn't steered in the correct direction.  I quite like the sidestep buffs, and somewhat mitigated the overall janky hitboxes of Tekken (Kazuya hitting someone who's laying down with a jump side kick for example, not that sidestep buffs fixes that)  Tekken felt better without moves that powered through getting hit. The tradeoff for doing that big, flashy, kinda slow move that does a lot of damage is supposed to be the risk of getting interrupted or dodged.   Every Heat Activation causing the exact same effect no matter who's using it is incredibly lazy in my opinion. It automatically setting up a longer combo makes the receiver (who will almost assuredly get hit by it near the end of a non-heat combo) have a frustrating time. Heat also is too accessible. It should not be available every round, or at the very least without earning it in some way. I also dislike how it automatically triggers after certain moves instead of via player input.  Rage Arts all being the same input is lazy. Them all hitting around the same area and being uninterruptable is also a bad call. The animations for them are cinematic for maybe the first 3 or 4 times you see them, then they're just time consuming. Rage Arts are also too accessible. I feel it either should be 1 use per match period or you need to earn it somehow, possibly even in exchange for the entire heat meter or something.  The customization lacks options for things such as gloves. Two accessory slots feels too few to do proper customization with that feature.  This is more/less a personal opinion thing, but I really miss when items or outfits would change grab animations or apply silly effects like putting a pie on the opponent's face for the rest of the round.
