I want to start by saying that I genuinely appreciated the direction Tekken 8 pitched, a faster, more aggressive game that encourages forward momentum. That kind of gameplay can be exciting and engaging for spectator and enjoyable for players. I’m not against change, and I’m not asking for a return to older games out of nostalgia.  But the way aggression has been realized in this iteration of the game feels oversimplified. It seems like there’s been a shift toward equating pressure with constant 50/50s, and mindgames with binary guessing rather than layered strategy. Many moves are safe, plus on block, and track movement. Defensive play often feels discouraged or outright invalidated. It’s becoming increasingly difficult to find moments where smart decision-making can turn the tide, because I’m often left with no real options except to guess.  More than that, the system now actively encourages you to press buttons simply because giving up your turn might mean losing the round. Once the opponent is in Heat, or you’re pushed to the wall, it can quickly become a life-or-death situation where 50/50 pressure is relentless, and of course, one wrong guess ends it all. That’s not about strategic aggression, that’s about forcing guesses where interaction used to be. Additionally, playstyles are starting to feel too homogenized. It's harder to express yourself through your character, and easier to fall into flowcharts that feel similar regardless of who you're using or facing.  What made Tekken’s offense work in past titles wasn’t just the pressure, but the subtlety of it. Movement baiting, fuzzy guarding, backdashing sidestepping and yes, sometimes throwing out a dumb option in neutral. All of it gave the game its depth. Offense was earned, not given by default. That’s the part that feels like it’s slipping away.  I’m not opposed to new systems. I’m not asking for mechanics to be deleted. But I do believe that Tekken is strongest when it encourages interaction, when pressure invites response, and when risk and reward are balanced in both directions. Right now, it feels like that balance has shifted too far into offense that plays itself.  Please don’t interpret this as resistance to innovation. It’s a request to preserve the soul of what made Tekken feel unique, a game of skill, knowledge, movement, and thoughtful interaction. I hope future patches can begin to reflect that philosophy again, but until then, I’ll be staying away from the game.

Sad that I'm writing this, there's an absolutely amazing game under all of the mess, but the developers seem set on doubling down on gameplay elements that the community at large do not want.  The emphasis on offense and the oppressiveness of the heat system make this feel more like a game of rock paper scissors than a game of chess.   The addition of offensive moves and buffs that leave few defensive options is bad for play at all levels. If you're a pro, there's less skill expression, and it shrinks the range of playstyles that can be competitive. If you're a beginner, then good f******* luck because it's even harder to learn good defense now than it's ever been. Homing moves everywhere, long range mids that are plus on block, canned stance-transition 50/50s everywhere. Single-minded focus on making offense easy has made it completely un-fun to play against. And when you do fail to defend, it's easier than ever to pull off a combo that lasts 10 seconds or more, which brings the back-and-forth pace of the game to a crawl. It used to be cool to see long juggles because they were difficult and showed some amount of player skill. Now it's trivial. Launcher -> Heat Burst -> Tornado -> Heat Smash/Rage-Art, rinse and repeat. It feels like as a defender you get 1-5 seconds of playtime to guess your opponents stance mixup, and then if you guess wrong you have to sit there for their huge wall-carrying heat-engaging combo to finish, before you get another 1-5 seconds to guess again.  The only sensible option is to mash harder and play more aggressively, but it makes for a very boring game dynamic.   I sincerely hope the devs listen to the community... I want to see the game be as good as I know it could be.   If someone made a mod that removed heat, removed rage, and reverted the characters back to their S1 moveset, you'd have a damn good game. Tekken has been around for 31 years and the core gameplay has stood the test of time. It doesn't need additional gimmicks layered on top to make for an engaging experience.

Focus more on fighting rather than who can abuse system mechanics first. The recent Season 2 patch has made this game into something where you don't need to think, just hit buttons and let the game play itself. When you win, you're angry because of what you had to fight against to scrape up a win. When you lose, you're angry because you don't feel like your opponent earned their win. Namco needs to revert the Season 2 changes and really revise the new mechanics added to T8. Until they do that, I'm done with this game.  [u][b]Pros[/b][/u] [list] [*] Highest quality visuals the series has seen [*] FINALLY Jukebox got added to the PC version [*] After buying the fight pass once, you can earn your "credits" back and use it for the next one [*] An effort was made to add more cosmetics [*] Crossplay finally [*] WiFi indicator for matchmaking games [*] Season 2 change - Ranked now runs off of your highest rank for all characters, less likely to run into smurfs [/list]  [u][b]Cons[/b][/u] [list] [*] Gameplay focuses too much on offense, defensive playstyles are NOT welcome by design [*] New mechanics encourage throwing things out and forcing your opponent to deal with it [*] Chip damage and "recoverable" health just don't work. Going to preface this by saying that I've not really played Tekken 8 for a while so I haven't really experienced the new season. That being said, I've had the game since it came out and I stopped playing after around 60 hours at the time as I was genuinely not happy with one thing: how overly aggressive the game is.  Heat is an awful mechanic that gives you BS options and access to a bunch of mix-ups and chip damage that is exhausting to play with due to being given each round. Side-stepping while seemingly buffed this last patch I don't think will ever feel good anyway, as I'd imagine there's still a ton of arbitrary rules to side-step each move that is simply impossible to be able to incorporate into your game plan and thus makes it feel random when it does work. And characters didn't really seem to have a clear identity either, with the system mechanics and framedata resulting in a lot of homogenous gameplay across the cast, with this recent patch seemingly doubling down on that and turning everyone into rushdown with forced 50/50s as part of their winning strategy.  Despite all the issues I had which did make me stop playing at the time, I've always hoped that the devs would listen to the feedback and improve the game, as their design philosophy for it has been bad and something that most players did not agree with since the game came out. But once I saw this season's patch and the uproar surrounding it, I've kind of lost all hope of that happening. They didn't listen throughout the last year, and are now doubling down on the hyper aggressive gameplay that just doesn't feel like what Tekken should be about.  So, unless there's a massive turnaround from the devs at some point (there won't be in my opinion), I would say if you were ever interested in getting into Tekken to not bother with this version. Maybe pick up Tekken 7 and see how that feels, or even try out one of the more legacy ones. They may not be getting updates like T8 is, but considering how destructive the changes have been to it I don't see that as a bad thing at all.

TLDR - s1 looked promising. Some issues but things were finally taking shape. s2 made the game feel like a beta version again and they also dumbed down the game to the point it no longer resembles tekken anymore.  OK. You pay 100 € for the game+season 1 pass. The balancing is a mess. Practically, a little more polished version of the playtests but still felt like beta. After you've bought the game, they introduce micro-transactions, battle passes and all these things literally no one cares about and little is done to fix the gameplay and balancing issues and the cheating/plugging epidemic (aka the important stuff). Bonus for selling a stage extra and not including it in the season pass...  The game looks promising and feels fresh and fun though. In time, the balancing gets better, the meta is more stable and you have a roster of generally overtuned characters. Some are a little too strong, some need a little help but overall you see the game is taking actual shape. Yes, the game has taken a more aggressive direction but still retains its complexity and depth in general.  Then, season 2 lands. Some positive changes, like ranking system overhaul, the ability to step from crouch to both sides and the combo realignment (not everyone agrees with the later but I think it's a positive change). And the rest is pure chaos.  Every character gets a ton of new combo tools. Combo damage and wall carry is through the roof. The game feels like T7 season 3. One launch into wall combo into on final mixup and the round is over.  Every character gets new tools/buffs to allow them to be "more aggressive". All characters become stance mixup characters, completely removing all character identity in terms of gameplay.  All the new stuff are introduced at once, apparently with little to no balance testing, making the game feel like a beta version once more.  The devs claim this is the "defense" patch, yet, despite the lateral movement buffs, every character can easily put the opponent in such frame disadvantage that sidestepping the mixup is impossible. And every character gets tools that track so much and have such long range that shut down movement as a whole.  They have over-simplified the game, to the point that, when pressured you have option a) or option b). Guess right and you win, guess wrong and you lose. There are no more layered mindgames (ie option c) beats both a) and b) but if the opponent does option d) they beat option c) but then you can do option e) etc.) Pure casino 50/50  I do not recommend this game to anyone interested in a serious competitive experience until (and if) the s2 mess is fixed. If you are a casual and want to play some cool matches, have fun with your friends, do cool combos and play story mode, then by all means go ahead.

To set the scene, season 2 of Tekken 8 is presently launching.  I have enjoyed playing Tekken since Tekken 2.  To date, I've played every Tekken game.  Throughout my life, I have dedicated energy to playing and following this brand since I enjoy it so much.   I think this may be the worst Tekken game I've ever played.  In my opinion, Death by Degrees is a more accurate representation of Tekken's formula and style than this game.  You can see it now.  You may wonder why I've spent hundreds of hours playing this game.  Why spend so much time on something you don't like?  Here's why: I've been frantically trying to hold onto the hope that everything will suddenly click if I play enough and level up enough.  I felt like I was missing something because I've always liked Tekken and didn't want to abandon a franchise that I've always appreciated.  The fact that I wasn't has already been established.  At first, players received Tekken 8 as a review copy without the battle pass.  A battle pass was implemented to get past the approval process once the official release date arrived.  Items typically acquired in Tekken games through in-game currency earned from Online Matches, Arcade mode, or even other party activities featured in earlier games like Tekken Bowling or Tekken Volleyball are included in this battle pass and every one that has been released up to this point.   This was an unpleasant surprise with Tekken 8, though, and now actual money is needed.  With the release of Season 2, they emphasized that the upgrades would favor defence choices more.  Currently, plus frames are common, with many moves or heat activations leaving no space for retaliation, and certain characters are completely broken.  I don't mean overpowered, but they have them too.    Paul can presently do f,1+2 into while standing 3, which bypasses the guarding system and hits every time.  To go even further, he can press 2 after that unblockable ws,3, and if you're near the wall, you'll get wall splat.  Which may result in you losing the match because you anticipated the move and blocked like a normal sane person (you should not have done that).  There are a myriad of comparable issues with the game right now.  There are numerous reasons why the game is in this situation, but it all boils down to who is currently in command.  This narrows down to Kouhei Ikeda as game director and Harada as an adviser.   All "heat" on this problem is thrown at Harada, who is spending his time with Tekken.  All positive feedback from T8 will be attributed to Ikeda's work on the game.  All flaws will hopefully be addressed with the next game, but ultimately, it is Ikeda's series now.  Many Soul Calibur devs have switched to Tekken development.  That is the current state of development for Tekken 8.  There are several reasons why the game isn't good right now:  Too many plus frames.  There are no true defense choices.   Terrible heat mechanics.  Many motions go off-axis.  Combo damage is really high.  Too many posture transitions (it appears like everyone is now Lei).  Stock/State Powerups.  Chip damage.   The look of prior games is also completely lost.  Despite having little to show for it, T4 continues to set the standard for excellence.  They merely required a hint of showy or crazy ideas in Tekken.  If you look at Clive, you'll notice that's been thrown out the window.  What's especially sad is that many players have tried to instill in people the idea that prior Tekken games were worse, but they don't have the fortitude to admit that the series has gotten worse.   It's a curious coincidence that Tekken Tag Tournament 2 didn't destroy Tekken, but Tekken 8, their most opulent and expensive title to date, is doing a greater job than Tag 2 ever did.

Revising after playing some more and giving the company time to realize their updated vision: oh my god lmao it's somehow even worse, don't buy this garbage.  I have no idea who this game is for, but it is certainly not for anyone who values being rewarded for learning and practice.  This is the first fighting game I've actually put time and thought into, and during Season 1 I was having a lot of fun learning the characters and systems. The aggressive play style was often frustrating against characters and moves I hadn't encountered before, particularly when massive screen effects were obscuring the animations, but it felt incredibly rewarding to learn how to deal with the moves and to pull off the correct counterplay in a match. I could feel myself slowly getting better at the game: figuring out my opponent through deliberate pokes and patience (which was particularly difficult for me), adjusting my play style and timing based on my opponent and their character, starting to apply movement and spacing to hit juicy whiff punishes, getting consistent with more difficult combo execution.  Season 2 has taken a massive turn away from everything I found interesting in the game. It included some good changes, but unfortunately they are inconsequential next to the flood of awful ones. There is no longer any reason to learn matchups since every character has the same gameplan: start attacking and pressure with moves that leave you with advantage on block and lead to a true coin toss situation where attacker risks a small punishment and losing their turn for the reward of taking away at least 50% (most likely more) of the defender's health. The game actively punishes you for patience and defense with chip damage and continued attacker advantage when you block. Every character also has incredibly strong offensive options to deal with the defender's movement, without risking anything or even gaining further pressure. It doesn't even seem to be worth it to practice more difficult combo execution since for my character at least they've made the easiest possible combo route the most effective one.  And then there are the technical issues. The game has been riddled with gameplay bugs since release, and with the big new patch not only were very few fixed, they managed to introduce a plethora of new ones. Online performance is also awful: even with the strictest connection quality settings, you'll run into games where the opponent is warping around the screen during normal movement and the game suddenly starts dropping frames randomly whenever the opponent's computer can't handle a new particle effect.  I really don't see a reason to play this anymore unless the developers, by some miracle, decide to completely reverse the design direction they've apparently chosen.

Tekken 8 era un juego excelente y muy recomendable antes del parche actual. Un juego con sus asperezas, pero muy entretenido y con cierta profundidad respecto a su ruptura con el molde de los Tekken anteriores. La historia es absurda y ridícula, como corresponde. Los personajes dicen cosas que les darían vergüenza hasta a los fans del anime más acérrimos. Los diseños son exagerados, coloridos y ridículos. Por eso amamos Tekken.  Pero durante este parche se hicieron cambios con los que ningún fan está de acuerdo. Cuando toda la comunidad pidió moderación y mayores capacidades defensivas, ellos solo mejoraron un poco el movimiento lateral, pero esto literalmente se vuelve irrelevante. Los personajes pasaron a hacer daño absolutamente masivo y absurdo, y ahora es común que los combos puedan ir de una pared a la otra en casi cualquier mapa, infligiendo más del 50%. Los buffs que hicieron provocan que los ataques anulen completamente la posibilidad de moverse. El daño a través del bloqueo se volvió mucho más masivo y opresivo. As much as I hate to say this, although there are plenty of people complaining online, there are also a lot of valid, constructive criticisms regarding season 2.  Out of all the 3D fighters, Tekken was always the one that stood out because of it's emphasis on movement and the depth of dimension of the game was much higher to others. Movement was one of the key defensive mechanics in the game; after labbing out moves that are steppable and actually stepping it in an actual match, makes you feel pretty good!  However, in season 2 of Tekken 8, it really did feel like it lost what made Tekken, Tekken. I truly believe that the game can workout being a much more aggressive version of its predecessors, but it CANNOT lose its original identity, which was what made it successful in the first place.  I had hoped that the company and developers would be slightly in touch of the community, at least listening to SOME part of what they had to say, but given recent events of chain blocking on Reddit and Twitter, I can clearly see that this was not happening, not in a million years.   It is one thing that the developers want a new iteration of Tekken, which is fantastic, but completely disregarding the community and blocking every single constructive criticism feedback posts from the content creators and everyone else, is another level of narcissism. Fighting games are becoming much more mainstream and accessible, but it just feels like Tekken is doing everything it can to stop the growth.  There are subjectively and objectively correct decisions and actions, I have only ever seen objectively incorrect decisions (Arguably subjective incorrect as well) from the game over the last little while. [h1]Tekken 8: A Disheartening Departure from Its Legacy[/h1]   The release of Tekken 8 represents a significant shift in the franchise's identity, seemingly tailored to prioritize profit from casual players at the expense of the gameplay mechanics that made Tekken renowned worldwide.  [b]Tracking and Sidestep Mechanics:[/b]  One of the most glaring issues lies in the tracking mechanics and the diminished effectiveness of sidestepping. In previous Tekken installments, linear moves could be avoided through precise sidesteps, with some exceptions requiring specific directional movement. These exceptions were clearly identifiable within the move list, ensuring players could adapt accordingly. However, Tekken 8 leaves such mechanics entirely to the discretion of Bandai Namco. The move list no longer flags exceptions consistently, and while certain moves are labeled as non-stepable, the majority of tracking moves lack such clarity. This lack of transparency demonstrates a troubling disregard for the game's fundamental principles.  [b]Loss of Strategic Depth:[/b]  Tekken 8 also abandons much of the strategic depth that defined its predecessors. Characters now come equipped with an abundance of simplified, overly potent tools—such as power crushes, throws that interrupt incoming moves, heat engagers, heat dashes, heat smashers, and Rage Arts. These features bear little resemblance to the mechanics that made Tekken iconic and are frequently exploited by casual players. The absence of mind games and nuanced decision-making has transformed the gameplay experience into one devoid of the intellectual engagement Tekken fans once cherished.  [b]A Fractured Experience:[/b]  In its pursuit of accessibility, Tekken 8 sacrifices balance and cohesion. The game's fundamental rules fail to apply consistently, and each character operates as an isolated, self-contained system with unique mechanics.  This design undermines the rewarding experience of gradual skill improvement, making the title increasingly unsuitable for dedicated players seeking growth and mastery.  In conclusion, Tekken 8 strays far from the principles that established its global reputation, delivering an unbalanced and unsatisfying experience. For those passionate about competitive play and skill development, this installment is regrettably unworthy of investment.

I would recommend watching tournament footage to see what's possible at the highest level, and to also learn how to deal with the aforementioned busted rubbish if you choose to get this game anyway, but with so many good games on the store, I think there's very little to feel FOMO over by skipping Tekken 8 unless they successfully stay the course and balance the game's glaring issues out in future.

Tekken 8 shuffles my certainties about what I know in the most confusing ways possible...inconsistency is a weird consistency that this game has.   It's confusing when you're trying to fully understand it and you play to absorb every possible situation you might run into inside the sockets of your eyeballs, in order to get better and react/punish your opponent as much as you can, without getting overwhelmed by them in return. It's confusing when geometries are like little sharpened thorns on your side poking fun at you when you're sure you've taken the best possible angle to extend the combo at the wall, and yet, to your shock and demise from this mortal soil, your oppenent drops on the floor, quickly rising up as the occasion presents itself to launch you straight in the air and finish you off, because that move that you did at the wall didn't hit as it should have.   3D games are surely not easy to manage for many reasons, hurtboxes, hitboxes, extensions, ducks, sidesteps and whatnot, and I'm maybe digging way to deep into this, but I think the scructural bones of Tekken 7 were a bit more sturdy and reliable when it came to some ordinary scenarios; aside the overall connection improvements that Tekken 8 successfully underwent, something about being less mechanically congested made Tekken 7 easier to follow, even if the game was more imprinted towards personal skills compared to Tekken 8 and more unforgiving.  Yet, you have to quickly let everything I just wrote pass through you and move on to your next battle if you want to enjoy what's underneath the rug because, when it works, it does wonders since there's something pretty satisfying that in the long run kept me personally coming back to it. It will always feel rewarding to win on your terms. Getting better is always the main reason why I boot the game in the first place (also my combos are sick and I'm the best yes of course I am). It is surely frustrating sometimes when things get ugly fast and are they are not under much of your control anymore, but, every character is broken and you have the same means as your opponent, so, for as much as it doesn't seem, it's a fair play while coming to knowledge. Stance mix-up based characters (there's a lot of them) will be the bane of your existance if you don't quickly develop some kind of counter defence for them and will make the game look like you're taking a willing walk into hell itself if you don't adapt fast enough. It's a rollercoaster if your temper gets the best of you, but I mean, no one is immune to salt.  Heat system is debatably dumb and demanded to be used at any cost if you wanna scale the ranks, also the most toxic community I've ever had the pleasure to interact with that lives under the FCG bubble, and I've had a bit of past experience with some lunatic gamers to begin with (Rocket League and MOBA's always come to mind when comparing them to this experience). The game is infested with so called "elitists", "purists" or "old guards", whatever they boast their title of "true gamer" to be, that are eager to give you that backhand compliment that under the lines it reads as "you are a scum you should have never won against me, so I'm gonna use my restricted vocabulary to make you notice that your victory was a fluke and undeserved" or straight insult you if you've clapped them with the rage art.  As you can witness, It's hard not to have split opinions about the game overall...it's a challenging child to have to bear but it gives fruits of your labor if tended accordingly, so, as any fighting game out there, it's up to you if you're liking it the way it is or you are waiting for a miracle to pick it up from the ashes of what the second year has been for the most part of Tekken 8 life. We're on a redeeming path that a lot of people shied away from since Tekken 7 saved everyone's ass. We'll see.

I rarely review games, but since i spent a lot of time and dedication to Tekken 7 and Tekken 8 (for a total of 2500+ hours, including offline events), i feel the need to communicate my dissatisfaction, and maybe help the devs to get back on track.  First: if you are a casual player, this game is still for you, it's fun, it has great graphics and effects, and all the appealing things a fighting game for casual gamers should have.  But: if you want to take it a little bit more seriously, not like a pro player, but let's say as a hobby, this game is in an almost unplayable state. Patch 2.0 was obviously implemented with small to no testing at all from the dev/balancing team, new moves don't work, they are outright bugged, or track in some odd way, or whiff with no reason to do so, Paul and Jack have game-breaking interactions. And let's talk about balancing: the developers told us they would have improved defensive and lateral movement gameplay, and then added 1 to 3 moves per character that do insane pressure and are impossible to evade, so they did not only gave us false promises, but they mocked us too.  Since i really care about this game, i often participated and organized events, tournaments and such, i must put a bad review on it, and hope the devs wake up from their "vision" and actually listen to the community. I would like to play this game again, thanks.  Funny thing is, there are some cool, small addictions to this patch, such as a visual cue to one-side tracking moves, and new visual/sound effects, it seems like there were two different teams working on this patch, that never communicated between each other, and one of the two were drunk all the time during work.

This is an incredibly difficult review to write, since I love the Tekken franchise and everything it's grown to become over the years. But after the recent updates, I simply cannot, in good faith, recommend this game to anyone who appreciates the technical, expressive gameplay this series is known for.  Let's get it out of the way. Yes, season 2 was awful. Sure, it's *one* bad patch, but the methodology behind this patch is what makes it so bad. The developers clearly don't care about the players, the long time fans who've been playing these games for decades, they're obsessed with building the game *they* want, damn everyone else. After the millions of comments and critical posts against what this patch did, the developers continue to stick their heads in the sand and pretend the negativity doesn't exist. It's pathetic and entirely unprofessional. There was no apology or a vow to do better, just anger and hate, which makes people very worried about this game's future. Only time will tell if we'll get fixes for the glaring issues, the 50/50 casino gameplay, the overpowered heat system and this game's obsession with rewarding mashing and reckless gameplay.  Even before the homogenisation of the entire cast with the launch of season 2, this game was way, way easier to play than any previous game in the series. The gameplay model rewards mindless aggression over strategy and tactical thinking. I'm all for games becoming more "accessible" to newcomers, but it shouldn't come at the expense of character expression, technical gameplay and a high skill ceiling. "Accessibility" should mean making it easier to learn the rules, not making the game so easy that anyone with a pulse can press random buttons and secure wins. Every match, no matter the character you play or are playing against, just feels the same. It's draining, playing the online modes in this game is a droning experience because every character has been retrofitted into the same playstyle. Characters like Lee and Steve have been forced into Harada and Murray's idea of "Tekken 8 aggressive gameplay" while tearing away unique features that made them fun to play and watch. The game feels incredibly hollow in a way that both casuals and competitive players alike will feel with every match. You may be able to avoid this sinking feeling if you play with friends in a more casual setting, but these changes are really hard to ignore.  The monetisation issues are really bad in this one and have been since season 1. This full price AAA game has multiple battle passes with costumes and cosmetics. Though optional, the character customisation options are a little lacking compared to 7 and it hurts that most of the really nice clothes, hairstyles and accessories are locked behind stupid battle passes with little to nothing else in them. Thankfully, they're pretty cheap and are entirely optional. However, what I cannot accept is the DLC model, where you need to buy DLC characters in order to practice against them. This is a disgusting pay-to-win scenario, where players who use DLC characters are at a distinct advantage over players who don't own said DLC. Not to mention that characters like Clive and Lidia are incredibly strong and warrant spending time to practice against.  Now, this is a more personal gripe, but I think the roster is rather uninspired. Not only are several Tekken 7 newcomers absolutely missing from 8, some fan favourites missed the cut. Characters like Josie, Julia, Lei, Bob and Eliza haven't made an appearance in 8 (yet), while Raven (who was replaced by his "master" in Tekken 7) returns to a resounding "meh" reception. There are only 3 new characters, 4 if you count the DLC (as of season 2's start) and 4 of Tekken 7's new characters returned. I understand that many of these characters have long standing fanbases and most of them warrant a spot on 8's roster, but it's a bit of a shame to see so many of the same faces. Certainly hoping that future DLC will fix this and bring back some fan favourites. Still, it's nice to see Jun again (though it makes Asuka's inclusion quite redundant) and Reina, Azucena and Victor are genuinely amazing characters in both design and gameplay. Again, this is a personal issue and is really quite minor, so don't pay too much heed to this part.  It hurts, because Tekken 8 genuinely has a lot to love about it. The game looks beautiful, it has a robust customisation engine for your character's appearance, the music is amazing and it has plenty of single player content to enjoy. The story mode is pretty good for a fighting game, though a bit standard for the Tekken series. I really love that you can change the music that plays on every stage, on the menu and in the different modes to any track from pretty much any game in the series. It's a really nice touch that gives the game more customisation options. This game also offers Arcade Quest as a solid tutorial story to get new players into the groove of Tekken, teaching the basics of movement, attacking and defending. Though, I'm fairly certain they could've done a better job, it's still better than just throwing newbies in without any sort of training.   In short, Tekken 8 has been incredibly disappointing lately and the horrible PR from its developers certainly hasn't helped. Despite all this, I remain hopeful that this game can make a comeback. If the developers decide to listen to the people who play their games and make proper changes, alongside some solid picks for the season 2 DLC pass, I think Tekken 8 might be able to save itself from the current spiral of degradation it finds itself in. However, as of right now, I cannot recommend this game to anyone, unless your intention is to play with your friends and avoid the online space entirely.  Edit: Season 2 has had several new updates that attempt to balance the game, yet a lot of the problems still remain. I'm still hopeful for the future, since changes ARE being made, but I'd still hold off on this game. Wait for season 3, then maybe consider Tekken 8.

Now, I'll admit I'm sort of a Tekken 8 apologist. In season 1, the game obviously has problems, I feel the balance was pretty good (of course there were higher tier characters, but high and low tier was not too far off), and the battlepass paid for itself and you would get the currency to buy it over time, really giving you a sense of progression to continue playing online. The game fixed a lot of things that were wrong with Tekken 7: less low parry reward, less incentive to backdash, better sidesteps, etc. Overall, though it has flaws and issues, I though season 1 of Tekken 8 was not so bad, and had high hopes for the future. The developers even stated that they were going to make defense more powerful, which is the main issue for most in the game.  Then Season 2 happened. A worrying livestream turned into a travesty of an update. Now look, I don't think it's so bad that I'm going to quit playing the game. Chaotic fun is still fun, and people play games with poor choices like the HnK fighting game made by Arcsys to this day. However, as much as I would like to ignore what is happening and have fun, this is extremely unhealthy for the longevity of the game. After the livestream I mentioned, the devs only listened a little bit, taking out the most agregious change, but told the community to wait and try the game. When the patch dropped for season 2, and it was the exact opposite of what they promised, they said wait half a month for us to fix it, and not only buried their head in the sand, but community leaders like Murray are actively blocking constructive criticism from notable members of the community instead of listening.   Look, I love Tekken 8. I really do, and I want this game to shine. I don't mind Tekken taking a more offensive approach compared to previous titles. But the way they are doing it is not great. Catch-all homing moves and overwhelming stance offense is okay when one or two characters have it and are balanced around it, but nobody wants the whole roster to be doing the same things on offense. It makes the game stale for new players, and goes against what old players like about the game in the first place.   I'd love to eat my words and re-make this review. I love playing this game! But I cannot ignore the poor leadership behind it any longer. Let's cross our fingers that one day the developers can figure this out and fix it like Capcom did with SFV.

Disappointing and Underwhelming - Tekken 8 Season 2  As a long-time fan of the Tekken series, I’ve been eagerly awaiting the next season of content in Tekken 8. Unfortunately, Season 2 has left me extremely disappointed, with several issues that I just can’t overlook.  First and foremost, the character balance changes are frustratingly inconsistent. While some characters got much-needed buffs, others were nerfed without clear reason or justification. It’s as if the developers made changes just for the sake of it, rather than with any thoughtful analysis or player feedback. The result is a highly unbalanced roster that makes some characters feel almost unplayable, while others are overpowered.  Then there’s the lack of meaningful new content. Season 2 promised new characters, stages, and game modes, but what we got was incredibly underwhelming. The new characters feel uninspired, with a lack of unique movesets or fresh playstyles. Additionally, the stages we’ve been given are either recycled from previous games or lack any real creativity. I was hoping for something exciting and innovative, but instead, it feels like a rushed attempt to push out content without much effort.  On top of that, the online experience is still riddled with issues. Lag and connection problems persist, despite the developers claiming to have improved netcode. The matchmaking system still feels broken, often throwing players into matches with drastic skill differences, leading to frustrating experiences. As someone who enjoys playing competitively, these problems are a huge turn-off.  Lastly, the lack of communication from the developers is downright frustrating. Players have been voicing concerns about these issues for weeks, yet the response from Bandai Namco has been minimal at best. It feels like they’re more focused on pushing out microtransactions and cosmetics than on addressing the core problems that are affecting the player experience.  In short, Tekken 8 Season 2 is a huge step backward for the series. It’s clear that the developers haven’t put the same level of care and attention into this season as they did with the base game, and it shows. Until these issues are addressed, I can’t recommend Tekken 8 to anyone who’s looking for a polished, enjoyable fighting game experience.

Hi, everyone. This is my first review ever here on Steam and it couldn't be to any other game besides Tekken. Unfortunately, this is going to be a bad and sad one.  Tekken has been part of my life for almost 30 years. Tekken 3 and 4 were part of my childhood and from Tekken 5 onwards I started to learn the fundamentals of the game.  Tekken 8 Season 1 was rough, unbalanced system with an one-way gameplay where the offense is so busted that you can see countless rounds in professional level where the defender just lose their entire health bar by just blocking with no counter play because a lot of things are plus on block, track your side steps, cause chip damage and so on.  For the entire year players gave feedback, the devs said they were listening to it and we were hoping that Season 2 would have addressed these problems properly. But no. They lied to us. They said on several occasions that this patch would focus on defense, but they lied through their teeth.  Season 2 doubled down the reckless agression, exactly the opposite of what the community wanted. Now it is a dumbed down game with a 50/50 festival. These current devs are killing characters identities, they're making all characters play the same way. They're removing techs from the game that were there for decades and no one was complaining. They don't know how to balance the game and they have terrible ideas!  I don't want to get into technical details here, but just so you know, they thought it would be a cool idea to make the player who successfully break a throw take chip damage! In which world this would be appreciated? Breaking throw is a hard skill in Tekken, they were punishing the experienced player who is able to break throws for years and also punishing beginners who were still learning the game and when they finally manage to break a throw, congratulations, here's your chip damage. Yes, they already said they will remove this, but it doens't change the fact that they thought this would be a cool feature to add to the battle system.  And as if that wasn't enough, the producers are blocking people on Twitter for just criticizing the game.  This game deviated far too much from what Tekken is and I'm afraid a couple of patches won't fix it. I wish they rollback the patch and started again. I'd wait patiently for this. It's sad to think the game will keep on this state for a long period, but we'll see.

[h1] A Casual Player's Review [/h1]  I will be purely reviewing the state of the game as a casual player and why I feel this way. I come heavily from a 2.5D Background like Tag Fighters and SNK games so take what I say with a grain of salt rather than a professional player's take.  The way I see how Tekken has evolved from 6 to 8(Tag 2 and 7 Included) the game has tried to evolve to also include mechanics which contemporaries have also dabbled with i.e. a Comeback mechanic in the form of Heat(Which is a mechanic I feel like is mimmicking SF5's V Trigger) and Rage which is a mixture of Mortal Kombat's Fatal Blow and Guilty Gear Xrd's Hellfire in the sense it gives you a buff when your HP falls under a certain threshold, and the need to make the game have a much flashier look to make it look cool. I'll be honest and I speak for myself it's a lot to consider.   It's a fighting game that very much embellishes it's style over substance identity which is holding the game back compared to the previous games before it, even Tekken 7 before S3 introduced over tuned DLC characters. With each major update introducing another new issue and the release of each DLC character being considered "Problematic" as well as the departure of Shimbori, Harada and now Nakatsu it's becoming a lot more difficult to believe in the remaining team at Project Tekken to be able to clean up the game and bring it into a state where everyone can be happy with it. I really won't be shocked if Project Tekken makes like Team Blue at ArcSys and eventually faulters into non existence.  Also personal gripe: DISABLE THE TOGGLE TO TURN ON AUTOCOMBOS IN RANKED. EITHER HAVE IT ON OR DON'T.  The sad part is I want to like it. I really do. This might be one of the best looking games in the series but I cannot really recommend the game as is as a causal player.

[Edit after patch 3.00.02]  This patch is one of the best patches Tekken 8 has ever received. Almost every character got much needed nerfs and not a single one got buffed. There is still a lot of changes needed for this game to be actually a good Tekken, but this is the "right direction", or the so called "back to basics" people expected. I hope to see more patches like this one throughout this season, therefore I change my review to positive to let the developers know, that this is what the game needs in my opinion.  [----------------------------------------------------]  I would never expect, that my first ever review is going to be a negative one.  I have played other fighting games like Street Fighter 6, Guilty Gear Strive, Granblue Fantasy Versus: Rising, etc., but Tekken 8 was the first game that I felt was the one I would stay with for a very long time. I believed I would be playing this game for hundreds or thousands more hours, slowly getting better and better, mastering my character, basics of the game, match ups and other unique situations. I am not so sure about it anymore.  With the arrival of season 2, the developers showed in what direction they want to go. They want to attract new players which are new to fighting games and Tekken, but the way they do it is horrifying. This game is getting easier and easier, complexity that made this game stand out is slowly vanishing. Every character has gotten new moves that are plus on block and homing, which make them basically stance mix-up characters, tearing out their identity. They seem to have their vision and do not care what the players have to say, so if the negative reviews and the bombardment of criticism on twitter and other platforms doesn't change anything, I might stop playing the game eventually, either because won't be able to stand this anymore or there will be no one to play with, because so many people want to drop this game now. Let me preface this as someone who started with Tekken 7 very late I got to enjoy a game that had years of balancing and while Tekken 7 has its fair share of issues I enjoyed it so much I spent close to a thousand hours learning, meeting new people and practising. I ended Tekken 7 at Tekken King rank when Tekken 8 launched.  Tekken 8. After the launch honeymoon phase I felt I could not get into the game yet I stayed optimistic that it would get better and I was just suffering from the loss of my main and a new mechanics stopping me from enjoying it, however after 200 hours with season 1 I know now this was not the case. The game has serious fundamental flaws that I feel break the Tekken feel. With season 2 now in full swing, these have been amplified ten fold.  Chip damage. It doesn't fit in Tekken, its oppressive rewards a OVERLY aggressive mindset and removes patience and reward that comes from it. I understand this is Tekken 8s ethos but it just doesn't work. it makes playing the game a chore.  Heat. While a fun concept and one I tried to enjoy it often leads to you being stuck with very little options to get out of the barrage of attacks your opponent is throwing out, mix in plus frames and chip and its a slog to get momentum back.  Defence. It's non existent. while season 2 changes sidestepping from crouch which is fantastic its hard to defend against tracking range three mids, +4 to +7 on block moves and stance pressure that always leads to a 50/50 situation. its hard to appreciate a small defensive buff when the act of blocking is punishing enough.  Speaking of 50/50s, every character boils down to them, find opening, heat engage, pressure, 50/50. The identity of every character has been homogenised into the same play style, its not fun and removes expression. Everyone is shoe horned into playing the same way no matter who you play in the character pool.  Now I am no Tekken 8 guru nor a Tekken Guru for that matter, but this just isn't it. I have tried to love this game I have but it is more infuriating then it is fun, Tekken 7 is not the best game by any means and was plagued with issues that are horrible even to this day but at least it was fun. We had an opportunity here to fix issues the community had with season 1 and make Tekken 8 a bloody good game, but the devs doubled down and made heat more oppressive and defensive options even more limited due to the new moves characters got and heat changes.  I'd steer clear for now. At least untill the game gets some form of fixes, it's just not fun. thats all it boils down to.

It's a great comedy game. If you're looking to beat up your friends in (at least what I consider) a beautiful looking game and have a good laugh as your lifebars disintegrate, it's pretty fun as games go. It's very beginner friendly in the sense that a large portion of winning strategies can rely on knowledge checks - but that's always been a part of Tekken. Combos are also very easy to do in Tekken compared to other fighting games: even a novice can spend half an hour or less and solidify a consistent, low-execution combo from a launcher that does somewhere from 33% to 45% of the opponent's hp. Again, this is nothing new - Tekken 7 also had plenty of combo damage off easy to execute strings. There's plenty to learn if you're trying to take the game seriously as well: every character can include forms of execution in their combos to create better situations, and building knowledge of the game will definitely increase your winrate. It's definitely not "random" in the sense that anyone can just do anything and it's going to work.  But all that said, Season 2 of Tekken 8 has made me want to uninstall the game and ask my friends if they want to play T7. But why? My character got buffed - he's way stronger than before, no doubt. But I don't want to play him. The most satisfying thing about Tekken isn't winning a round, or winning a BO3 - it's that you're engaging in an interacting and evolving player vs player face-off: one where you condition each other and make reads based on who you think the other is and what sort of options and OS-es they might tend towards. It's so satisfying to switch up your timing to land that counterhit, or chase down a sidestep and land a deep electric, or step the move you knew was coming to get a full back-turned launch. This stuff isn't gone with Season 2, but the amount of pausing and "feeling out" you're allowed to do has decreased a lot. Mixups are more "real" than ever in the sense that counterplay is often restricted to risky options. It's not a good feeling to feel punished for blocking a move that is a) hard (if not straight impossible) to step, b) comes out faster than 20 frames c) will absolutely massacre you if you DIDN'T block it. Because when it's so fast to come out, it starts to feel like the only real counterplay you have to these kind of moves is to hit the opponent before they have the chance to use it.  It's just not fun to play Devil Jin on this patch. I don't want to do any more fully charged unblockable mid hard-to-step guard crush vs +18 ob 50 damage CH+reset situation mixups. I don't want to press f+3 at my opponents and realize that if they didn't already jab me out of the air they're locked into an exceedingly dangerous (and potentially looping) situation. I'm so sick of winning games because "Oops you didn't block my electric and now I maul you at the wall in 2 interactions thanks to my absolutely ridiculous heat dash + frame launching mid vs launching low" - and all they did is buff every aspect of this. What's worse is that I no longer feel like I can apply all the interesting timing mixups I love when no one is incentivised to block. It's just got to the point where I feel bad for my opponent when it's my turn for offense; at some point, hitting people with fly 1+2 stops becoming funny and starts becoming sad while you and your opponent rps their way out of the looping situation.

I've held back from writing a review, and I'll keep this short because enough has been said about where Tekken 8 is at currently.   Coming off of Tekken 7's trailblaze, 8 had tons of momentum upon inception. A lot of the flaws from Tekken 7 were addressed in 8 and the developers- all of Bandai Namco seemed to have made big strides in polishing 8 during the beta tests before its official release. When 8 dropped, I didn't like it still. They did tons of things right and tons wrong, but I was willing to look past all of it as they delivered a fine product with 7 which I adore as a fighting game in the Tekken series. All of S1 I remained hopeful for a better, more polished Tekken 8 in the coming season. Obviously, that is not the case and the level of dissatisfaction from the community has reached an all-time high. My only suggestion at this point without being super negative is for BN to hire personnel who can interact and communicate with the community, share their ideas and vision for Tekken to see if there is any alignment, and for them to relay information back to BN and the developers what the community believes can make Tekken 8 great again. If BN won't do that, then this game is cooked because they dropped the ball hard in S2 given all the critique, feedback, and reviews from the player-base suggesting changes they believe would make the game more enjoyable and increase the player experience in the last year and change.  --- Update: Post Season 3 Release ---  Tekken 8 was a sinking ship from the very beginning of its release. It's sad to say, but having any hope in Namco to deliver real changes to the game is a farcry from reality because it seems like they've lost touch with how to develop the game where it reflects their beliefs and the community's desires. There's a total disconnect between tekken developers and the community, but the community is also to blame for this. Tekken 8 will not be able build enough momentum to get it to a place where it can drive significant traffic and have stronger appeal to fighting game players. I have been trying to stay away from the notion that this game leans to and favors casual play, but season 3 patch release was just weak and the current meta still plays a lot like S2. Tekken 8 has not been able to create its own momentum. Most of that was created from T7, and the current state of T8 is on a decline with higher levels of player disinterest. I've been playing fighting games a long time, and was until very recently a Street Fighter and 2D fighter enthusiast. I bought Tekken 8 because it looked good and the characters are cool.   There's been a lot of dooming in the community recently (And basically since release. Be honest.), and Tekken players are kind of famous for yapping about how ♥♥♥♥ their game is, so I was kind of ignoring the doom and simply trying to play the game. I'll continue to try to be fair, here's my honest review:  The Good:  Game looks great, is fun to play and has lots of very cool looking, different playing characters and lots of great looking stages that impact how games play out. The music is largely good and matchmaking pretty quick. There's enough modes to keep you entertained and the character customiser is a tad anaemic, but it's there. The game is presented well, and the matches are super fun. There's loads of depth in the mechanics and the systems and you can spend years learning a game like this. Indeed, the idea is that you do. The training mode is excellent and has a lot of great functionality. I love the Battle Lounge and the people you can bump into there.  The Bad: This game is built on legacy, so if you're new like I was it takes a long time to learn matchups, characters, movesets, frame data etc. The monetisation system for the game is a tad heavy handed. I understand a AAA fighting game costs a lot, but it has felt a tad like we're being asked to nickle and dime ourselves, or some of the pricing/functionality feels a bit predatorial (Miscommunication over stages being in battle passes, charging for old costumes in the new game, fight passes being a bit crap if we're honest, not allowing characters not purchased in training mode or replays etc.). Now, some of these things were walked back, but... they still tried it.   Now for the big one. The season 2 patch. I was waiting for Anna as I wanted to main her, and I am happy with her and am enjoying playing her. But overall, a lot of people who know what they're actually talking about aren't very happy, and that needs to be addressed. Hopefully this is a mistake that Bamco learns from and course corrects. In fact, I even think they will. I'm not affected by the things that bother pros as being a mid purple rank player, everyone's mashing mids, missing punishes and generally being scrubs, so honestly, I haven't perceived a difference. I trust Harada and co. will address the backlash and hopefully T8 continues to be a very fun game we can all continue to enjoy whilst Twitter melts down about it for a long time to come.  Do I recommend this game? Absolutely, but with caveats. Make sure you have friends that you can play with or get into the Zaibatsu discord and get on voice chat. Do not grind ranked all day on your own, actually try to learn the game and have fun, and the game will provide it to you.  I will retract this positive review however if Season 2 is the start of a doubling down on the mistakes of this failed experiment. I trust it is is not. Tekken 8 has become my favourite game to play, and has the potential to be one of the best of all time. Let's hope the devs get it there.

There are stark differences between a pastime and a hobby, and fighting games, more than many other genres of games, usually fall into the latter category - but after the Season 2 update I'm unsure of where I'd place Tekken 8. How to structure offence and hedge your defense has been replaced with a ton of forced casino-style 50/50% stance mix-up transitions from tracking, plus on block Mid attacks from full screen away. This is like removing the painter's ability to mix colors and create nuance.  There are several other issues with the direction of this Tekken entry that I won't go into. Just know that right now, if you're looking for a game that adequately rewards you for the time you put into it, with a heavy heart I'd have to suggest that you make another game your home.

Casino 8: A review.  My issues with this game and current patch:  Lets start with what I do like about Tekken 8: Game looks great, animations are new models look excellent.  I think making the game more accessible and easy to learn is good. All my favourite characters are in the game, and I enjoy playing them. Practice mode is better than ever. Online performance has gotten a lot better than in T8.  Now for what I don't like:  1. ) The erasure of character Identity: All character weaknesses have been addressed, and this has led to the problem that all characters (some more than others) can create very easy 50/50 setups with little effort, with minimal options for counterplay, other than just deciding to block low or mid. Every character is now a 50/50 machine. One of my main gripes with his game is the overwhelming design choice across the board, to give every character insane stance pressure. Stances are cool, and interesting, and having good stance options was some characters identity in the past. In this game, every character has transition into transition to multiple stances, heat engagers, launchers and now heat bursts into all of their stances.   They have also made characters much more easier to play. Sometimes this can be a good thing if a character is underperforming, but they straight up took away core weaknesses for characters. My own main, Jun comes to mind. What was her weakness? Had problems opening opponents up when behind. What does she have to compensate for this? GOOD DEFENCE OPTIONS.  Excellent block and whiff punishment, Reversals, Punch Parry, Cancans, and also had some good mid pokes. They addressed this by giving her unreactable, casino roulette gameplay out of her -again- stance pressure.   Jun just as example, but many other characters have been given similar treatments. The erasure of weaknesses, and therefore identity.  2.) Damage It is far too much. Off the aforementioned 50/50 focus, the damage you can get off launchers, wallsplats is huge. This is exacerbated by the chip damage situation. Some characters should be known as having weaker damage, some should be higher, this is a normal fighting game design philosophy, and their should be trade offs for either. But in this game, combo damage, especially at the wall is massively inflated. Everyone has access to +75 DMG combos, with wall carry gotten even easier.   3.) The Heat System Very popular opinion, yes. The heat system is just crazy. It is in essence, god mode. Within heat, you can experience the most horrendous gameplay loop of + frames into more + frames which further enforce this 50/50 guessing game that is so popular now. With this patch, heat has been improved with the addition of some extremely strong only draining the heat gauge now instead of using it all. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  I really like Tekken. I've played it for a very long time. I think the consensus on the game is that everything is too much, Tekken is a game of great complexity, and it is good to try and get new players on board, but not listening to your veteran players in this case is a bad decision.  I seen this comment on a youtube video somewhere but I agree with it:  The dev's need to think 'is this fun to play against' rather than 'is this fun to play'.

The Season 2 update might be the worst update in the history of fighting games.  It took a game that was close to capturing what made Tekken before 7 fun to delve into for hours, even as a casual fan.  While Season 1 had issues, mostly around the Heat mechanic, some adjustments to things like tracking and homing moves, and adjustments to some moves and nerfs to the top tiers it would have been going in the right direction.  As of Season 2 they went full send on the stuff everyone was not liking.  The constant in your face offense with little options as a defender to fight back.  Mostly due to the tracking that so many moves and strings had, side stepping was at some of its weakest.  One of the few things this patch did was make stepping feel better.  However, all of that is for naught as most of the cast now has some form of strong homing options, usually a mid, that is also plus on block.    Character identity is quickly disappearing as well.  Almost every character got adjustments to address their weaknesses.  The other thing is almost every character now has some sort of stance.  As a result most interactions are not, some string into stance into a 50/50 that usually leave the attacker safe if not plus on block.  All interactions are turning into this, long gone are the days of learning what a character wants to do and defend against that.  No, now you must flip a coin and guess right.  If you guess right more than your opponent, you win!  After a session the other night I reviewed my games, and that was almost every interaction, I didn't outplay them, they didn't outplay me.  Sometimes I guess better, sometimes they did.  Nothing learned, nothing gained,  That is the biggest sin of the game in its current state.  You can learn, and practice but it won't matter unless you know how to guess a coin flip better than the rest.  It is a mess and it sucks.  Despite it's issues, I had fun in Season 1.  It was the first time since DR that I got lost in Tekken again.  Until something happens with this patch, either reverting back to Season 1, or they fix this mess.  I can't in good conscious recommend this game.  I hate that this is where we're at, but this is the state of Tekken.  If it gets fixed I will gladly change my review.  Untill then STAY AWAY.

Season 2 might be the worst thing the devs have done to tekken, not just 8, but as a series.   Changing core mechanics for no real reason, looking at Ki charge in particular here. Patching out character weaknesses while massively amplifying oppressive stance based offence to allow war crimes like Jack's "Make Some Noise", all while touting about how much they are going to improve defence this season. All they've done is give everyone 100+ damage combos for free, made it so players if defending cannot take their turn back with absurd amounts of frame advantage, and just slapped homing attacks onto everyone.   As an example, Kazuya has ALWAYS had a weakness to side stepping to his left, it meant he needed to mix up his timings for things like dash electrics after the enemy side steps in order to continue his pressure / find an opening. What do Bandai do in their infinite wisdom? Give him a move that is homing specifically for enemies moving to the left.   This was a key characteristic of Kaz, and it allowed the enemy to be able to come up with some sort of game plan in order to actually make this a two player game.    Further to this, with the amount of homing moves just slapped into place, it seems to be a direct attack on side stepping, the thing that Tekken is known for, while in the same patch allowing players to sidestep left or right (depending on p1/p2 side respectively) out of crouch. It's confusing, misguided, and I personally do not think that the balance team are communicating  either among themselves or other departments.   One patch note for lars even had the gall to address when "opponents adapted and countered" his options, noting that it "became more difficult for Lars to effectively utilize his stances in battle" Is that not kind of the point of fighting games? Adapt, and counter? What patch notes like this show is that the devs view of improving defence for lars is to make his stances braindead so the opponent simply cannot adapt and counter them. They simply are not thinking.   I'm a king main, have been since launch. One of Kings weaknesses was that his grabs, while effective, did not track left or right for the most part. Now, not only do they track while in heat, but they also restore heat gauge, making them track for longer. I'm happy on a personal level he got a buff, not that he needed it, but on a fundamental game design level they have just patched out an entire weakness for king.   This patch isn't all bad, it's nice to see the punish and counter notifications in battle, along with combo damage. That at least makes the viewing experience a little more approachable, not that tekken needed it imo.   Until the devs actually get their head in the game, I cannot recommend tekken 8, which is a shame because I just had a whole podcast episode absolutely singing the games praises, and then they went and ruined it in what is possibly the worst April fools.

[h1] Animation & Art Style [/h1] the animation and art style are really pleasant and beautiful compared to tekken 7. honestly, it was one of the main reasons i bought the game : ) and i still really love how the characters are designed.  [h1] Music [/h1] as one of my friends said: “peak fiction.” okay, i know i’m exaggerating a little, but the music is just so good (especially the seaside resort. absolute 10/10.) [h1] Gameplay [/h1] where do i even start? i think what tekken 8 tried to do was make every character really Overpowered, so you could just pick whoever you think is cool and still be able to win with enough practice. in paper, that sounds simple: you work hard, you master your character, and eventually you climb the ranks (tekken king, tekken emperor, and so on.) but in reality? unfortunately, It doesn't work out that way : (. instead of true balance, what we ended up with is a game where every character specializes in something extremely annoying like:  king has insane grab mixups, dragunov has crazy pushback and pressure, Jun has a ton of safe launchers and plus frames, panda & kuma hit like trucks during heat mode and can chip away your health like it's nothing... and why even add the heat system to tekken? tekken 7, from what i heard, was already really good without it. so why bring it in? Just to make the game faster? there's no real point to keeping the heat during the game, all it does is make the characters even more broken. and the worst part? knowledge checks. [ for me at least : ) ] the process is simple: memorize and practice, over and over till you get it. but honestly? it's just boring... having to do this for every character completely kills the fun for me : (  [h1] Updates [/h1] i really hoped season 2 was some kind of april prank's joke. It feels like the devs didn’t listen to anything the community asked for : (. I mean... is it really that hard to fix the actual problems people have been pointing out for months? instead of fixing the game, season 2 somehow made things even worse. i didn't know it's possible to ruined the ruined... one of my friends said that harada meant to "surprise" us with season 2 changes. well... surprise, I guess. First, I want to say that having started playing TEKKEN games with TEKKEN 8, I love this game, but this Season 2 patch is VERY problematic and is completely ruining my enjoyment and interest in the game.  As a relatively new player to TEKKEN and fighting games in general, I can attest that the most frustrating thing for a new player is to be steamrolled by the opponent and feel like there is nothing you can do about it. This happens a lot in TEKKEN because it is a complex and often unintuitive game. But despite often experiencing such steamrolling, I still stuck with the game for a full year because I knew that even though a character or move might seem unfair, there are weaknesses to exploit if you know about them, and I was intrigued by the idea of getting good enough to use the counterplay. That way I could transition to playing the actual mind games with my opponents, which I find to be the coolest thing about fighting games.  This patch takes away all of my intrigue and enthusiasm. They have now made changes to most of the characters so that their weaknesses have been largely mitigated or removed and at the same time have been given extremely problematic pressure moves. These moves shut down pretty much all counterplay (like sidestepping and general movement), apply unconditional pressure and lead to 50/50 mixups where the only thing you can do is to guess for your life. And if you guess wrong, "here we go again...". So in other words, steamrolling now happens way more frequently at all skill levels and the mind games that I wanted to play are almost nonexistent now. It's basically a boring and needlessly frustrating game of steamrolling the opponent before they can steamroll you.  So to the devs: PLEASE revert the Season 2 patch ASAP! Keep the sidestepping changes, the extra HUD information in match, and the adjusted leniency of throw breaks, these are great! As for the new moves; back to the drawing table. If nothing is done very soon, I will go elsewhere and so will MANY others.

I remember when my friend first got me into Tekken 7. It was hard, very hard, and it was the first fighting game I had ever jumped into. We played it like a party game for months, practicing combos sometimes, and never really taking it seriously. I remember that day like it was yesterday as well, when I was at work and I was thinking about Lei Wulong, and I texted my friend that I wanted to commit to learning him. Fully learning him, down to the last string. And that was the day I created the Lei Bible for myself.  It took the better part of a year, but it was fun. I genuinely took months to learn everything about Lei, from his frame data to every move in every one of his stances. From his punishers to every one of his wall combos. I learned everything there was to learn about Lei, and I wrote them all by hand in a notebook of mine just so I could memorize and know Lei down to his core. With my friend's help and guidance, I learned and had Lei Wulong down to memory, and I dragged myself to Tekken God Prime with a character that the Tekken community thought was too complicated to play. It was gratifying, genuinely. I played honorably, ignoring dissent from some pros like TheMainManSwe who said that all you needed to do was spam Hellsweep and Razor Rush to climb rank. I wanted to earn a high rank off of my own skill and hard work, and before Tekken 8 came out, I beat that same friend who helped me become as great as I was, a Tekken God Omega Kazuya, in a first to 10 sparring tournament we held against each other. That was the first time I had ever beaten him in that game, and I was sure that as we both transitioned over to Tekken 8, the high I had felt that day would be felt many more times throughout the years. The high of honorably and respectfully winning a duel against an equally respectful and honorable opponent. Unfortunately, that spar we had would be the last time I ever felt high again.  Because Lei wasn't in the game at launch, I had to find a new main, and despite the fact that I had never liked Jin's playstyle when I had first started Tekken, his gameplay in Tekken 8 spoke to me now that I had a deep commitment to playing fair and honorable characters. Spamming, unfair advantages, and broken mechanics didn't make me feel like I earned a win against an opponent, and despite Jin being more flashy and bombastic in this game than he was in 7, I didn't feel like I had an unfair advantage above other opponents like I felt with other characters, so I chose him to be my main, and I learned him fast now that I knew what to learn. I learned everything there was to learn about him and committed myself to playing honest, and I was ready to get into ranked.  To cut to the chase, Tekken 8 just felt wrong. It wasn't the fact that new players were relentlessly spamming, something I devoted myself not to do. It wasn't the fact that any opponent had a built in unfair mechanic to just take your turn back after an opponent rightfully earned a punish, or the fact that anybody could throw out ultimates so easily that you'd get an entire round you earned the win on robbed from you because someone panicked and pressed one button. It wasn't even the fact that movement was heavily gutted, so I couldn't practice Korean Backdash to cause my enemy to wiff when they were being too aggressive. If it were just those things, I could have adjusted and adapted, changing my playstyle up so I could match their aggressiveness and keeping pace with my own. What made Tekken 8 feel so wrong was that all of this was heavily rewarded, while my honest playstyle was not. Spamming strings and moves you didn't understand the frame data for was now the new meta, and being honest was not a thing anymore. Anybody could just press any buttons instead of trying to be strategic and outsmart your opponent. Combos were a waste of time and barely did enough damage to matter. There wasn't respect in anybody's gameplay anymore. I never saw someone Korean Backdash and punish my wiff with a perfectly timed launcher, because that wasn't a thing anymore. I never saw someone notice that they used the same string twice in a row and backed off to clear their mind and not spam. Hell, I didn't even see anybody try to do flashy combos that required work. All that mattered was spamming and getting off a Heat Smash, and if the enemy gets you near death, spam Rage Art. Nobody needed to learn their character like it was back in Tekken 7. Nobody was trying to achieve victory, they just wanted to watch the opponent lose.   And believe me, I defended the game when it first came out. However, as time wore on, I realized I never got that high that I got from Tekken 7. I never felt like I beat the opponent because I read their next move and beat them with my knowledge, I only ever beat them because they had no idea what I was doing. Tekken 8 lost so much of its identity, and I tried to voice my concern to the community, but I was met with dismissive comment from people brand new to the series who had jumped on the bandwagon and wanted to act like they knew what Tekken was like before. Criticism that could have helped the game got drowned out, and eventually I dropped Tekken 8, followed by my friend who couldn't stand what the game had become following close behind me.   As a community, we feel dejected. Tekken is too easy now. They made every character beginner friendly but took out all of the hardest things in Tekken that you could learn. Player expression was gutted, as you probably have heard many people say, but its true. I've never seen someone in Tekken 8 do something that left me in awe and made me want to jump in and practice it, because its not difficult. Anybody who practices the game could do what any pro can currently do, and there's nothing skill-wise that can separate us. And unfortunately, our criticism and pleads didn't just get drowned out, but they got actively ignored by the developers. The devs only wanted to listen to the people who would sing Tekken 8's praise, and in response to everybody begging them to fix the game, they turned around and finished the job, thoroughly destroying the game with this second season. I'll admit, I haven't played the second season, so don't think I'm claiming something I'm not, but it doesn't require you to play it for you to know how bad their decisions were. They nerfed the already gutted movement system and doubled down on aggressive gameplay, to the point where you can't even sidestep mids. Oki is practically nonexistent. Defense is practically nonexistent. Its barely even a fighting game anymore. Its just a rushdown simulator, seeing who can press buttons faster than the other before their healthbars disappear. And the devs hear the outcries of their fanbase and would rather tell them to stop complaining, while thanking the few contrarians who defend the game who get proven to not even play it.   Let's face it, if the devs don't want to hear from us, then they don't want us here. Fine by me. I treated Tekken like a party game in the beginning, but grew to respect it when I saw how much time and focus I could put into it to improve my gameplay. Now, all people do is treat Tekken like a party game, and they don't ever grow out of that mindset because they're rewarded for doing so. So maybe Tekken is a party game now. This isn't the game I dedicated over a year to improving myself on. That game was left behind, just like we have been now. Tekken is dead.
