The Tekken 8 balance patch for the start of Season 2 has shown clearly that the direction the developers have planned for the game runs contrary to what makes the series enjoyable. They've sent a message that the initial problems with the games release not only [b]aren't being fixed, they're being worsened.[/b]  I want to establish my biases to appear as objective as I can. I'm not some oldhead set in my ways and nostalgic for some perfect edition that never existed, which is how I dismissed the early criticisms of more experienced players. I joined the series very late in to the prior entry, after the release of its last DLC. I had enough playtime to push through the noob frustration phase, and to learn how to play at a deep enough level to have a sense of what makes Tekken unique. That's not to say Tekken 7 was perfect, or that there weren't changes that needed to be made, simply that there was enough working that the more annoying elements could be seen past.  The devs seem to be scared of making the optimal play style how it was in tournament play in Tekken 7: players spending a lot of time backing away, and committing mostly to quick, low risk attacks, hoping to catch their opponents in an opening. [i]The solution appears to be to make a game where blocking is so difficult, it's not even worth it[/i], better off just risking an attack and hope you get lucky.  As I played Tekken 8 throughout the first season, I heard the complaints from top level players, but dismissed them: it doesn't really matter to me if a small percentage of players don't like it but there rest of us do. I refused to dislike the systems until I felt I understood them well enough. Eventually, it became clear to me and other vocal experienced players that optimal play wasn't about outplaying your opponents offence until they made a mistake that could be taken advantage of. Rather, the most successful strategy is rushing to be the first to the offensive so the opponent doesn't even get a chance to start. I don't want to be a player who complains because I don't know how to play well. [b]I'm complaining because when I play well, it's less fun.[/b]  The central feature, and problem, of Tekken 8's design is heat. Players enter heat with either a generic heat burst that can't be interrupted, and allows the player to act first if it's blocked, or various moves unique to every character. If a player entered heat with one of their own unique moves, they get positioned right in front of their opponent with a huge time advantage: the opponent has no way to dodge or interrupt, only block. Either way, when a player is in heat, all their attacks deal damage even when blocked, and the opponent is effectively forced to block, because every character has a heat smash, which has huge range, is very hard to dodge, does significant damage, and is advantageous to the attacker when blocked. In heat, the moves that are used to enter heat can be turned into heat dashes, which launch the opponent for a massive combo on hit, and give advantage on block so the opponent needs to keep blocking or risk getting counter hit. With all these combined, [i]your choices when your opponent is in heat are block, block some more, keep blocking, and hope you guess right[/i] if your opponent goes middle or low.  Once I understood the problems of Tekken 8's new design, I thought it was just an over-correction from Tekken 7's style, and would eventually be fine-tuned to a happy medium after some live fire testing. Season 2's patch was the wake up call that no such thing was coming. Despite a year of complaints about how frustrating it was to play against oppressive offence, the Tekken team have decided what the game needs is even stronger offence for every character. Instead of respecting what the players want, [b]they're stubbornly prescribing what they think we should want, and telling us we need to learn to like it.[/b]  The developer's interviews suggest that the objective of this design strategy is to make the game more exciting for new players, but I don't think it actually accomplishes that. An inexperienced player wouldn't know why what they're doing works, so they can't take full advantage of it. The standard of skill based matchmaking means that newer players are matched with other low skilled players, so they wouldn't need an oppressive core system that weakens the experience for everyone else, because low skilled players by definition could be beaten by anything. If a new player sticks with the game, and learns the optimal “go into heat, never let your opponent press” strategy, then they'll inevitably get bored when they figure out, that there's no more to learn about the game, just keep doing what you've been doing. I'm going to guess the actual target is fans of single player action games, who are used to playing against AI controlled enemies who can't interrupt you once you start attacking them, and the skill being rewarded is optimizing getting the most of your attacks.  If you haven't played Tekken and are considering buying it, as it says above, I don't recommend it. If you're expecting a deep, complex game that you can spend a long time improving in, the game works against you for it. If you just want to play briefly for the thrill of a simple action experience, the game doesn't offer much for you there. The story is... ok as far as the low standard of fighting game stories, but not something you really need to experience. The “special style” simplified control scheme is like overly restrictive training wheels that allow you to do so little, I don't see how it could feel like you're doing anything. It'd be jarring to switch to full controls, compared to something like Street Fighter 6, where modern controls give you most of your options, you play mostly the same way, and it becomes a meaningful decision between faster inputs or more options.  Don't buy Tekken 8. The development team have sacrificed a loyal fanbase to make a game for nobody.

Let me start by saying: I love Tekken. I’ve played it for years, and I’m deeply invested in what makes this franchise tick. That’s why I feel compelled to speak honestly about Tekken 8. While I agree with much of the criticism being shared online, I want this to come from a place of care, not cruelty. This game has potential—but it's being held back by some fundamental design decisions that I believe hurt the very identity of Tekken.  The "Aggression" Philosophy—Good in Theory, Bad in Execution The developers have made it clear that Tekken 8 is about emphasizing aggression. That’s not a bad direction on its own—but how they’ve implemented it doesn’t reward smart offense. Instead, it often rewards brute force.  Heat Engagers are the biggest example. Many characters now have long-range, mid attacks that lead to +17 on block and force you into oppressive stance mixups. In a game like Tekken, which traditionally gave defenders a toolkit to outthink or outmaneuver pressure (sidestep, parry, backdash, armor, counter-hit tools), this feels like a massive downgrade in gameplay depth.  If my only option is to block and guess in a 50/50 over and over again, the mind game of neutral disappears. Tekken always rewarded players for earning their pressure—now, too much of it is handed out for free. These plus-on-block situations don’t feel earned; they feel automatic.  Skipping Neutral Isn’t Aggression—It’s a Shortcut When someone can throw out a heat engager from a distance and immediately start a stance mixup, it bypasses everything that made Tekken’s neutral beautiful. If those moves must be in the game, they shouldn’t grant stance transitions at advantage on block. At the very least, make that part a conscious, punishable decision.  Let’s reward players for getting in and setting up, not just giving them easy access to oppressive flowcharts.  The Damage is Just Too High Heat Bursts and many character combos hit way too hard. When even basic sequences take off a third of a health bar or more, the pacing of the match becomes overwhelming. The game doesn’t breathe. There’s no room for long-term adaptation or reads when you’re dead in 3-5 mixups.  Tekken has always had explosive damage, but the current numbers are pushing it too far, especially combined with the new oppressive tools.  The Rise of the “God Buttons” Another issue is move diversity—or rather, the lack of it. Too many characters now have one or two “god buttons”: long reach, fast, safe, near-homing, low-risk, high-reward. These buttons do too much. They check too many boxes.  Part of Tekken’s depth used to come from specialization. You had to choose between tracking, speed, range, or safety. Now, too many tools give you everything at once.  Please Bring Back Defensive Options and Systems You Removed It genuinely feels like some of the deeper mechanics were removed not because they didn’t work—but because they required too much effort to balance or explain. Systems like oki, ki charge, and certain movement options are either gone or severely neutered. But these were the things that made Tekken unique and layered.  If new players are struggling, the answer isn’t to dumb the game down. It’s to create a robust tutorial system and community-driven learning tools. Tekken is at its best when the community is active, engaged, and empowered to share knowledge.  Visual Clarity > Flash A small but important note: the game looks great, but the visual noise has become a problem. Lasers, explosions, tornadoes—it's all a bit much.  I actually like the new HUD effects, but I think they should be redesigned to be more subtle and integrated into the actual action. For example, show damage numbers next to the hit (like FF-style pop-ups), and keep the tornado indicator visual only. Clean, readable, informative UI should take priority over cinematic flair.  What Aggression Could Look Like To be clear, I love aggression in Tekken. But the most iconic forms of pressure don’t come from looping 50/50s. They come from players dashing in, threatening space, baiting responses, and conditioning opponents. There’s nothing more Tekken than a high-tension moment where no one is pressing buttons—but everyone’s doing something.  Even ki charges added a fun layer: the user is at risk, the defender can read and punish, and both players are actively making choices.  Final Thoughts It’s frustrating because I truly thought Tekken 7 was a testbed for a better, smarter Tekken 8. And while some systems have evolved in promising ways (Heat can be fun when used thoughtfully), it feels like the wrong lessons were taken from Tekken 7’s success.  Tekken doesn’t need to be Street Fighter. It doesn’t need to chase trends. It just needs to trust in what made it special—and empower players to play, not just guess.  Please continue listening to the community, not just the loudest voices, but the thoughtful ones too. We're not here to tear it down—we want to build something better with you.

I spent a year learning back 2 loops with Lee and they removed the use for it by simplifying his combo routes. I've just reached a point where the investment is not worth it even though I've poured so much into it. If you're a newbie don't take this game serious. Attacks that give plus on block situations (favorable recovery situations) are no longer earned, but delivered on silver platters. Sometimes, you're able to duck under moves that do this, but they added dangerous mid attacks (must stand up to guard) to deter you from doing this. This means that if you try to do anything under this pressure, you're bound to get counter hit. The gameplay that results of this is that both players take turns doing 10 attacks each. Or, as many attacks as it takes until one player is dead. Often, it is the first player that enters Heat status that wins the round.  The game is guessing. There is no depth left. Attacks are changed so that they go through parries or reversals. Strings (sequence of attacks) that can be interrupted are no longer implemented. Many strings are implemented with high moves that you can normally duck under, but you're stunlocked during them so you can do nothing - it's very unintuitive. As I mentioned earlier, attacks get increased tracking, so sidestepping is not an option either. This results in dichotomous, two-way gameplay that means you either 1: try to retaliate to break up their attacks and risk getting counter hit, or 2: block and continue to block because attacking is not favorable for you. You may ask yourself: if I just stand there and block the other player's attack by attack, can't I just wait until the round is over if I have a lead in health? No, because in this game you take a lot of chip damage, aka damage inflicted by blocking!  Everything becomes easier to do. Attacks that has been in the series for more than 20 years change inputs for no reason. When I say for no reason, I mean it: Lee had his QCB+4 changed to QCF+4 (quarter circle back or forward motion, followed by right kick button). That's not even easier, it just messes up everybody's muscle memory! When you get hit by certain moves and fall to the ground, you used to have to hold back in order to roll back safely. If you didn't, the opponent can get free damage on you while you are on the ground. As a result, you now do the quick roll back whether you want to or not; it's automatic. No longer can you stay down to break up the opponents pace and timing. It felt really satisfying to do as well, even if it was the most obvious choice in most situations.  In Tekken, you may or may not be aware: each character has more than 100 attacks each. And there are almost 40 characters! Let me ask you this: why would you spend countless upon countless of hours to learn the frames and properties of more than 4000 attacks, if every character plays exactly the same in the end?  In the end, you have a game series that had a ton of depth, reduced into a game that requires way less skill, is way less interesting, has way worse match flow (defense is boring said who? Tekken 7 matches were action-packed!).  ...And for what?  So that it's more fun to watch? But if players don't have fun, the watchability will suffer. So that newcomers can have a better time? ...but will they though? They have to be on the receiving end of the endless onslaught all characters now has as well. And, once you get better at the game, you may come to the same realization I have.  If you're nostalgic about Tekken 3 or Tekken 5, sure, go ahead and goof around with some friends. That's what Tekken 8 is for. Thank you Namco for 20+ years of Tekken!

This review will stay negative until the problems addressed for season 2 here are acknowledged and dealt with. I won't speak about specific characters (except for a couple of examples), but rather the direction the game is taking, what made Tekken unique, and the design philosophy behind everything. The core mechanic of Tekken has always been movement. How you interacted with your opponent through movement was one of the core aspects of the game. Think about things like sidestepping a string, exploiting a character's weak side by stepping to said direction, etc. With the latest season 2 update, they've removed depth and skill expression in favor of oppressive offense and moves that cover a character's weaknesses. What this causes is very limited options for both the defender and the attacker, since now the attacker has moves that cover most if not all options of counterplay against a certain string, move, or character altogether, meaning there is less creativity when attacking. As an example of this, I'll use Kazuya. He's always been a defensive character, and his offense revolved around strong mixups from his crouchdash. The counterplay to this was that he was weak to sidestepping to the left, which beat every option. To address this, the Kazuya player had to implement new strategies like doing dash into electric which realigned and hit the opponent while they sidestepped. The defender now had another option, they could sidestep into duck to cover both options. The Kazuya player, once again, could adapt by changing his timing, wavedashing, mixing in with a quick mid like ws2 which was a risky option but would work on a read about the opponent sidestepping and ducking. What this created is a very layered gameplay, where both the attacker and the defender had to outsmart eachother. Now, Kazuya has access to a new move: uf1, which is a safe homing mid created for the purpose of negating his weakness of being stepped to the left, as stated on the patch notes ("(...) enabling him to agressively pressure opponents who rely on frequent sidesteps for defense"), which takes away from the nuance his approach to offenense had, and thus also taking away from the defender. This isn't unique to Kazuya, I'm just using this example to highlight a trend of covering character's weaknesses and taking away skill expression in favor of a more homogenized cast, where no one has clear weaknesses that can be exploited.  Adding to the homogenization of the cast, a lot of the characters now have moves or strings that transition into stance, some of them being + on block, forcing a mixup. This forced stance mixups aren't fun to play against, because it doesn't feel earned. If you transition into stance from a whiff or block punish, then the mixup is earned, but we're seeing transitions that force a mixup on block, further punishing defense, which I haven't commented on yet, but was a promise that they made about season 2 ("That's why for Season 2, we'd like to focus on defense in terms of the lateral aspects of a 3D fighting game"). The direction the game is taking is more based on stance mixup offense, which was restricted to certain characters and with room for counterplay (Hwoarang being an example of a stance mixup character that had holes in his offense that you could exploit).  Speaking of character weaknesses, that's what made each of them unique; having to work around those weaknesses made the gameplay much more dynamic instead of every character being able to do everything perfectly. But patching weaknesses isn't the only way they strip characters of their identity. Take for example Paul. He received new transitions into deep dive from different moves to further enforce stance mixups. Paul has never been a stance character, his identity was always that of a high damage, volatile but flawed character.  What this leaves us with is the question: Who is this patch for? Casuals will have a difficult time defending against this oppressive aggression, veterans who mained certain characters that have had their identities taken away, often leading to techniques that have been practiced and perfected for years becoming obsolete (Law's CH ws4 confirm into DSS comes to mind) and have already given their opinion about the nature of the aggression and 50/50 tendency this game has. Which leads us to the answer: This patch satisfies no one.

Season 2 has ruined this game. Over thirty years of refinement to some of the most technical and interesting game play in any fighting game, reduced to 50/50 mixups, atrocious balance across the board, and a general lack of understanding what has made this IP so popular over the years. The ability to not only learn a character and how to beat them, but to be able to learn your opponent and play THEM, is what has made Tekken so compelling if still being a little intimidating for those who are new. This patch seemed like it was going to adjust offense and tone it down while giving players more defensive tools for more counter-play and interactions with each other.   Instead, they triple or even quadruple downed on how brain-dead offensive this game has become. Heat while being an interesting mechanic was kind of the first red-flag that this game is going to have some shenanigans and BS that will be tough to get around. And after a year of making fixes along the way, Tekken 8 was close to feeling like a very balanced and refined game. However, this season 2 patch has knocked us back to square one and even some further than that. It feels as though we are back to the first beta test where heat was usable more than once per round.  I don't know who this season was for. It's not for OG's of the game, it's not even for casuals or newcomers. It has destroyed the one thing T8 has had going for it, was a delicate balance of counter-play options and engagements that felt as equal as they could for a 25+ roster fighting game. I don't know who is responsible for this at Bandai Namco; I don't know if it's Harada, Nakatsu (the NEW director of T8), or suits at Namco demanding the team to chase trends and make changes that other games are doing, but almost everything in season 2 is awful. What makes this worse is that there are some good changes; sidestepping being easier and having T8 be the FIRST game in the franchise to allow sidestepping into the foreground was enough of changes for season 2. But alas, we got way more than anyone wanted.  Don't play or buy this game until it gets fixed. It will; it's going to take at LEAST until the end of April apparently, which is too long. But either way, the respect and trust of the community towards project: Tekken is gone, and maybe for good. Now, we need to work extra hard to get back to what we had before S2. Such a shame... such a waste.  _______________________ Update as of the Season 3 Patch on March 17th, 2026:  This game is cooked. Simple as that. "Back to basics." "More deliberate." "A fresh start." These buzzwords were nothing more than marketing for the new seasons. Yes; they are going to be making future changes going forward in the coming  months, but this patch just shows they don't understand what people want. And even if they make meaningful changes, there are tons of interactions that slipped through the cracks that go against the changes they created. It's a failure on Project Tekken to understand their own game and the communities sentiments. The fact they didn't patch this game a single time for nine months after the disaster that was the launch of Season 2 and players waited for so long and this is what they got. They don't respect you. Please, find another fighting game to play that actually respects both you and your time. ___________________________ Update as of 5/29/2026:  Game is FINALLY starting to make changes that are generally healthy for the game balance wise. Heat is being toned down across the board, and we are now starting to see some hyper specific character changes. Now, it'll be interesting to see what happens because they are running out of nerfs to hear and will need to tackle characters on a case by case basis. We still have some really strong moves on certain characters but if they can generally continue to nerf the oppressive moves in the game, we can finally get Tekken 8 to a place it should've been a year ago. While Tekken players are notorious for often complaining about things that end up being minor, on this occasion, it is unfortunately everything we've been worried about and worse.  Season 1 was, on release, a big mixed bag because the system improvements that reduced Tekken 7's extreme turtling problem, and general performance improvements (which are the main reason anyone at this point would still pick Tekken 8 over 7), were shipped alongside confusing offensive adjustments that had a tendency to encourage a style of trying to out-offence your opponent and made the concept of playing heavily defensive outright detrimental, with many characters being given ways to force through their combos even against someone carefully blocking.  In addition, some character identity felt like it was being sidelined to make more room for this; a notable example in my opinion being Lee Chaolan, a character who had long specialised in evasive counterhits that made him extremely risky to press into, but traded that off for having very weak abilities to break open a defensive player, and therefore being very reliant on conditioning and reads against the opponent's buttons. In Tekken 8, he was gifted more ways to play rushdown offence and became depressingly good at it, while the only thing they could think to give him for a heat passive was "make his execution free".  As a community, some were in generally in favour of this, though the overall sentiment even among fans of Tekken 8 was that there were a few cases of characters simply being too good on offence, giving little room to the opponent outside of "guess-for-your-life" gameplay, which overshadowed many of the characters who had some critical weakness or weaknesses that could be exploited.   As Season 1 came to a close, the devs at Bandai told us that we were being listened to. They told us that season 2 would be a total overhaul that would greater reward defence and that they were focusing on it as being a defensive upgrade patch. The initial Tekken Talk livestream laid out their broad policy goals of toning down heat-based pressure, and bringing down enforced aggression as a playstyle in general.  The next Tekken Talk, the Anna Special, was not promising. Despite all they had said, they still were adding not only the ability to enforce even more mixup situations out of a heat engager, but they showed off several pieces of upcoming character changes - which revealed more stance mixes, more ways to get into those stances, and specifically these mixes were being given to already top tier characters like Jin and King. Add in other system changes such as taking chip damage even when a throw is broken, and it seemed like offence had been helped more than it had been hurt. But still, we waited for the patch.  We had to wait for the patch, because the devs uncharacteristically decided we weren't going to receive the patch notes until the moment the game itself was playable. And once we got there it became clear why: across the ENTIRE board, characters had had their offensive capabilities completely juiced. Every character summary came with the introduction that they were "improving offence" and in several cases outright removing primary weaknesses.  Once the patch was playable, things only got worse, as death combos were discovered. Setups that lead to bugged guaranteed damage from Paul, offence loops that literally could not be escaped from without taking a lot of damage from Jack, and more. So many characters had their counterplay completely shaved off and reduced to "correctly guess when I'm going to do a low". Lee got even more of his identity stripped out as various inputs and routes were made even easier for him.  The devs blatantly lied to us when they told us Season 2 would be defensive. They were aware of what was in this patch, and chose to tell us that anyway. The only thing they have even remotely responded to since then is saying they will remove the throwbreak chip. They have completely spat on the competitive scene of this game in favour of catering to people who barely play it; apparently this is their target audience now, and they want Tekken 8 to be nothing more than a total party game where someone with no experience is on a level playing field with someone who has devoted themselves to the series for 2 decades.  I cannot under any circumstance recommend Tekken 8 as it currently stands.

It genuinely saddens me to write this review, but given the current state of the game, alongside others in the community, I feel these issues need to be pointed out in the hopes that the development team will respond to the feedback soon and work on fixing the glaring issues. By all means, commit to your vision of an accessible game, but focus on making it easy to learn and hard to master, not easy to win regardless of skill level. Strike a balance between aggression and defensive game play that does not dilute the identity of the franchise so much that the aspects of Tekken that veterans and even new comers have grown to love are unrecognisable.  As someone who enjoys fighting games, but isn't particularly good at playing them, Tekken 8 was the first game in the franchise that felt accessible to me due to the Arcade Quest mode and the plethora of learning tools including the replay system, Super Ghost Battle, an in-depth practice mode with punishment training and combo trials to cut your teeth with getting to know your character while giving you a pathway to work up to learning optimal combos and online practice that was added via a patch post-launch.  Prior to playing this game, I had no friends on Steam due to rarely playing games online, however, after picking up Tekken 8 that quickly changed. As I continued learning the game and progressing on my journey with my chosen character, people began reaching out to me, either to simply say good games, and/or to give me advice and play sets with me to show me the ropes and to help me to both improve and enjoy the game on a deeper level. The Tekken community has been very helpful and welcoming. I now have 60 passionate fighting game/Tekken players added on Steam who I frequently chat to about the game and run sets with; this is genuinely the first time I have felt part of a gaming community.  With a variety of training tools at my disposal and a community of helpful and welcoming players I was able to chip away at learning the game and its systems while still having plenty to learn if I ever hoped to hold my own against higher skilled players. Though Season 1 was not without its issues, characters still had unique identities and play styles and any time a character felt overwhelming to play against I would hop into the replay, realise that there was a clear counter play, and, that I was pressing or moving when I shouldn't be, not stepping when I should be or not blocking lows, ducking highs and punishing when I should be. These were all things that were recognisable and gave me clear goals to work on.  With the release of season 2, character identities and play styles have seemingly been radically diluted or flat out scrapped; most characters have received buffs and along with the increase of chip damage and combo damage the game play has become extremely volatile; in online matches I'd either end up with my back to the wall eating chip damage and not being able to find a counter play, or, I would make a slight mistake and lose the majority of my health bar. To add to this, there are plenty of examples of broken or poorly balanced moves players have recorded. After hopping into my replays, and realising that this would be the experience until further changes and fixes, learning the game was no longer enjoyable to me and with defensive options continuing to be overlooked learning the game felt pointless and made the game feel less accessible to me.  There is a great game at the heart of Tekken 8 that has unfortunately been over shadowed by a series of radical changes and design choices with the release of season 2. I still very much feel that the game has potential and would be thrilled if the community's feedback was taken into account and the game was able to bounce back offering a fun and accessible game for newcomers encouraging learning, while maintaining the core Tekken experience that long-time players have come to know.  All I can do at this stage, is keep my fingers crossed that the community's voices are heard.

Having played with the Season 2 update prior to forming my assessment, I feel compelled to address concerning trends in the game’s current trajectory. While my critique stems from a place of genuine appreciation for the title, it is evident that recent changes have inadvertently shifted the core balance toward an asymmetric focus on overwhelming offensive strategies, undermining the intended emphasis on defensive counterplay—a stated goal of this "defense-oriented" patch.    The current meta now disproportionately rewards aggressive, unrelenting offense, leaving defensive options feeling ineffective and reactive. This has reduced matches to an over-reliance on 50/50 guesswork scenarios, where successful defense often hinges on luck rather than strategic skill expression. Such dynamics erode the depth of gameplay and risk alienating players seeking meaningful tactical interplay.    Furthermore, the homogenization of character kits is alarming. While the buffs to universal mechanics like sidestep may have aimed to improve accessibility, they have come at the cost of diluting unique character identities. Equally troubling is the decision to amplify already dominant “top-tier” characters, elevating them to near-uncontestable status rather than fostering a balanced competitive ecosystem.    Though efforts to welcome newcomers through streamlined mechanics are commendable, this should not come at the expense of strategic depth or roster individuality. A truly accessible game can coexist with nuanced, high-skill gameplay it requires careful calibration, not oversimplification.    I urge the development team to reassess these changes, recentering balance on rewarding skill, preserving character uniqueness, and ensuring that defensive play feels as viable and intentional as offensive pressure. The foundation for a great experience remains; it simply needs more thoughtful iteration to thrive.

I can't in good faith recommend Tekken 8 in it's current state.  I've been a long time Tekken player and lover of the game series. Tekken 8 unfortunately started in quite a precarious state in my opinion, and things have (mostly) just gotten worse.  The balancing for Season 2 (which just released) was the stone that broke the camels back. All of the major issues with the balancing of the game had been time and time again made apparent, both from community outcry, as well as seen from high level competitive events. With Season 2, instead of addressing these issues and attempting to resolve them, they 'doubled down' on most of them, making the problems with the game significantly worse than before.  Tekken has in the past, been a game where Defense is king, and Tekken 8 aimed to shake that formula up and make Aggression the highlight. While the idea in concept isn't a poor one, as it more easily gets people acclimated to the game and helps bring in newer fans as well as stir drama among older fans to keep the hype going, it did show a variety of issues in the early stages of the game, namely the Heat System as well as the damage just being too over-tuned. All it takes is 1 or 2 bad guesses in a 50/50 scenario and you're dead. And again, i'm not directly opposed to the idea of a more Aggressive Tekken than we have seen in the past, but it was overkill, and made the game feel like a lottery based system where you just throw all your crap at the wall and see if they can stop you, and 9 times out of 10, they cant and you just win for free.  With the new patches from Season 2, they made this worse.  While the lower-tier characters felt decent overall, the top-tier characters were just on a different level than the others, so understandably the community thought the best choice would be to nerf the top-tiers to bring them to the level the other characters were at (This would overall result in less needed balancing, reducing strain on the Dev team, as well as would more consistently keep the balance of the overall game in line, leading to less unforeseen circumstances). However the Dev team decided to instead buff everyone (INCLUDING the top-tiers). This resulted in not only the lower-tier characters not catching up to the high tiers in any way, but making the game extremely inconsistent and lottery based in its gameplay, further making the issues addressed previously with damage and aggression EVEN WORSE.  While Tekken has at it's core, been a fantastic game, Tekken 8 has been increasingly receiving dubious and questionable balancing patches made to the game (See; King), and unless this changes, I recommend anyone interested in Tekken 8 refrain until the issues are dealt with.

To preface; this perspective is one from someone who is a fan of many fighting games. I am not a professional, but I am proficient at a handful of fighting games.  Season 2 balance changes are the single greatest advertisement for Virtua Fighter that Sega could have ever asked for. I don't think there could have been a more tone deaf response to many people's complaints about Tekken 8. Any reason to play Tekken as opposed to other fighting games has been slowly removed from even before the release of this entry. Sure, the devs will allow you to sidestep into the foreground from crouch, but how often are you going to be sidestepping when every character has plus on block mids into stance 50/50s where your only option is to guess right on the high or low block?   The homogenization of the entire cast of characters has been mortifying to see. Characters are simply not allowed to have unique strengths and weaknesses. I mained Lee in this game, a character known for being slippery with evasive moves, strong counter hits, solid generic attacks, strong keep-out moves, and rewarding high execution and knowledge of the game's fundamentals. His strengths WERE contrasted by his weaknesses; many linear buttons (i.e. not very good tracking. best moves are weak to sidestep), not many hard hitting mid attacks, weaker lows in terms of damage and having the ability to continue offense after hitting lows. Offense is not Lee's strong suit, and you generally had to take greater risks when pressing the offensive. This has been his character identity, core pillars of his design for several tekken games. The developers decided to scrap his character identity, because not only did they nerf moves associated with his keep-out game, they decided his lows need to provide more offensive opportunity, allowing to you more easily continue the offensive after a successfully hit low. Then they gave him one button, plus on block power mids to go into a stance mixup, something completely alien to Lee's core identity. This is only one example of the mass homogenization of the Tekken cast, and it was happening in tekken 7 in the game's later patches, but not to this extent.  Bandai seems to want to cater to a casual audience, but for the life of me, I can't even recommend this to a casual or recommend this as a person's first fighting game. The offense is so smothering and so frustrating to lose to because it doesn't feel like you lost because you were outplayed or outwitted. It feels like you lost a coin flip.  If Bandai Namco's goal was to, in one fell swoop, alienate the core fanbase of their long running franchise and, piece by piece, remove remove or simplify every mechanic and interaction unique to tekken in the hopes they can make more money off an audience that doesn't play fighting games, then they have done it. Tekken 8 is a party game now. Worst april fools joke ever.

I genuinely enjoyed my time with Tekken 8 in season 1. I've played Tekken relatively casually for several years, and while I'm far from a high-level player. I was actually one of the people okay with the more aggressive direction the game initially took. It wasn’t perfect, but I had hope. I assumed Season 1 would be the rockiest part of the game’s lifespan. I thought, surely, they’d refine things over time. I thought they learned from the launch of Tekken 7.  So... What about Season 2? I got really exited to hear the devs talk about their plans to increase defensive options in season 2, while I thought the aggressiveness wasn't the biggest issue, my hope was that they would take the great elements of Tekken 8 and refine everything overtime. Tekken has always been a game where defense was actually arguably the most interesting part.  When the devs announced plans to add more defensive options, I was excited. Defense has always been one of Tekken’s most interesting aspects, and even though I didn’t think the aggression was the core issue, I welcomed a more balanced approach. I was ready to see the great parts of Tekken 8 polished into something even better.  Instead, what we got a season that feels like the opposite of everything that was promised.  The only real defensive "buff" we got was a slightly improved sidestep—but even that was overshadowed by almost every character getting buffs to tracking, aggression, and raw forward momentum. They didn’t tone down aggression; they supercharged it. Defensive players didn’t get tools—they got reminders that this game isn’t made for them anymore. Instead of refining the game, Want to sidestep? Good luck—everything tracks harder. Want to block? Get ready for chip damage anyway. Tech a throw? Cool, eat some chip for your efforts. Even throw breaks feel like losing interactions now. And somehow, even top-tier characters got stronger.  More coin flips. More 50/50s. More chaos.  It feels less like I’m playing against someone and more like I’m gambling with my character’s life every few seconds. The core systems aren’t helping me, it now feels like they’re actively working against me. And that’s a miserable feeling for a game that once prided itself on deep, thoughtful mechanics.  I was hoping for a season that encouraged player-to-player interaction, strategy, and adaptation. Instead, Tekken 8 has taken a big step toward becoming a party game—and not in a fun way.  People are frustrated for a reason. And if you’re wondering why so many are speaking up now, it’s because this season made one thing painfully clear: If this is the future of Tekken, I’m not sure I want to be part of it...

As a player with over 3500 hours in Tekken 7 I was very excited to see what the next entry in the series would be. My review is being written as of Day 3 of Season 2.  [h2] Network and PC performance [/h2] When the game released on PC it still had performance and network issues that were reported in the network test. As a user with a custom build machine that is tuned well and can play all the latest games on highest settings Tekken 8 still has performance issues at times. Every time I am on the character select screen the game will become slightly choppy when swapping and selecting characters. The game can sometimes crash on PC. Users that played Tekken 7 on PC will remember if you would alt tab there was a chance the game would crash. This is still on ongoing issue with Tekken 8.  Regarding net code issues, it still feels like Tekken 7 season 4. I am not a developer so I do not know what can be done to improve the net code but it is sad to see a fighting game release in the year that it did (2024) and have such poor net code when other titles like street fighter 6 and guilty gear strive have phenomenal roll back net code.   [h2] Presentation + content [/h2] The costume redesigns the characters received are a warm welcome and do a lot for the returning cast. The music and stages in the game are brilliant. Tekken 8 honestly has one of my favourite soundtracks in the series. I was really looking forward to the story mode as I was invested in seeing what happened after the ending of Tekken 7. The story mode was brilliant and is easily my favourite one iv played in a fighting game. Hopefully we can see a big follow up during a DLC release for Tekken 8.  Customisation is cool and I hope it continues to see free updates over time. The jukebox features is something I always wanted for PC users so it's nice to see us finally get it after missing out on it being a PS4 exclusive for Tekken 7.  I do wish there was more game modes available to play. For example having Team battle come back from the older entries would be really fun for offline play with friends or online in private lobbies.  [h2] Gameplay [/h2] This entry is very rewarding for aggressive play. The new heat system promotes players to stay on the offensive rather than  using movement and blocking to counter play their opponent.  With the new chip system you are punished for blocking and trying to play slowly to get into a better position. This is a huge change in the direction from the previous entry (Tekken 7) where you could use that games movement system to block and take your time to get out of situations. Since Tekken Tag tournament 1 (1999) players have been using movement (Korean back dash cancelling + sidestepping) to avoid these guessing situations and create whiff opportunities however with Tekken 8 having nerfed movement  (With season 2 they have buffed side steps which is nice but back dash cancelling still feels horrible) you will find yourself at times being forced to guess on a 50/50.  I think some of the hit effects are too much. When Clive activates heat and starts doing through his moves it really takes away from the fight and is too distracting.   Every member of the roster got some new tools coming into Tekken 8.  Characters have new single hit and combo strings to change how their game play looks and feels. Some users may find characters play vastly different than their previous entries (Jack-8) is a great example of this.  I think it is important that characters feel unique and have clear defined strengths and weaknesses. I am unsure what approach the developer team are taking with Tekken 8. But it feels to me that characters are starting to feel similar and lose their identity which is a first for a series that has so many unique and interesting characters. Take King for example. Does he need to have the best counter hit string in the game (DF+2,1) which you can hit confirm for a full combo? This does not make sense to me. As a wrestler type character he should be more focused on doing big single hits and using his cool chain throws.   There are currently 14 characters in the game with the guard break mechanic (Bryan, Clive, Devil Jin, Feng, Heihachi, jack, Kuma, Lidia, Panda, Paul, Reina, Shaheen, Steve, Yoshimitsu) which will break through your block and guarantee a follow up vs you.  In Tekkn 7 only two characters had this functionality (Lidia and Fahkumram) with Bryan also has a unique version of this mechanic since Tekken 3 (Taunt). Seeing it become such a normal part of the game really has made it no longer feel special.   With the latest update to the game (Season 2) we were expecting the developers to tone down how aggressive the game is and show us what defensive options they were working on. Since the latest patch characters across the board have become even stronger and more oppressive. More characters have access to 100+ dmg combos without rage and new tools to force you to block and guess on a 50/50 as you cannot use movement to escape situations. Chip damage is still a massive issue and heat lasts for too long when activated.  There are also currently some game breaking bugs from characters such as jack and Paul that have new moves that seem to have slipped past testing and are causing interactions that were not intended. It being only day 3 of season 2 more bugs could be found in the coming days/weeks. Hopefully we get an emergency patch to fix them.  [h2] Closing thoughts [/h2]  I am not sure what the future holds for the game.    I feel like Bandai Namco have been developing Tekken 8 to be enjoyable for the user on the attack without thinking how does it feel to be the user on the defending side.  Just because being on the offensive feels good doesn't mean being on the defending side has to feel bad. But with the core systems in place for Tekken 8 that is exactly how the game feels. From speaking with casual and pro players it does not seem that either group is happy with the direction the game is going.   I think the developers have lost sight of what made Tekken so much fun. It wasn't big flashy hit effects, over powered moves, characters having no defined weaknesses.  [list] [*] It was the unique characters and their specifics strengths. [*] It was seeing someone put years into a character and mastering what their specific game plan was and aspiring to be that great. [*] It was being a new player and seeing a clip of someone moving around the screen fast thinking "Wow how are they moving like that??". [*] It was the people who took the time out of their day to host online and offline events just for people to show up and play their favourite fighting game. [*] It was seeing people coming together from different countries to compete and change their lives [/list]  [b] It was the community.[/b]  And right now it feels like the developers are no longer listening to the community.  You can do as many collaborations and have as many guest characters as you want. If no one is around to play the game who will purchase the future dlcs you make?  I am lucky enough that I have a healthy offline scene of cool people who play for fun and want to improve. I hope the developers can open up a bit more with the community and maybe reach out for more feedback on future patches or ideas they have.  Everybody who purchased Tekken 8 loves the series. We just want to see it go in a different direction than the current one.  All the best   o/

Aside from the absolutely obnoxious balancing decisions made a few days ago, I have genuine concerns about Tekken as a whole.  I don't understand why this is the final straw with the community but they ignore everything else wrong with the game. Nothing wrong with only caring about the competitive aspect of the game but I don't think it's right that the folks who care about the story and the content outside of ranked match are almost entirely ignored. Tekken's story has been on a decline since Tekken 5 imo but Tekken 8 is different. It feels like the writers are telling us, "If you haven't checked out now, here's the time to do so."  Everyone who has played Tekken 7 knows that the game was centered around the end of the "Mishima Saga" and it "ended" with Heihachi's death. Almost immediately in season 1 of Tekken 8 he's back and canon?? Why even invest the time to making a cinematic story presented as a send off for Heihachi if you were just going to bring him back and almost retcon the entirety of Tekken 7? Every character that wasn't a Mishima got shoved off into character episodes in Tekken 7 and 8 like they're a nuisance. What made Tekken stand out was its unique cast of characters and seeing them be treated so poorly since Tekken 5 is a huge problem that can't be ignored anymore.  The mtx's also go unnoticed but I'd say it's a FAR greater issue than some frame data. Why are we paying so much for items that were free in the last game? We played Tekken 7 for 7 years we know what it looks like when we see it. Nostalgia costumes $4 a pop and on top of that there's a freakin' battle pass?? That's not including the season pass which is more money for the characters and stages but remember this is already a $70 game.   We've seen MUCH better and more in-depth customization in previous titles such as Tekken 6 and Tag 2, but it's severely lacking in Tekken 8 because most of it is behind a paywall and the flexibility of said customization isn't half as flexible as past iterations from over a DECADE AGO.  In previous titles such as the aforementioned Tekken 6 and Tag 2, A lot of customization items were unlocked through ghost battle and arcade battle. That's hardly the case in Tekken 8 since most of the items require real money instead of the in game fight money. Ghost Battle used to be fun to grind and obtain new items but that isn't present in Tekken 8.  Staple game modes like Tekken Force and Team Battle aren't present in Tekken 8, nor is the tournament mode added in Tekken 7. I genuinely want the soul to come back to Tekken and this isn't it.

𝗧𝗪: 𝗬𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗜𝗡𝗚!  i gotta admit, i had high hopes for the game despite it being already a 50/50-mania. being a casual member of the fgc as well as tekken games in general, i never actually got into fighting games competitively because i was just a kid going through school. and now i have the time and equipment to do so, i have picked up tekken 8. this game was never my first tekken, the first game i've played in the franchise was tekken tag in the arcades and i was at least 6 years old, and later at 2022 when i got a good enough device, i got tekken 7 to play with a friend. that being said, tekken 8 is (or was) the first tekken game in the franchise that i've been playing competitively, even though i know that i suck most of the time. but it was the enjoyment i got playing with friends and other either it be casual or competitive that got me to stay. sure forced 50/50s are a problem, sure the game is sometimes buggy, sure there are a lot of characters that are broken, sure the heat system is busted, sure there's a lot of tracking/homing that doesn't make sense animation-wise but i still enjoyed it because this is what i think pushes people to adapt and get better (forced 50/50s, bugs, and excessive tracking/homing will STILL be a problem which should be sorted out).    this leads me to this fiasco that is the most recent patch of the game, season 2 (ver 2.00.01 shown by that unnecessary watermark on the top of the screen when you're in an active game). more 50/50 pressure, more chip, more tracking, more bugs, the kind of stuff that makes me want season 1 back. why is it that way? i don't entirely know aside from the fact that the devs want the core of the game to stay aggressive. nothing wrong with wanting the game to stay aggressive, but if THIS is the result of that intention, i don't know what else to say. and aside from the egregious amount of added stance transitions and 50/50s and bugs, there are more things in this patch that personally annoy me which i will now list in the following as well as reasons why i find it so annoying:   - making move inputs easier (reducing the amount of execution and challenge).   - axis-correction when you execute a generic combo slightly off axis. (reducing creative combo routes and even potentially reducing off-axis combos that lead to higher overall damage).   - excessive tailspins (washes down character identity. no, seriously. doing a tailspin after a tornado then activating heat while the opponent is still in the tailspin state is probably one of the coolest things in this game imo. and to my knowledge, (correct me if i'm wrong) not every character can do that which in my personal opinion gives the player a reason to make combos and adapt without it. but the fact that you can do more of that in a single combo, hell, before a tornado and heat activation, just dilutes everything).   - more chip damage (need i say more?).  - ALMOST ALL of the cast's ability to be able to do a t7 super akouma vs chikurin TOD.   - replacing the ch property of ki charge with something lame (reduces smart plays/setups as well as reducing the reward for the risk).  - THE CAMERAMAN!! (update 2.00.02-03, i have been getting into FAR more situations where the camera man keeps making me fumble for no reason after some bs. i know it was fairly uncommon back in season 1, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's egregious now. i don't know if this has anything to do with season 2's automatic realignment when doing combos, but by god is it just not fun)  - [2.00.03 update] game eating my inputs. (dunno if this is just me, but i've been noticing the game's eating more of my inputs and isn't translating my notations into the game very well which costs me a lot of my matches, so i'll give this one just a tiny bit of a benefit of the doubt).  all of this accumulates to one thing, lack of player expression/creativity.   will i stop playing this game? probably not. the tekken series is one of my favorite fighting game franchise and even with the mess that's going on all at once, i still have hopes for the game. but i can't blame a lot of people, especially professional players, for giving this game heat, not the one the devs added in the game. everyone's distrust for this game as of now is valid and i truly hope that this game will take more steps forward than back.   thanks for reading my yap.

The Tekken series has been a part of my life since 2010. My closest friend and I put thousands of hours into the series between 6 through 7. I grinded rank, I practiced all the time. I love the Tekken series and it legitimately is a part of who I am. You will probably be able to find me in a nursing home and find me talking about Tekken. And when I eventually get to that nursing home maybe I'll be happier because I won't remember Tekken 8.   I've watched what I call "Modern Gaming" poison this series since the early days of 7 where DLC characters were pay to win strong, frame data was paid for, and Rage Arts and Rage Drives were implemented to cater to the legendary "FGC Spectator", a mythical person who only pays attention to a game if it has sparkly effects, meters, and cinematic supers. Genuinely I think they're insulting the intelligence of FGC Spectators that they wouldn't enjoy a more grounded tactical fighting game that is more about outwitting and outfighting your opponent.   I detest the heat system. I detest rage arts. I would very much like to play the game and not have to watch constant screen flashes and cinematics. I would like to listen to the soundtrack and not have to hear the constant bass drop of the heat system. I'm gonna use a buzzword phrase and state that it betrayed the vision of tekken.   I hate that every character needs a stack mechanic or install mechanic. I'm not playing tekken to get my good boy points for pressing a button combo, again marketing to what I can only imagine is a small child who loves seeing stacks increase like jingling keys in front of them.   I hate battle passes and paid customization! How dare they charge me for a costume that was from tag 2. That is genuinely insulting. Why would I grind a battlepass in a game that is this awful to play?   And the thing that frustrates me the most is the story. Bringing Heihachi back just makes me feel like an idiot for being so invested in the writing. As a fun fact: Nuclear tensions in America were very high in late May of 2018. We thought that nuclear war with North Korea was going to break out. The tekken story was so important to me, that I watched the leaked story mode cutscenes for tekken 7 online a week before the launch, specifically so that if I died in nuclear war, I could at least know if Kazuya beat Heihachi. I know thats stupid, but that's what tekken meant to me. And then a few months ago they just.... Take backsies huh? To say nothing of the very poor story mode that came packaged with Tekken 8 at launch.   I know that everyone is hating on the current patch as well. And looking at the changes I watch as they add more terribly offensive pressure and damage tools to each character, add more stances and more stance rushdowns, and I can't generate any more anger for this.   My Rage Meter is empty, my heat for tekken is zero. I'm watching a game series that I spent thousands of hours on sputter out and die and I have been asking myself for weeks "Did I waste my life playing tekken? Why was I spending so much time on this series?"   I would estimate 2500 hours of my life feel wasted at this point considering that all that skill, reaction, and space in my memory that tekken occupies has been wasted by what I feel is corporate greed (microtransactions, battle pass, DLC balance), and catering to the non-real FGC Spectator (rage arts, drives, heat, stances)  I don't like any other fighting games except for Soulcalibur and I have tried so many others. I don't enjoy any of them as much as I like my favorite 3d fighting game that at this point is dead to me, and might be dead forever. I don't know if corporate decisions are trying to kill tekken, I don't know if someone actually thought these changes were good ideas.   I miss tekken. I miss playing tekken with my friends. I would like if tekken 5, 6, or tag 2 were released on steam.  Maybe I'll go back to 7 because while I had complaints it was nowhere near as bad as this.   Thanks for reading if you did.  I want my favorite game back.

My Tekken Journey: From Love to... Whatever This Is  My journey into Tekken started with the free-to-play Tekken Revolution on PS3, and then TTT2 on the same console. Say what you want — that game was awesome. From the very beginning, I was hooked by the variety, the polish — everything felt super intentional. You could sidestep, backdash, crouch, poke with jabs... it felt tight. The way button presses matched the movement on screen was just chef’s kiss — it really gave you that "I’m in the fight" immersion.  It wasn’t overloaded with mechanics, yet every character had a massive movelist. There was this weird feeling of lightness to it — the kind of game you could sink hundreds of hours into and still feel like you’re learning something.  I jumped into Tekken 7 around Season 3 and stayed till the bitter end, all the way to the release of Tekken 8. Man, I loved T7. Sure, it had its flaws — Kunimitsu, Akuma, Marduk's dumb takedowns — but those felt like quirks, not game-breakers. At its core, Tekken 7 was beloved because it was understandable. You had time to block, think, adapt, switch up your strategy. It played more like chess than a brawler. That’s what made tournaments so dope — watching someone run Jin (a mid-tier pick) against busted stuff like Geese and actually win felt insane.  And then... Tekken 8 dropped.  And the soul of the game? Gone. That familiar feeling — gone. Now it’s all about guessing games, flashy mechanics, and way too much sugar sprinkled on top. The new Heat system? It just bloats the gameplay. Instead of outplaying your opponent, now it’s just: press Heat, armor move, and dump your 50/50 pressure. You and your opponent sit there mashing like two headless chickens until someone explodes.  The strategic flow? Dead. Now it’s monkey mode. Press buttons, get banana. 🍌  They promised they’d fix it. Harada — we trusted you. We hoped you’d actually listen to us, the players who sink hours into this game and spend real money on it. You said you heard us. That you’d add more defensive options — which, in player language, meant: “We’ll chill out the game, tone down the aggression, make things a little more readable.”  Season 2 drops. Boom. Fresh batch of 50/50s, more crazy moves, more plus frames, more chaos.  I’m not coming back to this game I once loved — not unless the soul of Tekken comes back. Right now, this thing? It’s a body without a heart. A shell. A cyborg. Tekken used to feel alive. Now it’s just a machine.

Hey, I’m Saki. I just want to take a moment and talk about the current state of Tekken 8 as someone who is new to the series. I got into FGs through tag fighters like MVC3 & DBFZ. I appreciate the chance of you taking the time to read this thread.  I wanted to start by saying how I started. About 5 years ago one of my cousins introduced me to Tekken 7 because of his love for the boxer Steve. It seemed like an interesting game and I was sort of familiar with 3D because I liked playing Maxi from the SC series.  That day didn’t turn into much since I got on to mash every blue moon, but we recently got into an era that I would consider the golden era of fighting games. New games for a bunch of returning series going above and beyond. So when I heard Tekken 8 was coming I wanted to learn.  Fast forwarding to its release it had its issues, but that’s every game. The important part was the core was still very fun to me. I didn’t dive into the game yet because I was in my journey to Master rank in SF6 since that was also essentially my first SF game.  A few weeks ago I accomplished said journey with Jamie. With that finally off my chest my interest was peaked with starting during Season 2 and playing Anna. I would say I’m very familiar with most FGs out because I love playing them all and even watching tournaments even when I’m not playing them.  Sorry for the long backstory, but this is where the real meat of it all starts. I read the entire patches notes, played around with them myself, and even watched other creators or pros do the same. As someone who is new I can’t speak towards balance per se, but I believe you guys may have made a big mistake. Firstly, as directors of the game I trust you. I always do for game since you have a vision for the game and want to get that vision to everyone. Even though there may be some pushback along the way it usually ends well. However, for this patch I have a few important things I feel was disregarded.   First, character identity is something I believe is EXTREMELY vital for fighting games. Strengths and even more so weaknesses are what make characters who they are. I feel that quite a few of the adjustments we’re removing said weaknesses in the name of “strong offense”, but I would like to ask where does that offense end? I know people don’t want to block so you give them the fun of offense, but that’s not necessarily what an aggressive game means to me. I think it should be reconsidered.  Second, would be player expression/creativity. After going through it in my head this goes along with my next point as well so this one is just going to be a bit longer. I feel as though player expression is constantly being reduced and that’s not good. With the combination of characters losing identities and you guys take of stances I believe a lot of players are losing the freedom of making decisions. Especially with this patch the stances in this game to me feels like you are trying to hard to hold my hand and walk me through my offense, but then it also developed into deciding my oki, and pressure. It feels like it’s trying to hard to play the game itself and avoid human error/mistakes and I believe that hurts player expression/creativity. I believe that this one should really get looked into and possibly consider the chance that it’s taking too much of our decision making.   I’m going to stop here. I really want to learn Tekken 8 and im still going to. So I just ask that you guys look into this patch and see if adjustments can be made to further better the game. I know everyone is frustrated and angry, but this is years worth of game knowledge and experience being ripped away. I hope you made it to the end and possibly take time to think of on this. It’s just my perspective as a new player. Let’s work with the community to make Tekken the great series that it has been. Thank you!

The overemphasis of oppressive offense with very weak or no counterplay could actually end this game, when it has the potential to be the best in the franchise. The foundation is there, the design decisions, especially when it comes to new game systems and game balance, completely lost the plot.  That is the summary, for anyone interested, hopefully someone working at Bandai Namco or the Tekken Team, please keep reading for the constructive criticism of a competitive player who introduced multiple casual players into the game. This is a combination of the sentiment of the competitive community, friends I have asked and my own opinion on what the issue with this game is. This is entirely focused on the core gameplay loop the players will spend the most amount of time in.  The issues of this game are: - oppressive offense This is created by too many safe + frame moves with either excessive tracking or homing properties and hitboxes that are just too big and extend too far in the 3rd dimension. That is combined with mixup situations that are a 50/50 guess for the defender, at most you have 3 defensive options, which are all too weak, dangerous and inconsistent for the defending player. Tekken always had mixups, Tekken never had this many 50/50 mixups. Blocking or powercrushing often are the only options because of the frame advantage or the tracking / homing properties.  - bad movement Movement always was THE defensive option in Tekken and it is the weakest it has ever been. Backdashing and spacing is completely ineffective due to the low distance and slow speed of backdashes, combined with insanely large hitboxes from the attacking player. On top of that, a lot of moves (like paul uf2) recover insanely fast even when the attacker whiffs them, to the point that punishing on a whiff is also inconsistent. Sidestepping/Sidewalking does not work either because of said frame advantage and tracking/homing issues. Movement does not work as a defensive option anymore or at least not well enough. It can mitigate some situations, but since the season 2 patch not nearly enough.  - lack of defensive options / the issue of "Reversal Break" Since movement is so greatly mitigated by overtuned or outright overpowered moves that shut it down perfectly, Tekken would need something to compensate for that. In it's current state, there are two mechanics for this, Powercrush and Parrys. Both of them are completely ineffective due to the excessive frame advantage and the new mechanic "reversal break" which breaks through powercrushes and Parrys. Both mechanics had well established counterplay. Powercrush? loses to throws and lows. Parrys? are extremely punishable on whiff and can be countered with specific moves (lows, knees/elbows if it is not a strong reversal) Reversal Break completely overwrites this counterplay, and moves that have the reversal break property usually do not carry any significant amount of risk or decision making with them. Just press them, it works. Reversal break should be either a decisive, risky decision like a parry, or not be in the game at all. Powercrushes and parrys are not strong enough to require a whole counter mechanic, they already have a risk associated with them.  - lack of character Identity Define characters by their weaknesses, not their strengths. Each patch keeps removing character weaknesses, creating an ultimately boring cast of allrounders who can all do everything. Defining character's by their weaknesses creates a stronger bond for the player and more interesting gameplay because you have to play around your own weaknesses and use the strengths you have. This is the part that my casual friends especially complained about.    - The Heat System I actually like the heat system, but I feel like it is dominating the game too hard and it happens too often. A state like heat should be a big exciting moment of the match, not something you activate every 30 seconds. The advantage gained on heat is too strong especially with it's frame advantage situations. The other issue is Heat Burst as a combo extension. While this is cool, with how common Heat is, it drastically increases the average combo time of the game to the point that combos can take up to 20+ seconds. for a game with 60 second rounds, that is just too long, and I like the idea of heat! Imo Heat should change in one of two ways: - make heat a building meter that carries over between rounds (similar to burst in Guilty Gear), this allows for more finetuned balancing because the amount of meter gained can be adjusted per character, and activating heat feels like a big moment and a strategic decision instead of just that thing you activate constantly for your extra damage and free mixups. - create defensive heat mechanics to counteract the overwhelming offense/add more strategic decision making. What if there was either a defensive heat mode or mechanic? One that for example improves your movement, gives your opponent more pushback on block, or a heat parry that drains the opponents heat meter and resets to neutral? Anything to give the heat system a defensive layer, right now as an exclusively offensive snowball mechanic it feels one dimensional and not fun.  Either way, all of these things ruin what could be the best fighting game of all time, and unless a quick statement and an emergency patch that actually addresses these issues happens, I can not recommend the game. I will not purchase any additional DLC (I have decided not to buy the Season 2 pass) and I will not promote this game until these issues are addressed. The frustrating part is that all of this is fixable with patches. The infrastructure is there, the Developers and the Publisher just please need to execute on it. I don't know if they will at this point, but I sincerely hope so.

Season 3 Edit: Tekken Devs continue to lack the foresight to see the impact of their own changes but more importantly, have chosen to blatantly ignore community feedback. Season 2's oppressive, roulette-styled offense lives on without being touched upon, new moves/changes found in Season 3's patch go far as even enhancing these opportunities and continue to reduce the weaknesses found in all the characters. It's alarming that the key phrases this patch notes seems to focus on (by verbatim) are to make offense "easier" or more "streamlined." The game continues to be volatile as ever with every matchup being a minefield with the risks of being caught up in a character's "streamlined" and "easy  to use" offense. As if the changes and new moves to characters weren't enough, Namco also decided to add a couple more landmines to the field by revisiting the idea of Tekken 7's most controversial patch of adding a "new tactic" except instead of bouncing off a wall, certain attacks will now instantly break the floor to extend for a combo, a feature that's reserved for mid-combo decision making. Aside from the absolutely ridiculous animation, this unnecessarily more to the volatility of Tekken 8, which is the opposite of what most people were hoping for in this game. To give what little credit I can, some characters did have sensible nerfs, but for the overwhelming majority of the roster which have received either no changes or only received buffs, this was hardly anything in respect of the current gameplay environment.   Finally if the lack of foresight on new attacks wasn't enough of a problem, the lack of extensive testing of their own changes has led to new unintended interactions or the REVIVAL of old bugs. To list what was found within the 24 hours of Season 3's release: -Jack's 1 Frame speedup to Gamma stance has allowed for an infinite combo on downed opponents who are in a Face Up Head Towards position by repeatedly using his ground electric shock attack. -Steve's 2 Jab into Albatross 2 (or Quick Spin 2) will again whiff against opponents against the wall at certain angles. This was a bug that was found in Season 2. -Heihachi's new move (ub 1+2) can be instantly charged to the maximum version of the attack if the input was simply mashed on. Instantly charging chargeable attacks by repeatedly pressing the input was a bug that was found previously before in Season 2. -Lee's bB4 into Hitman stance uf4 does not spike properly for its intended followup attack and will result in a juggle state if done quickly enough (which is an incorrect interaction) -While being struck after Lee's Hitman 1+2 into Hitman transition will result in Lee being punished, despite being a unpunishable attack. -While wallsplatting Heat Smashes were removed, whiffing the initial attack of the heat smash will still be able to wall splat opponents if they are struck from the 2nd or 3rd attacks of the heat smash (Hwoarang, Leo, and Heihachi are examples) -While Bryan's Snake Eyes ff1+2 cannot wall splat anymore for a continued wall combo, hitting an opponent near a wall still enables Bryan to pick up the opponent to get a wall combo anyway (using his d3+4). This is an unintended interaction that was found on Feng about a year ago in Season 2 that is now found on Bryan again. -While not a bug, but an unintended interaction and another show of lack of foresight, Xiayou/Ling's fF3 on Counterhit can combo into her backturned launcher (BT4) when hit on later active frames/spaced correctly.  As noted above, you can see that many of these bugs or unintended interactions are quite alarming as about half of what was listed were previously fixed interactions that were found in Season 2. It shows a clear lack of testing and a lack of care from the dev team. I'm sure these will be fixed again shortly but it's a clear showcase of mediocre work of what is Season 3's big "back to basics" patch.  Season 2 Review: The game and its characters are way too oppressive and the execution in balancing shows a lack of foresight on how the changes will affect the meta of the game or how they drastically change the identity of characters away from their iterations in previous Tekkens that "legacy Tekken fans" were known to love and play.  The overall direction focus of being offensive is a great and understandable decision coming from Tekken 7's defensive meta, but the enforcement of 50/50s along with the decision to reduce complexities to enable newer players makes Tekken 8 lose its pride as a movement-heavy neutral-based 3D Fighter that the franchise is known for and is a unfun approach to discourage extremely defensive gameplay/strategy. I really cannot recommend buying Tekken 8, especially not at full price. You could consider buying it if it's on a significant sale (50% or better), but otherwise it's not worth it, especially after Season 2 very bad balance changes (which hopefully will get quickly patched).  Cons: - For the given price tag (at full price), having to spend money to buy DLC-characters, not just to play them but to train against them in Practice Mode, is an extremely big negative; - Right now (early Season 2), game is totally unbalanced (I will not repeat here arguments which have already discussed in-depth elsewhere by players who are much better at the game than me); - Some character interactions seem absurd: in some slow-motion moments, you can see characters limbs going across each other, but only one of them hits, and if you don't know frame-data (and the logic behind the game), it seems a bug; - Too much time and too many clicks to get to go into match-making from the start of the game; - Some animations are sloppy and/or counter-intuitive regarding the gameplay: for example, a character looks intuitively "hittable" (or punishable), like he dropped his guard, but in reality he is not (also the opposite may be true); - The game doesn't really teach you much: truly learning the game most likely will require reading or watching guides online, and then a lot of practice.  Pros: - Season 2 added useful indicators (like Punish, Clean, Counter, Tornado, ecc...) and I consider this to be the only significant good change they did; - You may love some character(s) and/or have nostalgic feelings towards one (or more) of them: playing your favourite character(s) may feel fun and satisfactory (at least as long as it lasts, and also as long as playing against other characters does not undermine your positive experience); - Cross-platform play, and the game online typically doesn't lag (at least, in Europe).
