Review for Patch v.2.00.01   Season 2 has made the game much less enjoyable, but I already didn't enjoy the game very much from launch. The developers have a track record spanning multiple games of making REACTIVE balance changes which leads to improper or nonexistent game testing and consideration of what the changes do to game systems and the roster of characters as a whole. This has led to short-sighted "fixes" which tend to either break the game/character, or lead to another workaround which in turn has led to the developers becoming frustrated and removing the mechanic completely from the game.   An example would be addressing the issue of Akuma's reset juggle near the end of Tekken 7's life which led to removing the tech from the game and affecting several characters who in rare situations were also able to do reset combos, and Akuma finding a workaround and still able to do the reset anyways. Now in T8 S2 they have removed many ground tech traps such as Lee's wall reset, forced stance transitions on some characters disregarding the player's freedom and making characters play more similar to DLC characters for the sake of plus frames, removed counterhit from Ki Charge which has been something in the game since Tekken 3 and utilized to great effect by many players some of which were widely known for being the only character specialists to use Ki Charge setups, and overall homogenized most of the roster of characters despite stating that their focus for T8 was on character identity and unique playstyles. Characters that used to be classified as "defensive or defense focus" playstyles feel weak if you try to play to their archetype, but if you play how the game "wants" you to with an aggressive focus and forced 50/50s you will find more success. There is very little player expression or freedom, and the game feels less fun because you rarely feel like you are adapting and outplaying your opponent, only that you snowballed harder and forced more favorable situations for your character by dominating your opponent with offense, when a big part of what made Tekken special in previous games was watching what your opponent was doing and reacting or adapting to them, forcing yourself to come up with different strategies against not just different characters but different PLAYERS themselves. Now the game doesn't require you to think deeply about the human you're fighting against because every character you play has the same solutions built into their kit to force the opponent to guess, and the "balance" has removed any unique weaknesses your character had before. If not for a huge community uproar, S2 would have launched with chip damage on throw breaks on the RECEIVER effectively punishing YOU for CORRECTLY breaking a throw and rewarding the thrower with health; luckily this was reverted days before the patch went live.  The developers openly stated that they heard the feedback for more defensive options and less oppressive offense in season 1 and then promised the players that there would be defensive changes, but also doubled down on their plan for the game to be offensive focused. Since Season 2 has launched none of those promised defensive changes feel present in the game because the game overwhelmingly buffed offense again, adding more tracking moves alongside the absurd amount of tracking already, more oppressive frame advantage moves, less counterplay against those moves, less whiff punishes, less reward for strong defense,   In Tekken 8 I rarely feel like I am playing against the player themselves and almost always feel like I'm playing against the character they're playing. The rare exception being long sets in player lobbies and between friends. Ranked sets are too short and don't allow players to show their unique playstyles nor do they allow for opponents to recognize patterns and player tendencies. I fail to see how any of these changes are a positive for new players or legacy players. Both types of players don't feel rewarded for beating their opponent in core fighting game and Tekken fundamentals such as whiff punishing, block punishing, spacing, pressure, reads, frame traps, tech traps, knowledge checks, mental stack, combo adjustment, stage and distance awareness, combo variety and wall carry, deciding between oki combo enders and damage enders, huge life deficit comebacks, clean and stylish play, etc. All things that make Tekken special and not only fun to watch but to play, feel like they've been taken away in favor of short term rewards and more "wins" on paper due to making more correct guesses in a match.   Speaking from experience I believe these short term gains won't help players grow and absorb the legacy skill that Tekken games are known for which in term encourages the player to think, reflect, and be creative in planning their own strategies not only for Tekken but any fighting game as well as discovering and seeking out the character archetypes they enjoy in different fighting games. Tekken 8 only teaches the player to "be persistent and you'll eventually win" And when you win; most of the time you won't be able to explain why. You won't be understand why and if you were the better player overall or your decision making because of how many guesses you were forced to make. But the devs seem to think getting ranked points and promotions to shiny new ranks based on a more fair ranking system is enough for most players. This is a failure on the developers to all players and doesn't retain what I consider to be one of the most important things in a Fighting game and the Fighting Game Community.  I really cannot recommend this game to anyone who enjoys fighting games and I truly believe this serves as an example of everything wrong with modern fighting games. The current developers of Tekken 8 are very selective about feedback and tone-deaf. They select a complaint, address one aspect of the complaint, band-aid fix it and expect us to praise them, but fail to see the bigger picture of why the complaint was made in the first place and the deep-rooted problems in their current design philosophy. For every 1 time they genuinely listen to the community and make a change that benefits the game and the players, they do 10 things wrong whether its balance, dumbing down or killing special attributes of characters, and breaking or outright removing game mechanics.

It's ironic; the first time I thought to review this game, I wanted to leave it a positive score -- a score that would have been a no brainer for me. The roster is replete with vibrant personalities, and the gameplay, although by no means perfect, had a (somewhat) coherent vision and philosophy; aggression (in the form of pressure with and without heat moves), evasion (in the form of crushing and stepping), and player expression: these 3 qualities stuck out to me as the core elements that underpinned Tekken 8's identity. To be sure, some of these aspects were disagreeable to members of the Tekken community, especially its aggression, which some (many?) players derided as overly tuned. I wasn't fully onboard with the criticism. I agreed that certain characters (what's up Yoshi?) were a bit too powerful compared to the rest of the cast, and that some heat smashes (including that of my main, Asuka) were too difficult to sidestep, but I thought these were issues that easily could have been remedied by a simple patch. It was my honest opinion that even with its flaws, Tekken 8 sat atop the throne of 3D fighters.   With Season 2, the throne has been abdicated.   'Abdicated' implies some sort of intentional self-sabotage which was entirely planned on the part of Bandai Namco. It is a weird claim to make, but at present it's the only way I can make sense of the almost kamikaze-like direction taken by the director(s). Characters are now shadows of their former selves; every character can abuse their plus frames and chuck attack after attack after heat move after attack after heat smash after attack, to the point where the cast has become largely homogenised. Speaking as an Asuka main, she's completely lost her identity as a defensive character. She's just much better at playing aggressive than she is playing defensive. Her identity is a far cry from her original vision. It's no surprise that Fergus, a top Asuka main, titled his latest video about the character 'I Don't Recognize Her Anymore'. I've also heard about more than a few Zafina mains who felt as though the latest season made her too offensively oriented. Some of the balance changes are extremely questionable as well. The top tiers simply did not need buffs. Certain characters, such as Lee, also received what seem to be disproportionate nerfs, but don't you worry Lee mains: Bamco compensated by giving him buffs that make him more suited to the rushdown style they seem to have in mind for virtually every single character in the roster. It's disappointing, but above all it's confusing. The minds behind Tekken 8's balance patches seem to enjoy a significant social media presence and they doubtlessly know how the community feels about certain decisions. After all, it was vocal community push-back that prompted them to roll back the bizarre decision to impose chip damage for successfully broken throws. They most certainly knew the lay of the land, and so my question is simply this: Why would they make changes that they knew the community would dislike? Before the patch, we were promised buffs to the game's defensive options. This announcement was met with a great deal of fanfare, as several community members thought that an antidote to what they believed was an overwhelmingly aggressive game was on the way; they felt heard. So you can imagine the reaction of the community when Season 2 served to amplify the game's aggression to an overwhelming amount instead of toning it down. I don't know. I want to enjoy Tekken 8, I really do. If the devs truly did not know how the community would react to the new season, then they know now. It's incumbent on them to give the players what they want. No more pandering to a nebulously defined, perhaps even nonexistent contingent of 'casual' players that would get mowed down by the new system anyway. Please listen to the players who are actually offering criticism. It may serve you guys well.

Bandai Namco and the Tekken development team have lost the plot with Tekken 8 Season 2.  With buffs to characters who absolutely did not need them, jumbling some characters' playstyles by lowering the effectiveness of signature tools, and a greater emphasis on 50/50 mixups through stances, character identity is being forcibly removed from the game, whilst blind aggression no matter the character is becoming more and more rewarding. This is being done to make the game easier to access (not my words, the developers in several patch notes list that characters were difficult to play and wanted to simplify them), but the problem becomes that new players will be pushed away by veterans who use legacy knowledge in tandem with the potentially exploitable systems, whilst said veterans lose faith in the game due to the team behind Tekken 8 removing what gave the game its identity and competitive fun factor. Ironically enough, figureheads from the development team stated that this season for the game would focus more on defense, but the changes to the defensive aspects were limited, made irrelevant by the plethora of additions to characters (sidestepping being buffed whilst more moves would beat out sidesteps), or simply done by removing legacy knowledge because it's "unfair" (certain setups being beaten by simply blocking on wakeup).  I cannot in good faith recommend anyone purchasing this game or any of its bloated amount of add-on content (Season Passes, a stage that wasn't included in said Season Passes, the awful microtransactions, the pointless Battle Passes that re-use assets from Tekken 7, even numerous crossovers with Nike and Chipotle of all things) in the state that it is in. In fact, I believe this game and its balance philosophy will not change unless the hard-headed team behind it are removed from working on the game.

I absolutely hate that I am even typing this, but I don't want to see the passing of my favorite fighting game franchise without at least giving it a decent send off. First off, I would like to thank everyone who worked on Tekken throughout the years. I love that the game had a face, well two faces in Harada and Michael Murray who I could tell were really passionate about the series. Unfortunately, it seems we have hit an era where it has become more important for the game to look fun than to be fun and frankly this is something that plaques Street Fighter a bit too. This era of fighting games is so concerned with pushing offense forward to create big moments that it doesn't stop and realize that defense is even an element of gameplay, let alone a key part.  During the life of Tekken 7 comments were made several times about how Harada didn't appreciate the defensive play toward the end of rounds when the tournaments got to the top players. The Korean backdashing, feint, backdash, sidestep, etc finals might be perceived as boring to the casuals and that was a sin because making money means more casuals picking up your game so they needed to be wowed with what they saw on twitch. I can understand that and I loved the addition of the slow motion camera when two fighters were low on life and we waited to see who struck the final blow. Also, I frankly thought Korean backdashing needed a rework so the end of a round didn't devolve into a showcase of avoidance. I was hoping they would do small changes that altered the distance moved, the speed at which it could be done, the ability to defend straight out of a backdash, maybe even make it so if you did backdash and canceled it into a block you would take a little chip damage from a move that hit your defense. Some small tweaks. Instead we got offense is your defence, overtuned damage in combos, wall to wall juggles doing 100 points of damage and leaving the downed opponent open to a 50/50 that ends the round.  Part of what got us here is the new heat mechanic. Heat is interesting and it didn't have to break the game. It just needs to be more restricted. If it was an activation that could only be done if you are 20% or less life and they did away with the low life rage damage boost so it couldn't be combined to do absolutely absurd damage that wipes off 70% of a life bar on a launch it could be cool. Also, there is no world in which the heat system should be able to regenerate its own gauge. Once activated it should diminish over time and when you use it chunks should vanish weather you hit the opponent or not. We should not be seeing 20 seconds of this state so an entire round is basically one guy just crushing the other with heat mode 50/50s ad nauseam.   Furthermore, this notion that chip damage regenerating in any way makes up for the increased damage is just misguided. I understand the desire for chip seeing as the aforementioned tournament finals often turned into a defensive showcase which wasn't explosive or exciting, but why not make it so chip only occurs where a player defends as a canceling of a backdash or when they defend against big power moves like Paul's Phoenix Smasher. That would be more acceptable than taking 60-80 points of chip while my opponent has heat activated and is just 50/50 ing me into oblivion and making me feel like I am playing Marvel vs Capcom 2 without the tag partner.  This game could have been great. It looks amazing. It feels fluid. I want to love it, but season 1 was a bit lackluster thus my mere 40 hours or so played. I was hoping that season 2 would bolster defense and make me fall in love with the latest iteration of a series I have loved since the 90's, but the entire defense change list seems to be increased fluidity of sidestepping and the ability to sidestep from crouch while the remainder of the patch is devoted to giving away +frames, wall splat, and tracking on tons of moves to everyone. This makes for a flashy game, but not a good game. The attack options are as wide as an olympic pool, but they devolve into shallow mix ups and rabid unga bunga gameplay. It is the sugar high that quickly leaves you feeling empty.   At this point I hope this game redirects its course, but I don't expect it to. Last week I was hopeful of one of the upcoming DLC characters being my main. Now, I am not spending another dime on this game unless I see changes first. Thank you Team Tekken past and present for the many years of enjoyment from the day I saw Tekken 1 in the arcades and thought King was bad ass as a teen all the way to 7. I can't tell you how many thousands of hours I spent playing 3, Tag, 5DR, 6, Tag 2 (yes I was one of the ones that really enjoyed it), and 7. Perhaps I will come back to 8 later and love it in the future, but regardless it has been a hell of a run. Now, I have Virtua Fighter 6 to look forward to while I play Tekken 7 and VF5 some more.

I hate to just jump on the hate train with these reviews so I'm going to try and leave my honest, constructive criticism without just bashing the new season only.   tl;dr first, then I'll elaborate after (I tend to ramble)  [h1] Positives [/h1]  [list]     [* ]Generally improved UI from previous games     [*]More accessible than previous games     [*]System mechanics are genuinely fun, if overtuned     [*]Characters look and sound great     [*]Highly requested features, such as instant rematch and UI improvements are finally in the game [/list]   [h1] Negatives (not just from S2 update) [/h1]  [list]     [*]Aggression is very powerful, which is fine, but defense does not scale properly alongside it     [*]Some bizarre decisions made with the power of some moves     [*]Standard fare, predatory monetization practices such as a battle pass that you can't return to or obtain past a certain date     [*]Less compelling story and character presentation compared to previous games (subjective, admittedly)     [*]A lot of characters are just very annoying to deal with. Even if you're an experienced player who understands a matchup, the interactions the game pushes do not feel rewarding to play out a lot of the time [/list]   [h1] Things worsened by S2 [/h1]  [list]     [*]Every character became much more annoying to deal with     [*]The aggression that was pushed already in S1 was enhanced for every character, which makes the roster feel very samey in my opinion. There are exceptions, but for most characters, you really just need to go all in all the time or you're not playing to your character's full potential     [*]Strong aerial tailspins are fun to use, and a lot more characters have them, but it makes wall carry even more insane and combo theory feels like it may just come down to doing as many combo extenders as you can. In total with heat and stage hazards, you may see 6 or 7 combo extensions total in one juggle. [/list]   [h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]  S1 of this game was flawed but genuinely fun to play. There were some characters that showcased the game when things were abused to their maximum, and personally I did not like the experience that those characters created for players. Now in S2, every character is heading more in the direction, and the cieling for aggression has been raised even further. I have to admit that I have a bias against games with incredibly strong offense as I'm a defensive player, but to me the beauty of tekken was how you could use defensive knowledge and movement to make your opponent hesitate to push their offense too far.  Tekken has always leaned towards very defensive gameplay. I do understand why Bamco wants to push aggression in Tekken, and I'm okay with it on principle. I just think it is going a bit far and the defensive improvements this season are nice, but not enough with how much they buffed characters' control of the neutral and mixup potential. Trying to move around and read your opponent to punish their offense feels like a losing battle, and it feels like Tekken has lost a very important part of its core identity by neglecting that. If offense is meant to be this potent, then defense should be appropriately tuned to be a viable and equally potent choice as well. Currently in Tekken 8, if you are trying to play defense, you're really just throwing away an opportunity to play offense.  I am not a game designer, but I try to understand why certain decisions are made. I simply cannot agree with the decisions that have been made for this game. I believe the game at its core is a fantastic experience. Heat is a fun an interesting mechanic that has a lot of potential, but it's tuned in a way where it's a great source of stress to deal with. Combos are fun to engineer, but every character is juggling you for over 10 seconds every round, and the oki situations at the wall are often miserable. You could say that you just shouldn't get hit, but it's an inevitability with how forced the mixups get, and how they loop into each other. If you want to defend yourself, (not even play defensively, just defending yourself) you have two options. Either guess right, or hit them first. You can sidestep, but there are a lot of options built in to cover that that will kill you so hard, and with the amount of plus frames that exist in this game, sometimes you can't afford to try it.   If this is your first tekken, or you just enjoy this type of game, that's great and I hope you continue to have fun. For me and many others, it's just not very well designed.

I held out on reviewing this game because throughout Season 1, Tekken 8 felt like a game that launched with glaring issues but could eventually evolve into one of the most enjoyable and competitive Tekken games of all time. This is unfortunately not what happened.  Season 2 is a masterclass example of how to be completely tone-deaf to your community as a developer. The general sentiment toward Tekken 8's launch was that forced 50/50's and streamlined offence, as well as the homogenisation and over-simplification of core character identity and mechanics, was not very interesting and at times quite frustrating. Couple that with the overbearing and at times egregious heat system, and you have a game in which it feels painful at times to be the defending player. It is worth mentioning too that alongside this there were other glaring issues like chip damage, strings that tracked much too well, moves with too many properties baked in such as heat-engaging power-crush wallsplats, over-tuned heat smashes and other smaller things like strange camera behaviour at the wall. This pursuit by the developers for the players to interact by introducing overwhelming offensive options had more or less been unhealthy for Tekken 8 during Season 1, however it seemed to improve slowly over time as the developers removed things such as homing throws, full tracking on heat bursts and key changes to pertinent moves on problem characters etc. All of this, alongside the implication through marketing that they would be changing their focus in Season 2 toward defensive counter-play and options as the defender, lead the community to believe that all of this would addressed. For me, and possibly many others, I took this to mean that they would be fine-tuning frame data, adjusting hit and hurtboxes thoroughly, re-evaluating heat per character as well as heat smashes, and generally just balancing down as all characters felt like they had the potential to be quite strong in Season 1 with some characters standing out a little more so.  Season 2 however has proven that as of this moment the developers do not understand what makes Tekken, as a core concept, fun and engaging as a fighting game. Being one of the only majorly successful 3D fighters, Tekken is loved for it's depth in movement and options, both defensive and offensive. Season 2 has moved toward a direction of streamlining offence further and patching out character weaknesses and flaws, turning majority of matches you play into what can feel like a boring pseudo-2D guessing game depending on your opponents' character. Many changes feel like blanket solutions to changes that should be made to specific characters. The two biggest examples of this to me are the Ki Charge change, and the buffering sidestep change. Starting with Ki Charge it feels like they didn't understand how to nerf setups that certain characters had available to them and so instead, arguably lazily, they decided to change the property of the system entirely and as a result removing a lot of what could be considered player expression/identity. To this same end, the buffering to sidestep also seems out of touch to me on the basis that sidestep is already strong in Tekken 8 and although it can feel like it's not working well enough at times, this to me does not read as a problem inherently with sidestep but as an issue with the moves you sometimes attempt to step. There are many long-range linear moves within Tekken 8 that for no apparent reason, track relatively decent to either side, and rather than adjust the hitboxes on moves such as these to properly represent the animation, we instead are buffing sidestep. To make matters worse, there are many strings that track and realign exceedingly well for no justifiable reason and even with a well-timed sidestep you often have to block anyway, and in certain situations can't even punish your opponent. Without going further into patch details, many characters' changes in Season 2 involve considerable focus on offensive capabilities as well as strengths from stance and in heat, seemingly encouraging players to interact with their opponent in forced ways and making them guess or just deal with outright annoying plus frames.   Simply put, it appears that the Tekken team would prefer to have the average player be forcing situations with plus frames, chip damage and heat, locking down their opponents and limiting the use of the 3D component that many loyal fans love this franchise for. This direction and philosophy for Tekken is one that limits creativity and reduces interesting interactions in matches in favour for much more streamlined and repetitive gameplay, resulting in players not being able to separate themselves with player expression simply because it is not optimal, and in the case of Season 2, even patched out.   As a footnote I'd like to include some minor things that do not substantiate a negative review on their own but coupled with everything else, deserve to be mentioned.   Time-gated battlepasses - Really? On a full priced game? Fair enough to charge microtransactions, it's a choice and that's fine, but to time gate them to capatilise on FOMO is once again tone-deaf. Has no one learnt anything from Helldivers?  Unforgotten Echoes - This DLC is playable for free as a continuation of sorts to Tekken 8's story mode, so it's hardly fair to use this as a basis of why the game is bad. This is not that. Why I point this out is merely because I did not find this to meet the typical quality expectation of Tekken content. I liked Tekken 8's main story and I enjoy the whacky, silly over the top ♥♥♥♥, but this was different. Without spoilers, the reference to a major plot point from a previous Tekken is lazily handled, not only showing the writing to be poor but also just disrespectful to the source material. By no means does this make Tekken 8 bad, but it doesn't make it better either.  Netcode - Now this may be speculation because I am not involved in this technical space, nor do I understand it and therefore am not qualified to speak on the inner workings of this system. However, as a player, I feel that I have noticed a gradual degradation in the quality and consistency of network conditions online. I should state that I have an incredibly stable and high-speed ethernet connection, and even against other ethernet opponents, I have noticed this drop in quality. I obviously can't prove this so take it with a grain of salt, but I did feel that it was worth mentioning.  As a final note, I do hope this game begets much improvement but it can only happen if the developers begin to listen, so voice your discontent if you feel similarly. I initially wanted to buy the Season 2 pass before it's release as I expected Armor King to be included and for my potential enjoyment of this Season to be much higher, yet it seems I will be holding on to my money instead as if the game continues in this direction I can't justify that investment. If you have been thinking about taking advantage of the 30% off sale, as much as it hurts me to say I would strongly suggest you reconsider and wait for the game to see improvement over time.

As a long-time Tekken fan, I had high hopes for Tekken 8, but unfortunately, it feels like the developers completely ignored the community’s feedback and doubled down on everything we didn’t want.  One of the biggest issues is how aggressively they’ve pushed 50/50 mix-ups. Instead of refining the neutral game or adding more defensive tools, they’ve made mix-ups even stronger, forcing players into constant guessing situations with little room for intelligent counterplay. We asked for better defensive options, but they gave us the opposite.  To make matters worse, plus-frame moves leading directly into stances have further ruined the flow of the game. It makes dealing with pressure feel suffocating, removing opportunities for counterplay and rewarding blind aggression over thoughtful spacing and timing. This isn’t the Tekken we love—it’s a chaotic, momentum-heavy mess that prioritizes flashy offense at the expense of skillful defense.  It’s frustrating to see Bandai Namco disregard the feedback from dedicated players who have supported the series for years. Tekken 8 could have been a true evolution of the franchise, but instead, it’s a game that alienates the core fanbase in favor of mindless aggression.  If you enjoy constant pressure with little room to breathe, this might be for you. But for those of us who love Tekken for its depth and strategic play, this feels like a massive step backward. Save your money and don't buy this season pass  Final Verdict: Disappointed.

As someone who started with Tekken 7, I was excited to see where Tekken 8 would take the series. But instead of refining what worked and made it fun, the game makes baffling changes that frustrate BOTH newcomers and veterans.  On paper, the shift toward simpler mechanics (homogenized characters, removed techniques like Law’s DSS and oki mindgames + many more) seems aimed at accessibility. But in practice, the hyper-aggressive offense-heavy gameplay creates an oppressive experience for casual players. Without the defensive depth of past games, newcomers get steamrolled by relentless pressure, leading to frustration rather than fun. Meanwhile, veterans lose the nuanced gameplay that rewarded mastery, leaving neither group truly satisfied.  Worse, the heavy focus on monetization (overpriced skins, battle passes) makes it clear where the priorities lie. Instead of fostering a balanced, rewarding fighting game, Tekken 8 feels like it’s chasing short-term profits from players who’ll drop the game in less than a week. First time leaving a review on any game, but I have to because of the state of the game.  to preface, i've been playing tekken since tekken 4, so a little more over 20 years. This is the worst tekken of all time, and its not even close. You can scratch that--its just a bad game overall, even when you look at it as a standalone game.  I'll try to keep it as short as possible for anyone who is looking at the reviews to buy the game:   [*] Gameplay: its very one-dimensional and formulaic. Pop heat burst, chip damage, end with heat smash--round ends. Every character does the same thing and has the same fighting style--rush-down. It's initially fun to see all these particles in your screen, but quickly becomes old. [*] Defense in this game is nonexistent. Once someone begins their offense, your turn is over and now you simply wait for the next round to start. [*] Once you actually get to play the game, you're actually just a glorified spectator. Every move has a mini-cinematic where your character says some weird anime ♥♥♥♥ mid combo. You can see this during heat engagers, heat bursts, heat smashes, rage arts, and random moves. A combo that should take 5-8 seconds actually can take 15-20 seconds between all the cutscenes in the combos. Its not fluid at all. [*] The game strayed far from its original inception. Its no longer based on martial arts with some goofiness sprayed every here and there. it is straight up an anime game with corny and badly translated lines. [*] Monetization: they reused the same assets from tekken 7, except now theyre charging you for it. a new haircut on a character is $3, and the battle pass is even worse. A random tshirt form the battlepass will cost you anywhere between $2-$20 to obtain. [*] Developers: out of touch. the game has been chaotic to say the least with the community being vocal about the changes, and the developers turned the other way. All of the feedback that was provided was simply ignored. The few times that they respond to feedback, its usually sassy, passive aggressive, rude, immature, or a combination of all. Read through Harada's or Murray's twitter to see for yourself. So if you want a game where the developers listen to its community, then this game is not it.  All that to say that I love this franchise and I am only writing this review because its one of my favorite game title of all time and I am extremely disappointed that the state of the game is a steaming pile of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Dont get fooled by the shiny particles on your screen or the graphics (which are really good)--the gameplay is soulless, bland, and boring.

Tekken 8 started with a great foundation but since day 1, the devs have constantly struggled to balance the new "heat" feature that they implemented. In Tekken 7, no one really liked the meter system, not even the people who played characters that had meter. it was hard to balance and the dev team simply ignored all the complaints about it. In the end, they added meter to EVERY character in Tekken 8, Season 1 of Tekken 8 had rough edges, but still had potential, just a nerf here, a buff there, if the dev team properly understood and took in feedback from the players of the game, they could've easily had the game in a fun, playable state.   The dev team DID acknowledge community complaints, and constantly told us they were holding off from patching the game for the sake of the competitive scene, so everyone had to suffer with all the messy situations and poor balancing for the sake of the competitive scene, but then the dev team decided to patch the game to cater towards the casual scene, and ignore all the competitive players complaints and queries. They had a "push push push" mindset with the game, where they only said to themselves "will players enjoy pressing these buttons and winning?" and never "will players enjoy having to defend against this?".  season 2 PROMISED a "defensive patch", and they showed they understood that Tekken 8 was TOO aggressive and lacked fun counterplay. they announced that they were buffing sidesteps, increasing buffering on certain actions, and a bunch of other things that were all GOOD. But they also have a habit of "if we buff this, it'll be too strong, so we'll buff this aspect of it as well". They made grabs easier to break, but then made it so the defender who BREAKS the grab takes a small amount of damage. They buffed sidesteps, but then increased the number of homing moves and situations where you CAN'T sidestep. They nerfed certain parts of characters, but then EXTREMELY buffed them in other areas, as a quick example of this, they acknowledged Yoshimitsu and how strong he is, and decided to nerf his frames and damage on some of his moves to reduce his overall combo damage output, but then they buffed him everywhere else, and it feels like he has MORE safe moves, MORE oppressive situations, MORE mixups, and his combo damage is still extremely high.  I had high hopes for season 2, but they really fumbled the bag and made the game worse. It's insane to think season 1, despite all its problems, was better balanced than season 2. They introduced MORE bugs and glitches as well.  I've completely lost faith in the direction of the game, and the dev team, and have decided despite loving and playing the Tekken series for over 20 years, I'm quitting the game and I've uninstalled the game.  I'm done trying to be patient and waiting for the dev team to fix their issues, because at this point it feels like they never will.

I'm going to keep this review as civil as possible.  I’ve been a dedicated Tekken fan for nearly two decades. Through all the ups and downs in life, Tekken has always been my go-to escape—something I could rely on for enjoyable and unforgettable experiences. Whether I was casually spending my lunch money at the arcades or attending events with friends to watch tournaments, Tekken has always been about more than just gameplay. It’s about the memories, the connections, the laughs, and the challenges, all built on the solid foundation of Tekken’s complexity. With Tekken 8, the shift towards a more aggressive style was initially disappointing, but I could still appreciate the game for maintaining its unique balance, rewarding both offensive and defensive play. However, with the release of Season 2, it feels like everything that made this series great has been completely disregarded.  What happened to Tekken? The game has taken a significant step backward in terms of design. The complexity that defined this series is gone, replaced by a system that relies too heavily on guesswork. At this point, Tekken might as well be rock-paper-scissors with better graphics. There’s no depth, no strategy—just an endless cycle of random guessing with a touch of spacing thrown in here and there. Where’s the skill-based decision-making we used to enjoy? Where’s the thrill of mastering the complex systems that made Tekken such a rewarding experience?  Season 2 feels like it was made for people who have no interest in learning the game or improving their skills. The intricate mind games and strategy that once defined Tekken have been watered down to a point where the game now feels hollow. The characters no longer feel distinct, and every match seems more like a gamble than a true fight. It’s honestly frustrating and disappointing.  I won’t be refunding this game because I’ve been a fan for so long. However, I can’t help but feel deeply disappointed to see the franchise fall into this state of mediocrity. I never imagined I’d feel this way about Tekken, but right now, I have zero desire to play. I’ve invested so much time and energy into this series, and this feels like a betrayal. I hope that one day, the players will have a real voice in the game’s design. I honestly can’t believe I’m saying this, but looking back, we all took Tekken 7 and the earlier games for granted.  If I could offer a suggestion, though it’s probably not going to be considered, it would be to roll Season 2 back into the Season 1 system and gradually fine-tune the moves like they did before.  I truly wish the series the best and its fans to soon wake up from what appears to be a bad dream. My hope for a light at the end of this miserable tunnel continues to thrive, but for now, I’m reinstalling Street Fighter 6.

I'm going to break with the majority of complaints here and offer a different criticism: this game is poorly optimized for portable devices.  As someone playing mostly on a docked Steam Deck, it's baffling that there's no option to tune down the glut of unnecessary particle effects and background animations. They're completely extraneous to gameplay, so why are they mandatory?   Running into slowdowns is extremely frustrating for both myself and people I play against, doubly so because it should be a relatively straightforward issue for the devs to solve. I have to single out Clive as a singularly bad example of this - a character with so much going on on-screen, even when using basic moves, that it's unmanageable at portable resolutions and framerates. The Steam Deck "Playable" verification, and its assertion that the "default graphics configuration performs well" is misleading. A stable 60fps is a prerequisite in a fighting title.  Perhaps you'll find me pedantic for saying this, but the release version of the game was, by all accounts, better optimized for the Deck. I had held hopes things would improve from there. Instead, it seems that subsequent patches and character drops have only eroded the compatibility. Tekken's mechanics are relatively simple so I don't think this is a computation problem - it's a graphics optimization one. This is a shame because the quality of life perks like instant rematches, improved labbing, are all great. I'll leave the well-trodden issues of balance to other reviewers at this time.  Ultimately, a "Season 2" while not even providing support for the latest FSR 3.1 for low-end systems feels lazy to me. The Tekken Store gets more attention than core gameplay. I refuse to have to potato mod and risk a ban in order to hit stable frames. All said, if you're playing on a lower-end device Tekken 7 is a better package at the minute.

Over the course of the last year the Tekken team has continued to stray from the formula that their fans have loved. I can understand wanting an aggressive game and hoped that Tekken 8 would turn out similarly to Tekken 6 and Tag 2 where you play a very close and fast paced neutral game against your opponent. However after a year of bug fixes and data collection the team has decided to cut down the already emaciated state of the defending. They promised more defensive options but instead are transforming the game into one of forced offense by giving the aggressor better frame advantage on both hit and block, and a better situation for the aggressor after they get hits by making moves do more damage, launch, or wall splat.  The new moves are a joke, some unnecessarily given to the strongest characters and others outright invalidating the weaknesses that are core to the character's identity. If the team's vision is to make an oppressive fg that wants both players to push for advantage then the defense needs to at least be good enough to give an out to the defender that can make a hard read.

Been playing tekken for years and this was my first recent tekken game since tekken 6.  While tekken 8 might look great and at first glance feel great, once you start learning the game, you realise how far away it has strayed from what tekken has had an identity for. This game has gone from a knowledge based, skill expressive game to being a very offence oriented game (which sounds fun until you are on the receiving end and realise how miserable it feels to have people constantly throw nonsense at you that would have never even been remotely balanced in previous games).   The damage and frame advantage is insane in this game, as well as having every character have good wall travel in long combos, having straight up broken tools in heat where as the defensive player just has to hold back until they die or the attackers heat ends. And a lot of "interactions" have now just turned into a 5050 guessing game where you have no choice but to gamble on what your opp will do which will usually lead to 30-70% of your health being lost for guessing wrong.  Unless you have been living under a rock, s2 is one of the most hated updates I've ever experienced in a game, and the reason for this negative response is:  -The devs admitted the game was overtuned, had too much of an offensive focus, and heat was being used in uncreative ways while being unintendedly strong.  -The devs went out of their way to promise us they would make changes in s2 and address these isssues by having a "defence focused update".  -The preview live streams barely included defence changes while demonstrating changes that would have the opposite effect of what they promised.   -There was outrage and we as players were told to "wait until the patch drops before we complain"  -Despite it being crystal clear that none of the changes we were upset about were actually good for the future of the game, we waited  -S2 drops and HOLY COW almost EVERY CHARACTER got BUFFED?????  -This is the complete opposite of what they promised and what we wanted. It was so much worse than what we could have imagined. Strongest 5 characters we were BEGGING to be nerfed, got a slap on the wrist but then "to compensate" got huge buffs anyways, changing absolutely NOTHING in the grand scheme.  These include:  1) more moves tracking and better, making sidestep(a defensive option)  2) moves having better frames, keeping the pressure on the defending character and having the rush down stay for longer  3) moves completely gaining too much unneccessary utility, removing the skill in knowing what to do in certain situations as the new broken move covers every defensive option, which just dumbs down the game  note there was a few great buffs on sidestep but the other changes are so overwhelming that it has made this completely irrelevant.  But one of the WORST changes is that they have changed so many of the fan favourite characters by removing what made them unique / difficult and making them function like every other character. Not only are the characters (like Lee) not remotely the same any more, they made changes that would only benefit a new player that wouldn't play the game long term because even intermediate players are fed up from the state of the game. All the work and effort put into learning the mechanics are thrown out of the window.  Some of these changes are so bad that if you played a character you'd think NO ONE tested these changes or knows how to play that character. On top of that since this was dropped on 1st April I was COPING so hard that this is just the most expensive, worst april fools joke ever, which is why I am only making my review the next day.   So that is why this update sucks. It's straight up disrespectful.  I will be uninstalling and so should you if you are as unhappy as me you should too, as i feel it's the healthiest way for both myself and Namco to realise how bad this was. The overall meta and balance of the game has barely shifted. There are characters who have barely been touched since aprils disastrous patch and are still waiting for proper balancing. Tekken 8 season 1 was very good but definitely had some glaring problems...problematic characters, inconsistent sidestepping, the overpowering heat system, and the prevalent rushdown 50/50 casino battles just to name a few. Instead, they doubled down on the things everyone has been complaining about. In the first interview video that was posted the developers touted this as a "Defense Update" and provided some information that excited everyone. And then the Tekken Talk...Oh the Tekken Talk. Everyone got buffed! Installs for everyone! Chip damage on throw breaks! Even the newest character seemed to be quite good from what was demonstrated. I was understandably very nervous but I wanted to wait to play the actual patch before I made any judgement.  Season 2 releases. I can confidently say this is not Tekken anymore. Characters have been buffed like crazy where stances and 50/50 situations are enhanced. Characters with defining weaknesses have been buffed to the extent where that previous weakness is gone and it feels like they all have been homogenized into one distinct playstyle. Heat is even more broken now and I feel there is even less strategy than ever before. This feels like something out of Strive but if I wanted a game like Strive I would just go play Strive! So much for the so-called "Defense Update." Yeah sidesteps are better I must admit but does it really matter if everything tracks and has homing? Even if the devs come out soon and go "We hear you we are working on a fix we apologize blah blah blah" It is completely UNACCEPTABLE that they let this release in this state regardless. How did some of the changes make it past testing? Paul has a ToD and moves that do damage ON BLOCK. Jack has a string that can only be escaped by Power Crush. HOW did this make it past testing?   Enough said

I’m no Tekken pro player or oldhead. I started playing with Tekken 7 release and immediately fell in love with the immense depth of each character and all the crazy dynamics situations you can get in. In other fighting games I found that most characters felt similar too each other. Each character didn't just have a large number of fluff moves they each had unique gameplans, strengths, weaknesses, and quirks. Even though most characters mostly punch and kick they each felt quite unique and the longer you spent on each one you could really start expressing how you like to play that character in a way I hadn't found in any other fighter.   Some characters are super technical, requiring precise inputs for a competitive advantage. Others focused on landing a small number of massive damaging combos that were hard to execute but were weak in the neutral game. Some focus on evasion an countering opponents over aggression. I say all this to emphasize Tekken has never been a solely defensive or offensive game. Every character had it's own unique strengths. Some better at offense and some better at defense with game systems designed to try and keep all of these playstyles balanced together.   Tekken 8 made a massive change to this variety and forces a much more aggressive play style on every character. The implementation of the heat system and the balance changes made to each character have forced players to be more aggressive or struggle for wins. The risk reward ration has been shifting significantly in favor of the attacker every patch since Tekken 7. Tekken 8 took this to the next level. Now you can gamble a 'risky' launcher in your opponents face and if it lands you get half their health bar and are in a 50/50 to lose the round. If you blocked that 'risky' launcher you get one tenth of their healthbar and go back to neutral. This was already a thing in previous Tekken games but in Tekken 8 your defensive choices besides block and guess have slowly been going away. With Tekken 8 release and now with Season 2 offense/defense risk reward has become absurd. You can easily take most of your lifebar successfully blocking long and complex strings of pressure which require you to constantly guess between: Block and take chip or duck and risk getting totally deleted.   Season 2:  Myself, along with a large part of the community have been hoping that with some balance changes and tweaks to the systems the game could have turned into not just the core experience we loved but something new and special in it's own right. Sadly, this has not been the case. With the release of Season 2 we have seen a brutal homogenization of the cast, Ironing out the wrinkles of all the unique and interesting play styles. Characters have had many of their weaknesses patched out and their strengths focused on string based offense into a forced stance 50/50 and repeat. Not to say that characters didn't exist before which focused on overwhelming your opponent with strings and stances (hwoarang players) but those strengths made those characters special and they had weaknesses in their defense to pay for that oppressive offense.   Now it seems that most characters have good defensive options compared to the insane anime fighting game level of offense in the game. Tekken isn't just about taking your opponent to pound town in the corner and mauling them with 50/50s till the guess right and then take you to pound town. It was about variety, some characters flail in your face, roll around on the ground and throw pizzas at you while others in the right hands could form a defense so dense and slippery that you can never grasp on to them and everything in between. Sure pro play was dominated by safe gameplay in older games but 99% of players are pros and can enjoy any of the playstyles. By making all the characters offensive powerhouses that are pretty much forced to flail in your opponents face you take away the variety and character expression that made Tekken special.   Unless the devs make a massive U-turn and change direction completely (which I highly doubt) then this will probably kill all of my interest in the game going forward. Overall, If you want a game to really sink your time into and build up a deeper appreciation for a competitive game then I can't recommend the game. The game is cool if you want to play for a week or two and do some silly moves with friends but as a serious competitive product. The developers have repeatedly and obviously ignored pleas from the community to change direction over years and they seem hostile to the idea of listening to community feedback.

I almost never post reviews but I feel a need to write this considering how much time and effort I've put into Tekken. I got into the series in Tekken 7 Season 2 and became a huge fan. Watching top level players compete in tournaments was about the coolest thing I've ever seen. Players showing the full potential of the characters, having an large wealth of knowledge and skills, being able to express a lot of personality with different play-styles. I developed a real passion for the game, and felt like I found something that I truly resonated with. So I decided to put in lot of effort in order to become better at the game because of that passion.   So when Tekken 8 Season 1 came out, I actually was a big defender of the new entry. I thought it was a start to something that had a lot of potential, and that with time it could become something great. That is if they were willing to listen to community feedback and make some major changes to the heat system while giving a boost to defensive options. So I can't explain to you my disappointment with this game after the release of Season 2. Were it feels like not only did it not reach it's potential they didn't listen to anything we had to say.   Tekken 8 Season 1 had a lot of controversy after 1 month of the game coming out when they added the Tekken Shop, which the community hated thinking it was a cash grab. Then the stage DLC situation was awful where they didn't clearly communicate that you would have to purchase the stage DLC separately despite buying the ultimate edition of the game, and that's just naming a few. So Tekken needed a big win with Season 2, a fresh start and something for people to start looking forward to with the future of the game. Unfortunately they dropped the ball again.   For Season 2 they did several interviews stating that their goal was to increase defensive options for the game, when in actuality it feel like their goal was the complete opposite. When they continue to buff offensive options of characters, giving them moves that iron out their weaknesses like giving Asuka more offensive options to open up the opponent or Kazuya more homing moves to deal with people stepping him, it feels like they remove character identity and counter play which makes the game fun in my opinion. When they continue to hyper focus on the utilization of Heat, and constant aggression, it feels like it comes at the cost of defensive options. In fairness they did add things like allowing you so Side Step in both directions while in a forced crouched state, or allowing you to buffer a Side Step making it easier to deal with block stun situations, but they added these things and give a large portion of the cast plus on block homing mids that defeat the purpose of buffing movement. Not only that, but the current state of the game is broken where you have bugs like Paul's F1+2 allowing an unblockable follow up with WS3,2 because they gave the character a stance transition, where combo damage is excessively high, you get punished for breaking throws receiving chip damage, while they stated they would remove this it does not change the fact that it is currently in the game and is something we have to deal with.  I'll try to make a quick and list my thoughts of the Pros and Cons of game and why you should or shouldn't buy it.  PROS  - Graphics are incredible it's truly one of the best looking fighting games hands down - Story mode is great, Tekken has never had amazing writing when it comes to story telling but there's a lot of passion and effort in the story mode it's definitely worth playing -Lots of great content, like Tekken Ball, Arcade mode, Character endings, etc. -Tekken Lounge is cool idea, a bit cartoonish also wish there was more to do  -Great Tekken for new comers, lots of options for people to pick up and play with special style, etc. -the removing of Magic 4's and the overall nerfing of counter hit utility was a welcome change in my opinion -Some reworkings of Characters are actually interesting -Having a powered up version of your character (Heat Mechanic) is an interesting idea in theory -Load times are quite quick and instant rematching is great  CONS  -Forced 50/50 and mixups situations are horrible -Heat Engagers being +17 on hit and Heat dashes being +5 on block is too oppressive -Many character reworkings are horrible such as Yoshi, Kuma, Jin,(I'm a Jin main btw),etc. -Throws were homing in S1 which they removed but brought back in S2 being homing for King in Heat Why? -The removal of character identity by the homogenization of characters and moves (example every Mishima type character has a PEWGF now when previously Kazuya only possessed it) -Lack of overall counterplay for many situations -Ranked system is still broken you can’t get win streak bonus points but still get lose streak punishment points -Many controversial situations such as Tekken Shop, Stage DLC, and lack of listening to community feedback

I'm writing this as a big fan of Tekken. I started with Tekken 2 and Tekken 3, played Tag 1 and Tekken 5 for a while, but I never owned a console beyond the PS1. Because of that, I only played Tekken rarely and occasionally until Tekken 7 (2,175 hours) and Tekken 8 (861 hours) at the time of writing this review.  In T8, offense is overwhelmingly strong and easy, while defense is risky, restricted, and exhausting. This alone has made the game tiring and boring to play and watch after just a year. No matter how well or poorly we play, on average, half of our time is spent attacking and the other half defending. It makes no sense to prioritize and enhance one half of the game (offense) while neglecting the other (defense). That’s not how you create a great fighting game—that’s how you end up with a half-baked one. And with the Season 2 patch, Tekken 8 is now even worse than that. Every flaw in the game has been amplified fivefold, making Tekken 8 a truly bad game.  Furthermore, 95% of defensive play is matchup-specific, buried under an endless list of moves and animations. The developers keep gatekeeping talented newcomers by piling new moves on top of old ones, making each new title less accessible and more confusing. Years must be invested just to engage in meaningful mind-games against an ever-growing and ever-changing pool of moves, frame data, and characters—hoping for a slight dopamine boost while merely trying to keep cortisol levels in check during defense. It’s a lazy and uninspired way to add complexity and depth. Quantity doesn’t equal quality! No number of attacks will make the game engaging if the core mind-game revolves around a dull, forced 50/50 mix-up. How long can we enjoy winning, and how long can we ignore the frustration of losing when it all boils down to a simple coin-flip guess?  On top of that, Tekken’s archetypes have completely lost their distinct characteristics, turning every character into an uninspired jack-of-all-trades. Even the unique identities and playstyles of competitive players have been diluted by Tekken 8’s forced offensive gameplay.  Uninstalled. I’m both happy and sad to have made this decision.

I’ve spent a good part of my life playing Tekken. Not just playing—living it, studying it, pushing it to its limits. I was a pro player. I’ve felt the thrill of victory, the sting of loss. But now, with Season 2 of Tekken 8, I barely recognize the series. It’s not the more aggressive direction that I’m criticizing—on the contrary, I loved that vision at first. But the execution was a failure. Tekken 8 is a beautiful empty shell: fast, flashy, "aggressive"… but hollow once you look past the surface.  ❌ A painful lack of vision What made Tekken unique and deeply satisfying was the respect for each character’s limits. You had to understand your weaknesses, play around them, cover them up. You had to study your opponent’s flaws, look for openings, punish. That was the thrill—the micro-decisions, the spacing, the timing, the movement. The art of earning your mixups. Not a free 50/50 because pushed one button. Earning a mix-up opportunity used to mean something. It was a reward. A peak moment. Now? You get there without effort. You spam, you force, you rush—who cares if it fails, you’ll get another shot in three seconds. And that’s the saddest part. It feels like the devs don’t even understand their own system anymore. They patch blindly, overhaul core mechanics with no coherent philosophy, stack new systems on top of each other with no regard for clarity or elegance. Everything is loud, everything is blunt, but nothing is precise. Tekken isn’t a game of mastery anymore—it’s a game of consumption. Add to that: - A €40 Season Pass - Battle Passes that offer nothing meaningful - Cosmetic packs on top of a full-price game - Monetization that feels like a premium gacha And you start to wonder whether Tekken is just dressing up as a fighting game while selling loot boxes in disguise.  I’m not just disappointed. I feel betrayed. Tekken has been with me since childhood. It was a journey, a bond, a conversation between me and the game. Now I feel like that story is ending. Not because I’ve changed—but because Tekken has turned its back on what it was. This isn’t rage. It’s sadness. Because I wanted to believe we still had a future together.

You spend most of the time standing there trying your best to block against a barrage of ridiculous attacks, unblockable moves, launching grabs. And, forbid that you actually try to do anything, because a single launch will have you in the air for half the round, take most of your health bar, and lead to a bad okizeme setup afterwards where you are forced to deal with a horrible mixup.   Moreso. The devs have shown that they do not care at all about player feedback. Everyone was begging them for nerfs and better defensive options, but instead, nearly every character has been buffed. Tekken historically was a unique, tricky, but highly rewarding game with a lot of mental stack options. Now, even if you're winning, the game is frustrating and honestly kind of boring.   Certain characters feel effortless, they can do whatever they want. Nobody has any weaknesses, and every character is the same archetype of stance transition into mixup into insane damage.   Tekken devs don't want you to block, everything just encourages random mashing, and it's really annoying, and now they've shown that the game will not improve.   I don't recommend this at all, and Tekken is my favourite game. Maybe one day it will be better, but right now, they are doubling down on all the worst aspects of the game.

If you are new to Tekken, and to fighting games in general, this game could be the one for you. But if you're an old-school Tekken enthusiast, then no. Then you should avoid this game like the plague.  Why? Because this game is not Tekken. It carries the name, the sound, and the looks, but it is not - I repeat - a Tekken game. Where Tekken used to be easy to learn, but extremely hard to master, with each character having their strengths and weaknesses, they pretty much eliminated all of that in Tekken 8. Now almost every character in this game has the tools for every situation. Some would call that balance; I call it what is - lack of depth.  Yes, the ones who play this game on professional level still crush the newcomers and people, who have actual lives outside of playing video games, so of course there are those who still claim the game requires actual skill to be good at. But when even the professional players publicly mock the game for having become a braindead slugfest due to its many faults, you know Namco has a turd in their hands.   The entire Heat system is so badly designed I almost believed it was done by an Indian developer; and the Rage Art attacks has become the ultimate "I Win" button, that cannot be stopped by anything other than another Rage Art attack. In Tekken 6 (and 7?) you could at least stop it with low attack or a throw. Now, whenever you see your opponent going into Rage mode, you are pretty much forced to stay back and let them initiate lest you get clocked by a blow that will take one fifth of your health.  And then there are the hackers, that the developers of this game promised to deal with back during Tekken 7. Now they even refuse to acknowledge the rampart cheating, script-kiddies, and whatnot that you encounter, when playing online. Hell, they actively ignore any inquiries towards their policy against cheaters if confronted in public; one of the leads of Tekken 8 - Michael Murray - even blocks you if you try and ask him about it. Or anything really. That man has skin thinner than a toilet paper. But is it no wonder, with how often he must have been used to wipe Harada's backside lately?  The music in this game is...okay, I guess? It's Tekken, so if you're familiar with the music from the previous tittles in this franchise, you know what you're going to get. Hard techno inspired metal rifs and not much else.  The stages in this game are pretty, I give them that, but still manage to feel lacking in comparison to the older games. Hell, they used to have snow back in Tekken 5, that moved when you walked on it. Now we don't even get footprints on the sand while fighting in the beach; not even a dust cloud after you body-slam your opponent to the ground.  And the effects; my God the effects in this game. It's not quite as bad now (10.6.2025) as it was at launch, but some of the characters (Clive, especially) have moves that can blind you to what is happening by just throwing his magic attacks and whatnot. It's bloody ridiculous.  In conclusion? This game was not made to cater to the old Tekken players, or hardcore enthusiasts of 3D-movement style fighting games. It was made for the casuals. It looks pretty, I give them that, but it is perhaps the worst designed fighting game in the past ten years or so - at least. Tekken 8 is a Tekken game that lost it's identity from the very beginning. In the hopes of making the game more "exciting" for people who don't love what Tekken truly is and always has been, a game of defensive reads, advanced movement and in depth mind games. Tekken 8 from release was a game that focused on pure guessing and snowballing offense without complex options to respond with, often boiling down to outright guessing randomly, whereas before Tekken was a game of gathering information and saving it to later use to your advantage for a time when it would be the right time; you will die playing this way in Tekken 8. Now with the release of Season 2, the dev team has confirmed that they have completely lost sight of what makes Tekken as a series actually worthwhile to invest time into. The cast has lost all of their unique identities and all been given extremely similar gimmicks, installs, stance mixups etc. Some characters are completely unrecognizable from their past iterations, whereas before legacy knowledge would be rewarded in almost any previous competitive Tekken game, characters like the mishimas have been changed into something completely new to appeal to a newer audience. Overall I think that Tekken 8 has been fundamentally flawed from release and I think it would take a miracle to save this game now, even reverting Season 2 is settling for less and sadly Tekken 7 being left in the state it was (being a testing ground for Tekken 8 mechanics and offense) means that there really isn't a lot of places to go from here, unless Bandai Namco truly does something about this.

I love Tekken.   That said, the direction this game is going will destroy the Tekken franchise if allowed to continue.   The Tekken team is continuously sacrificing the competitive integrity of their game in favor of easy to run offense with no counter-play. This I can only assume is an attempt to make the game more fun and enjoyable for people with zero understanding of Tekken or fighting games in general. The design decisions regarding system mechanics and character balance seem to be aimed towards the utmost casual audience, allowing players with zero or next to zero skill to compete with experienced players (This is straight from the Tekken team btw, the lead game designer Nakatsu has communicated this sentiment several times).  Considering that the past year of Tekken 8 has seen next to no actual balance changes, the community has had a lot of time to play and analyze the state of the game. The community has also been extremely vocal about exactly the type of changes we were expecting so that T8 is able to grow and blossom into an extremely deep and rich competitive experience. This blatant disregard of their community by the Tekken team has left me feeling betrayed, and my faith that this game will improve has been lost.  Even if they spent the next year continuously nerfing system mechanics and broken characters, they still wouldn't be able to undo the damage that version 2.0 has done to the game without completely reverting version 2.0 and restarting from scratch.   So, after 800+ hours played at this point, I feel obligated to give this game a negative review and encourage other players to do the same. I wish we as a community didn't have to go to such extremes to get our voices heard, but unfortunately, money seems to be the only language Namco knows how to speak.  I hope someday in the future I can delete this review and replace it with a positive one, laughing at how silly this version of T8 was.

This started out as a genuinely fun game to play and despite the frustrations with the end of season 1, there was still a lot of skill expression and fun learning its quirks. It was easy to forgive season 1's flaws because the game did not have an arcade release to test the waters. Maybe the smoothest launch a modern Tekken game could get. Hats off to that.  Season 2's initial balance patch is very confusing. I got one character (Lee) to God of Destruction at the end of Season 1 and play a few other characters, so I hope that I can provide enough insight to the game beyond casual play. I don't mind the casuals; please have fun at your pace, but do keep in mind that the problems in this patch that more experienced players take issue with will inevitably trickle down to the casual base.  There were a lot of changes that were meant to "fix" flaws in characters, which is fine to a degree, but they overcompensated with a lot of the buffs and changes on a lot of characters–some of which ruined their identities. For example, part of the fun of Kazuya is that he gets destroyed by sidesteps and his tracking moves are risky, which demands that optimal Kazuya play involves movement, timing, and reading your opponent. Now he's given more tracking moves, which ruins the fun of succeeding with him and counterplaying him.  The fun of Tekken was that each character had very defined strengths and weaknesses, and there just seems to be a whole litany of plus frame pressure and forced stance pressure minimize defensive play (and I like Lidia!). There appears to be more safe, if not possibly plus homing moves added to a game that was trying to emphasize the game's buffed sidestepping. As a result of overtuning, it feels like there's less skill expression and loss of character identity. I actually like and appreciate getting bodied by someone who can pull off something that clearly looked tough to set up or was ultimately risky, and some of that's kind of gone now that they've given a lot of characters too many good solutions to the complex problems that Tekken's movement and systems have always demanded.  At the crux of it, it's not about whether or not a character got too many buffs or nerfs, but rather that the changes–even the buffs–clash with character identities. I personally do not like playing against Steve, but admire his playstyle and design philosophy around finding counterhits and openings; I find it hard not to respect anyone trying to pilot the character, so I'm kinda gutted that they're forcing the character to play more into Lionheart stance mixups instead of the things that make him cool as a character even if those options may technically be beneficial. It'd feel almost as uncharacteristic as giving Zangief a projectile to technically cover a weakness.  I don't know how they can bring this back. They're gonna have to straight-up delete some stuff that they added.

To preface this - it's currently the launch of season 2 of Tekken 8. I like Tekken, I've played Tekken since Tekken 2. I've played every Tekken game to date. I like this franchise so much that I've spent energy following it and playing it over the course of my life.  This game is quite possibly the worst Tekken game I have ever played. I would consider Death by Degrees to be more true to form to Tekken's formula and aesthetic than this game.   You can see right now I have hundreds of hours in this game, you might be asking why? If you don't like it - why spend so much time. Here's why - I have desperately tried to cling onto the idea that if I played enough/ranked up enough it would suddenly click. I've also always liked Tekken and didn't want to drop a franchise I've historically enjoyed so I thought I was missing something.  I wasn't and that point has been proven now.  Tekken 8 was given out to players initially as a review copy without a battle pass addition. Once official release came around a battle pass was added to bypass the review phase. This battle pass and each one afterwards till now contains items which were normally obtained in Tekken games through in-game currency obtained from Online Matches or Arcade mode or even other party modes added in previous games such as Tekken Bowling or Tekken Volleyball.  However with Tekken 8 this was a unwelcome surprise and now it requires real world money.  This is why Tekken 8 now has a asterisk with the message "This product has experienced one or more periods of off-topic review activity".  This is not one of those times.  With the launch of season 2 they emphasised that the updates would favour defence options a bit more. Currently plus frames are rampant with many moves or heat activations which leave no room at all for you to retaliate and certain characters are utterly broken. I don't mean overpowered either but they have them too.  Paul can currently do f,1+2 into while standing 3 and it will bypass the guarding system and hit every time. To go even further, he can press 2 after that unblockable ws,3 and if you're at the wall, you just got wall splat. Which will possibly lead to you losing the match because you anticipated the move coming and blocked like a normal sane individual (You shouldn't have done that).  There is a plethora of similar issues with the game right now. There are many reasons the game is in the state that it is in but it comes to who's currently in charge. This narrows down to Kouhei Ikeda now being game director and Harada becoming an adviser. All "heat" on this issue is directed towards Harada who is sun setting his time with Tekken. All positive notes to take from T8 will be accredited to Ikeda's work on the game. All drawbacks will be learned from for the next game hopefully but ultimately it's Ikeda's series now. Many Soul Calibur developers have transitioned to Tekkens development.  That is the state of Tekken 8's development right now.  There is a bunch of issues why the game is not good right now: Too many plus frames. No actual defensive options. Terrible Heat mechanic. Many moves hitting off axis. Combo damage is incredibly high. Too many stance transitions (Everyone is Lei now apparently). Stock/State Power ups. Chip Damage.  The aesthetic of the previous games' are also lost entirely. T4 still holds the bar for the best with so little to show for it. They only needed a hint of flashy stuff or ridiculous concepts in Tekken. If you look at Clive you can see that's been thrown out the window.  What's also really disappointing is that a lot of players have tried putting the thought into peoples head that previous Tekken games were worse and they don't have the stomach to actually say the series got worse.  It's a really funny twist of fate that Tekken Tag Tournament 2 didn't kill Tekken but Tekken 8 - their most lavish and expensive title to date is doing a better job than Tag 2 ever did.
