[h1]Without a doubt the exact opposite of what anyone wants from a Tekken game. Incompetence and laziness reigns supreme.[/h1]  So Season 1 was a fairly obnoxious state of constant plus-frame mixups, some problematic moves, pockets of limited counterplay and a Heat system that really needed toning down to allow the freedom of opportunity for both players to play (you know, the thing Tekken has always been known for). There was an chance for Namco to turn the game from something a bit lacking back into something great.  However, Season 2 is now a full blown circus and the clowns are the only ones left in charge.  We now have huge plus-frame moves that flow into more hugely plus-frame moves with zero counterplay. Just about every character has gotten some sort of stance transition move into a guaranteed mixup. These offer no defensive scope other than just "guess", or get hit and take in the realms of 100 damage simply because you had the gall to block wrong once. Did you want to utilise movement or specific timings to get around some of these options? Well good luck with that buddy because Tracken 8 with it's Unreal Engine 5 sloppily coded hitboxes guarantee you'll get clipped on even the most linear looking moves and lucky if you're even able to mash an armor move in time to save yourself.   Worse still, the vast majority of these scenarios are both when you get hit and when you block something, so most games simply devolve into back to back 50/50s regardless of whether you're on offense or defense.  Some absolute banger changes also included defenders receiving chip damage on throws that they successfully broke (yes you read that right, well done for defending yourself properly!), and Heat Engagers being landed allowing you to go into full crouch for yet another layer of inescapable mixup that some characters can make heretical use of. All of this wrapped up in a a patch that promised to focus more on improving the defensive aspects of the game by...buffing out damn near most characters weaknesses, giving everyone the same lazy "new move into stance of choice" buttons, "install" states for nearly everyone, and homogenising everyone into an offensive powerhouse that plays exactly the same.   Other stupid changes include straight up removing legacy mechanics like counterhit ki-charge properties that weren't even close to competitively problematic, and outright babying on other mechanics that nobody asked for. Seriously, are you telling me the modern fighting game player absolutely needs a shortcut input for a quarter-circle motion because it's too complex? Is this 2XKO???  The people "balancing" this game are an absolute joke. Never before have I seen such a tone-deaf approach to game development, and that doesn't even begin to include the top brass and their attempts to eke out as much money as possible through micro-transactions, battle passes, and flaky DLC practices that seek to trick consumers into getting less than what they were expecting. Old reviews slamming the stage DLC will get you up to speed on that one but the TL;DR of that one is simply corporate greed on Namco's part.  All in all it seems my favourite childhood series since Tekken 2 has finally caught up to the same garbage standards seen from every other "AAA" developer / publisher these days.  I sincerely hope there is a crowd large enough to cater to whoever the hell Namco think are out there that want a game that plays like this, because if not it's definitely going to die a very quick and undignified death and deservedly so.

Skill expression, combo knowledge and attack inputs have been streamlined, removing satisfaction from performing mechanically intensive combo routes and ruining countless hours building up muscle memory for a character. Every character has been reduced to the same boring play-style: pop heat > easily apply heavy plus frames > transition to stance > 50/50 for your life. After the constant feedback from the player-base for over a year, it should be clear to the dev team that being on the receiving end of this mind-numbing offence with barely any counter-play simply isn't fun, and the reverse effect of having to succumb to the same method of play just to win is not gratifying. In May of last year, the Tekken team publicly stated that they would refrain from patching the game's balancing for the rest of the year, continuing their statement saying they would consider the feedback gathered throughout that year and adjust for season 2. During this time, what the Tekken development team refers to as "Veteran Tekken players" have voiced  their feedback in the favor of toning down the overall strength of offense significantly in this game. The idea behind this being that counterplay to offense was very difficult in season 1.  Instead of taking the feedback of Veteran Tekken players for what it is and implementing it within what fits inside of their game vision, as they publicly stated they would, they go in the opposite direction. The game balance in season 2 offers even stronger offense with the main available counterplay being a guess between high/mid/low, or frametrap/pressure extension. Before season 2 officially released, they stated that defensive movement was going to be enhanced, in order to make playing around this absurdly strong level of offense possible. This ended up not working out as stated.  Overall Tekken 8 was a disappointing game from the start, but given the benefit of the doubt seeing as it was Bandai Namco's first no-arcade Tekken game release. Now I'm disappointed much more by the decisions made for game balancing in season 2, considering their communication throughout season 1. And finally I'm disappointed by Bandai Namco because of their misrepresentations of season 2 ahead of time. Mentioning on multiple occasions that defense would be enhanced, but that hasn't turned out to be the case.  Very unfortunate! TL;DR: The developers seem to ignore community feedback and continue making changes no one asked for.  While this is my favorite franchise, I can no longer, in good conscience, recommend this game. As of writing this review (April 1st), I can’t help but feel like this is an elaborate April Fools’ joke. That being said, my opinion may change in the future, but only if Bandai Namco actually listens to the community.  Since launch, many players (myself included) have criticized Tekken 8 for taking an overly aggressive direction, favoring:  50/50 situations (mix-ups that lead to massive rewards with counterplay reduced to guesswork).  Severe disadvantage scenarios (where a single mistake, i.e., getting hit, can leave you practically stuck in a cutscene).  Overtuned moves and characters, making balance feel nonsensical.  Today’s new season (patch/update) has only made things worse. To say I’m disappointed would be an understatement. Instead of addressing these issues, Bandai Namco’s balancing team has doubled down by introducing even more overpowered moves, leaving the Heat mechanic untouched, and outright ignoring the biggest complaints that have been voiced since launch.  This isn’t just about the latest update, TEKKEN 8 has had issues from the start:  Lackluster battle passes that offer recycled, low-effort rewards (many of which were free in previous games).  Unfair monetization practices, such as leaving new stages out of the season pass without prior notice. Worse still, while they later added the stages to the character/stage pass, they excluded players who had purchased the Ultimate Edition or season pass prior to doing that. Effectively ripping off early supporters.  Poor communication, with little to no transparency regarding updates or requested changes from the community.  Misleading statements, such as claiming Season 2 would focus on "defensive play in the lateral aspects of a 3D fighting game", when the changes suggest the opposite.  Online matches are still unstable after 14 months FFS! As an online focused fighting game, TEKKEN 8 requires a solid ranked matchmaking system. Yet, over a year since launch, the netcode remains inconsistent. For example:  A 5-bar wired connection (which should be optimal) often results in laggy, choppy gameplay.  A 3-bar Wi-Fi connection, which should be worse, can sometimes work better than a 5-bar wired match.  This kind of instability is unacceptable in a modern competitive fighting game.  Ranked is stupidly designed. Tekken uses a first-to-two format. Meaning the first player to win two matches wins the set. In theory, this is fine. However, players can simply leave after the first match. If they encounter an unfavorable matchup or an opponent they struggle against, there’s no incentive to stay. This defeats the purpose of the first-to-two format entirely.  Cheating is inevitable in online games, but Bandai Namco has done little to combat it. This issue has worsened since Tekken 7, yet there seems to be no real effort to fix it.  I’ve given this game far too many chances, but I’m done. If Tekken continues down this path, it risks becoming another SoulCalibur. A once great franchise now essentially dead.  I tried to remain optimistic. I didn’t want to contribute to the negativity surrounding the game. But after 14 months, there’s no excuse.  Bandai Namco, do better.

Before i type this review i wanna mention that i've been playing this series since the arcades of Tekken 2 when i was young. It has been a year and some months since the game came out, some patches happened and characters released so i guess it's fair to write something about it now.   Let's start with the "sway" from the freedom of customization (which is the lesser important problem but still a big one for longtime fans), now the game has an in-game store filled with poor cashgrabs things that range from a literal sphere to some premade costume or a horrible white t-shirt with some decal on it at the price of 5 bucks (all items were free to obtain with ingame currency in previous games.) On top of it there's a "battle-pass" in game which just bloats you with more of those  (most recycled from previous games or really low effort content) and isn't really appealing to finish at all. The further problem of those things are that there was no announcement regarding them if not some days prior to the FIRST patch, they were literally hidden to reviewers and the like. Also to buy the premium pass you have to overspend your coins and aside of that, the DLC prices are absurd as usual, so more scummy cashgrabs.  PS: The only good customization that i see from time to time being worth getting freely from ghosts in the lobby are the artworks, which are worth the praise and use for the amazing community that worked on them.  The story was probably the best part of the game, aside of some niche situations, it would have been better to improve it further with more battles like that of the tekken force rumble you play in some chapters. Even better if they put some of those scenarios from Tekken 6 where you would walk around places with your characters. Aside of the arcade mode and the ghost battle (which i'll summarize after) the game lacks some good singleplayer content and there's lots of ideas to improve it like the ones i mentioned. If you play a lot with friends and want to try something else, there's Tekken Ball at least, returning from previous games which is a nice alternative mode, would be happy to see bowling again as well.  I forgot to mention things about the ghost battle. It feels way more clunky to move around the menus to start it and even if the "ghosts" are somehow a bit better (by a smal margin) to fight against and get rewards/item currency, the way you have to get back to the lobby to change stages gets you bored fast, especially if you want to try stuff you practiced offline and want to get a handful of it before hopping online.  The battle system itself feels like a gamble everytime you play, the very first iteration they showed of this game was probably the best look of it as the in-game mechanic of "heat" was something rewarded to you during the match and not given at the start of the round. Now that Season 2 is out every character has been lacking its identity (further making everyone very easy to use, once again dividing the need of handy characters) since the dev team toned down on most (if not all) okizeme strategies, setups, ki-charge mindgames and so on, in favor of flashy lengthy combos, forced 50/50s situations distributed to everyone in the cast. The battle system team working on the patchnotes barely understands the needs of all the players categories (newbies and pros) and mostly ignores the negative response from the community toward the "overly-aggressive" focus on the gameplay, giving away false hopes of adjustements that when you try them you know they just fed you lies.   Now we're at a point where i think the community is further straying away and has zero want to further discuss with whoever is in charge of deciding the changes for the game and the future of it is looking really bleak. I love the series and the characters since i've grown along with but the way the state of the game is, does not engage me at all.

I feel like this is just a culmination of what Tekken was for the past 20+ years, and perhaps Yutaka Kounoe is being proven right, with regards to what he said about the direction of Tekken games after his departure.   "So does Kounoe like the recent effort between Capcom and Namco? "I have no interest in the Street Fighter X Tekken crossover. I haven't played it. The Tekken that emerged after I left has fallen below my expectations. It's a lot easier to create 'arrangements' of old games than to make something new. To still be relying on Tekken even now is proof that Namco's real strength has disappeared, and I'm shocked by the decline in creativity and development ability. It's shameful to call yourself a developer or a creator if you can't design new games. Relying only on collaborations that will sell well shows a lack of imagination, and it's not going to set the world on fire."  In some ways, it feels like a huge exaggeration, but it's hard to deny that the Tekken series has been characterized by the lack of innovation. New things get added all the time, but it's always done through small iterations on the existing formula, unlike something like Street Fighter's complete revamp of core mechanics.  Until some point, it was easier to look at it as not "lack of innovation" but rather an attempt to continually refine the existing formula to the point of perfection, a goal similar to that of Tekken's rival series, Virtua Fighter. That idea started to crumble in Tekken 7. It made some obvious concessions for the sake of streamlining the gameplay, making it more approachable for beginners and more flashy for spectators.  With Tekken 8, the idea of trying to "refine" something is completely gone. It's impossible to say that people in charge want to take Tekken formula to its peak, when all the things that defined the series are getting hammered down for the sake of broader appeal. The reasoning that pops up over and over during dev talks and patch notes is that certain elements are made easier, more intuitive, stronger, or more consistent. That might sound fine in vacuum, but within the game, that usually translates to weaker defense, stronger offense, higher combo damage, more homogenized cast, and lower execution barrier for things that should by all means demand higher level of execution. Defense has always been one of the more difficult things to learn in Tekken, and it seem like the solution BN arrived at was to make offense so strong that staying on defense is detrimental. You have to actively go on the offensive and gamble by taking risks if you want to turn the tides.  Going back to the beginning, this is why it feels like a culmination of what Tekken was for the past 20+. It's a series that had no vision for improvement or change, because every time changes were introduced, it got a little bit worse, only surviving thanks to those changes not being severe enough, and having an incredibly strong foundation that was mostly established in T3/Tag1 and then calcified in Tekken 5, after the severe Tekken 4 backlash reminded them what people did and did not want in their Tekken games.   Even with Tekken 4, Harada said that many of its changes were made because he was listening to feedback, and putting together a frankenstein out of disparate voices, rather than trying to make a game that he specifically wanted to make. Despite having some interesting redeeming qualities (better storytelling, great atmosphere, uniquely interactive stages), it was still a result of trying to calculate a "perfect sequel" that follows up best-selling Tekken game to-date with everything fans could want! Tekken 8's blunders seem to be result of the same thinking process. People told us Tekken 7 was too defensive so we made a Tekken game that is very offensive. Now that this has terribly backfired, Harada is still trying to put together some emergency round table to discuss what the game should be.  Not every game that follows a singular vision is good, but even a bad game designed by committee will never be better than a bad game that was a result of genuine passion.

I've been very tolerant and hopeful for this game, up until today.  It was okay that after release and the positive reviews have settled in they released an in-game shop where you could buy legacy outfits for your characters that were otherwise available in previous games.  It was okay that the game came out in a very imbalanced state, as this is the first time there is no beta-testing in Arcades as it used to be. Tekken historically needed innovations for each iterations to experiment and try out things for better or worse.  It was okay that DLC characters are released in overpowered state to then later on be nerfed as a business decision.  It was okay that some mechanics simply either did not work or were ridiculously inconsistent. These are to be fleshed out over time, especially since the game was completely rewritten in a newer engine.  What's not okay is, how blatantly there is a decision towards erasing anything and everything, that made Tekken Tekken in the past, especially with the release of Season 2 right now.  The game now is stupidly simplified and robs the players (both the attacker and defender) from the trees of decisions to at best, rock/paper/scissors - where in my opinion sometimes there isnt simply a scissor anymore and just rock and paper.  There is a clear mindset that the direction the game director wants the game to head towards is flashiness with very in-your-face effects and anime-sque moments to hopefully bring in newcomers. All while neglecting the hardcore veteran playerbase and what they wished the game offered.  There is an unprecedented power creep that this season has introduced onto all available characters, while in previous a discussion round (Tekken Talk) the clear direction that they envisioned and broadcasted for the new season changes was to loosen up the currently overagression-driven state of the gameplay, and to enhance defensive options. Despite all that, most of the changes introduced was simply power creep for all characters, and limiting interaction options for the players.  I was very enthusiastic about the franchise ever since I rejoined the scene in 2019 after like a 12-15 year hiatus since childhood, but the current state of the game just doesn't allow me to overlook the issues anymore.  Tekken is losing its' identity, and makes my decision how I want to spend my time a little bit easier from now on... Not playing it.  Edit: Welp, after 6 months of hiatus I touched the game again - tiny steps have been made, but there's still a long way ahead for the devs to fix the game.

Let me break down to you how a match usually will look in this game: - Round start lotery, even if both players do a jab at the same time it will be fully random. - The player with frame advantage, or a better timing does a mid/high that is at least +5-+15 into stance transition - Stance 50/50 usually resulting in another guess situation. Here we have two paths: - You guessed right -> You block, sidestep, crouch. Either you put your oponent in a 50/50 situation or launch him for about 1/2 or even 70% life and put him in a wakeup 50/50. - You guessed wrong -> Your oponent puts you in a blender resulting in same thing as above. If you like this style of quick gameplay where mostly you will be in a casino with your oponent, please suit yourself. If not (like me) please avoid wasting money on this game. If you're just looking for a casual fighting game that you can just mash on for 30 minutes, this is probably a good option. Wouldn't recommend the game for anyone looking for depth at this point.  This game launched with the philosophy of "aggression", which is not really what this series has been known for. Defensive options in this game are limited and running your offense will carry you an unbelievable amount.  Season 2 was touted as an update where the devs wanted to make defending better and giving the defender more options. The playerbase has been saying that all of the offensive mechanics (heat engagers, heat smashes, 50/50s everywhere) were way too much. We got a buff to sidesteps (which is great), but every other change on the patch notes was buffing offense by giving characters more plus frames, more 50/50s, more homing moves, and more stance transitions. Not to mention that instead of nerfing specific character interactions with game systems that were unintended, the dev team will instead remove the system for the entire cast.  It's understandable that the devs want T8 to be distinct from previous entries, but this game feels like it cares about nothing beyond drawing in new players, whether they stay or not. Execution has been reduced a significant amount, knowledge checks have been removed from many characters, and many strings or moves you previously needed to react to with movement/ducks have been changed to no longer require this. All of the changes in Tekken 8 have been done to appeal to a new player and seem accessible, when in reality, all this is doing is removing depth from the game.

This is a 2D guessing game that features some characters from an old fighting game franchise called "Tekken", which lasted from Tekken 1 until Tekken Tag Tournament 2. It's fun to see these classic characters in a different genre of games, although this game can be frustrating, specially for avid players of the older games. Tekken 8 is filled with panic buttons and mechanics designed specifically to frustrate players that valued the design of past games, such as heat, heat smash, power crushes and rage arts (introduced in Tekken 7).  It also introduces characters designed to infuriate and be hated by 95% of the players, such as Victor and Clive, that look completely out of place fighting any other character and on any stage.  This game contains long movies that will keep you staring at the screen for up to 25 seconds, they call these "combos" and "rage art". I recommend alt-tabbing as soon as you get launched and get some work done while your opponent performs his combo, as they are like 15 hit combos on average now, unlike the 3 to 5 hit max damage combos in Tekken 3.   They supposedly introduced new mechanics to make the game easier to pickup for beginners, but I think the result has been exactly the opposite: Tekken is more complicated than ever before, as all the moves already had so many properties to be studied (frames on hit, frames on block, frames on counter hit, tracking to one side, track to the other side, range, is it a special mid or normal mid, how punishable is it on whiff, does it hit grounded, does it work on this combo, is it guaranteed after that other move, does it have extensions, is it a launcher, does it guarantee any other move afterwards or they can block even if at -15, etc.), and now they add heat... which changes some of these properties for many of your moves, while adding even more moves that you can perform only while in heat. So, in addition to all the other properties, now you have to consider "does it start heat, what if I'm already in heat, does it end the heat state, is it a counter hit launcher on heat??".  Overall, this is a game with pretty graphics, decently well optimized, with local multiplayer so you can pretend to have fun with friends and family, and works well. I have not experienced a single crash so far. It's not fun, but it's a decently well developed software.

Tekken 8 – A Step Forward, Two Steps Back  Tekken 8 was supposed to be the next big leap for the legendary fighting game series. Instead, it ends up feeling like a chaotic mash-fest, completely missing the strategic depth that defined previous entries.  The gameplay is flashy but shallow. The new Heat system looks cool on the surface, but it's wildly unbalanced and encourages random button mashing over tactical play. Defensive tools have been nerfed into the ground, making the game feel heavily skewed toward brainless aggression. What used to be a game of precision and timing is now often won by whoever mashes the fastest.  Character balance is a mess. Jin, for example, feels absurdly overtuned — hands down one of the most overpowered characters in the game. Dragunov and Heihachi? Land a combo into Heat, and the round’s basically over. The gap between top-tier and low-tier characters is painfully obvious, and certain matchups feel like a total waste of time.  Then there are the nonsensical in-game moments — situations where nothing makes logical sense. Whether it’s bizarre hitbox interactions or mechanics that seem to ignore the laws of the game itself, it feels like Tekken 8 wasn’t properly tested or balanced.  Visually, the game is stunning. The soundtrack is solid. But all of that means nothing when the core gameplay feels so chaotic, shallow, and unfair. If you came for the tight, thoughtful combat Tekken is known for, prepare to be disappointed.  Final Verdict: Tekken 8 is not a worthy successor. It plays more like a flashy arcade brawler than a serious fighting game. Fans of the series who appreciated its depth and balance will likely walk away frustrated. To preface: I am a complete newcomer to fighting games, all of my thoughts here are from the perspective of someone who has no frame of reference from previous Tekken games. The most I did before buying this game was watch some Youtube guides to understand the game's basic mechanics and if it looked like something I'd like to play.  Choosing between a positive or negative review was a difficult choice, I greatly enjoyed the core gameplay but there were many annoying things in the game that compounded into me ultimately going with a negative review. At one point I even uninstalled the game, only to reinstall it later just to get another fix (Which was excruciating since it's a 100+ GB game). Here are my thoughts on the game's various pieces in no particular order.  The Story - The story mode was the first thing I did in the game, and I was not very impressed. I watched all of the cutscenes summarizing previous games, but even with that the writing was simply abysmal. Extremely generic anime writing with very little depth to any of the characters. The whole thing took me maybe 4-5 hours to complete, so I'm sure a fighting game veteran would likely blitz through the whole thing. Annoyingly, the story mode did not offer much in the way of a tutorial, so most of my learning was pausing at the start of a fight and scrolling through the move lists. The character episodes were even less, you got a brief introductory cutscene, a few fights, than an end cutscene, without adding much more depth to the characters.  Arcade Quest - To be perfectly honest, arcade quest might as well have been the real story mode. It was better in basically every way. A more in-depth tutorial that focuses on whatever character you're playing, a sense of progression as you travel to different arcades fighting stronger and stronger bots (even if they're absolute garbage once you start learning your fundamentals). The writing is still generic as hell of course, but it was fun.  Tekken Ball - Tried it once, didn't care for it... that's all.  Fight Lounge - Seems like an interesting way to introduce a more social aspect to the game. You can chat with people, play against them over and over, and even practice with other players which is really cool. The main downside though is that playing against people is clunky, you have to go to a set of machines, go through a loading screen into a queue, to then "match" against the person. It's very awkward, slow, and unintuitive.  Customization - The customization is alright. I like the ability to freely change parts of an item/clothing to any color you want, and it's a feature I wish more character creators would adopt. The amount of items you can equip is a bit underwhelming, options for facial features like hairstyles and eye colors are especially limited, and the inability to add or tweak things on full body outfits feels rather restrictive. Still, it gives enough creative freedom to pull off some really good looking and/or goofy outfits, as well as cosplays.  Monetization - This is a $70 game. If it just had cosmetic microtransactions, I'd find it distasteful but ultimately not care too much since it would be just that, cosmetic. Unfortunately, this is not the case for Tekken 8. You have a battlepass, and paid characters and stages. Making people pay for decades-old characters in a $70 game is criminal, and I hate that ♥♥♥♥ like this is normalized in the gaming industry as a whole. Hell, the worst part for me is that you can't even choose the characters in practice mode if you don't own them, so you can't even lab them unless you have somebody willing to practice online with you.  Practice/Replays - The practice mode is phenomenal. The sheer amount of options and settings you can adjust allows you to practice any scenario, positioning, combo, punish, etc. Additionally, the ability to view replays, as well as take control while watching them is a fantastic. A very well thought-out mode.  Quickplay/Ranked - Okay, time for the real meat of the game. Starting out, I got my ass handed to me, as was expected. I slowly worked my way up to Garyu over the course of a few months as I learned a character or two, slowly working on my fundamentals and figuring out how to stop getting hit by stupid ♥♥♥♥. (Disclaimer: I still get hit by stupid ♥♥♥♥, and I cannot break throws, such is life.)  The learning process was extremely fun, getting a feel for the game's movement and applying more moves and combos into real matches was a blast. The ability to infinitely rematch in quickplay was a much needed addition, as it allowed me and a complete stranger to keep beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other while learning our characters' matchup, this was peak enjoyment of the game for me. Unfortunately, reaching the Garyu/Shinryu threshold is where issues with the game became more prevalent.  I understand that much of the game's population is within orange and red ranks, but the skill disparity just doesn't make sense. Sometimes I would get matched up against what felt like green ranks who didn't understand frames and just button mash as you obliterate them. Other times, I would get matched up against what felt like blue ranks who promptly beat my ass. They ducked every high and grab, blocked or parried every low, performed insane wall-carry combos, etc. I'm not sure if smurfing is that prevalent or red ranks are just THAT wide in the range of skill, but matches like these became so common that it just wasn't fun.  Additionally, reaching Garyu is where the game's aggressive nature became much more prevalent. I met more people that would just absolutely rush me down with characters like Nina, Heihachi, and Reina with constant plus on block strings and 50/50s. Now let me say, I understand that these are mostly knowledge checks. I understand that each of these characters have gaps where you can sidestep, jab, crouch, etc to get out of the rush. What I'm saying is that situations like these are where most of the fun vanished. I play games in my free time after work and weekends, I like Tekken 8, but I want to play other games too. For a single character to have the ability to completely shut you down unless you decide to go and lab them for extended periods of time feels ridiculous. It feels like red ranks are a wall that halts all of your momentum until you decide to start extensively labbing, it was a very sudden difficulty spike and smothered out a lot of the enjoyment I was having with the game.  Now, the above wouldn't bother me nearly as much if most of these issues didn't seep into Quickplay, but they do. Huge skill disparity, some characters forcing you to adapt or die, relatively common lagswitching and plugging. It all just feels like a coin toss as to whether or not I'm going to actually enjoy a match. (Also, WHY are people with 20%+ disconnection rates allowed to play the game without any penalties, and WHY don't you at least get a win on record whenever somebody DCs?)  Heat & Rage - I believe my problems with the aggressive gameplay are exacerbated by heat smashes and rage arts. The damage boost from rage as a comeback mechanic seems fine, what I HATE is rage arts. A fast, hyperarmor, high damage move that ignores all hits and throws and forces you to watch a cutscene is not fun. I've lost track of the amount of times where I get someone down to low health, and then the entire match turns into a spacing game of who's going to press the "win button" first. I don't like heat at all, the core gameplay already feels robust, but adding heat smashes and oppressive chip damage just takes away from the game.  As of this review I've uninstalled, I REALLY wanted to like this game, but the constant back-and-forth of enjoyment and annoyance has finally worn me down. Might play more, might not, but without a serious overhaul of the game's aggressive nature, I don't see myself playing much more of this game.

Tekken 8 – the fighting game hyped to the heavens. But does it live up to it? 🤔 Well... yes and no. As someone who’s been grinding MK11, MK1, and SF6 these past few weeks, here’s my honest opinion. ✅ THE GOOD 🔥 The Golden Middle Between SF and MK MK1 – great story, but online is absolute pain. 💀 SF6 – godlike online, but have almost no story mode. Tekken 8? It has both. A proper story mode,  and solid online with good netcode and matchmaking. 🎨 Graphics  Looks absolutely stunning.  Stages are 🔥 – fully 3D, interactive, and destructible.  🧥 Customization Huge W for character customization. Finally, a game where we can dress up our mains however we want. SF6 and MK1, take notes. This should be standard in every fighting game. 🎭 The Roster – Pretty Solid Great mix of old and new characters. ❌ THE BAD 🥴 Gameplay – Feels Random and... Jelly? Hard to explain, but something about Tekken 8’s combat feels weird. 🤔 Played as Victor, and he just steamrolls everything. Got 5-6 wins in a row without knowing a single combo.  Switched to another character – immediate ass-whooping. Balance issues? Yeah, probably. 🏀 The Combat is Basically Juggling The only real strategy in Tekken? Kick your opponent into the air, juggle them like a clown, and smash them into a wall. 🎪 If you can do that, your win rate is 98%. Skill? Optional. Fighting game or juggling simulator? Hard to tell. 💾 This Game Eats Storage for Breakfast We all know Unreal Engine 5 games are massive, so TK8 is not an exception. I barely managed to fit MK1, MK11 and Tekken 8, on my SSD. Had to put SF6 on an HDD, and guess what? It still runs fine. What does it mean? Tekken 8 is very hardware/storage-hungry.  Tekken 8 is a good game if you: ✔️ Love fighting games 🎮 ✔️ Enjoy the lore & story mode 📖 ✔️ Want to wreck people online (or get wrecked) 🤼 But how long will the fun last? For me – not very long. I keep coming back to SF6, and still checking out MK1 updates, but Tekken 8? It might not have that long-term grip. Maybe I’m just not a Tekken guy. Final Score⚖️: 6.5/10

[b]Tekken 8 launched with incredible promise, showcasing polished visuals, refined mechanics, and a solid competitive structure that felt like a worthy evolution of the legendary fighting game franchise. My original review reflected that excitement, but with the release of Season 2, it's clear the direction has shifted in a way that undermines everything longtime fans loved about the series.  The aggressive mechanics, once a breath of fresh air, have now spiraled into flashy, over-the-top movesets that feel more suited for Soul Calibur than Tekken. The legacy of tight, grounded combat has been replaced with cinematic flair and excessive effects that distract from the core fundamentals. This isn’t the Tekken we’ve known and loved, it's something else entirely, and not in a good way.  The new moves introduced in Season 2, have dramatically shifted the meta, prioritizing spectacle over strategy. Characters now feel bloated with tools that diminish the nuance and spacing that defined high-level play. The Heat System, once a promising mechanic, now feels intrusive and gimmicky, forcing a style of play that betrays Tekken's legacy of balanced, defensive-optional gameplay.  Visually, the game remains impressive, but visuals can't carry a competitive fighter alone. The core gameplay identity is being lost. With every patch, it feels like Tekken is becoming more of an arena spectacle than a technical, mind-game-heavy fighter. If this is the direction Nakatsu is pushing, fusing Soul Calibur flair into Tekken, it’s time to seriously rethink leadership on the design team. What was once a celebration of legacy now feels like a franchise losing its identity.  I never thought I’d have to update my review this way, but after hundreds of hours invested and witnessing the changes brought by Season 2, it’s clear Tekken 8 is no longer the game I was excited about at launch. It had the potential to be one of the greatest in the series, but this path? It's a misstep that may cost the trust of its most loyal fans.[/b]

Launched in January 2024, it’s a visual and mechanical powerhouse, driven by Unreal Engine 5, with aggressive, fast-paced combat that hooks both newcomers and veterans. Long standing franchise veteran Katsuhiro Harada, a Tekken visionary since the ‘90s, infuses this installment with his signature flair—think destructible stages and a Heat system that rewards bold play. His influence shines in the game’s competitive scene, a cornerstone of its identity. Tournaments like EVO and CEOtaku thrive on Tekken 8’s depth, with rollback netcode ensuring crisp online matches, though pros still debate balance tweaks like Heihachi’s return. The latest DLC drop, Clive Rosfield from Final Fantasy XVI, adds a fiery twist. Released December 19, 2024, as Season 1’s finale, Clive brings sword-slashing Eikon powers and his pup Torgal to the roster. It’s a bold pick—fans clamored for Tifa, but Harada’s curveball pays off with a flashy moveset and the stunning Phoenix Gate stage. Tekken 8 remains a competitive titan under Harada’s watch, and Clive’s crossover cements its wild, evolving legacy.

For starters, Tekken 8 is definitely a better product than Tekken 7, and even if you are new to the fighting game genre, this would be a good place do start. I think its better to divide the review in 2 parts, one for complete begginners in Tekken and FGC in general and the other for FGC players, since a lot of the concerns that some players have does not affect new players at all or are very specific in regards to gameplay. Feel free to read both parts, but if u are a newcomer, I highly recommend to stop at the first half, as reading throughout the specific game mechanics can make you feel like the game is too complex, and all that complexity [b]does not apply for begginers[/b]. With that said, lets move on.  [h3] For Tekken or FGC newcomers [/h3] In relation to content, not only Tekken 8 delivers a good story mode, great customization options (compared to other concurrent competitors), good characters, amazing stages and a good learning curve (this is a Tekken characteristic imo, not exclusive to Tekken 8, although 8 it does it slighty better i think) and the game itself is very good looking, graphically speaking.  When it comes to the more technical stuff (ike bugs, stability, frame rate, etc), I can say I never had any issues with the game excluding some people on ranked with a really bad connection (but even those were rare and its not actually a game issue) and some times those players with a bad conection would be reconized in my game as if I was low on fps and the game would downgrade to medium/low settings. While that was annoying, it only required me to go to the configs and change it back so nothing game breaking here. I'm not a shill for the Tekken series or Bandai Namco, but a lot of bad reviews of the game page that I saw are criticizing using Tekken 7 as comparison.  And just to clarify, while the bad reviews and critics comparing T8 to T7 aren't in itself invalids, it worth reminding that T7 launched in 2015 and had its last update in 2022. Comparing the amount of gameplay changes and customization options between these 2 games are not very fair. [b]Don't let those bad reviews convince you to not try the game.[/b] It has a demo that you can download and try for yourself and if you are still not sure, consider getting the game when it is on sale. You will not regret because the game is, indeed, very good.   [h3] For Tekken fans or other FG players[/h3] Ok, now to the specific stuff.  When it comes to the gameplay mechanics, Tekken 8 is more aggressive game beacuse of the new Heat System. Heat rewards you going in not only because the system gives you advantage (a good amount of +frames) situations, but it also lets you recover a lot of gray health/chip damage (wich is also and new thing in T8). While in a vaccum that does not translates to a bad mechanic, a lot o people are used to Tekken being a more neutral based game, where you would win by having good reflexes and whiff punishing. And since Tekken is a very traditional game, that does not get mechanically changed that hard from game to game, there are a lot of people unhappy with T8 trying to follow the "modern" trend and forcing you to interact with the oponent a lot so the game fells more dinamic, while also adding a big amount of 50/50 situations you are put on. Contrast that to T7 where high level play usually involves the 2 players korean-backdashing like crazy and only interacting every now and then, you start to understand from where these critics are coming from. First of all, the game being now hyper agressive is a valid critic. I'm started in the FGC playing Street Fighter 5 and current play 6 at high level, and the amount of pressure you get from most of the cast in that game is absurd and I grew used to that being normal. And although I really dont feel that the game is so hyper focused on offense that you cannot play defensively, I understand that some people want the game to play like the past titles. Second, no, the game is not "filled up with 50/50 situations". I understand that a lot of disavantage situations when you get comboed to the wall, knocked down, and then you get put on what it seems like a 50/50 of blocking a hellsweep or mid safe launcher and lose 60% health (or the round entirely) when you guess wrong. But believe me, 99% of those moments are not "true 50/50". You just don't know the matchup, you missed the tech, you are not using get up options right or are not stepping to the sides. And also, if you got put on what seems like a 50/50, its your fault for being on that place to begin with.   The other big critic I see on the Steam reviews are people criticizing the lack of skins and the forced battle pass. And not, I also dont like battle passes, but the game was develop with a huge budget and if the current battle pass systems is what it is as a necessity for bandai keeping adding new characters and stages, so be it, there are a lot of worse monetization on other games and the Tekken 8 BP is not that bad. And about the free customization options that we had on T7, we usually remember a game for its lasts moments and not the mid state (I played a lot of SF5, believe me, we forget how bad things used to be). T7 had a lot of things going for it at the end, but it did took 6~7 years of development to reach that place, and since the first year or so of Tekken games are more focused on the arcades, is usually after season 2 that the content start goind hard.  [h3]To Sumarize / TLDR.: [/h3] I was going through the reviews just out of curiosity and that convinced me to write a review myself.  [b]T8 may not be perfect, but it is amazing. Probably the best fighting game at launch we ever had.[/b] The game is fun to play and watch, very appealing characters and stages, and a very good entry to the FGC.  There are changes not very welcomed by the community, yes, but most of it are personal opnions and not a critic about the game quality. RN there are not that much customization as seem in the previous game, but the game is not out for that long so be patient. If you are a FGC player or newcommer to the genre, T8 can be very fun and may be your game. Also a lot of huge streamers played the game in the recent months and had a blast, even sticking to play it till today, so go search for one you like and watch their experience to help you decide to buy the game or not. If you want, Andrewjrt, a big Overwatch youtuber, has some great videos on his first times learning the game and is very funny and worth watching (may get you hyped up!)

Tekken 8 continues the legacy of one of the most iconic fighting game franchises, and it does so with a bang! From the moment you launch the game, it’s clear that developers Bandai Namco have pulled out all the stops to deliver an experience that both honors the series' roots and innovates in exciting ways.  Visuals and Sound First and foremost, the graphics in Tekken 8 are a feast for the eyes. The character models are incredibly detailed, and the arenas are vibrant and full of life. Every punch, kick, and special move is rendered with jaw-dropping precision. The sound design complements the visuals perfectly, with bone-crunching effects and a pulsating soundtrack that keeps the adrenaline flowing.  Gameplay and Mechanics The gameplay in Tekken 8 is both accessible to newcomers and deep enough for veterans to appreciate. The controls are tight and responsive, making every fight feel satisfying. The new mechanics, such as the "Rage Drive" and "Power Crush" moves, add layers of strategy and excitement to the battles. The game also boasts an extensive roster of characters, each with their unique moves and playstyles, ensuring that there’s something for everyone.  Story Mode and Content The story mode in Tekken 8 is engaging and well-crafted, with plenty of twists and turns to keep players hooked. It delves deeper into the Mishima family feud, providing a rich narrative backdrop to the intense combat. Beyond the story, Tekken 8 offers a wealth of content, including online multiplayer, practice modes, and various challenges that keep the replay value high.  Conclusion In conclusion, Tekken 8 is a triumphant entry in the series. It combines stunning visuals, thrilling gameplay, and a compelling story to deliver one of the best fighting game experiences available. Whether you’re a long-time fan or new to the series, Tekken 8 is a must-play. It’s a knockout in every sense of the word.

Waited a while to write this and with season 2 around the corner I feel like this is the best time to do so.  Long and short I think Tekken 8 is an exceptional fighting game and should be tried by anyone interested. I think its fully deserving of the price tag and I'll quickly explain why.  Pretty much all fighting games are value dependant on how much you expect yourself to play the game. Most fighting games have a story mode, arcade and extra gameplay modes however 99% of your time is in the lab and online.  DLC has been a questionable situation with Tekken 8 so I'll sum it up quickly. DLC characters are far from over powered (so far) with the worst being Clive who is annoying to fight against and A tier in the right hands, this isn't a free win character by any means though and all DLC characters so far have been handled brilliantly and well designed aside some crushing 50/50 gameplay on Eddy and Lidia, but the more we experience these characters they're far from free wins.  Battle pass is a thing but I don't care here or there, gaming developers need an income of cash nowadays with the cost to make AAA games, and the Battle pass is completely cosmetic and optional. My only annoyance is the stage DLC, but I refuse to rank a game down based on one mistake they've said they'll address in the future.  So how's the game? Put simply, amazing.  Tekken 7 was in arcades for a few years and even at launch was a mess, it grew into the game we love over years. Tekken 8 was straight out of the oven and into the hands of the masses despite a few Betas, in short the game is a blast and fantastic.  I've reached Tekken King which is by no stretch good, my experience with ranked so far has been two fold. In one was its amazing and when its good its great! Somedays however you get win quits, bad connection and more but this can happen with most games, it would be nice for Tekken Team to find solutions to this ASAP.  The game with heat, supers etc I still truly believe is fairly balanced. Lots of people will tell you "Old Tekken is dead", or "Heat burst, heat dash, win" or "Don't get launched". That's just stupid.  Season 2 is around the corner, hopefully we will see some improvements.  EDIT: Season 2 is ass  EDIT 2: Season 3 is ass

As a long-time fan of the Tekken series, I can't help but feel deeply disappointed with the latest entry, Tekken 8. What was supposed to be a fresh, exciting addition to the iconic franchise has instead turned into a frustrating and broken experience, with endless issues that completely derail the core gameplay.  First and foremost, the introduction of new characters has done more harm than good. Take Reina, for example. She feels like a token character thrown in for diversity with no real substance or unique fighting style. Her moves are overly simplistic, her combos feel uninspired, and overall, she lacks the depth and charm of many of the earlier characters. If anything, her inclusion feels more like an attempt to appease a certain group than a meaningful addition to the roster.  Then there's Xiaoyu. Why is she still in the game? Her moveset has always been a bit of a mess, but now in Tekken 8, she's somehow worse. The animations for her moves are stiff, the hitboxes are inconsistent, and her juggling capabilities have been made even more frustrating. While she was always a tricky character to deal with, her ability to spam mixups has now reached a level of absurdity. It's one thing to counter a skilled Xiaoyu player, but when all you’re faced with are endless, repetitive strings with little to no counterplay, it becomes infuriating.  Eddie Gordo... where do I even begin? Eddie has always been a polarizing character in the Tekken series, but now he's become a symbol of what’s wrong with the game. His endless spams of flips and kicks are borderline unbeatable, leaving opponents with few chances for a fair counter. He’s been overhauled into a mindless button-mashing character, where the focus is less about skill and more about exploiting ridiculous mechanics. It’s not fun, it’s not fair, and it most certainly isn’t strategic. If you want to win with Eddie, all you need is a good old-fashioned "button-mashing" session, and the game practically hands you victories.  Moving on to Lidia, the new addition that somehow feels more broken than most of the returning fighters. While her moveset on paper looks strong, in practice, it’s a nightmare. Her specials have absolutely no recovery time, meaning that once she gets going, it’s nearly impossible to regain control. The balance is severely off here, and it often feels like you’re fighting against a character who is way too overpowered for the competitive scene. Every match against a skilled Lidia player feels like an uphill battle, where one wrong move can cost you the entire round.  But perhaps the most frustrating issue with Tekken 8 is the overwhelming amount of spams that dominate gameplay. It’s hard to even enjoy a match when you’re constantly subjected to the same repetitive moves that offer little opportunity for counterplay. Between Eddie's mindless flip spam, Xiaoyu's endless mixups, and Lidia's unblockable pressure, the game's core design is in shambles. These spams overshadow the technical aspects of the game that once made Tekken stand out. Where’s the strategy? Where’s the emphasis on skill and timing? Now, it’s just about who can spam faster and more efficiently.  This brings me to the larger problem with Tekken 8's gameplay loop. The matchmaking system feels more broken than ever. It's clear that the developers have shifted their focus away from balancing and refining the mechanics in favor of flashy graphics and cheap gimmicks. Even in the higher ranks, you'll find yourself up against endless combinations of spam tactics that leave you helpless. The once-proud Tekken franchise, known for its rewarding depth, has been reduced to a platform for button-mashing, frustrating combat that will leave you questioning why you ever invested in the game in the first place.  At this point, I honestly think Tekken 8 has taken a massive step backwards. Instead of refining and perfecting the mechanics that made Tekken the legendary series it is, we’ve been handed an unbalanced, spam-heavy mess. If you're someone who enjoys strategic, deep, and fair fighting games, you’ll find nothing but frustration here. The developers have made poor choices with character design, balance, and overall gameplay direction. Tekken fans deserve better than this, and I can only hope that Tekken 9 will course-correct the mistakes of this disastrous entry. Until then, Tekken 8 remains an utter disappointment.

Tekken is the first fighting game I played with the intention of learning it. I never played many fighting games before, only some casual Smash Bros. and 30 hours of GG Strive. In my opinion, Tekken is fun, especially playing and learning it together with friends. Every character in this game is complex, with its own game plan. Discussing how to counterplay other characters and explaining how to counterplay your own character makes this game super fun and competitive. I really enjoy learning the combos and hard moves like the electric. As a player who hasn't really played on a controller before, it’s also fun to learn how to play with a controller.  Sometimes Tekken can be really frustrating, for example: playing against King (some random throws and a lot of mix-ups) or playing against characters you've never seen before. It’s just a constant learning and practicing of the art of Tekken, which makes it so much fun for me.  All in all, I would recommend Tekken to all kinds of players who are willing to put the time into learning the game. It’s expensive, but it’s worth it because you can have hundreds of hours of competitive experience in this game.  I rate this game 8/10.

I want to preface this by saying I love aggression, I want to fight as if I'm actually trying to kill someone in any game I play. Aggression isn't my issue with Tekken 8. I have issues with the way it's been implemented as sacrificing everything else that would balance the game better and make that aggression feel rewarding. I bought the game at launch and at first I was a defender of the Heat system because it felt like an uno reverse trap card, pressure tool I use so I can catch ppl with a B+3 or a F F + 2 if they block it, or a nice combo ender before fishing for my next link. It definitely felt fast paced in a way that matched my adrenaline. But as time has gone on I think Heat needs an overhaul, it needs to be toned down. It has the same issue I find with launchers ever since the T7 days; launchers have become too free. Recently I've been playing Tekken 5 on my PS2, and that game made launchers far more technical, more difficult, but if you could pull them off many options opened to you as a reward. If you weren't launching you were playing the neutral/footsies game looking for your opening or just doing solid combos and pokes. You were expected by the game to develop two sets of skills, a side for the neutral interactions of basic combos, and then a more technical side for executing and following up launchers. Launching was a threat constantly in the background, whereas from 7 to now practically everything launches. This is a common complaint where because of how easy it is to launch even if you're mashing, you don't really play the game past a certain level, so much as you get hit with a launcher then spend the rest of your life watching a combo that lasts 10,000 years. Rinse and repeat. It's boring. It's repetitive. It only encourages rote memorization over creative responses. It takes you out of the game.  Heat just compounds the issue by scaling damage done to ridiculous levels; it allows you to be aggressive to the point of overwhelming the opponent or being overwhelmed so in the end one person isn't getting to play at all. That doesn't feel like a fight to me. A fight should be us beating each other to death, one upping each other, clashing with every interaction and considering what the next move should be. If I wanted to beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of a pillow I'd do that in my room, and if I wanted to be someone's helpless speed bag I'd go to a boxing gym.   That brings out the other issue, the lack of defensive options, predominantly fluid movement controls. Sidestep is abysmal in this version. Trying to sidestep itself feels sluggish as ♥♥♥♥, and even if you try it your opponent's aggression is so overwhelming because they're trying to get you first throwing everything and the kitchen sink at you (and why wouldn't they want to go for the steamroll when movement is slow, blocking still causes damage, and Heat is easy and launchers are easy etc), that your sidestep is interrupted before it truly starts and you're back in launcher limbo hell. I've seen people complain that the game is all 50/50s now and I think that's an exaggeration plus it's a fighting game no ♥♥♥♥ you're always considering 50/50s- HOWEVER that doesn't excuse limited attack variety (launchers + "I can only move forwards" mentality), or limited defensive tools. Instead if we're keeping Heat I think you should only get to use it once per round IF you can land a launcher, with launchers themselves requiring more technical inputs to create a ceiling for them to be used as a trade off. Launchers would put you in Heat state then apply Heat damage to any launch combo you perform afterwards, ending when that combo is finished. You should be able to at least sidestep circles around the enemy if you don't want to give us back KBD too.  Personally something like Tag 2's sidestep would be nice for me. There should be no chip damage. Chip damage just makes defensive planning even more worthless, because yes you can get health back if you retaliate but like I said with movement and waiting for openings, it's so easy to get choked out you may as well forget it and eat the chip.   This isn't the worst game in the world, it can still be fun especially if you play with people who choose not to or can't capitalize on launch spam so my matches become slugfests and pure reading, but it took the blandness that was starting in 7 and has made the blandest, most one track minded modern Tekken yet. I can't recommend it to anyone except other people who like me are so into fighting games you just wanna have a finger in as many pies as possible. I play because I want to play, because I'm sadistic, because I love slugging it. My ass is never going to a tournament or a local. That doesn't mean there isn't room for improvement here, and there's much that can be improved to bring this game back down to Earth instead of being robotic and one sided to best succeed.   Microtransactions and the sneaking in the pass system nonsense is also garbage, you don't need me to restate the obvious but it is. And only a total shill wouldn't be even a little bothered at the fact that the game revolves around your debt card from something as minor as cosmetics to as major as getting to unlock or train against locked characters offline.    Even DLC stories suffer from this because the stories just serve as smaller ads to encourage you to buy the new characters featured. Unfortunately developers of the current landscape from all over have realized it's easier to skip the middleman of making you unlock ♥♥♥♥ via progress and instead play with your head to make you give them money. I'll preface this by saying I'm not a hardcore fighting game player. I loved Tekken 3 and a few others way back in the day but have barely touched a fighting game since the PS2 era. So in theory I should like the noob-friendly approach Tekken 8 has taken with the heat system and "special style", but in reality I hate it.  All the common criticisms of this game are completely valid. Here are my main gripes: Matches are more about luck and button mashing than skill. You can waste your time learning a character and their combos only to get destroyed by one launcher followed by single button mashing. Miss a block and your entire health bar will usually be gone before you ever get a chance to attack. It would improve the game significantly if they simply added options to disable special style and heat in PVP. They cheapen the game so much and I'm baffled there isn't an option to turn them off. Bamco could at least make it where you have to earn heat instead of automatically starting with it in every round. I don't have an issue with rage arts other than the long unskippable animations. It's a mechanic that actually makes sense and becomes available when your health is low. But adding free heat in every round on top of rage arts is way too excessive.  I've used at least half the roster and have yet to find a character I really like. Usually in fighting games I like the majority of the characters so much that it's hard to choose a main. Here they all feel the same, they all feel slow and heavy. Movement doesn't feel smooth or fluid, yet the game forces you to play fast and aggressively. The gameplay in general just isn't fun. Even when I win matches it's not that satisfying and feels like I won because of pure luck instead of skill. i.e. my opponent messed up before me and got caught in an inescapable combo against the wall. In other games I can have fun and relax even if I'm getting my ass kicked, and wins feel earned. Not in Tekken 8. Why waste time playing it if it's not even fun to win matches and just a stressful experience in general?  It's a shame that other franchises like Soul Calibur, Virtua Fighter, and DOA have fallen by the wayside. For me they're much more fun, more balanced, and have more interesting characters. This game is getting a ton of backlash and rightfully so. I regret buying it and would refund if I could. Guess I'll have to bite the bullet and force myself to keep playing a little more, but will be sticking to casual modes from now on and sure as hell won't be buying any DLC. Hopefully the devs will listen to players and make some improvements but I won't hold my breath.

Before you read further on, know that I am by no means a long time Tekken fan, this is my first one, but I am something of an avid fan of fighting games, and most of my issues come when comparing it to the other of the big three right now. Those being Street Fighter 6, Tekken 8, and Guilty Gear Strive.  What kills the game for me is two big things, for starters, a lack of defensive options not named Parry. Its nothing new for a character to lack such options, hell its the whole idea being a Rushdown character, but when the most you have for defense is basic blocking and parrying, you're not gonna have much you can really do beyond go for a punish or counter, and one wrong move usually results in your loss. The other big issue is, at least from my experience and poking around, most characters don't really differ in their core strategies, by which I mean Launchers are the be all end all practically. There are characters with some quirks that to keep them distinct, but their game plan doesn't really change from character to character, as basically everyone wants to just get in with a launcher and do whatever string they like, making a lot of the cast blend together in terms of what does make them unique, at least in my mind.  This isn't taking into account stuff like Namco just being a bit of a crap, how every character stat wise basically acts the same, move bloat being absolutely insane with some characters only having a handful of moves they care about out of potentially a hundred, and in general my personal thoughts on Heat as a mechanic, which in short: I don't think its interesting, if anything its just there, I guess.  I don't doubt there's a reason people enjoy the series, its lasted for 8 games and probably more if we count crossovers and spin offs (I'm not really concerned about an exact number), but I don't really get it, clearly I'm missing something, but I don't feel a desire to come back to this when SF6 and GGST are right there. Those games have their own sets of problems, but at least the core game doesn't feel like a coin flipping contest at a casino 98% of the time.

I played a lot of Tekken 8 on PS5 before I upgraded my PC, hence my low hours. However, I can say that Tekken 8 truly has done an amazing job of feeling like a Tekken game while innovating and making it a lotttt easier for new players to get into the game. If you've never played a fighting game but want to, I recommend it. If you've played Tekken before and are thinking of getting back into it, I recommend it. If you played Tekken 7 and are wondering if you should go to 8, I recommend it.  I've been with the series since the 1st Tekken on PS1, and I think this is the first time I could confidently recommend the game to people who have never even played a fighting game. The training modes, the story mode that helps you get used to things, and the Special Style mode which allows you to do combos with just a single button press all make it easy to learn the flow of combat.  To be clear, Tekken is a very deep game. A lot of it is like learning grammar: sure, you COULD try to remember all the rules and execute everything perfectly, but that is not very feasible annnddd it sucks. Instead, go into it thinking of every round as practicing conversation in a language you're learning. You'll make mistakes, you'll mess up, sometimes it'll even be embarassing, but if you stick with it you'll have an entirely new avenue with which to explore something great.  I love Tekken and I love Tekken 8. Not much more I can say, really.... except that Yoshimitsu is my favorite gay space ninja, obviously.

I expected a balanced, thoughtful experience, but what I got was a masterpiece, a divine intervention that freed me from the shackles of neutral and defense. No longer do I concern myself with trivial concepts like footsies or adaptation—I have ascended. Why adapt when I can just spam one move and get a 50/50? I’ve converted to the sacred religion of Jackology, where we gather once a week at our local game tournament to jack it off in the name of plus frames and enlightenment. Honestly, Dragunov’s whiff punishes are so 2020—Jack-8 gives me instant gratification, and frankly, I’m addicted.  Season 2 has made some drastic changes—changes that, while the community may dislike, have made the game infinitely more fun and interesting. "The Heat System's overpowered," they say. “It’s too braindead,” they cry. Uh, hello? How is forcing the opponent to constantly guess between 50/50s "braindead"? It’s innovative. Every Heat Engager now leads to a 50/50, ensuring that decision-making is a thing of the past. You didn’t want to think? Well, now you don’t have to. Just press buttons until something lands. It’s like an auto-pilot feature for your fighting game experience. Moves now seamlessly transition into stances that provide even more 50/50s—because why settle for just one when you can have an entire buffet of options? And Oki setups? Gone. Who needed them anyway? The real Tekken experience isn’t about calculated pressure or wake-up reads—it’s about relentless momentum. If you want to play footsies, go play Street Fighter. Each match, I must methodically plan my decision-making around which move will best lead into my sacred mix-up. The answer? Gamma uf+1+2, commonly known as the Gamma Clap—where I clap the cheeks of my opponent, ushering them into a true 50/50 mix-up scenario. “But that’s so cheesy!” you say. Oh really? Is it cheesy to go for high-level strategy that guarantees a win? Do you call LeBron James’ slam dunk “cheesy” too, or is it just an effective use of his athleticism?  This is, hands down, the best Tekken has ever been for the series—a game focused on skill expression, creativity, and execution. People are all like, “Tekken has turned into a button-masher’s paradise,” and I’m over here like, “You know what? Exactly. That’s the point.” Tekken has always been about making bold, decisive choices, and with the Heat System, you’re just making your choices faster. Now, every match is an opportunity for creative expression—whether it’s using Gamma Clap into 50/50s or just mashing through the entire opponent’s defense like a hot knife through butter. Tekken has taught me the core fundamentals of approach, punish, block, and, of course, one-and-done the moment my opponent figures out my gimmick. One-and-done isn’t defeatist; it’s just a methodical way to ensure no one gets too comfy.  And with these sacred teachings, I have ascended to Tekken King. Now, whenever someone complains about the game’s mechanics, I just look at them and smile—knowing full well that their complaints are just the soundtrack of my victory. The more they moan, the more Zen I become. I’ve transcended. So let them cry about “Rage Arts being too cinematic” or “Heat Engagers being too powerful”—I’ll be over here, sitting on my throne, counting all my perfect victories.

Here's my whining.  I'm a Tekken newcomer and this is my first Tekken game. I came from MK11-MK1, so I'm definitely not the kind of person to take too seriosly when it comes to balancing complaints and so on, as I'm more of a casual player (Grand Master in MK11 and 1 and Battle Ruler in T8). But if you're the kind of person like me, and deciding if maybe Tekken is what you've been looking for, this review is for you.  I was definitely fed up with MK1's cameo spam BS, getting zoned and mixed to hell with almost unblockable setups by people who could've as well been orangutans with gamepads pressing two buttons. I decided to look for a more "honest" fighting, I didn't like the visual style of SF, and Tekken always was in the back of my mind as "THE figthing game".  At first I was really impressed by Tekken 8, it definitely has a lot of good things going for it. The amount of effort put into the game is very respectable. The customization is nice, although a lot of it is paid. The quality of life features are amazing, it's almost everything you could ask for. The only quality of life thing I found lacking was being able to keep recorded moves for opponents in practice between launches of the game. When it comes to just basic things like ease of watching replays or doing things in practice mode, or finding other people, or their games, the bar has been raised so high for me with Tekken 8 that I don't think it will ever be beaten by another fighting game.  Gameplay-wise its incredibly satisfying and learning new things, managing to pull them off in game, or just solving your opponents gameplan are top-notch dopamine rushes. Way more satisfying than it was for me in MK.  The community seems quite nice, a lot of information is available for the new players, and there're character specific discord servers with many active members discussing latest tech.  Why am I not recommending this game then? The answer is simple - expectations from the player. There's a 25+ year old history of Tekken games, with moves and characters straight up passing from previous to the next one, with additions. At this point, there're 120-150 moves/strings on average per character. Some characters have up to ~200. A lot of moves are similar, and fall under a whole family of similar moves (for example, many characters have a variation of Bryan's "snake edge" move, that is a slow reactable low homing launcher that is launch-punishable on block). You can recognize those moves and adapt during the match, especially if you're familiar with the game. Same goes for strings mostly, many three hit strings come in pairs, only different in last hit - it's either a duckable plus high that you can full launch on read, or a mid that is -13 or so that you can do a smaller punish for. Usually there's an answer for every move, you just have to know it. Yes, for thousands of moves. For 30-40 characters.  It would've been nice if you could semi-casually play the game and learn the matchups and move counterplays as you play and gradually go through ranks. But to me that doesn't quite seem possible.  Some characters in the game have simple and clear animations and strings, you can learn them by playing against them. Others...well, let's just say you can play 10 games in a row against them and learn next to nothing unless you just decide to give up on playing the game and simply lose experimenting while blocking them or trying to press some button. And even then you will learn almost nothing useful, because the next time you see that character you will forget everything. Or maybe they will just use some new 20 barely distinguishable moves.  The female characters are notoriously rage inducing to play against for the new (and not only new) players. As one of the pros, Ulsan, recently said "This game makes you hate female characters". They're very evasive, their animations I found to be extremely unpredictable. Some of them will hit you a few times and then almost fall to the floor and stay there for some moments, and then just suddenly jump into your face defying any laws of physics when you try to press. They will do flips after flips after flips, dance around the screen unpredictable, turn around and spin, giving you unreactable lows. Your jabs will whiff when you try to take your turns, sometimes their moves go under MIDS. You won't even understand where one string ended and the other began. It's heavily aggravated by the sheer number of stances developers put into the game which allow those characters to continue pressure almost endlessly without you being able to recognize the situation.  Many characters have 3-4 stances with up to 20+ moves, good luck playing against Hwoarang, Steve, or Lidia without spending many hours in labbing. Then there's King. He's the grappler character. Teching throws in this game supposedly (?) can be done on reaction by looking at which hand/hands were used to grab you. If they grabbed you with their left - you press 1, if right - 2, if both - 1+2. For most characters you only need to press 1+2 vs (1 OR 2). The throws have 12 frames of startup, and a 10(?) frame break window.  I will admit it, I can only tech throws that I spent time in practice mode learning how to recognize and tech without thinking, and I'm not too good at it. Maybe it's just my boomer reaction time, but anyway, King has around 20 throws with different tech options, AND some of them don't even follow the "left hand - 1, right hand - 2" rule. You HAVE to train teching them.  Some genius also at some point in the series decided to add one or two 10-hit strings to almost every character. Have fun memorizing those sequences of lows and mids and highs for 40 chars. Have fun getting downranked if you don't.  Now I will get to my point - you can play the game and enjoy it. But at some point you will start hitting 50% of your matches being HARD knowledge checks by stances like Lidia/Hwoarang. Or grappler characters like King/Nina. Or unrecognizable string spam by the likes of Steve or Lili. Or whatever weird things Yoshimitsu does. Or Xiaoyu/Zafina going under your mids. Or Devil Jin flying away randomly. Or Alisa chainsawing you though block when you helplessly watch. There's an answer to all of these, and the answer is labbing for days and weeks and months, and reading articles, discords, watching videos, watching your replays, etc. I think you're supposed to spend more time in practice than in the matches. Otherwise ranking feels almost insurmountable, and a game of luck.  Or do what I did and get a friend to play against, it's very fun and rewarding. Maybe find some players in discords and steam friends. Don't buy it in hopes of playing ranked. Don't even go there if you're new to Tekken, there's no reason to not just play quick matches instead.  Also matchmaking system is one of the worst I've ever seen. There's a system called "Tekken prowess", which is basically a hard MMR tied to your account that you can't really lose. It pretty much only grows. You want to try a few characters? Well, now you only get to play against people who had twice your rank on their one character. There's no escape.  I will admit that I'm not very good at the game. I will also admit that I get frustrated with it more than I should. But hopefully it will at least give some overview to someone else like me. Thanks for reading :)

TEKKEN 8 is a game that, at one point, was made by talented people. However, it seems that these talented people have lost their voice because the art direction, stages, and characters all look and sound great but the game itself has robbed these characters of gameplay personality and made it nigh impossible to appreciate the model and background work. The TEKKEN franchise has sped up to the point where the game is exhausting to play for any longer than 30 minutes and 50/50s are indeed something that will be on your mind a lot. Ranked has been tuned so that pluggers are not punished(atleast not harshly enough) and players can't derank until red ranks which puts red rank players way closer to purple and blue rank players. With the new ranked system they might as well remove the Kyu ranks and the green, yellow, and orange ranks. Rage arts can't be funny punished with rage art. Armor moves are supposed to be used more often now but it feed into a weird gameplay loop of attempting to get offense going and characters with good armor moves can finally take advantage of what was once a niche mechanic. Certains throws track and are unbreakable which make sidestepping even more unreliable than it already is. Sidestepping wouldn't be as much of a nuisance if strings wouldn't gain tracking mid way through or moves extending hurtboxes into hitboxes which get you scooped up despite being behind people. TEKKEN team is taking a long period of time to balance the game and I can only hope that season 2 with the system changes will make the game a little more bearable.
