I think i'm done now. I gave it a whole season and, even with my favorite character finally making it back since Tag 2, I can't recommend this game *SPECIFICALLY* to people who have played and enjoyed any Tekken games from Tag 2 and before.  The game is gorgeous, the lobbies and netplay run like butter, and the customization and extra features like Tekken Ball is extremely nice to have. The season pass is also very fair, with BN giving out the currency to buy the season pass with the only restriction being you play the game. Pricing structure for the costumes isn't for me, but it doesn't seem predatory... yet.  My issue is that the gameplay. It's hyper polarizing, which seems to have been the point. T7 created a big system of "haves" and "have-nots" with it's implementation of rage mechanics, with T8 tripling down on it with heat. Clive's moveset cements that fact even further, as his moveset and heat mechanic blend very well together and do things that everyone else in the cast could only dream of, like his maddening corner carry on the largest stages in the game. It's absolutely a blast to watch as the game is super flashy but, at least from the viewpoint of someone who has played older Tekkens, playing in the confines of T8's systems feels so lopsided at it's core. You are either winning big and flying completely free, or you're being absolutely dogged by your opponent and unable to do much about it because movement in general doesn't feel as good, what with a lot of major strings having amazing tracking even on whiff. Not to say you CANT move, but that it feels much harder to do so than it used to be.  *Tl;dr* If you're new to Tekken or haven't played one in years, give this game a try. It's an absolute treat and extremely easy to pick up and play (Play Victor. I hated fighting him, but love seeing the chaos he brings lol). If you're an oldhead like me, and you've come to these reviews for validation on why things feel off, it's not just you. The game is different and scary and amplified the formerly small parts about tekken that were only mildy annoying before, but are now glaringly frustrating and unavoidable.

[b]As a professional Alissa player, my standard operating procedure in Tekken 8 involves casually detaching my own exploding head to use as a projectile and turning my arms into chainsaws to carve through the competition. However, navigating the game's recent history on Steam has felt like trying to execute a perfect flying kick while suffering from a severe motherboard malfunction.   When Bandai Namco first dropped the game, it was a visually stunning, adrenaline-fueled masterpiece that beautifully updated the King of Iron Fist Tournament. Then came the heavily criticized balance updates, which essentially turned high-level competitive play into a highly stressful casino. The developers managed to spectacularly mess up the delicate balance, tweaking the new Heat system and offensive buffs so much that years of painstakingly mastered defensive skills were entirely invalidated. Suddenly, almost every character on the roster could force you into an endless loop of unreactable guessing games, making it incredibly frustrating to play a highly mobile, poke-heavy android when a single blocked attack could leave you pinned to a wall questioning your career choices.  Thankfully, it seems the development team has finally looked at the frantic, frustrated pleas of the community and realized that turning a highly technical 3D fighter into an aggressive slot machine might not have been their finest engineering decision. The most recent patches prove they are finally coming around to fix the mess, actively pulling back the overly generous frame advantages and tweaking the mechanics so your opponent cannot remain in an unstoppable, powered-up state for three business days.   They are restoring the crucial balance between risk and reward, meaning I can finally go back to methodically annoying my opponents with calculated chainsaw mix-ups instead of just praying I guess correctly against an endless barrage of attacks. While the Steam version still occasionally pairs you in matchmaking with someone playing on a Wi-Fi connection beamed directly from the moon, the core game is rapidly healing. Tekken 8 is finally returning to the beautifully chaotic, skill-expressive martial arts sandbox it was meant to be, making it the perfect time to boot it up and start handing out robotic beatdowns once again.[/b]

The meticulously detailed character models, dynamic environments, and fluid animations create a truly immersive experience. IGN  Robust Single-Player Content  Tekken 8 offers a wealth of single-player modes that cater to both newcomers and veterans. I  Enhanced Online Experience  The online component of Tekken 8 has been meticulously crafted to ensure a seamless and competitive environment. Diverse Character Roster  The game boasts a diverse roster of over thirty characters, each meticulously designed with unique move sets and playstyles. This variety ensures that players can find a character that resonates with their personal preferences, enhancing the game's replayability and depth.    Positive Reception and Accolades  Tekken 8 has been met with widespread acclaim from both critics and players alike. On Metacritic, it holds a commendable score, reflecting its status as a standout entry in the series. Critics have lauded its dynamic combat, robust content offerings, and stunning presentation, solidifying its place as a modern fighting game masterpiece.    Conclusion  In summary, Tekken 8 elevates the franchise to new heights, offering a comprehensive and exhilarating experience that appeals to both long-time fans and newcomers. Tekken 8 Season 2 didn’t just make me want to improve at fighting games—it cemented it. I came in expecting a balanced, tactical experience, but what I got was a divine masterpiece that freed me from the chains of neutral and defense. Who needs neutral when you can just press a button and mash Heat Engagers until your opponent submits? Why think when you can just let the game do all the heavy lifting? While the community is off crying about frame data and matchup charts, I’m out here living my best life—because you know who doesn't care about frame data? Jack-8.  I’ve long since left my old main, Hwoarang, in the past—he's just not cutting it anymore. I thought he was the “cool” choice, with his flashy kicks and “I'm the martial artist of the century” attitude. But really? Hwoarang was like the kid who shows up to class with a bunch of fancy moves and never does his homework. You get all these cool combos, but what’s the point when you can’t even get a solid hit in? I’ve found true enlightenment with Jack-8, the real powerhouse. Why worry about footsies, punishes, or adapting when you can just hit one button and get an automatic 50/50? I’ve converted to Jackology, where we gather once a week at our local tournament to jack it off in the name of plus frames and instant gratification. Hwoarang’s flashy kicks are so 2019—Jack-8’s plus frames give me the rewards I’ve always deserved.  You ever just think about socks? Like, they’re just little fabric tubes that hug your feet and keep them warm, but somehow they manage to be a huge part of your day. We wear them, we lose them, we stuff them into shoes and forget about them until we need them again. The whole sock game is just a constant cycle of getting new socks, losing them in the laundry, and trying to pair them back up like some lost souls searching for each other in a dark drawer. What’s the point of even matching them up anymore? Does the sock even care if it's paired with its twin? Maybe socks are just symbols of the deep, unspoken chaos in our lives—like the Heat Engagers in Tekken, a constant game of guesswork that just keeps us moving forward.  Season 2 has made changes that have sent the community into a frenzy, but I see it as Tekken’s shining moment. "The Heat System is overpowered!" they say. “It’s too braindead!” they whine. Uh, hello? Forcing your opponent into a guessing game of 50/50s is not braindead—it's brilliance. Every Heat Engager now leads to a 50/50, and guess what? Thinking is now optional. Why bother with strategy when you can just hit buttons and see what lands? It’s like buying a self-driving car and taking a nap while it handles the road. Every move now flows into stances that provide even more 50/50s—because one 50/50 isn’t enough when you could have a buffet of them. Oki setups? Gone. Who needs them when you can just bulldoze your opponent with constant pressure?  Now every match is a sacred journey where I choose my one true path: the Gamma uf+1+2, AKA the Gamma Clap. I clap the cheeks of my opponent and send them straight into the 50/50 abyss. “But that’s cheesy!” you say. Oh, you think that’s cheesy? If being effective is cheesy, then sign me up for the Cheese Club. Do you call LeBron’s slam dunk “cheesy” too, or do you just appreciate the sheer effectiveness of it?  Tekken 8 Season 2 is the finest the series has ever been. A true work of art focused on skill expression, creativity, and execution. The haters are out here saying it’s turned into a button-masher’s paradise, and I’m sitting back, smiling, because that’s exactly what it is. Why try to think when you can just be fast, bold, and creative? The Heat System has turned every match into a chance to show off your unique playstyle—whether you’re Gamma Clapping your way to victory or mashing through your opponent's defenses like a hot knife through butter.  Tekken has taught me the real fundamentals: approach, punish, block, and, of course, one-and-done the moment my opponent figures out my gimmick. One-and-done isn’t cowardice; it’s efficiency. Why let them learn your tricks when you can just end it right there?  And now, thanks to my newfound understanding, I’ve ascended to Tekken King. Every time someone complains about “Heat Engagers” or “Rage Arts being too cinematic,” I just smile, knowing that their cries are the soundtrack of my inevitable victory. Let them whine while I sit on my throne, collecting perfects and basking in the glory of my ascension.

The Tekken series has always been one of my favorite fighting game franchises, but Tekken 8 has been a huge disappointment.  First, the DLC decisions are baffling. Locking legacy characters behind paid DLC—especially someone who's been part of the main cast since the original Tekken—feels like a poor choice. It doesn't sit well with longtime fans and makes the roster feel incomplete.  Second, the gameplay has been simplified to the point where it often rewards repetitive, low-risk offense. Many players can rely on the same strings and flowcharts repeatedly, and it often feels like your defensive options are too limited once the pressure starts.  The community has also become increasingly toxic. It's common to run into players who taunt, emote, or act disrespectfully after winning, and the game doesn't do much to discourage that behavior.  Finally, I'm not a fan of the Heat system. It makes extending combos and maintaining offense much easier than in previous Tekken games, and it often feels like a free momentum swing rather than something that has to be earned. As you climb the ranked ladder, matches become less about adaptation and fundamentals and more about abusing gimmicks, knowledge checks, and repetitive offense.  Tekken 8 still has great visuals and solid core mechanics, but the gameplay direction, monetization decisions, and overall online experience have made it far less enjoyable for me than previous entries in the series.

Long road from the Playstation days of old to here, but I've enjoyed that road very much. I really, really like this title. It's not perfect, but luckily, I never expect them to be. The game play though, it hits everything right where I want it to. The fights feel more tense then ever with that new heat mechanic. It took me a couple of hours to really get what I was doing and where I was going with it, but once I got it, man, it was a ton of fun.   Every character that I used from earlier titles feels more streamlined than ever (after you get through that pesky bit of time in practice to see whats changed.) Not too much changed from the earlier games either. For the most part, you can pick up who you used before and still play them fairly competently right out of the box, which is appreciated in any evolving title.   The characters look better than they ever have in my humble opinion. They all look great, and have really been spending some quality time in the gym. I can't as of yet mention the quality of story mode. I haven't yet given myself the pleasure, but the character arcade endings are just as stupid and satisfying to collect as ever they were. (What is up with Dragunov? Why can't he build anything right? Ever?)   I'm pleased that the money for customization for you favorite toons comes very very fast. You pop yourself a cool million just for clearing one arcade ending for a character, and even the in and out fights net you very quick cash that adds up to a whole lot in the blink of an eye. The cash shop stuff feels quite scummy, and I won't be purchasing anything that was in older titles. I don't know what developers think when they do that. It was an old asset, you put zero extra work into it, so you get zero extra cash for it.  The price on this one is steep. Even with my love for Tekken, I would only say buy it on sale like I did. I waited a pretty long while, but it was worth the pick up at the discounted price tag, easily. I feel it's a must buy for any Tekken and fighting game lover without a doubt. And I'm not going to lie here, but the game did get added points from me because I main Steve, and generally alternate between him, Bryan Fury, and that Can't build a damn thing Mr. Dragunov, and they happen to put them side by side in the character select which makes my life even easier.  Would recommend for sure. Dear developers, please quit shelving Lei...

Today's Tekken is so different than prior Tekken games that its hard to respect this once great fighting game even based on its older earned reputation. If many of the mechanics were kept the same or similar(defensive mechanics???) while evolving other aspects of gameplay, movesets, and UX, the core greatness of Tekken would come through and deliver another great game, but that isnt what Bandai Namco chose. i have played a lot of this game and a lot of tekken in general. I am uninstalling today for good.   tekken has always had a lot of knowledge checks, and thats okay. one of the best parts about tekken is getting bodied by a character's flowchart, hitting the lab, figuring out the options, and then beating it next time.  that being said, the game's new design concept with hyper focus on aggression/oppression has created a bunch of situations where the ONLY option for defense is guess block, and if you guess wrong you die. this is not an overstatement. there are way way too many plus frame set ups in this game. if you can predict what an opponent is going to do, you should have the option to avoid by movement, defense, or choice offense. but since there are so many plus frame set ups ON TOP of heat which gives plus frames, the meta has devolved into heat engager-mix up-oppression-chip with plus frames-heat smash-wall mix up.   It's not that defense has no reward, but the amount of knowledge/execution it takes to play defense properly vs spamming offense makes this game super frustrating. I am a defensive player and i always loved tekken because of how many options there were for counterplay against aggro opponents. But if i am defending a character who is in heat and attacking me, it is not worth the risk to make a defensive read. its better to just sit there and eat the chip and hope i land a heat engager and can do the same thing back. THIS IS BORING.   I made it to tekken god with my main and blue ranks with a handful of other characters. i'm nowhere near GoD and recognize that there is a lot more I could learn to play better. I am not blaming the game for my lack of skill or practice. I just don't think the amount of effort i need to put in for match-up specific defense is worth it in tekken 8 like it was in the older games. Defensively this is the hardest fighting game i've ever played and offensively it's the easiest. when i stopped trying to play defensive and just focused on steam-rolling i climbed way higher and enjoyed it much less. the identities of the characters have all been replaced with rushdown mix up.   maybe i'll check out season 2 but i can't see the game changing much since this is the direction they went with. sad to finally say goodbye but it's been toxic for a long time and i am not happy playing it anymore. wish they had made it different.

Pros: -Story mode is pretty good. Obviously a setup for our next main antagonist in the inevitable Tekken 9, but "wraps up" the father-son rivalry of the Mishimas in a pretty over-the-top way. -Very pretty character models. The main menu even gives you close-up views of whatever character you choose to show off how well made they are. -New characters are pretty memorable. Not a huge fan of how they try to play off Azucena as Lili's new "rival" (c'mon, Asuka is and always will be Lili's main rival!), but other than that I enjoy all the new designs.  Cons: -Microtransactions galore. Remember when you used to be able to unlock cool stuff through your hard-earned points from treasure modes and arcade? Not anymore. Bandai Namco just wants your hard-earned real life money now. Unlockables are pathetic in this game and even the actual shop is pretty barren. -Base roster sucks. Half the characters from the previous games that should be base roster at this point are either completely missing or released as DLC. Like I said, Bandai Namco are just getting greedy at this point. -Even some stages are locked behind DLC. I mean come on, you can't get any greedier than that. Characters are at least somewhat understandable, but even stages aren't safe? -Music isn't as memorable as previous titles. This is more of a personal complaint, but I miss the feelings that some of the old Tekken music invoked. This game doesn't have the same memorability in that category, save for maybe the final battle song.  If you really want to play this installment of Tekken, at least wait until it's majorly on sale. Don't be a fool like the rest of us and pay full price for a half-baked, money-sucking game.

As a former Mortal Kombat player, I thought it was time to get acquainted with something new. Tekken 8 was my pick and the feelings I have from the game can be described as follows: Pros: - Graphics are smooth (background is immersive, so are the looks of characters themselves). - Story mode gives us a redemption arc as well as finding peace with your inner demons (which at least some of us can relate to). Have to say a word about the DLC episode - the way Heihachi was saved from inevitable burning alive is underwhelming. Let the old man retire, he did his worst, he tried his best, now it's time to rest. - Jukebox - change the music on stages whenever you feel like it!  Neutral aspects: - Customization (unlike other major fighting games as of now) gives you the opportnity to dress your character as a character from other games, movies, cartoons (including anime), and so on, and so forth. The opportunities are limited only by the boundaries of your own fantasy. The thing is, more othen than not you have no choice but to spend money on the things you want the most. It's up to you, but still, a feeling of unpleasantry sits deep inside.  Cons:  It's no secret that game truly perfect doesn't exist, now I'll say a bit about the things you, my honorable review reader, might have read elsewhere, but still, give it a go: - Balance (an issue which flows through the fighting game genre as a whole) - some characters are the easy way to obtain rounds while others require much more skill and dedication. In Tekken 8 it's either mash and smash or spend a great deal of time trying your best to learn the character trying not to smash your head on your gamepad/keyboard/whatever suits you the most - and there's no guarantee you'll prevail. - Product behind paywall (we all remember the story with Genmaji Temple, hope the devs learned their lesson for the future (I doubt it), and the fact that we have a battlepass (excuse me, the fight pass) in quite an expensive game from the start (this is no Valorant or other free-to-play games that gotta rely on extra paid content to keep the flow of life). UPD: - As of now, they added Clive from Final Fantasy XVI - a mixture of Miguel (visually) and Dante from DmC (gameplaywise) - we alreasy have Yoshimitsu's katana and Victor's takemikazuchi, no need to add yet another swordsman, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. If the trend keeps up, we might as well have a King of the Iron Sword tournament - send Geralt of Rivia the invitation, he'll show you how it's done.

I admit, I didn't play much Tekken before T8. I got all endings on emulated T3 and I played a little bit of T6, but I never got too invested in the series. That changed in 2023 during my visit to Poznań Game Arena when I got to try T8 before it got released. Despite not knowing how to play the game, I had a great time and sometime later, I purchased a physical copy of T8 at the local electronics' store. This isn't really a review, but more of a history lesson on how we got to this point from a person who's interest in the series peaked with this game.  Tekken 8's Season 1 was the absolute peak of this game. There were some complaints about some characters being too aggressive or having their playstyle changed for whatever reason, but it wasn't all bad. The community had a great time, I was having fun, and Tekken devs didn't have groups of angry players wielding pitchforks in front of their office, at least until they didn't give players who paid for the most expensive version of this game access to Genmaji Temple stage. Unfortunately, it was the most balanced season of them all. When preparing the mandatory balance patch for S2, Tekken devs made one of those most bizarre decisions I've seen in any live-service game. They promoted S2 patch to fix the biggest problems with this game, but they doubled-down on them instead.  Tekken 8 Season 2 rolls around and it's a disaster. Most characters were super buffed, or at worst, had their playstyle changed. I'm a Lee main, so watching the devs try to turn him into a rushdown hurt my heart. I quit playing the game during this season and decided to keep playing older Tekken games, because I got very interested in them. Saying that the situation was bad is an understatement, but it was still salvagable. The playerbase was still willing to give Tekken devs one last try. Clearly, the balance team with a conscience would listen to the bigger part of the community and fix the game. At some point, Harada left Bandai Namco and I feel like the devs' incompetence was one of the reasons why, assuming that he was against what they were planning for this game.  Tekken 8 Season 3 trailer rolls around. The devs promised that this season will be a return to Tekken basics. Did they listen? Is the game playable now? In a better world, that would've happened. Unfortunately, Tekken devs completely failed the assignment and everyone in the roster got buffed. The remaining trust in the devs from the community faded the moment they've read the patch notes, and nobody believes in the game getting the balance patch it deserves in Season 4.  That brings us to now. Tekken 8 had the potential to be one of the best Tekken games. The devs had everything they needed to realize that potential, but the urge to make the game appeal to a casual audience was stronger, and we ended up with a game that rewards button mashing rather than outsmarting your opponents. I can only recommend Tekken 8 in its current state to non-competitive fighting game players and those who like dress-up games, because the character customization is actually pretty good. If the game ever gets fixed, I'll consider returning, but until then, I'll keep playing older Tekkens and other fighting games.

Arguably the best Tekken game to ever release. I felt like with Tekken 7 a lot of the aesthetic and identity was lost. Tekken 4, 5, 6 and TT2 had amazing identity, graphics and style that made Tekken what it was. 8 brings back its style, identity and flow that we've all been missing in T7.  The roster consists of 32 characters, each with their own unique fighting style, moves, and combos. It holds a rich story mode, a variety of online and offline modes, and stunning graphics and sound.  Story mode picks up where Tekken 7 left off, with the final showdown between Kazuya Mishima and his father Heihachi Mishima. We explore the origins of the Mishima family feud, the secrets of the Devil Gene and its orgins as well as the fate of Jin Kazama, who is missing after the events of Tekken 7. The story is presented in a cinematic style, with fully voiced cutscenes and dynamic battles.  Gameplay is fast-paced, fluid, and responsive, with a balance of offense and defense. There are new mechanics, such as the Heat mechanic, which allows the player to unleash powerful attacks as well as recovering health, chip damage and Power Crush, which allows the player to absorb some damage and continue their attack. The game also has a variety of stages, each with their own environmental hazards and transitions.  Online mode is robust and smooth, with a ranking system, a replay, and a spectator mode. We also have cross-play between different platforms, allowing players to challenge each other regardless of their device. Sounds are impressive and immersive, with realistic character models, detailed animations, and expressive facial expressions. There are diverse and dynamic soundtrack, featuring rock, techno, and orchestral music. The voice cast is of talented actors, who deliver their lines with emotion and personality.   To sum this overall great package: Positives: + Amazing gameplay + Phenomenal Design and graphics + Stages, characters and moves are perfect + Tekken Ball + Online Lounge and online modes in general are smooth except Day 1 Release + We can use all Tekken soundtracks in the game from T1 all the way to T7 and 8 + The Story is awesome. Really well done. + Easy to get into. Arcade Quest and the tutorial really help out bringing the best in you. It's easy to practice, easy to learn and very hard to master. + The Ghosts AI is actually capable and useful. What a great design choice and implementation.  On the negative side: - Not enough customisation options. T6 is still the GOAT in that regard - No Tekken Force - The sound of punches isn't as satisfying as T7 but it's good enough still  Tekken 8 is a must-play for fans of the series and newcomers alike, as it offers a satisfying and thrilling fighting game experience. The game has a lot of content and replay value, as well as a deep and engaging story. The game is a masterpiece of the genre, and a fitting conclusion to the saga of the Mishima family.

I do recommend the game, with the caveat that you do not take it seriously in any way. It's crazy fun and the characters are all very interesting with very cool moves to master. I play Alisa mostly and I think she's hilarious! The story mode is great. However, for competitive play online this game is honestly a nightmare and it always leaves me feeling disappointed and annoyed. Is that a good feeling to have after playing a video game? There are a number of reasons why this is the case for me, but the primary reason is the rage art, a devastating, uninterruptable attack that any player can spam at will when their health is low. You will be hit by it a lot even if you make conceited efforts to block or avoid it. You lose so much health from this attack it's unbelievable. Because of the rage art, in many cases, the loser gets to win, and that drives me absolutely crazy. Would it not drive you crazy too? What were they thinking in including this stupid and unfair mechanic? I can't tell you the number of times I have dominated a match and been on the verge of winning only to be spammed with the rage art at the very end and lose. Why? Because I played better than my opponent? There's this absurd situation that often happens at the ends of rounds where both players have rage arts available and you're both sidestepping around like idiots both too scared to go in for an attack. It really goes against the idea of playing aggressively in Tekken 8, which was supposed to be the whole ethos of this sequel. If you're aggressive in Tekken 8 you will probably not be rewarded, instead you will get punished hard. The air juggle system in Tekken 8 is utterly ridiculous. I honestly am sick and tired of watching my character being flung around through the air helplessly like a rag doll, yelping in pain for half of the match and being unable to do anything about it. I feel sorry for my opponents who are forced to do the same when it's my turn to air juggle. Sometimes an entire round can be lost on a single launcher, first move, with a huge air juggle combo string that takes away all of your health in one go. It's very impressive that some players can pull this off, but it's still unfair and should not be in the game. They balanced the damage so that you can't be completely defeated in this way most of the time, but it's so frustrating being forced to just sit there and watch, waiting for a chance to get back up and not be launched into the air again. Honestly after a while it just gets boring. I often think of what I could be doing while I wait. Maybe making a tasty sandwich? It would have been great if you could use your heat system engage to escape an air juggle, but alas that's not in the game. That would have improved things immensely. Getting back up when you finally do regain control is also a joyless experience. You either roll to the side or get pummelled by ground attacks, some of which can launch you into the air again! Did I mention that King can grab you while you're on the ground and do a leg break that you cannot counter even if you're at pro level? Who on the dev team thought of that? I've never played a game where I spend so much time having no control over my character. It's kind of extraordinary really. Going back to a 100% control game like Resident Evil or Streets of Rage 4 after playing Tekken 8 always feels very nice. Don't get me wrong, Tekken 8 is a great fighting game. Mechanically it might be the best fighting game ever made, but that's sort of the problem. It's too extreme for its own good. Tekken 8 is mechanically so great that I keep trying to play it even though I kind of hate it at the same time. Just try to accept the absurdity of it all and you will likely enjoy yourself overall as I do. Mastering all of your moves is very satisfying and I love that the game is super hard. I've had some great matches where I genuinely had a lot of fun, and for that, stomaching the drawbacks of this game is ultimately worth it.

Real Tekken begins when the crowd is roaring, but all you can hear is his voice, low and teasing—"Is that all you got?"  Real Tekken begins when you land a perfect electric, and he groans—low, frustrated, turned on. He bites his lip, whispering, “Good punish…” Real tekken begins when you win and barely have time to process before he’s on you, his hands grabbing your face, his mouth crashing into yours. All heat and desperation, the adrenaline—it’s intoxicating. Real Tekken begins when he growls against your lips, “Run it back.” But you both know the only thing getting run back tonight is each other.  Real Tekken begins when you’re tangled in hotel sheets hours later, still arguing over frame data between kisses, his voice husky as he murmurs, “You only won ‘cause I let you.” Real Tekken begins when you pin his wrists to the mattress and whisper, “Then block next time.”  Real Tekken was never about the game. I have been playing since Tekken 2 and to be honest with you although I have big gripes with the game if we had a neutral score in Steam I would still recommend you this game. Tekken 8 is really pricy for europe and monetized in a money grubby manner. The MAP DLC, the Battlepass, but my biggest problem, the in map ads. Although the in map ads have no defense, The Map DLC has been adressed by the devs and they gave a compensation for it, while the Battlepass always rewards you with more Tekken Coins than its cost, and its not that hard (However I think its prizes are not that good either.) What I want to focus on is the gameplay. And As someone who saw Tekken at its most basic AND Tekken at its most complex (TTT2) I love how welcoming to both casuals and pros, this game is. I am not great at Tekken, I think I am green or yellow rank? But I always have players better or worse than me that I can play against in online. I always have the greatest single player mode of any fighting game ever created: Super Ghost Mode available too. ( Not to mention how overly cheesily yet absolutely amazing Story Modes were) I love how the graphics, one of the single greatest achivements of the biggest Tekken Games (T3 and T5) are finally up to par and look incredible. (Compared to T7 which geniunely looked worse than TTT2) As someone who hates grapples (buffed) and loves parries (nerfed), I can STILL say I love the new techs and mechanics. I hate panic buttons yet I love how much opportunity Heat Mode creates, I love how Heat Smashes make you feel cool without you actually taking the game serious. I love the community that keeps creating around games like Tekken WHERE YOU CAN STILL BE A NOOB. Where you can go in ranked and not get your ahh handed to you by a skilled af 11 year old who does a %80 combo on you. Most of all I love that there are many things that I don't know or outright know wrongly about the game because I am only a green rank. I have so many more good things to say, such as Customization (without the paid skins :( ) or Jukebox (which doesn't have the Story Tracks) As you can see every "good" comes with a lil paranthesis "bad". So in Tekken 8's general case the  good are the developers who make and balance the game (while the publishers are the mones who make one of the worst monetizations ever) Let your voice be heard so we get some solutions like the last 500 coins but please don't review bomb this amazing game so hard that we stop getting new players. -A fellow Asuka and soon to be Lee main

After the disaster that was the release of Season 2, it's no wonder the title remains at "Mixed" reviews at the time of writing, one quick look at the review graph for the game tells it all.  The overall fan reaction to Season 2 of Tekken 8 was such that the game's main balancing team was entirely replaced with employees that had previously worked on Tekken titles in the past, but was such reaction to Season 2 warranted?  Yes!  Not only did they increase the game's focus on aggressiveness and non-stop offense, but they directly LIED to the fans saying that "Season 2 would see defensive options increased and revamped." Throughout the marketing campaign for it, the Tekken spokes-people continuously refused to show this "buffed defense," and every single time would showcase new and improved ways they were increasing offensive focus. The fanbase held its breath tightly awaiting the release of Season 2 with a healthy dose of hopium, praying that these so-called improved defensive options just hadn't been showcased.  Sadly, by the release of Season 2, that hope turned into rage, as a solid percentage of the fanbase realized that almost every single change and addition in Season 2 was created with a single-focus: Simplification and Offense.  Since then, things have been better however, patches have crawled us back to a solid place once more, the game that had been horribly butchered is starting to piece itself back together, even if slowly. The new DLC characters, once the focus of so many fears, have turned out to be incredibly healthy for the game, no doubt thanks to many changes done by the new/old balancing team. If you were to ask me after the release of Season 2 if I had any hope left for this sad sad excuse of a game, I'd probably take a day to piece my thoughts together, but now I do have hope.  Tekken 8 has the foundation to be the greatest Tekken ever made, from the mechanics to the cast, it can all be balanced to be what every Tekkenhead has hoped for, all I can do is pray that the developers realize what makes Tekken so great and roll back on the baffling decisions of Season 2, something every patch since then has thankfully done, even if at a slow pace.  Things are looking bright once more, even if that brightness is dim, and even if many still cannot see it, rightfully blinded by what the game had become.  I'm holding my breath for the changes coming in the future, and for the decisions the Tekken Team will take regarding their flagship title, as they have shown both capability and unwillingness, potential and inaptitude. It took me 1 year to save up for Tekken 8 and in that 1 year period I could only buy the original version without dlc. In the first 7 hours when playing Tekken 8 the shock culture is very very much felt as if I was playing a different game, everything feels new starting from the appearance of the UI, the system, and new features such as the lobby where we can customize the chibby character as an identity, and of course customize character skins which in my opinion are freer than Tekken 7 even though I had heard that custom character skins were better in Tekken Tag 2 tournament but because I just played the Tekken game series from Tekken 7 so I think so far the best character skin customization is in Tekken 8.  Now, let's discuss the mechanics of this game. Since whenever Tekken implemented the heat system similar to Max Mode in King of Fighters or Drive Impact in Street Fighter, and according to me, the heat mode seems slightly unfair? Maybe, but the heat system benefits and harms equally. When we almost complete a combo, we can use the heat burst to keep our enemy airborne, allowing us to continue the combo beforehand. However, if the regular combo isn't extended, we can use a move with heat engagement to add damage to the previous combo or even continue it until hitting the rear wall, which is very advantageous. On the other hand, as victims, this is extremely disadvantageous since once we allow our enemies to use heat combos on us, the incoming damage often seems illogical or difficult to anticipate—examples include Kuma's heat engager, Lars' low attack heat engager, and many others.  Additionally, in my opinion, the walls in Tekken 8 are slippery. For whatever reason, every time I corner my opponents with several moves, they end up slipping to either side rather than staying stuck to the wall, thus ruining my combo attempts and getting attacked back by the opponent. This happens multiple times with different characters, indicating that the walls in Tekken 8 are indeed quite slippery. This contrasts sharply with Tekken 7, where opponents sticking to the wall tightly rarely moved left or right.  Furthermore, some characters' moves became easier to perform in Tekken 8 compared to Tekken 7. These adjustments certainly helped new players entering the world of fighting games, but certain characters possess new moves that are hard to anticipate or even buffs on existing ones. An example is Alisa Bosconovitch's circular saw move; in Tekken 7, it could be canceled by pressing button 1/JAB, whereas in Tekken 8, Alisa's start frame is incredibly fast, making it nearly impossible to execute even with the fastest Jab input. Another case is Eddy Gordo; honestly, I'm puzzled by Harada's thought behind adding one button that triggers numerous moves, akin to releasing ten-hit combos in Tekken 7 but simplified to just pressing button 3 it should probably be adjusted further.  Lastly regarding buff stacking, as widely discussed lately, Heihachi receives a permanent buff during Round 3 marked by an 'engine logo' visible below HP bars. This additional damage is highly unjustified, and I strongly dislike this buff stacking system. Only DLC characters appear to have these buffs, implying that we must pay to climb the ranking ladder easily. Initially seeing this buff stacking mechanism reminded me of Heihachi from Tekken or Aldous from Mobile Legends: Bang Bang. Clearly, I am deeply unsatisfied with this buff stacking system.  All of this is purely my opinion based on my experience playing Tekken 8 for the first 18 hours. Despite all its shortcomings, Tekken 8 is still very enjoyable to play. If you encounter toxic players who like to ki-charge at the end of a match or even comment on your Steam account, just block those players in both Tekken 8 and on Steam. This way, you should encounter them less frequently during online matchmaking.  Oh, and one more thing: the visual effects are indeed stunning and impressive, but for me, some attack effects are overly extravagant. They are so flashy that they make my eyes blink and end up getting me hit by my opponent.

Tekken 8 continues the legacy of one of the most iconic fighting game franchises, delivering a refined experience for both longtime fans and newcomers. Developed by Bandai Namco, Tekken 8 brings new mechanics, an updated roster, and improved visuals, all while staying true to the core principles that have made the series a mainstay in competitive gaming for over two decades.  [h1]Gameplay and Combat Mechanics[/h1] At its core, Tekken 8 stays true to the fast-paced, hard-hitting gameplay that fans love. The combat system remains as intricate and technical as ever, offering a deep, rewarding experience for players who are willing to invest time in learning its nuances. Every character brings a unique playstyle, from lightning-fast combos to more deliberate, power-based moves. The game’s signature fluidity is still there, making each fight feel dynamic and rewarding as players string together devastating combos and counters.  A standout addition in Tekken 8 is the Heat System, which adds a new layer of strategy to combat. Heat Mode allows players to temporarily boost their attack power, speed, and access to special moves. This mechanic encourages aggressive play, giving fighters a powerful tool to turn the tide of battle. The new system feels like a natural evolution of Tekken’s already fast-paced combat, offering even more ways to outsmart and outplay your opponent.  The game also introduces Expanded Rage Arts, allowing for more visually spectacular, high-impact moves. These flashy finishers add a level of excitement to each match, rewarding players for building up their Rage Gauge.  [h1]Visuals and Presentation[/h1] Tekken 8 is a visual powerhouse. The game runs on a new, highly refined engine that brings character models, stages, and animations to life in stunning detail. From the intricate textures of each fighter’s costume to the fluidity of their movements, the visuals make every fight feel impactful and cinematic. The stages are beautifully designed, with vibrant, dynamic environments that react to the action, further enhancing the sense of immersion.  The visual updates also extend to the game’s cutscenes and story mode. The character animations are smoother, and the attention to detail in facial expressions and fight choreography creates a more engaging narrative experience, which is a welcome addition for players who enjoy the Tekken storylines.  [h1]Character Roster and Customization[/h1] Tekken 8 introduces a variety of new characters while retaining many of the fan favorites from previous games. The roster is well-balanced, offering a wide range of fighting styles and personalities. The return of iconic fighters like Kazuya, Jin, Heihachi, and Nina adds a sense of continuity, while newcomers bring fresh dynamics to the game. Each character feels unique, with distinct moves, animations, and playstyles, ensuring that players can find a fighter that suits their preferences.  Character customization also returns in Tekken 8, allowing players to personalize their fighters’ outfits, colors, and accessories. The deep customization options let players create a fighter that feels unique to them, adding to the replay value and appeal of the game.  [h1]Online Play and Competitive Scene[/h1] Online play in Tekken 8 has been significantly improved, with stable netcode that provides smoother online matches. The game’s matchmaking system works well for both casual players and those looking for a more competitive experience, and the improved online infrastructure is a crucial step for keeping Tekken relevant in the ever-evolving world of esports.  For competitive players, Tekken 8 offers robust online tournaments, ranked matches, and a well-balanced experience that ensures the integrity of the competitive scene. The game’s combination of technical depth and strategic play makes it a perfect fit for esports, and it’s likely to continue attracting top-tier players from around the world.  [h1]Story and Narrative[/h1] The story of Tekken 8 builds on the intense family drama that has defined the series, focusing on the rivalry between the Mishima family and their quest for power. As always, Tekken’s storyline is filled with twists, betrayals, and emotional moments. While fighting games are not typically known for their narrative depth, Tekken manages to deliver a compelling story that helps drive the motivations behind each character’s actions.  While some players may not be drawn to the story mode as much as the competitive gameplay, it serves as an engaging way to explore the game’s characters and lore.  [h1]Conclusion[/h1] [i]In conclusion, Tekken 8 builds on the franchise’s rich history while introducing new mechanics, updated visuals, and a host of gameplay improvements that make it one of the best entries in the series. The Heat System, enhanced Rage Arts, and stunning visuals elevate the experience, while the refined combat mechanics ensure that both casual players and competitive veterans can enjoy the game.  Whether you’re a longtime fan of the series or new to the Tekken universe, Tekken 8 offers something for everyone. Its blend of accessible gameplay and technical depth, combined with a strong roster of characters and a thriving competitive scene, makes it a standout title in the fighting game genre. Tekken 8 not only continues the franchise’s legacy but sets a new benchmark for what a modern fighting game can achieve.[/i]

Tekken 8 is a really hard one to review because I'm almost exactly in the middle.  I think Tekken 8 is probably one of the most solid fighting games I've ever played. It plays great, the soundtrack is as good as you'd expect from a Tekken game, the graphics look great and the story is enjoyable as well as the Arcade Quest gamemode which I enjoyed way more than I expected to. I would definitely recommend the game itself to anybody who likes fighting games.  However, what I think holds it back and I don't recommend is the overall Tekken 8 experience. The game is very good but to enjoy this, you pretty much have to be the type of player that enjoys the whole ranked online competitive scene as this is the main focus with modern Tekken which I think is huge shame.  Gone are the days of Singleplayer content for fighting games. No more Team Battle, Survival or Time Attack. Now to unlock certain cosmetic items that were actually previously free to earn in Tekken 7, you must first buy into a battle pass that at the moment and what I assume is going to continue to be the only way, is levelled by playing online.  Honestly, it's not the battle pass that offends me, it's the fact that a chunk of the items are just assets pulled from the previous game that require us to play a side of Tekken not everyone wants to play. I actually like some of the micro-transactions. I think bringing back classic outfits is really cool and if it supported the game and helped it grow, I would 100% spend a few pennies to play as T2 Yoshimitsu. But I feel at this point, it'd only support online which I don't really care about too much.  At the end of the day, If you're someone looking at buying this, I would definitely suggest doing a bit of research into what game modes are available to you and if you would enjoy them.  TL;DR The game is good but no game modes. I cannot believe I'm stating this, but Season 1 is dearly missed despite its problems. My initial review was positive but, as a long time fan of the franchise since Tekken 3, I feel obligated to update it and refuse to go back on my word until significant changes are made. The community has been voicing its opinion regarding the aggressive gameplay of Tekken 8 since the launch of the game, pointing out the lack of defensive options to deal with the overwhelming offense. Some people provided respectful and constructive criticism and ideas towards making the game feel more like Tekken, and Season 2 came in ignoring most (if not all) of that feedback, doubling down on what made it not Tekken. Defense received a buff yet it is hardly noticeable as most of the characters got more safe moves, more tracking, more plus frames, more forced 50/50 mix-ups... It's absolutely a guessing simulator now. Online ranked matches are a nightmare and I cannot recommend anyone to go at it in its current state. This is a competitive 3D fighting game from an established IP that many people love. It should not be getting such drastic (dare I say harmful) changes. Sadly, it is being ripped apart. Let's just hope things get back on track and Tekken 8 becomes as successful and fun as it can be.

The game  has really came far in development from the initial release and feels like it has the most important aspect of Tekken returning back to the franchise. No matter how powerful the move, no matter what character the other player picks, there is always an answer in your characters kit to match and overcome the problem set by the game or opponent. Despite a profusely greedy season pass, the game itself plays in a way that other fighters of this era fail to comprehend, and make for a game play experience where you can always learn something new at any level every play session. There is a reason the players of this franchise from 30 years ago are still willing to learn the new games and system mechanics of this IP rather than returning to support the older titles or attempt to make HD remakes. It is because the developers of this game know what it takes to make something better than the last and include more player decisions in each iteration instead of bogging down what the game was prior into something less complicated for new players. It may not be the best Tekken of all time, but that's because it came out in a gaming market where your wallet is never off the table and your time actually enjoying the game is irrelevant to a companies bottom line.

It hurts me to write a negative review for Tekken 8, it truly does. It was probably my most antecipated game of 2024 and when the honeymoon phase ended, what I ended up with is a mix of bad decisions taken without most players best interests in mind.   First the pros, to take it outta the way quickly. The graphics are the best ever. The soundtrack still isn't stellar as Tekken 5's and/or Tag 2, but still a good step away from Tekken 7's WUBWUBWUWBWUB. [u]It's the best Tekken for beginners[/u]. This is as much of a pro than it's a con, but more on that later. The netplay and load times are much better than Tekken 7's weird wifi netcode and massive load times.  Now the cons. Tekken 8 took a turn for the worse when it decided to be more aggressive in order to create matches more exciting to watch in tournaments. It used to be a [i]fairly[/i] balanced game but now it's a mashing festival where every character lost what it made them special in the first place. It feels like everyone has absurd plus frames, 50/50s, stances and shiny secondary special gimmicks. The game has no longer that tension, that spark that made it so special. I feel like I've played Dead or Alive matches slower paced than Tekken 8 ranked matches, and if you've played DoA before you know what I mean, that game is crazy fast.  All of this because Harada knew he wouldn't be able to luck it out the way he did with Tekken 7's competition when it launched. At the time there were basically no competition, since Street Fighter 5 had a bumpy launch and the other games didn't really matter. So he gambled his way making Tekken 8 the cocaine addict it is. The problem is that instead of being FUN to play, and it is somewhat fun, it doesn't feel like you're playing a true TEKKEN game. It feels like you're playing a spin off made for crazy kids mashing buttons. If you're still reading this (and I thank you for that), remember when I told you that this is the best Tekken for beginners? It's easy to get into the game loop because the game feels more approachable than before, despite having no real tutorial or useful beginner friendly tools, just like before. It does have a simplified attack setup but that won't help beginners in the long run. The problem is that all these beginners will most likely drop the game when the next Tekken comes out and realise that [i]boy, last night was crazy, gotta get up and go to work now [/i]. When Tekken becomes TEKKEN again, player retention will go rock bottom because Tekken 8 is not the way this franchise is supposed to play.  Or I can be really, really wrong and this is what Tekken has become. Then I guess I'll just go ♥♥♥♥ myself.   Anyway, this review is already long and I haven't even started about the Heat system yet. This MISTAKE replaced Tekken 7's Rage Drives and is basically half of the reason this game sucks so much right now. Every character takes all I've mentioned so far and cranks it up to 11 when Heat is activated. Characters like King will put you in a 50/50 every damn round using Heat, Reina won't let you press buttons until Heat is over (Reina main here, best goth gf ever, SUBMIT TO ME yes mommy). Not to mention how much Heat harms the flow of the battle with lenghty animations and camera movements. It's just bad. Visually, the game is getting more and more over the top and I think that's fun, since Tekken is no longer about martial arts and we even have a walking weapons safe John Wick silver daddy frenchman now, but honestly some animations are just annoying when you're being forced to watch it every damn round.  I won't say anything about the story mode because I don't care about this bad anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.   And of course, to wrap it up, we have all the microtransactions all over again, yayyy... Extra characters that should've been in the launch roster but you have to pay extra to play with. I hate Eddy with a passion but locking him up behind a paywall? Not to mention Heihachi, but he was supposed to be COMPRETERY DED, right Harada? I never wanted to punch Harada in the face so hard before. Then they launch the character but charges extra for his stage! And how they address this joke? "Here players, have 500 coins to spend on completely useless and stupid ♥♥♥♥". It's all gone to hell, guys. We're so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ now.  Thank you so much for making this mess of a game, Harada. You decided to cater to everyone but the former playerbase of this game. Former veterans hated it, the pros you fondle so much hated it, and all the new players will go away once you realize how much of a mistake this game is and makes things right again next time, because they'll be completely destroyed when they're forced to play TEKKEN how it's supposed to be. Dead or Alive 6 was a failure because of the same mistakes, essentially: forgetting what makes you so special. We've all seen it happen before.  See you in Tekken Tag 3, Tekken 9 or Tekken REBOOT-tentative-name, guys.

I got to Raijin before I gave up playing ~1 month after Lidia came out.  Cons; Winning is not gratifying. I enjoy fighting games for the interaction between players within a match and because I find defending fun. I enjoy reacting to what the opponent does, blocking, and punishing. There's just too much guessing for me to have fun. Tekken 8 all comes down to unrelenting pressure built out of plus on-block moves and constant 50/50 mix.  - 90% of the time you do not win because of your own skill, but simply because you kept wildly flailing your arms at the opponent.  - Defence is awful. Unless, of course, you study every character's move list in-depth. That may sound like an appealing leisurely activity some, but unless you want to become a 'Pro', it's death to the idea of playing the casually for fun. Until you reach the enlightenment of knowing your opponents constant string of knowledge checks, you will not be having fun defending in this game. - Overall monetisation of this game is dreadful. Battlepass isn't great. Not being able to do replay takeover versus DLC characters is awful, and as time goes on, there seems to be more and more issues with the DLC practice. Such as the big stage controversy with Heihachi.  Pros; However, I can understand that for those who enjoy being a gorilla and like the idea of unrelenting pressure, then Tekken 8 is much more of an appealing pitch than any other fighting game. It's by far the most offensive game that you can buy right now.  If you don't mind the offensive philosophy, you'll be rewarded with; + Great visuals. There are some great VFX and the overall quality of the game is top of the line. Being able to see the muscles tensing during certain moves is genuinely amazing. + Sound design is fantastic. All the sound effects are great and there are a few great new songs. + Quality of Life. Being able to choose your own music for each stage + it's accompanying final round is massive. There's replay take-over which is great at helping you learn match-ups. Crossplay works well, and the rollback is functional.

Story definitely came out swinging, its the best story mode in Tekken so far. Hopefully they finish off the Mishima saga with the same impact in T9 whenever that comes around.  In terms of graphics and art style, the high fidelity plus running on a more modern engine does the game justice, each character look amazing, despite the obvious favouritism (I'm looking at you Law and Feng).  Gameplay wise, they moved in a different direction compared to T7; with more of an emphasis on aggression and mixups compared to its previous iteration. Despite this the core mechanics is still Tekken; I believe that the negativity (and initial outburst) towards T8's new direction is because there weren't any balances towards the HEAT system and people still had T7 in their minds. If anything T7 could've been like T8 but there was already an established meta from its 1-2yrs being out in Arcade before every other platform.  The micro transactions are disgusting from a community perspective, but I can see why it was implemented from a business view. It doesn't subtract from the base game though, you are getting what you paid for (not including additional purchases). Even if you decide to stop raging and really learn the game (StarCraft franchise player here, if you know you know) presuming your network latency isn't absolutely fantastic, it's basically impossible to learn against other live players. Coming from Tekken 7, most people would likely have been more than satisfied with relatively minor changes, with a focus on addressing low risk/high reward safe pokes and CH tools that made Tekken 7 a bit too defensive and perhaps uninteresting from a spectator perspective.  However, that could've been addressed without this overwhelming heat system, and without giving everyone oppressive stances with power crushes that constantly force guess situations on block.    In this current state, I cannot recommend the game to any new players.  It's a shame since Tekken 8 did improve in a number of other areas - netcode, online functionality overall (i.e. reduced time between matches), graphics, etc.  But the gameplay just isn't there like it was in previous games.  Unless you're already an addicted Tekken fan, this isn't a good time to get into the series, and future support is questionable.

I think part of the problem with Tekken, along with every single triple A game that includes online services, will be the battle pass.  Do not let it fool you, its there because Bandai Namco wants it there, not because it adds to the game, its to line the pockets of those who helped fund the game. In some cases, this can work out for both the producers and the consumers - in Tekken 8's case, it doesnt work. It does the bare basics for a battle pass, and doesnt try to do much with it. I think part of what makes Fortnite battle pass interesting is the fact you could earn your way into buying the prem battle pass it offers with just simply playing the game. Tekken, I have to play for 80 hours as part of this review going up and ive only heard 300 coins, (almsost all items are 400 coins and more) with the free 500 coins coming in the next few days. Ive only owned the game since july so theres been progress done to make my enjoyment worthwhile, but it does only so much.  I think by the time this game gets to a season 3 and 4 (which it will, everything with this games gameplay, story, character roster, stages and music makes it a perfect game), I hope the battle pass, as well as the overall online system for this game gets revamped enough to feel inviting. Until then, be wary of those who wish to make this game out to be bad, or poorly produced. Its a great fighting game, might be the best one in years, but the over montezation doesnt suit Tekken, or any game. Its one step closer to fascism that people will overlook due to legacy status. Play this game, but denounce the level of capitalism that comes with it.

It's the newest installment in the franchise, yet arguably the worst one so far. Virtually nothing they added to the game was for the better. The new mechanics do nothing to improve the gameplay regardless of if you are new to the game or a veteran. You could remove things like Heat and Rage Arts and you would be left with a better game. The roster is sterile with a terrible wave of DLC and awful newcomers. The new lobby system is a complete disaster and the company has shown complete incompetence at every front: balancing, netcoding, dealing with cheaters, being transparent about paid cosmetics, etc... Off the top of my head I cannot think of a single thing the developers actually managed to do well with this game. Asuka doesn't even have a neck and every female has the same face and body. Every male looks the same from the neck down too. The customization is somehow worse than Tekken 6 even though it has been over a decade since then. I can't even call it Tekken 7 with a fresh coat of paint since it's strictly worse and has half the characters, but I guess the graphics do look better...  And fast forward a year and now I can't even call season two of Tekken 8 a version of season one of Tekken 8 with a fresh coat of paint. It is somehow strictly worse than launch Tekken 8. The fact that they could launch what has easily been one of the absolute worst serious patches in a well regarded competitive game (probably of all time) like this is absolutely shameful, and they did it all while continuing to parade their completely obtuse season pass with all but one piece of content hidden behind a wall, and the continued early access gimmick. It's actually pathetic. The beginning of S2 of Tekken 8 is so bad that the competitive scene has had to pre-emptively consider banning characters, something you rarely see in modern fighting games. It is laughable and yet this is supposed to be among the most polished and well established franchises in the genre. After decades all they managed to do was make a game significantly worse than something a far more competent group of folks at Namco made on the PS1. Well at least Anna looks nice I guess...

I trusted Bamco and Harada, along with his friend Murray, but that trust has come to an end. I’m hoping to see a new balance patch that will nerf this circus ASAP, but I guess that's just a dream. I’ll continue playing the game because I love the Tekken universe and the characters, but the characters I love are starting to disappear with each new patch. I may drop this game in the future if it continues to add more aggression and erase characters’ identities with every update.  It’s quite depressing that a game with so much potential, one that gave me core memories with my friends and the people I met in this community, has become so horrible. Stay strong, Tekken Community.
